US State Department Approves $2.68 Billion Air Defense Sale to Ukraine
The US Department of State has approved a potential Foreign Military Sale to the Government of Ukraine for Air Defense Development Upgrades and associated equipment valued at an estimated $2.68 billion, the US Bureau of Political-Military Affairs announced on September 18.
If finalized, Ukraine will fund the purchase through a combination of European financial contributions and US Foreign Military Financing (FMF) appropriated during the prior administration. The FMF funds will be credited as a US capital contribution to the Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund via a 1:1 reimbursement framework.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine remains heavily dependent on constant replenishments of air defense interceptors to shield its cities and critical energy infrastructure from sustained Russian long-range missile and drone strikes. With Russian forces launching thousands of aerial weapons every month, securing a multi-layered defensive shield is essential to prevent widespread destruction of key civilian facilities and maintain the country’s operational stability.
The requested procurement package includes non-major defense equipment, specifically S-300 Clone missiles, GAM-67 missiles, and Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket missile systems, the US Department of State wrote.
Kyiv also requested Improvised Transporter Erector Launcher 1.5 units, mobile launching system modification kits, RPS 202 counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) radars, erectable mast trailers, major modifications, and maintenance support.
Additional elements of the potential sale encompass spare parts, consumables, accessories, repair and return support, software, technical publications, transportation support, and engineering and logistics services provided by the US Government and contractors.
“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic progress in Europe,” the Department of State said in a statement.
The statement also noted that the sale will enhance Ukraine’s ability to conduct self-defense and regional security missions while maintaining that the equipment will not alter the basic military balance in the region or adversely affect US defense readiness.
Principal contractors will be selected through competitive procurements under the Federal Acquisition Regulation.
The European Union had previously approved $7.1 billion for Ukraine under the Ukraine Support Loan framework, clearing the way for Kyiv to purchase American PAC-3 Patriot interceptor missiles via NATO's PURL mechanism . The funding allocation includes specific exceptions to standard conditions to accommodate high-value Ukrainian-made drones as well as critical US-manufactured air defense systems.

Trump Signs Sweeping “Sanctions From Hell” Bill Against Russia Into Law

Trump Signs Sweeping “Sanctions From Hell” Bill Against Russia Into Law
US President Donald Trump signed sweeping legislation into law targeting Russia’s energy, defense, and maritime sectors, the White House announced on September 18.
Formally designated as the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” often referred to as the “sanctions bill from hell,” the law was named in honor of the South Carolina Republican Senator who died in July after being a long-standing advocate for aggressive economic measures against Moscow.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The bill gained final congressional approval after passing the House of Representatives on Wednesday following its passage in the Senate last month.
The landmark legislation specifically targets Russia’s primary revenue streams by imposing secondary economic measures on third-party entities and allowing the president to levy tariffs on foreign nations that continue to purchase Russian energy exports, Reuters wrote.
It also targets Russia’s defense industrial base, major financial institutions, and the illicit “shadow fleet” of tankers used to circumvent international oil price caps.
Critics and foreign policy analysts noted that the legislation grants the executive branch broad discretionary authority, enabling the president to impose secondary tariffs that could remain in place far beyond his administration. Despite these concerns, supporters emphasized that restricting Kremlin revenues is essential to weakening Russia’s war economy as the invasion of Ukraine continues, according to Reuters.
The Russia sanctions bill was previously stalled in the US House of Representatives due to opposition from corporate lobbying groups and concerns regarding expanded tariff powers.
After overwhelmingly clearing the Senate with an 86–11 bipartisan vote, the bill encountered significant resistance from corporate giants—including ExxonMobil, General Electric, Ford, and Pfizer—over potential tariff impacts on American consumers.

Murder trial of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi’s former relatives to begin
Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong, 31, his father Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother Anthony Kwong, 35, face a joint count of murder
The High Court will hold the first trial hearing on Monday for parties to sort out preliminary issues. Jury selection is expected to take place later in the week before the prosecution delivers its opening speech.
The 28-year-old influencer’s death came to light in February 2023, when parts of her dismembered body were discovered in a flat inside a three-storey village house in Tai Po’s Lung Mei Tsuen.
Choi’s former husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, will stand trial on a joint count of murder. The trio have also been charged with preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body.

The UK suspiciously reeks of the late-stage USSR
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:58:00 UTC
16:58:00 KST

The UK suspiciously reeks of the late-stage USSR
“The era of Westminster is coming to an end!” the nationalist leaders of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland declared this week.
John Swinney, Rhun ap Iorwerth, and Michelle O’Neill gathered in Cardiff to sign an agreement asserting their nations’ right to self-determination, as they called on London not to obstruct referendums and outlined their preferred futures beyond the UK, including EU membership for an independent Scotland and Wales, and Irish reunification for Northern Ireland.
In Russia, the meeting has already been dubbed Britain’s version of the Belovezha Accords, and the comparison is tempting because, as in 1991, political leaders from three of a state’s constituent parts gathered around a table to discuss a civilized divorce.
But the resemblance largely ends there, given the driving force behind the Soviet Union’s dissolution was its largest republic, Russia, represented by Boris Yeltsin. He joined his counterparts in dismantling the state that Moscow built, but no representative of England attended the Cardiff gathering, and Westminster has shown little enthusiasm for presiding over its own retreat.
The participants were also considerably more cautious than their Soviet predecessors, so they signed as party leaders, making the declaration a joint political initiative rather than an agreement binding their governments to secession.
This distinction exposes the central weakness of the Cardiff Pact. Its signatories want to leave the UK while remaining within the constitutional framework that holds it together. Their ambitions therefore depend on political and legal processes they don’t control.
Ireland’s experience offers an uncomfortable historical comparison, as the settlement that opened the way to independence followed two years of guerrilla warfare. Today’s nationalist leaders are pursuing an entirely peaceful route, through negotiations, elections, and referendums, but whether London will accommodate them is another matter.
Scotland has already encountered this obstacle. In 2022, the UK Supreme Court ruled that the Scottish Parliament couldn’t legislate for an independence referendum without Westminster’s consent, and after the close vote in 2014, London has little appetite for another.
Public opinion presents a further difficulty. Scotland remains divided down the middle, whereas in Northern Ireland, the figure cited for support for Irish unity is around 36% and Welsh independence remains a minority position, however much its advocates have gained politically.
Swinney wants another Scottish referendum by 2031, but his counterparts have offered no comparable timetable and their agreement establishes a direction of travel, but supplies neither a departure date nor a convincing explanation of how they will get there.
Britain’s dissolution is therefore hardly imminent, but nevertheless, London would be foolish to dismiss Cardiff as an exercise in nationalist theater.
Some British coverage attributed the meeting to an ill-judged intervention by Prime Minister Andy Burnham when he suggested that referendums in Scotland and Northern Ireland might be considered if there is broad public consensus, before attempting to narrow the implications of his remarks.
Qualifications rarely travel as far as the original statement and nationalists heard an opening and acted accordingly.
Yet an unfortunate choice of words can’t explain the forces behind this gathering. The more immediate political background was Labour’s local elections defeat in May, which strengthened nationalist parties and created favorable conditions for cooperation and Cardiff gave that cooperation a common platform.
However, the deeper problem is the condition of the British state itself. In 2014, many Scots supported independence because they believed London ignored their interests and governed badly – and since then, Westminster has supplied little reason for them to reconsider, as economic stagnation and trained public services have steadily eroded confidence in the established order.
Conservatives and Labour have each promised renewal, only to leave voters wondering whether either possesses a credible plan, while Reform and nationalist parties have moved into the space created by that failure. Their proposed remedies differ, but their appeal rests on a shared conviction that the old arrangements no longer work.
Brexit sharpened this argument, as Britain’s departure from the EU in 2020 changed the calculation for those considering a future outside the UK. Previously, independence meant leaving a state that already offered access to the EU, but now nationalists can present separation as a route back into it.
The choice, as they frame it, is between joining a larger, more successful economic and political community and remaining attached to a declining imperial center, still occasionally tempted to compensate for its weakening position with displays of former grandeur.
This argument doesn’t remove the economic risks of independence, nor does it guarantee EU membership, but it gives separatists something more persuasive than a historical grievance: A competing account of where prosperity and security might lie.
Cardiff matters principally for this reason. It did not produce a mechanism for dismantling the UK, but it brought together politicians willing to imagine what might follow it and an alternative once discussed separately in Edinburgh, Cardiff, and Belfast has acquired a shared political expression.
It’s far too early to suggest that Burnham will be Britain’s last prime minister, as states can survive years of disillusionment, and nationalist declarations are easier to sign than to implement.
But Westminster’s problem is that preserving the union requires more than obstructing its opponents, and it also requires giving people a convincing reason to stay.

NATO military chiefs tell industry they are ready to buy
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:57:42 BST
16:57:42 KST

Allied chiefs of defence have sent what NATO describes as a direct and united message to the defence industry that allies are ready to buy at scale, and that industry must be able to deliver with speed, scale and predictability, the alliance stated.
The message came from the annual Military Committee Conference, held in Copenhagen on 18 and 19 September, bringing together the 32 allied chiefs of defence with the two strategic commanders, General Alexus Grynkewich as Supreme Allied Commander Europe and Admiral Pierre Vandier as Supreme Allied Commander Transformation.
Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, Chair of the Military Committee, set out the purpose of the meeting as moving from commitments to delivery. He said: “We, the NATO Chiefs of Defence, together with SACEUR and SACT, will do the work that follows from the Ankara Summit, as we shift focus from committing budgets to delivering on capabilities that will enable NATO to deter adversaries and defend the Euro-Atlantic area.”
He added that the conference would address “collective deterrence and defence, innovation and technology, and accelerated adoption of new defence capabilities”.
His language on Russian activity over recent months was considerably blunter than the rest of his remarks. “Over recent weeks and months, we have seen once again the reckless behaviour of Russia, including airspace violations, drone incidents, hybrid activities and attempts to test Allied resolve,” he said. “Let me commend Allied forces for their swift, professional and effective responses to these incidents. NATO remains vigilant. NATO remains ready. And NATO will do what is necessary to defend every inch of Allied territory.”
General Michael Wiggers Hyldgaard, Chief of Defence of Denmark, said: “Today, in Copenhagen, NATO Allies once again show their commitments to strengthening the Alliance, bolstering our innovation and technology and our support for Ukraine. We will do what it takes to defend our common freedom and transatlantic security.”
Alongside the industry message, the conference covered implementation of the summit decisions and capability targets, and the acceleration of allied readiness and the ability to operate across multiple domains.
Allied nations also elected General Carsten Breuer, Chief of Defence of Germany, as the next Chair of the Military Committee. He takes up the post in summer 2027 for a three-year mandate, succeeding Admiral Cavo Dragone.
The line to industry echoes the commitments made at the Ankara Summit in July, where allies pledged to strengthen industrial resilience by expanding manufacturing capacity and removing barriers to defence trade within the alliance, launching the NATO Front Door for Industry and agreeing a Strategy for Industry-NATO Cooperation.
The Military Committee meets in Chiefs of Defence Session twice a year at NATO headquarters in Brussels, and once a year holds a conference hosted by a member state, with the next plenary meeting due in Brussels in January 2027.

Japan to assist Solomon Islands to hold fair elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:56:25 UTC
16:56:25 KST

Amir Latif Arain
20 September 2026•Update: 20 September 2026
Japan will provide up to 430 million yen ($2.8 million) in grants to help the Solomon Islands hold fair elections, Kyodo News reported on Sunday.
Tokyo will provide technical advice and assistance to the local election management board to run unified elections scheduled for 2028 in collaboration with the UN Development Programme, the Foreign Ministry said.
"Being strategically located in the Pacific, strengthening relations with the Solomon Islands contributes to the realization of a 'Free and Open Indo-Pacific,' based on the rule of law," the ministry said.
The "contribution marks a significant milestone in bilateral cooperation, reaffirming Japan's commitment to democratic governance and inclusive development in the Solomon Islands," the UNDP said in an earlier statement.
The UN agency added that it is expanding the support already extended to the Pacific country by Australia, Britain and the EU.
Tokyo's latest move is seen as part of its efforts to strengthen ties with Pacific island countries where China has been increasing its clout.
Solomon Islands' Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who took office in May, has signaled a departure from a pro-China stance of his recent predecessors.
After taking office, he announced that his government would review the agreement during his visit to Australia in June.

China may be building mothership for giant submarine drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:52:13 UTC
16:52:13 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Satellite imagery suggests China may be building a mothership to carry extra-extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicles (XXLUUVs).
Images provided by US geospatial intelligence company Vantor show a vessel under construction at the Hudong-Zhonghua shipyard in Shanghai, The Telegraph reported.
Defense analyst H I Sutton wrote in Naval News that two types of XXLUUV have been observed undergoing tests in Hainan. He said China is the first known country to have developed full-size uncrewed submarines.
The vessel has a well deck and a large internal hangar that could house the submersibles, Sutton said. He estimated that it could carry four XXLUUVs in the hangar or a larger number of smaller vessels.
One of the observed submersibles measures 35 meters long, while the other measures 45 meters. They are approximately six to eight times the overall size of the US Navy’s Boeing Orca XLUUV, according to Sutton.
Sutton said the vessel would probably serve as a mobile tender, maintaining the XXLUUVs and keeping them out of the water when not in use. It could also launch and recover the vessels during combat missions.
The XXLUUVs appear intended for long-range combat operations, Sutton said, “potentially including deployment off the west coast of the US during periods of heightened tension or conflict.”

Taiwan to hold 5 TV debates for nuclear power referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:52:03 UTC
16:52:03 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Central Election Commission (CEC) will hold five nationally televised presentations or debates ahead of a Nov. 28 referendum on using nuclear power to stimulate the economy and abolish the government’s “nuclear-free homeland” energy policy.
The referendum, designated National Referendum No. 22, asks voters, “Do you support the government using nuclear power to boost the economy and thereby abolish the ‘nuclear-free homeland’ energy policy?”
The five televised events are scheduled for Nov. 12 at 3 p.m., Nov. 14 at 7 p.m., Nov. 16 at 3 p.m., Nov. 18 at 10 a.m., and Nov. 20 at 7 p.m. The Legislative Yuan will nominate representatives supporting the referendum, while the Cabinet and authorized opposition campaign offices may nominate representatives opposing it, per a CEC press release.
People seeking to serve as opposition representatives must first apply to establish a campaign office under Article 20 of the Referendum Act and complete the registration procedures by Oct. 15. Those seeking to represent the supporting side must register through the designated representative with the legislature, which will submit its list to the CEC.
Representatives nominated by either side must sign a pledge confirming that they will present the position they have been selected to represent. Failure to sign will be considered a waiver of participation in that session.
Applications to establish campaign offices and recruit staff must include an office registration form, a staff roster and electronic copies, as well as copies of staff members’ national identification cards or household registration transcripts issued within the preceding three months.
The commission said each city or county may have no more than one such office, while the number of staff members, excluding volunteers, is capped at 100. Offices may not be established in government agencies, schools, legally established organizations, regular polling or vote-counting locations, or other public places.
The Nov. 28 vote will be Taiwan’s fourth national referendum concerning nuclear power since 2018, when voters approved a proposal to remove the statutory deadline for ending nuclear power generation. In 2021, voters rejected a proposal to restart the Fourth Nuclear Power Plant. A 2025 proposal to resume operations at the Third Nuclear Power Plant if regulators deemed it safe failed to pass.

Taiwan’s 7A Drones signs US market agreement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:51:39 UTC
16:51:39 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s 7A Drones and the North American Taiwan Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Association signed an agreement Friday to market Taiwan-made drones in the US.
The company and association signed the memorandum of understanding at the Asia UAV AI Innovation Application R&D Center in Chiayi, with County Magistrate Weng Chang-liang (翁章梁) witnessing the ceremony, per CNA.
Association members then received a briefing on Taiwan’s drone industry and practiced operating drones at the center.
Association President Arthur Chen (陳世修) said Taiwan’s drone industry is at a turning point amid geopolitical changes and growing demand for supply chains that exclude China. He said the association aims to use networks of Taiwanese businesses across the US to promote Taiwan-made drones.
Chen said US government agencies are seeking non-China supply chains and gradually replacing drone systems and components supplied by Chinese companies. The shift presents an opportunity for Taiwan’s drone industry to enter the US market, he added.
Weng said Taiwan has strong capabilities in small and medium-sized drones, while the US specializes in large drones. He said drones could become a key Taiwanese industry as countries work to establish supply chains that exclude China.
7A Drones CEO Dwayne Hsu (許新勝) said drones are aerial platforms integrating AI computing, encrypted communications, sensors, and precision controls. He added that Taiwanese companies are highly flexible and able to customize products for US clients.
The association said the US is seeking to reindustrialize and rebuild domestic production capacity for defense and commercial drones. The partnership will connect Taiwanese technology with US industry to address gaps in local supply chains and improve systems integration, it added.

Turkish Tulpar medium tank fires with Leonardo turret
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:50:30 BST
16:50:30 KST

Otokar and Leonardo have completed integration work and live firing trials of the Tulpar medium tank fitted with Leonardo’s HITFACT MkII 120 mm turret, a configuration intended to combine main battle tank-level firepower with the mobility, protection and modular tracked architecture of the Turkish platform, the companies stated.
Before any rounds were fired, engineering teams from both firms carried out an integration programme covering the mechanical, electrical, electronic and software interfaces between the hull and the turret. Functional checks, safety inspections and system validation activities followed, and the companies said these confirmed the performance, reliability and interoperability of the integrated system.
The vehicle then moved on to a series of live firing trials conducted under both static and dynamic conditions, in which the integrated weapon system was assessed across a range of representative operational scenarios. According to the two manufacturers, the weapon system, fire control system, stabilisation performance and overall system functionality met all planned test objectives. They added that the campaign validated Tulpar’s growth potential and its flexibility for future mission requirements.
Sedef Vehbi, Military Cluster Head at Otokar, said in the joint press release:
“The successful completion of this programme demonstrates TULPAR’s capability to integrate advanced large-calibre turret systems while delivering the mobility, survivability and firepower required by modern armed forces. It also reflects Otokar’s engineering excellence and our commitment to developing modular architecture, enabling rapid integration of mission-specific weapon systems to meet diverse operational requirements of our customers. This achievement reinforces the strong engineering collaboration between Otokar and Leonardo and highlights the capability of both companies to deliver integrated, high-performance land combat solutions for international users.”
Luca Perazzo, Deputy Managing Director of Leonardo’s Defence Systems Business Area, was also quoted in the release:
“We are pleased with the outcome and proud to showcase the technological excellence of our systems. The integration of our HITFACT MkII turret onto the Tulpar further demonstrates turret’s modularity. The HITFACT turret is currently the only system in the world equipped with a 120 mm smoothbore gun offering the same firepower as an MBT system, while being capable of being integrated onto a light or medium platform and of employing the new guided Vulcano 120 ammunition for precision-guided engagements. This turret is just one of the weapon systems that Leonardo is able to offer today, alongside the HITFIST family of medium-calibre turrets, which can be equipped with Leonardo’s proprietary 30 mm X-GUN technology.”
Tulpar is Otokar’s modular tracked armoured combat vehicle family, and its scalable design covers a gross vehicle weight range of 28 to 45 tonnes. Otokar says the common architecture allows a high degree of hull and subsystem commonality across variants, and that the vehicle can be configured for roles including medium tank, infantry fighting vehicle, fire support, air defence, mortar carrier, recovery and medical evacuation. The company also states that the platform has been tested in demanding climatic and terrain conditions and offers high levels of ballistic and mine protection.
The HITFACT MkII itself is described by Leonardo as a lightweight, modular and fully digitalised turret, fitted with panoramic electro-optical sights for both the commander and the gunner. It can accommodate either a 105/52 mm rifled gun or a 120/45 mm low-recoil smoothbore gun, and Leonardo states that the design is qualified, in production and in operational service. The firm describes it as the first large-calibre turret carrying a high-pressure main battle tank gun that can be integrated on both wheeled and light tracked vehicles. For protection against uncrewed aerial threats, the turret can also be fitted with the HItrole counter-UAS remote weapon station mounting Leonardo’s new Blaze 30×113 gun.
Otokar, part of Turkey’s Koç Group, produces 4×4, 6×6 and 8×8 tactical wheeled armoured vehicles, tracked armoured vehicles, uncrewed vehicles and turret systems from a 552,000 square metre production site in Sakarya that employs more than 3,500 people. The company has supplied military vehicles to NATO and the United Nations since the 1980s and says it has more than 33,000 military vehicles in service with over 80 users in around 50 countries. Leonardo, for its part, employs more than 62,000 people and reported new orders of €23.8 billion and consolidated revenues of €19.5 billion in 2025. Both companies said they intend to explore further cooperation opportunities.

Stabbings in Bondi Beach and the Blue Mountains have led a series of crimes in NSW over the weekend, with three of them domestic violence-related murders.
In Sydney's Bondi Beach, Sergei Mitnik was charged with the murder of an elderly woman in her 90s inside a unit. He did not apply for release on Sunday when he appeared in a bail court hours after being charged.
The woman was found with significant stab wounds to her torso about 5.15pm on Saturday and died at the scene.
Mitnik, who police said knew the woman, was arrested at the home before being charged with domestic violence-related murder.

16:46:00 KST

NATO is fully prepared to counter any potential Russian military escalation along the alliance’s eastern flank, Chair of the NATO Military Committee Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone said.
“The alliance is ready, the structure is ready, the soldiers and the weapons are ready,” Dragone said, according to Politico.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Dragone stated that NATO continues to expand its operational capabilities across the eastern periphery, reinforcing both troop levels and materiel readiness.
While allied commanders did not dedicate the Copenhagen summit to reviewing specific recent warnings issued by individual member states, Dragone underscored that the alliance possesses comprehensive operational blueprints to defend every inch of allied territory.
The operational documentation, comprising roughly 4,000 pages of classified regional defense plans, outlines response protocols ranging from localized border crises to large-scale military incursions.
The comprehensive blueprints build upon the three regional defense plans formally approved by NATO heads of state at the 2023 Vilnius summit, establishing assigned forces, pre-allocated defensive sectors, and rapid reinforcement routes across the continent.
“Allies are ready in case of escalation. In case of an attack, we know what to do,” Dragone said. “Russia’s irresponsible behavior over recent weeks and months continues to test allied resolve, aiming to undermine confidence and weaken our unity.”
Ukraine, Russia, Hard to Reconcile on Black Sea, Turkish Minister Says
The admiral emphasized that the Kremlin’s coercive tactics have produced the opposite effect, consolidating allied resolve rather than fracturing collective defense.
“These attempts do not divide us. They hone our tools, make us more united and determined,” Dragone added.
4,000-page defense plans
The defense frameworks discussed in Copenhagen represent NATO’s most comprehensive overhaul of collective defense planning since the Cold War.
Under the 4,000-page blueprint, NATO has transitioned from rotational reassurance deployments to pre-assigned combat formations capable of executing high-intensity defense from the first hours of a conflict.
The plans divide the European theater into three geographic zones – the High North and Atlantic, the central European and Baltic corridor, and the Mediterranean and Black Sea regions – linking national defense forces under supreme allied command.
Allied defense planners have focused heavily on logistical mobility, air and missile defense integration, and rapid troop positioning along NATO’s eastern frontier, aiming to deter conventional aggression through pre-positioned equipment caches and standardized command architectures.
NATO officials noted that the plans provide automated response options for commanders to scale readiness postures immediately if Russian forces mass near allied boundaries.
Eastern flank alerts
Dragone’s public assurances arrive amid contrasting assessments delivered by frontline European leaders regarding specific vulnerabilities in collective air defense.
Speaking in Washington, Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs cautioned that most NATO member states would struggle to intercept a mass Russian missile assault if the conflict spreads beyond Ukraine.
Rinkēvičs warned that aerial warfare and unmanned systems are advancing at “lightning speed,” warning that Western procurement cycles and defensive preparations risk becoming obsolete by mid-2027.
The Latvian head of state highlighted severe bottlenecks in securing Patriot batteries and surface-to-air interceptors, a shortfall exacerbated by the depletion of American stockpiles during military operations in the war against Iran.
Frontline states have also voiced alarm over deniable Russian incursions designed to probe allied resolve without triggering an overt military retaliation.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned parliament that intelligence dispatches indicate Russian plans include staging hybrid drone and missile incidents across eastern Europe, aiming to portray NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense guarantee as “more theoretical than practical.”
Concurrently, US President Donald Trump stated that Russia has already attacked Ukraine’s allies for “about five years,” treating Russian hybrid warfare, physical sabotage, and cross-border airspace breaches as an established reality facing European partners.

IGArchitects builds tokyo house from field of structural timber walls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:45:22 UTC
16:45:22 KST

forest of timber walls replaces a conventional room sequence
House of Wall Forest in Tokyo, Japan, by IGArchitects explores how the spatial clarity and structural presence commonly associated with reinforced-concrete architecture can be translated into timber construction. Rather than using timber to create a conventional sequence of rooms, the house is organized around a series of structural walls. These walls simultaneously define space, carry the building, guide movement, and frame views. The spaces emerge between and around them, creating a continuous sequence rather than a collection of enclosed rooms.
all images by Ooki Jingu
a strong timber framework opens the house to changing uses
The project deliberately gives timber a sense of mass and permanence. Its structure is expressed clearly, creating a spatial character closer to that of a reinforced-concrete building while retaining the material qualities of wood. Openings and gaps between the walls allow light, movement, and views to pass through the house. Although the architectural framework is strong and clearly defined, the resulting spaces remain open to different uses and interpretations. For the design team of IGArchitects, House of Wall Forest is part of an ongoing investigation into architecture as a durable framework for living. Rather than prescribing how a house should be used, the architecture establishes a strong spatial order that can accommodate changing lifestyles over time.

'Voices From The Last Days Of Freedom': Showcasing the pre-communist Cuba we lost - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:37:33 UTC
16:37:33 KST

Cuban American Genie Milgrom is a researcher, historian, and author who has published extensively about her family’s connections to Medieval Spain. In The Cuba We Lost: Voices From The Last Days Of Freedom, she revisits the period from January 1, 1959, when president Fulgencio Batista fled the island, to the 1962 Bay of Pigs invasion.
Below are some excerpts from her book, which showcases the personal accounts of those who were young children when they fled with – or without – their parents and families as Communism took over. And while, as Milgrom notes, the Cuban exiles went on to thrive and contribute vastly to the United States, I am reminded of a 1967 Spanish-language song by singer-songwriter Luis Aguilé that expresses the feelings this book lovingly revisits: “When I left Cuba, I lost my life, I lost my love... I left my heart buried.”
From the introduction
This is not an easy book to write, as I find myself reading and recalling events and emotions that had been kept hidden deep inside me for more than six decades. As I recount my own history and read and listen to the stories of the contributors to this book, I do so with tears in my eyes...
I read the accounts of dolls’ heads being yanked off, of a soldier taking the doll away from a toddler, or of witnessing a bombing in a department store in Cuba, and the pain is palpable.
January 1, 1959, at 3 a.m., Fulgencio Batista fled Cuba after having been in power for seven years.
At the exact moment that the wheels lifted off the ground toward the Dominican Republic, the Communist regime of Fidel Castro claimed victory over the island nation. Rebel forces quickly entered major cities, including Havana. Fidel Castro began a triumphal journey across Cuba and entered Havana on January 8. A provisional government headed by president Manuel Urrutia was established, while revolutionary leaders began to gain control of the military, police, and government institutions. The first trials and investigations of former Batista officials also began during this same period.
The dominant mood across much of Cuba was one of celebration, hope, and expectation. Large crowds welcomed the rebel leaders, believing that democratic elections, along with a constitutional government, as well as political freedoms, would soon be restored.
At the same time, families connected to the previous government, the military, and especially the business sector experienced major anxiety about the future. While optimism remained widespread, the first signs of political division and uncertainty were beginning to emerge underneath the revolutionary enthusiasm.
Perla Abrams, nee Ziegenhirt, recalls
My uncle was ministro de gobernación, a member of Batista’s cabinet; we have translated it as “secretary of state” in the past. His name was Santiago Rey Perna. My dad was a captain of police but served as my uncle’s assistant.
We left Cuba and went to Santiago de Chile, where we stayed for a few months; then we traveled to Mexico City before settling in Miami. I was five years old in 1959 when my family had to flee Havana.
The revolution was successful, and the barbudos [“bearded ones”] wanted to apprehend my uncle. My uncle was part of Batista’s regime and, with my aunt and father, took refuge in the Chilean embassy. The ambassador was extremely brave and risked a great deal by not giving them access to my relatives seeking asylum. They did manage to escape and reach Chile, where the rest of the family soon followed.
There were beautiful memories... My pretty cousin turning 15 and having the party of the season. It was very glamorous, with all the debutantes of that time attending. A platform was constructed over the swimming pool which connected all our family homes in Santa Fe to serve as the dance floor. The beauty of this remains with me still.
... my father surprising me with a “chemis” dress in my size, which was all the rage in Havana, and high-heeled shoes also in my size to go with it. That was a good memory that I cherish.
I remember my aunt’s breakfast room, which had a tree with a little real monkey that I found fascinating, and I also recall my uncle’s collection of cat statues... beautiful cats made of all kinds of materials. We subsequently heard that the collection had been sent to Russia after the revolution.
Little did I know that this beautiful life would soon end.
My mother, brothers, and I flew to Nassau... until we were able to reunite in Chile with the rest of the family. Our lives would never be the same.
I recall my mother telling me that our house staff were the people ransacking our home after the revolution, and how they removed all my beautiful dresses. I have a mental image of this happening, but it materialized from my mother’s story and not from witnessing it.
The rest of the memories of that glorious golden age arise from family stories: My father saying how no fruit was ever sweeter than our Cuban fruit and how our sugar was so superior to others that you only needed a fraction of what you use now to sweeten your coffee. How there were no better mangos or avocados; and so much more.
My father would tell me how lucky we were and proudly describe the high modern standard of living enjoyed by Cubans in Havana in the 1950s... He would explain how generous the US was in its negotiations with us for the purchase of our sugar, for example.
My parents so loved their country, and they could never fully accept that they would not be returning. My father and two cousins all fought in the Bay of Pigs invasion and spent two years in prison until the Kennedy administration traded farm equipment for their freedom. That was an especially dark period in my childhood. My mom was left alone with three small children, with only the support of my dad’s family.
It must have been extremely hard for him to do, but he felt it was his duty to fight for Cuba’s freedom. The day the men returned, we picked my dad up at Dinner Key Auditorium [in Miami, where 10,000 Cuban exiles gathered on December 23-24, 1962, to welcome home the freed prisoners of Brigade 2506 following the Bay of Pigs invasion], and this was the day of the greatest joy in our family history. ■
THE CUBA WE LOST: VOICES FROM THE LAST DAYS OF FREEDOM
By Genie Milgrom
Milgrom Publishing
300 pages; $20

Most Israeli Jews fast on Yom Kippur, while over half take part in prayer services, survey finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:37:23 UTC
16:37:23 KST

Three-quarters (74%) of all Israeli Jews fast on Yom Kippur while over half (57%) participate in the day’s prayers, a new survey from the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) found.
About 63% of Israeli Jews fast fully and 11% fast partially (part of the day or in some years), but the figure varies across secular, religious, and non-religious traditional Jews.
Among secular Jews, less than half (47%) fast on Yom Kippur, with 28% fasting fully and 19% partially, while the number among non-religious traditional Jews and religous Jews is significantly higher.
Some 90% non-religious traditional Jews fast on Yom Kippur (77% fully and 13% partially), and 97%–98% of Haredi (ultra-Orthodox), religious, and religious-traditional Jews fast fully.
According to the survey, more Mizrahi Jews fast on Yom Kippur than Ashkenazi Jews and those of mixed background, with 81% Mizrahi Jews fasting fully and just about half (50.5%) of Ashkenazi Jews doing the same.
Only a small number of those who reported fasting partially or not at all are older, according to the survey data, suggesting the reasons are more linked to health or principle.
There is little variance between the genders of those who fast, the survey found, as 65% of men fast fully, compared to 61% of women. By contrast, 13% of women fast partially, compared with 10% of men.
A breakdown by age shows that the gender difference exists only among the aged 18–44; among those over 44, the proportion who fast fully is the same for men and women.
How many Israeli Jews participate in Yom Kippur prayers?
Of those who participate in Yom Kippur prayer services, 51% attend Orthodox services while a minority (6%) attend Reform or Conservative services.
Most religious-traditional Jews (90%) participate in Yom Kippur prayers.
Among non-religious traditional Jews, 67% participate (9% in non-Orthodox services), and among secular Jews, the number drops further, with only 20% participating (7% in non-Orthodox services).
In total, between a fifth and a quarter of Haredi, religious, religious-traditional, and non-religious traditional Jews participate in Yom Kippur prayer services, alongside 11% of secular Jews.
Of those who participate in Reform or Conservative services, half are secular and 48% are traditional.
Men participate in Yom Kippur prayers at a slightly higher rate than women, with the difference reflected clearly in Orthodox prayer services, where 54% of men participate in Orthodox prayer on Yom Kippur, compared with 48% of women.
Another 6% of both men and women participate in Reform or Conservative prayer services.
Differences across gender
Differences between participants genders are also pronounced among traditional groups, with 76% of men and 56% of women participating.
Mizrahi Jews also participate in Yom Kippur prayers at a higher rate (68%) than Ashkenazi Jews and those of mixed background, with the numbers at about half (50% and 51%, respectively).
However, non-religious traditional Mizrahi Jews have a lower rate of prayer participation which sits at 63% while that Ashkenazi Jews (74%) and people of mixed background (76%) is slightly higher.
Among secular Jews, the rate of Yom Kippur prayer participation among Mizrahi (22%), mixed (22%), and Ashkenazi Jews (18%) is similar.
For 18% of Israeli Jews, attending synagogue on Yom Kippur is their only synagogue visit of the entire year, including 37% of non-religious traditional Jews, 21% of religious-traditional Jews, and 16% of secular Jews.
Among those who attend synagogue services on Yom Kippur, 32% say it is their only synagogue visit during the year.
The survey was conducted by the Israel Democracy Institute in July–August 2026 for the "Religion and State in Israel Biannual,” with a sample of 1,002 Jewish respondents aged 18 and over, and was representative of Israel's Jewish population. The fieldwork was conducted by IPanel. The maximum sampling error is 3.1%.

Thousands of IRGC, Basij volunteers march through Tehran in show of defiance against US, Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:37:17 UTC
16:37:17 KST

Hundreds of thousands of Iranians participated on Friday in a rally organized by the regime in Tehran, in the largest display of defiance of its kind since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Participants said they were prepared to take up arms and defend the country after months of war and a worsening economic situation in Iran, the Associated Press reported.
The rally was held as part of an initiative called “Janfada Iran,” meaning “those who sacrifice their lives for Iran.” Participants marched through central Tehran in combat uniforms and carried flags, while crowds along the streets cheered them on. Some protesters stepped on US and Israeli flags and chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
In the days before the rally, state media called on the public to join the initiative and announced that limited training in the use of assault rifles would soon begin.
The volunteers are intended to serve as an additional layer of defense alongside the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Basij militia, which has played a central role over the years in suppressing protests against the regime.
Tehran IRGC commander General Hassan Hassanzadeh told state television that more than 600,000 people had already registered for the program and that the regime expects more than 1 million people to participate in training. Iranian television estimated that more than 300,000 people took to the streets of the capital on Friday, although the figures could not be independently verified.
Basij head says recruits will be 'nightmare' for Iran's enemies
The new head of the Basij, Hossein Taeb, announced at the opening of the rally that the volunteers would be ready for “comprehensive defense” and that similar events would soon be held in additional cities. He said the new recruits would become a “nightmare” for Iran’s enemies.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, military commanders, and other senior regime officials watched the parade.
“I came to tell Trump that we Iranians are not afraid of his threats against our homeland,” said Marzieh Afaghi, 24, who attended the rally with her husband and young child. “No one throughout history has managed to invade Iran and remain there.”
The rally also served as an opportunity for the regime to display military equipment. Air defense systems were deployed on the streets, and female IRGC fighters wearing black head coverings were seen alongside machine guns mounted on vehicles.
The IRGC also displayed drones of the type used in attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran claims responsibility for tanker attack in Strait of Hormuz
At the same time as the events in Tehran, Iran claimed responsibility for an attack on the oil tanker Trend, sailing under the flag of Togo.
According to state television, the tanker was targeted because of what it described as an “illegal attempt” to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said a vessel was struck by a projectile and that a fire broke out onboard, which was later extinguished.
According to UKMTO, the number of vessels passing with US military assistance off the coast of Oman averaged 24 per day over the past week. However, overall maritime traffic in the area remains about 90% lower than in the period before the war.
Iranian attacks and threats in the strait have severely disrupted oil and natural gas shipments from Gulf countries to markets around the world.
Expanded Basij enables greater suppression of future protests
According to AP, the recruitment initiative also has domestic significance: expanding forces aligned with the Basij could strengthen the regime’s ability to suppress future protests.
In January, shortly before the outbreak of the war, Iran saw some of the largest nationwide demonstrations in the country’s history. The protests began over the economic crisis and expanded into calls against the government.
Human rights activists claimed that more than 7,000 people were killed in the crackdown on the protests and that tens of thousands were arrested.
In May, government officials claimed that more than 30 million of Iran’s roughly 90 million residents had volunteered through an online form or at public events to sacrifice their lives for the regime.

Expansive exhibition in Jaffa gives Gaza border artists a chance to air their trauma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:37:16 UTC
16:37:16 KST

As emotive art showings go, Voices from the Gaza Envelope has most of them beat. The voluminous group exhibition opened at the Amiad Center in Jaffa on September 14 and features more than 200 works from some 75 artists. The vast majority of them come from our southern communities near the border with Gaza and, hence, experienced the horrors of Oct. 7, 2023, firsthand.
Shosh Segev certainly did. On that fateful day, the septuagenarian multidisciplinary artist was at home, on Kibbutz Kfar Aza, with her husband, Benzi. “Our house is right next to the young people’s quarter,” she explains. “There were terrorists inside the residential secure spaces (mamad) in those homes,” she adds.
The Tree of Life
When the IDF eventually made it to Kfar Aza, just 5 km. east of Gaza, one of the soldiers tried to pry the Hamas gunmen out by using a bulldozer to smash the windows of their hideouts. Unfortunately, when he reversed towards Segev’s house, he knocked down a Prosopis cineraria tree. However, that mishap turned out to be a cloud with a life-saving silver lining.
“The tree, which was massive, probably 6 meters or more tall, crashed into our balcony,” Segev recalls. “It blocked the sliding glass doors at the rear of our house. When the terrorists ran out of our neighbors’ mamads, they couldn’t get into our house from the back, because of the tree. Since then, I call it the Tree of Life.”
For the past three years, Segev, who has several works on show in Jaffa, and her husband have been living at Kibbutz Shefayim along with some 100 other families from Kfar Aza. That’s a long time to be in temporary accommodation. She says she and Benzi have been given another year to stay at Shefayim before they return to their – by then – rebuilt domicile down south.
“Benzi doesn’t want to go back at all, and I am ambivalent about it.” She says they have a persistent feeling their home has been violated. “I used to live by the maxim that my home is my castle, a place where I can feel safe and secure. But that isn’t the case anymore, not since Oct. 7. Now I’m afraid to go back home.”
That sounds like a challenging state of affairs but, like all the exhibitors in Jaffa, at least Segev has an outlet for her trauma, her fears, and her pain. But you won’t see that too clearly in her work. She primarily engages in painting, but there are also merry papier-mâché figures in her extensive portfolio. The latter seem to burst with bright, rich colors, exuding a sense of optimism and hope. Neither of those sentiments is in generous supply these days for many of us, particularly among the likes of Segev, who still bear the deep-set scars of that terrible day.
But, unlike the majority of the other exhibitors, you couldn’t tell that from her post-Oct. 7 work. “If I feel down, I wait until my mood lifts before I get back to work,” she notes. “I can’t create out of depression. For me that just doesn’t work.” Segev’s acrylic paintings are mostly awash with color, and convey a sense of joie de vivre. Her slot in the Jaffa collection, which was curated by Iris Elhanani and initiated by the Gershoni Foundation to support artists from the Sha’ar Hanegev region, in collaboration with the Sha’ar Hanegev Regional Council and the Sha’ar Hanegev Community Center, takes in a couple of paintings and a fetching polychromic mischievous-looking papier-mâché character.
Stubborn as goats
Daniel Ohana’s brace in the exhibition grabs the eye and also tugs on the heartstrings with gusto. He clearly has a thing about goats. His mosaic-looking paintings present the sturdy milk-giving farm animal in an alluring manner that imparts something of a sense of the creature’s subconscious. “The goat is an animal of contradictions,” he explains. “It can fall prey but it is also more readily associated with survival in extreme living conditions.”
Ohana takes the metaphor a step further, into national climes. “For me, it symbolizes the character of our nation: stubborn, fearless, always pushing itself to climb higher towards the summit, against all odds.” Stirring words indeed, and his artwork is no less moving and impressive.
He has the existential Oct. 7-related credentials for his place in the exhibition. “I am a born and bred resident of Sderot and have always lived in the shadow of war. And having experienced Oct. 7 close up, for me my attraction to this figure [of a goat] is essential escapism.”
That comes through in spades in his delectably crafted paintings. “Through these two works I chose to take the experience of survival – collective and my own – and transpose it to an animal that refuses to succumb to the conditions that nature puts before it,” he declares. “This is an attempt to find strength, beauty and optimism in a place where it is all too easy to fall, and to remind us that we too, just like the goat, are always climbing.”
Bringing in the crowds
There are, indeed, positive messages to be gleaned right across the spread that fills the cavernous venue, which, Elhanani informs me, was made available gratis by the Municipality of Tel Aviv. “They and Mayor [Ron] Huldai have been very supportive,” she says.
The curator also pulled out several stops to help Gaza border artists get their lives back on creative track. She was instrumental in organizing an auction of works by Israeli artists in London, with the proceeds going to funding the establishment of studio facilities for evacuated artists.
She is well-versed in the work and lives of many of the artists, and is delighted to have the opportunity to push their art out there, to culture consumers of all ilks. The Amiad Center, she says, fits the bill on various levels. “It is a very large space. It is a wonderful venue. And we get thousands of people coming to see exhibitions here. I’ve curated shows that have drawn 25,000 visitors.”
That’s pretty good going, and a traffic volume which Establishment art repositories such as the Tel Aviv Museum would be more than happy to bring in. Not disparaging the Jaffa location one iota, I still wondered whether Elhanani might have been happier to have Voices from the Gaza Envelope run over at the more prestigious downtown venue on Shaul Hamelech Street. “Yes, of course, I’d like the Tel Aviv Museum to take the exhibition on. The question is whether they would want to.” Her intonation and facial expression clearly conveyed her skeptical take on that.
From the collective to the personal
Oct. 7, And all its corporeal and emotional fallout, comes through time and again across the display, and in all sorts of guises. Limor Klein Tivoli went for a definitive military apparel hook and embroidered a broad range of faux military unit insignia that tell the story of that cataclysmic event down south going on three years ago now, in her own unique way.
Her set goes by the highly suggestive moniker Where Did You Serve? It comprises a complement to a series she called Trauma Treatment, which she contributed to the Women Relate War: Voices from the Front exhibition, which took place earlier this year. That show, in turn, fed off stories related by female soldiers who took part in running battles with the Hamas terrorists on and immediately after Oct. 7, 2023. “This body of work was inspired by my encounter with the testimonies of female combat soldiers following the events of Oct. 7,” Klein Tivoli says.
The line she took was to try to portray some of that battlefield emotional detritus in physical aesthetic form. “I focused on the way in which trauma continues to be absorbed into the body, in memory and daily life, even after the actual event is over,” she explains.
Where Did You Serve? was sparked by the testimony of a particular soldier. “She is dealing with PTSD. Her story served as conceptual raw material for looking at the possibility of translating an ongoing psychological experience into visual language, and examining the tension that exists between the female experience and the military system which is associated with codes of strength, hierarchy and belonging.”
That led directly to Klein Tivoli’s choice of epaulet insignia, and the way she flexed military aesthetics into a very different philosophical domain. “The insignia – a definitive symbol of identity, belonging and role – are diverted away from the original meaning. They stop representing a military unit and become repositories of personal memory, vulnerability and resilience,” she expounds. “They enable us to consider the relationship between the collective and the individual, force and fragility, and between an institutional symbol and personal testimony.”
Klein Tivoli manages that artfully by delicately crafting designs that, at first glance, appear to be bona fide army shoulder tags. But as you spend a 
moment or two getting into the colorful compositions, the finer details begin to filter through with their patently non-military components, and extramural line of thought and execution. That is partly a result of the time Klein Tivoli spent in Japan, where she learned to note and leverage the minutiae of everyday life around her.
Blood flowers across the earth
There are so many images that flash before our eyes when we recall the carnage at the Nova Festival and the kibbutzim and moshavim near the border with Gaza. The color red has dual, and ambivalent, significance for that area of the country. Nature lovers may be familiar with the Darom Adom – Red South – festival, which takes place there towards the end of winter when the whole region is swamped by anemones as the normally arid plains sprout thousands of the beloved red flower.
Yaffa Solomon took that ubiquitous seasonal highlight and ran with it every which way. “The anemone is primarily a memory of the earth on which anemones bloom after the rain,” she says. Her contribution to the exhibition in Jaffa takes the form of a large sculptural affair with dozens of ceramic red flowers with elongated metal stems. Her sweeping artistic rendition of the Oct. 7 tragedy features thousands of crafted anemones she installed across the Nova site, and at other relevant locations such as the Oct. 7 victim section of the cemetery on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem.
She recently also finished work on a book on the floral memorial venture called Anemones Before the Rain. The tome is due out for distribution in the near future. I asked about her choice of temporal preposition. Her response brought tears to my eyes.
“When the dry and arid ground of the Western Negev was soaked with the blood of the murder victims [on Oct. 7], it was dyed red with the blood of the fallen. That is the same soil that, after the rain, drowns in the red of the anemones. The war broke out on the same ground where the anemones bloom after the rain.” Hence also her choice of material for her grand sculptural tribute. “It is a metaphor. The ground is the clay [of the ceramic flower heads], and the blood is the anemone which also plants hope in us, and reappears anew every year.”
There is no missing the angst in Nadine Bar-Noy’s portraits. The monochromic paintings drip with melancholy and a sense of inner searching for tranquility or, at the very least, acceptance. “She lives in Sderot,” Elhanani tells me. “She is still in shock after Oct. 7. She is suffering, badly.” That spills out of her works in a – hopefully – cathartic outpouring of her sorrow.
Furrows of life
Brit Einstein from Kibbutz Magen, less than 5 km. east of Gaza, was one of those who chose an active response to the trauma. “She was evacuated to Jaffa and then went back down south to work on a tractor. They were short-handed down there,” Elhanani explains.
Einstein’s stint plowing the fields on the kibbutz left her with an enduring image of the furrows. She subsequently photographed them and then transposed them into a set of nuanced monochromic paintings that convey the texture of the parched pre-autumnal rains soil, and the stillness of the air as the violence of the barbaric Hamas attack hovers over the future crops.
Orly Landber Tokolevsky’s ceramic set feeds off a pragmatic view of emergency situations and is a delight to the eyes. Her ceramic work is called Residential Secure Space Kit and comprises deftly fashioned items that may serve one well in such dire circumstances. A hefty-looking colorful glazed bowl contains an apple, a pencil, paintbrushes, and even a wad of dollar bills.
“There are some wonderful works here, with some big-name artists too, like Eyal Asulin,” says Elhanani. “There are works that express the sorrow, and there are others that impart optimism and hope for the future.”
Bridging the mortal artistic divide
The exhibitor roster also includes creations by artists murdered on Oct. 7, such as Aviv Atzili, Haim Perry, Roy Idan, Eliko Reichenstein, and Yuval Reviya. “Their work is shown alongside that of artists who continue to create today, creating a dialogue between voices that endure and voices that were silenced. The exhibition is not only an act of remembrance, but also a testament to artistic resilience, hope and continuity,” the curator notes.
There is quality art to be found among the ashes of the ravaged southern communities. “Our goal is to reveal the extraordinary artistic richness of the Western Negev and to present outstanding contemporary art that continues to flourish despite loss and devastation,” Elhanani states. “This exhibition speaks about the strength of artistic creation and the resilience of the human spirit.”
There are a number of events lined up for the exhibition, through to the closing date of October 3. There will be a conversation with South African-born former hostage in Gaza Aviva Siegel, from Kfar Aza, about her book The Main Thing Is to Wake Up to a New Morning. Siegel wrote the book together with journalist and author Amir Tibon, about her experiences on Oct. 7 and in captivity in Gaza. There will also be live dance and music, and film screenings.■

www.tel-aviv.gov.il

Nearly 150,000 people participate in final slihot ceremony ahead of Yom Kippur at Kotel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:37:15 UTC
16:37:15 KST

Approximately 150,000 people participated in the final slihot prayer service at the Western Wall ahead of Yom Kippur on Saturday night, marking the conclusion of 2026's traditional gatherings.
The gathering began in the early evening hours and reached its peak during the central ceremony at the Kotel, with participants standing in the Western Wall Plaza and spread across nearby balconies and throughout the Old City's alleyways.
Due to the large number of participants, the gathering was also broadcast on giant screens at the outskirts of the plaza, on the walls of the Jaffa Gate at the entrance to the Old City, and at IDF Square (Kikar Tzahal).
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, Sephardi Chief Rabbi of Israel David Yosef, Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi Kalman Meir Bar, Rabbi of the Western Wall and the Holy Sites Shmuel Rabinowitz, and Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion took part in the ceremony.
During the event, Netanyahu offered a prayer for peace and another for the safety of the IDF and Israel's security forces. Israel's chief rabbis similarly prayed for the peace and unity of the Jewish people.
Western Wall: Jewish people's beating heart
“This month has once again proven that the Western Wall is the beating heart of the Jewish people," Rabinowitz said in his address during the ceremony. "From every corner of the country and from all parts of the people, multitudes came here: members of every community, opinion, and outlook, those who wear a kippah and those who do not, and stood together as one person with one heart."
"Together we offered prayers for the success of IDF soldiers, for the recovery of the wounded, for the consolation of the families, and for the peace and unity of the people of Israel."
"From the holiness and spiritual elevation of the Selichot gatherings, we enter the new year with great hope: a year of healing and consolation, of victory and blessing, and above all a year in which we remember that we are all one people, sharing one destiny and one prayer," he concluded.
Former hostages attend slihot ceremony
Also in attendance were former hostage Eliya Cohen and his wife, Nova survivor Ziv Abud, as well as former hostages Rom Braslavski, Elkana Bohbot, and Ohad Ben Ami.
"Father in Heaven, I have come all the way to the Western Wall in our beautiful homeland to tell You I’m sorry," Braslavski wrote in a late Saturday post to X/Twitter. "I’m sorry that I didn’t do more at Nova. I’m sorry for all the times in captivity when I broke down, when I doubted, when I lost faith."
"I always knew in captivity that You would save me. I always knew that You would not let me remain in Gaza. I felt You with me in Gaza every single day, every single hour."
Braslavski went on, noting that every time Hamas attempted to convert him to Islam, he "did not give in to their pressure. Even in captivity, I always knew that a father would never abandon his children."
"A year ago, on the most recent Yom Kippur, I was a prisoner of Zion in Deir al-Balah. And today I am free at the Western Wall," he said. "On my way to the Wall, I passed by and saw the Al-Aqsa Mosque. With God’s help, Father in Heaven, You will return that to us as well."
In its own statement, the Western Wall Heritage Foundation added that nearly two million people visited the Kotel throughout the month, including former hostages, bereaved families, IDF soldiers, and members of Israel's security forces.
The foundation also completed its preperations for the Yom Kippur prayers, which will take place at the Western Wall Plaza throughout the fast and end with the Ne’ilah prayer and the blowing of the shofar on Monday night.

2 Dead in Moscow Region, Drones Hit Oil Refinery in Russian Capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:35:56 UTC
16:35:56 KST

Two people died in one of the biggest Ukrainian drone attacks on the Moscow region and an oil refinery in Russia's capital was hit, authorities said on Sunday, as Russia enters the final day of parliamentary elections.
Ukraine and Russia have continued attacks on each other's energy infrastructure despite an announcement by U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday that they had agreed to stop.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on his Telegram channel that the biggest Ukrainian drone attacks had been thwarted, with Russia downing more than 1,600 drones since Saturday, including 450 headed for Moscow.
Several drones reached the premises of the oil refinery and one hit an apartment, Sobyanin said, adding there were no casualties in the city.
"The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections," he said. "The adversary failed to achieve this."
Reuters witnesses heard blasts in Moscow and saw plumes of smoke billowing from the site of the Moscow refinery. The scale of any damage to the facility was not immediately known.
Ukrainian strikes have knocked out a significant part of Russia's oil refining capacity, triggering oil product shortages, fuel price increases and long queues at filling stations in many regions across the country's 11 time zones.
The Moscow plant, which has been targeted multiple times, processed 11.6 million metric tons of oil in 2024, producing 2.9 million tons of gasoline and 3.2 million tons of diesel, the latest available data shows.
Ukraine has not commented on the attacks. Both sides say they do not target civilians.
In the wider Moscow region, in addition to the two deaths, 400 people, including 70 children, were evacuated from a 21-storey apartment block in the Ramenskoye district and a number of homes were damaged, said Governor Andrei Vorobyov.

CNN, MS NOW, POLITICO journalists denied access to the White House after Trump said he'd bar them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:30:53 UTC
16:30:53 KST

The White House Correspondents’ Association, led by Fox News’ Jacqui Heinrich called on the Trump administration to immediately restore access to the representatives of the media organisations it barred, arguing that the move sets a dangerous precedent for free speech.
Reporters from three major news organisations were denied access to the White House on Saturday, a day after US President Donald Trump said he was barring them because of reporting he found to be “fake news.”
The media outlets, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, have previously been targeted by the Republican president, particularly CNN, who Trump kicks his antics up a notch, regularly mocking their reporters and lambasting their authenticity.
The actions were a clear escalation of Trump’s long-running efforts — in the courts and through administrative action — to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable, and the latest test of First Amendment protections in the United States.
Trump said on Friday that he would ban all three outlets because of coverage he disliked.
White House reporters from the two cable networks — Betsy Klein of CNN and Akayla Gardner of MS NOW — both went live to report they’d been turned away, their press badges deactivated, when arriving for their jobs at the White House.
Soon after, Politico said its White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett was also denied entry and had her badge confiscated. All three news outlets hinted at legal action.
“We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights,” Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in a statement to the Politico newsroom. A CNN statement said the network “will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account."
And MS NOW said it “intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”
In his second term, Trump and his administration have routinely punished certain media outlets, both in the courtroom and through regulatory action.
Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms — insulting them in briefings, or in his recent speech at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner, where he called CNN’s Kailtan Collins “very dumb and unhappy”.
The White House Correspondents’ Association President Jacqui Heinrich called on the administration to immediately restore the three outlets' access.
“The implications extend beyond these organisations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future,” she said.
“The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinise those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favourably.”
The move follows the president’s decision last year to bar Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events in retaliation for the news outlet’s decision not to follow his lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico.
The AP said that it would note, when appropriate, that Trump had ordered the water body, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters, renamed the “Gulf of America.”
The US news agency filed a lawsuit against their barring, and the case remains ongoing.
Since returning to office, Trump has pursued other legal action against a variety of different outlets, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC.
His administration is also involved in a long-simmering confrontation involving ABC over renewal of its broadcast licenses.
The AP said on Saturday it supported the news organizations banned this week. In a statement, the news cooperative said: “No news organisation — or person — should be retaliated against by the government over the words they use.”

Alex de Minaur has returned to form to seal Australia's Davis Cup progression, with the hosts beating Poland 3-1 in Brisbane also thanks to some earlier doubles brilliance.
The world No.9 found top gear on Sunday at Pat Rafter Arena, beating Kamil Majchrzak 6-3 6-3 to clinch a 3-1 result that sends Australia into the Cup's penultimate round next year.
With his backhand and serve firing, de Minaur followed up his 57-minute annihilation of Maks Kasnikowski on Saturday with another therapeutic response to a disappointing second-round US Open exit earlier this month.

Earlier, Max Purcell's scintillating tiebreak tennis alongside rock-solid Rinky Hijikata swung their doubles match, and the tie, in Australia's favour.
The pair's 7-6 (7-3) 6-3 defeat of Jan Zielinski and Karol Drzewiecki followed the win and the loss posted in singles by de Minaur and James Duckworth respectively on Saturday.
Purcell, on the comeback from a controversial 18-month anti-doping ban, turned the match on its head after a tight first set progressed to an inevitable tie break.

An unforced error from Poland was followed by two more Purcell winners, and he then held his nerve on a series of low volleys to eventually clinch the set.
Hijikata then held impressively and, after missing two break-point chances, nailed a forehand return to nab the match's only service break.
That was all Australia needed, with the composed pair energising the sold-out Pat Rafter Arena to secure a pressure-relieving victory in 77 minutes.
Australia's win followed a shock loss on the road to Ecuador earlier this year that plunged it into the must-win encounter against Poland.
The Aussies still need to win next year's qualifying round, against an opponent still to be decided, to progress to the finals in Italy in November, 2027.

Weak Ukraine Air Defense Threatens Poland, Defense Chief Warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:19:00 UTC
16:19:00 KST

Failing to supply Ukraine with sufficient air defense systems and interceptor ammunition directly increases the military threat to Poland, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz warned.
Speaking before lawmakers, Kosiniak-Kamysz stated that Polish fighter jets were scrambled again overnight to secure national airspace amid Russian missile and drone barrages targeting western Ukraine. The defense minister emphasized that recurring incidents along NATO’s eastern frontier can no longer be interpreted as accidental deviations.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“These are no longer isolated incidents; this is planned aggression against NATO member states. It is not an accident, it is the strategy of the Russian Federation,” Kosiniak-Kamysz told parliament, as reported by broadcaster TVN24.
Kosiniak-Kamysz criticized opposition parliamentarians over statements questioning defense aid to Kyiv, arguing that rhetoric seeking to curb military assistance aligns with Moscow’s strategic objectives rather than Poland’s national security interests.
“Missiles fall and drones fall one kilometer from the Polish border,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said. “If Ukraine does not have air defense assets, if it does not have ammunition to shoot down these drones, most of these drones will fly through Ukraine and reach Poland. Is that what you want?”
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 19, 2026
Border drone threats
The defense minister’s remarks followed an address by Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of the right-wing Confederation (Konfederacja) party. Mentzen had criticized the condition of Poland’s armed forces, pointing to shortages in domestic artillery ammunition reserves, deficiencies in reserve personnel training, and inadequate civil defense and bomb shelter infrastructure.
Responding to the criticism, Kosiniak-Kamysz insisted that sustaining Ukraine’s frontline interception capability remains the most effective operational barrier preventing Russian aerial munitions from penetrating deeper into allied territory.
The debate in Warsaw coincides with a series of cross-border security alerts along Poland’s eastern frontier.
On Sept. 13, Russian munitions struck within two kilometers of the Polish border in the Volyn region, damaging a commercial filling station near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk checkpoint and hitting the locomotive of a passenger train operating on the Kyiv-Warsaw rail corridor.
Polish air defenses and allied aircraft stationed along NATO’s eastern flank have repeatedly entered elevated readiness postures to monitor incoming Russian strike waves, with military planners cautioning that the deployment of high-speed jet-powered drones increases the margin of error near international boundaries.
Regional missile defense integration
The parliamentary debate follows Poland’s formal accession to a European defense coalition dedicated to countering ballistic missile threats alongside Ukraine and nine other European nations.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Poland’s participation during a joint press conference in Ukraine on Friday, Sept. 18.
Tusk characterized Poland’s initial omission from the initiative’s July launch in Paris as an administrative misunderstanding that has been resolved, noting that Polish defense enterprises are reviewing options to contribute industrially to joint interceptor programs.
The coalition encompasses Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, the UK and Ukraine, aiming to establish collaborative production lines and integrate regional radar architectures.
During their bilateral talks, Tusk and Zelensky also discussed the formation of the “Carpathian Eight,” a proposed regional security and economic format designed to reinforce infrastructure resilience and institutional alignment between Central European states and the EU.

Witnesses heard blasts in Moscow and saw plumes of smoke billowing from the refinery site. It was not clear what damage the facility had sustained. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.
“The biggest attack by enemy drones has been repelled. Since yesterday, more than 1,600 drones have been shot down across all fronts. Of these, 450 were approaching Moscow,” Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said in a statement on Telegram.
