In Belgium, an 800-year-old medieval structure was discovered with the help of moles
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
10:16:57 EEST
16:16:57 KST

In Belgium, an 800-year-old medieval structure was discovered with the help of moles
Kyiv • UNN
Near Damme, 2,810 archaeological fragments were found in 814 molehills. Among them was a brick gate dating from the 13th–14th centuries.
In Belgium, moles helped archaeologists uncover the remains of a medieval estate. In 814 molehills near Damme, researchers found 2,810 archaeological fragments, including remains of a brick gate dating from the 13th–14th centuries. The Arkeonews publication reported this, UNN writes.
Details
The finds pointed to the existence of a brick entrance gate dating from the 13th–14th centuries and provided new information about a medieval rural estate that had long disappeared from written sources.
In total, the researchers recovered 2,810 fragments weighing slightly more than two kilograms. They included construction debris, ceramics, metal objects, and fragments of natural stone.
The ceramics helped refine the dating of the site. Among the 294 fragments, locally produced gray pottery predominated, followed in quantity by red pottery. Decorated ceramics, proto-stoneware, and imported German stoneware were also found. Overall, the finds span a period from approximately the 12th to the 15th century, although most date from the 13th–14th centuries. This makes it possible to confidently attribute the gate to the medieval period.

Estonian experts say social media should be improved for children instead of banned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:15:00 UTC
16:15:00 KST

Estonian experts say social media should be improved for children instead of banned
The European Union is discussing a safe‑internet regulation that includes several restrictions planned for minors' use of social media. While EU plans propose setting a minimum age of 13, Estonian social scientists argue that blunt bans will not solve all problems and may even create new ones.
Tallinn University media professor Indrek Ibrus is critical of the EU initiative, saying the planned restrictions conflict with children's fundamental rights.
"In my opinion, it's generally a pretty bad idea," Ibrus said, explaining that it ignores the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. "Children must have opportunities for self‑expression and free access to information to support their development and identity. Any age‑based restriction on access to information essentially disregards children's rights," Ibrus said.
According to Ibrus, the European Commission is effectively giving up by proposing restrictions.
"Instead of working on these environments, these platforms, these spaces in a way that would make them safe and suitable for children, the European Commission throws up its hands and gives up. They don't have the strength to deal with regulation, even though the regulatory framework — the Digital Services Act — already exists and simply needs to be enforced. In a sense, children are being sacrificed because of the Commission's own inability," he said.
University of Tartu media studies professor Andra Siibak agreed that relying solely on bans and restrictions is not the best solution, highlighting the need to change platform business models. Siibak said it is positive that the EU demands concrete measures from service providers to make platforms more protective of children's rights, well‑being and privacy.
Like Ibrus, Siibak pointed out that all these recommended changes are already written into earlier EU regulations — whether the Digital Services Act or the AI Act. "The European Union itself must start thinking carefully about how to demand these changes from platforms and monitor that they actually implement them," Siibak said.
Tallinn University participation‑culture professor Katrin Tiidenberg warned against overly rigid bans, citing Australia's experience.
"Based on what we know from Australia and how their ban doesn't actually work, children under 16 are still online, which mainly means we don't know what they're doing on social media or where they're logged in," Tiidenberg said.
One of the biggest questions surrounding the EU Kids Act is how to verify users' ages without massively violating people's privacy.
Ibrus sees major risks in age verification. "It may be a direct privacy intrusion, and it may also be harmful in the sense that platforms could use identification for more precise profiling of users, which can be dangerous in several ways," he explained.
Ibrus added that although the EU is developing a digital wallet solution that could provide secure infrastructure in the future, any restrictions must be approached with extreme caution.
Siibak also noted that finding a reliable and transparent age‑verification method is currently difficult. Attempts with facial‑recognition software have not worked, and young people easily bypass restrictions using, for example, their parents' documents.
"We know from Australia's experience how skillfully young people bypass such age‑assessment apps and solutions. To access a platform, they show their parents' documents or take a photo with a famous footballer's poster in the background instead of showing their own face. Young people certainly have many ways to get around such systems. Finding a method acceptable to all member states will be a very difficult discussion," Siibak said.
Tiidenberg also stressed that mechanical age‑verification methods bring risks. "It's a very important issue, because if it means a child must log in with an ID card, then it means everyone must log in with an ID card. We want to avoid mass surveillance and monitoring of which sites we visit and who does what. In my view, maintaining freedom is important," Tiidenberg said.
"That doesn't mean age verification cannot be done in a reasonably safe way, but the method must be developed very carefully and not by quickly trusting the first private company that says: 'Look, I built you a solution,'" Tiidenberg said.
Experts say protecting children and young people on social media should focus on improving the platforms themselves.
Tiidenberg highlighted the need to pressure platforms to create well‑being‑oriented and responsible design. This means placing strong emphasis on curbing addictive algorithms — for example, giving users the option to choose between a chronological feed and recommendation algorithms. She also supports separate child‑ and youth‑friendly accounts (for example, ages 13–15) where harmful content is automatically limited.
Ibrus reminded that in addition to tightening rules, it is important to support young people's digital skills and critical thinking instead of creating artificial barriers that do not actually protect them online.
"Instead of bluntly banning communication environments because they may involve certain risks, those risks must be addressed. Platforms must be adapted, regulated, existing regulations enforced, and at the same time media literacy must be developed for different age and social groups," Ibrus said.
Tiidenberg added that digital skills are important, but a person can be both competent and helpless at the same time — including children.
"Critical awareness is very important, but obviously children have different self‑regulation abilities at different ages. Even many adults do not have very good self‑regulation. You may know something is harmful to you, but you still may not be able to avoid certain social media content," she said.
"Skills are important — they are part of the toolkit — but they are not enough if we allow user interfaces to be designed manipulatively, because they still measure the user's slowing finger while scrolling. If we do not regulate how quickly systems must respond when I say that I or my child does not want to see certain content, then digital skills alone are of little use," Tiidenberg added.
On Thursday, the European Commission adopted the safe‑internet regulation (EU Kids Act), which increases children's online safety in the EU. The package includes proposals to ban social media use for children under 13 and to require companies providing online services to create safe accounts for children.
Under the proposal — which EU member states and the European Parliament will negotiate — accounts for children aged 13–15 would be under parental control.
Social media and video services, online games and AI‑based companions and chatbots intended for users under 18 would be subject to a list of permitted and prohibited activities.
--
Editor: Mari Peegel, Argo Ideon

China's consumption shifts toward smart, health-related products: commerce ministry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:14:08 CST
16:14:08 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's consumer market showed a stronger move toward smart, health-related and higher-quality products in the first eight months of 2026, with sales of smart glasses on major platforms surging 120 percent year on year, the Ministry of Commerce said on Sunday.
Sales of electrocardiogram monitors jumped 75 percent during this period, while those of action cameras and organic food rose 26.9 percent and 7.4 percent, respectively, according to an official with the ministry.
The latest breakdown offers a closer look at changes within China's consumer market after official data revealed that the combined retail sales of goods and services rose 2.5 percent year on year in the January-August period.
Demand also remained robust for a range of consumption-upgrade products. Sales of communication equipment increased 16.3 percent, while cosmetics items registered growth of 6.1 percent, and sales of cultural products and office supplies were up by 6 percent.
In contrast, sales of petroleum products fell 6.1 percent year on year in this period, which the official partly attributed to substitution by new-energy products.
Services continued to outpace goods consumption. Retail sales of services expanded 4.9 percent in the first eight months of 2026, 3.9 percentage points faster than retail sales of goods.
Demand for tourism consulting and rental services, as well as cultural, sports and leisure services, maintained relatively rapid growth during the summer holiday season, as Chinese consumers increasingly spent on services alongside physical goods, according to the official.
Consumption growth also continued to spread beyond major cities. Rural retail sales of consumer goods reached 4.4 trillion yuan (about 651.65 billion U.S. dollars), up 2.3 percent year on year, and 1.3 percentage points faster than the growth recorded in urban areas.
Boosting consumption remains a policy priority for China this year. In July, China unveiled a five-year plan for expanding consumption, outlining measures to upgrade both goods and services consumption and expand quality services in areas including catering, tourism, elderly care and healthcare.
China has also expanded policy support for smart and energy-efficient consumption. Under its 2026 consumer goods trade-in program, backed by ultra-long special treasury bonds, subsidies cover automobiles, six categories of home appliances and four types of digital and smart products.
Smart glasses were included among the nationally subsidized digital and smart products for 2026, with eligible purchases receiving subsidies of 15 percent of the sales price, capped at 500 yuan per item. ■

Public memorial held for former HKSAR Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:13:50 CST
16:13:50 KST

HONG KONG, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- A public memorial was held in Hong Kong on Sunday for Tung Chee-hwa, former vice chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) and former chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR).
Tung died of illness at the age of 89 in Hong Kong on Sept. 8. He is regarded as an outstanding contributor to "one country, two systems," a renowned patriot, an outstanding social activist and a close friend of the Communist Party of China (CPC).
Tung served as vice chairman of the 10th, 11th, 12th and 13th National Committees of the CPPCC. He was the first- and second-term chief executive of the HKSAR.
While Tung was critically ill, the central authorities expressed deep concern over his condition. President Xi Jinping and other central leaders instructed the Liaison Office of the Central People's Government in the HKSAR to convey best wishes and demanded all-out efforts to treat Tung.
Following Tung's passing, Xi Jinping, Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi, Han Zheng, Hu Jintao and others expressed their deep grief in various forms and extended sincere condolences to his family.
Shi Taifeng, a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and vice chairman of the CPPCC National Committee, Leung Chun-ying, vice chairman of the CPPCC National Committee, Wang Dongfeng, vice chairman and secretary-general of the CPPCC National Committee, Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macao Work Office of the CPC Central Committee and of the Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office of the State Council, and John Lee, chief executive of the HKSAR, attended Sunday's memorial service.
The memorial service started at 9 a.m., with all those present observing a moment of silence. Leung, vice chairman of Tung's funeral committee, presided over the event.
Shi, chairman of Tung's funeral committee, delivered a speech at the event, reviewing Tung's life and highlighting his important contributions to the country, to Hong Kong, and to the society.
Following the speech, all participants bowed three times to Tung's portrait, came up in turn before his remains to pay their final respects, and expressed condolences to his family members.
Leaders from the central government institutions in Hong Kong, senior officials from the HKSAR government, HKSAR deputies to the National People's Congress, HKSAR members of the CPPCC National Committee, and representatives from various sectors of Hong Kong also attended the memorial to pay their respects. ■

Russian Election, Cast as Test of Support for Ukraine War, Enters Final Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:10:45 UTC
16:10:45 KST

A parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for Russia's war in Ukraine entered its third and final day on Sunday, with the ruling United Russia party expected to retain its dominance in a political system critics say does not tolerate dissent.
The State Duma vote, the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, is likely to be presented by the Kremlin as evidence of public backing for Putin's policies and for the war, Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II, now in its fifth year with no sign of ending soon.
Most anti-war candidates were barred from the ballot. Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party, which has polled in the single digits in recent years but hoped to tap into war fatigue, said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the vote for comments about the conflict deemed illegal by authorities.
Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news are punishable by lengthy prison sentences.
The Kremlin says national unity and some censorship are necessary during what it calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine. It casts the conflict as part of an existential struggle with a hostile West and says Ukrainian intelligence services and other enemies are stepping up efforts to stir unrest inside Russia.
Putin on Friday accused Ukraine of trying to interfere in the election, citing what he said was a Ukrainian strike on the home of an election official in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region that killed Yelena Astanina, the official. Reuters could not independently verify details of the attack and there was no immediate comment from Kyiv.
Russian electoral officials also said on Saturday that an online voting system in Moscow had come under cyberattack. Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a "pseudo election."
Despite what most experts see as the election's predictable outcome, the NEST think-tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, whom Russian authorities have designated "a foreign agent", said the vote could still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.
"The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on the ballot," it said in a note.
It said the Communist party and the New People party could attract votes the authorities would prefer to go to United Russia. Both parties have consistently voted in line with United Russia on major issues.
Putin told the nation in a televised address before the election that the vote would underline support for Russian troops fighting in Ukraine.
"Your choice, and your will, will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory, and love for our homeland, and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us," said Putin.
Initial results are expected to start emerging at around 18:00 GMT on Sunday, with more complete results available on Monday.

Unification Minister Chung Dong-young, however, pushed back on the concern, saying humanitarian medical aid should not be tied to North Korea's military policy and that the North's medical conditions are dire enough to warrant urgent support.

Don’t discount Reform because it's had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happen | John Harris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:00:09 UTC
16:00:09 KST

Despite the energised start Andy Burnham has made as prime minister, plenty of his party’s MPs and hardcore activists are still haunted by a familiar sense of insecurity. Underpinned by a political version of impostor syndrome, it runs deep – and, bar the odd spell of Labour optimism, it always has. So it is with the battle between Labour and Reform UK that will define an election that could arrive much sooner than some people think, and a widely held ambivalence on the left about the possibility of Nigel Farage’s party taking power. Reform is apparently in deep trouble, yet also still in with a serious chance. How come?
Investigations into the party and its leadership’s finances by both the Metropolitan police and parliament’s standards commissioner may worsen Reform’s woes. Those investigations predate the two recently announced £36m donations from the crypto tycoons Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, which themselves risk being backdatedly ruled illegal and are reportedly already being spent on 400 “field agents”. The two mega-donations symbolise two connected stories. One is about the possible buyout of our fragile democracy. The other centres on how, from much of the public’s perspective, all the allegations about Farage and his party might have already turned into an indecipherable blizzard. So, although Reform is down, it is still far from out.
But the reasons for that extend much further than money. Reform still has a serious chance of either leading or forming the next government because of the same basic fact that Burnham says he has come to avenge: that since the crash of 2008, millions of British lives have pinballed from one crisis to the next, leaving many people resentful, insecure and plain scared.
If anyone hadn’t already noticed, ours is an age of fear: of economic insecurity, wildfires and unprecedented weather, seemingly unending wars, and massed and chaotic human movement. Reform – and the Tories – lean into all that anxiety, offering the kind of crass solutions (witness Farage’s recent promise of a state of “national emergency” as soon as he takes office) that only heighten people’s sense of crisis. Labour, meanwhile, can only offer another variation of its age-old answer: modest hope and constructive change. Such will be the choice sooner or later presented to voters. And in that sense, the next election will be more emotional than political.
Make no mistake: the campaign has effectively already begun. If, for instance, John Healey’s first budget is not peppered with vivid symbols of a different approach to the economy, it will threaten to be a very serious dud, with lasting consequences. Moreover, at some point during the autumn – presumably beginning at the Labour conference – we will start to get a sense of Burnham’s 10-year plan. He will have to talk about AI, and its dire threats and huge opportunities, and the climate emergency – a subject he has so far been strangely reluctant to address. But he will also need convincing answers to less apocalyptic problems. Right now, I can think of no better example than the million or so young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) who have mums, dads and grandparents terrified – fear, once again – on their behalf.
He is also going to have to walk some very precarious tightropes. We all know what sits behind much of the public’s feelings about immigration: as well as misapprehensions about the relevant numbers – which are actually going down – and straight-up racism, too many working lives sit on the borderline between the official and illicit economy, and are defined by “employers being able to import cheap agency labour to undercut existing pay and conditions in the name of free-market orthodoxy”. Those last words were once uttered by that sainted socialist Jeremy Corbyn: they were intended as a rational explanation for yet another example of people’s deep sense of worry.
From that vantage point, footage of so-called small boats is bound often to spark a callous and fearful response. To many people, such sights look – look – like proof of even more people who have come to disappear into the cracks that run through our labour market, and then surface offering to work longer hours than you, for a lot less money. That makes you feel even more scared than you already were. And as any student of the 20th century knows, nothing warps politics – and helps demagogues – like that kind of anxiety.
A visceral dread is now the basis of the picture of modern Britain – and England in particular – offered to the public by Reform, the Tories and their allies in the press and online. We are, in fact, living through the comprehensive reinvention of English rightwing politics as a byword for angst, fury and paranoia. Anything that could reasonably be termed conservatism is nowhere to be seen: their England is now a country where summers are spent willing on unrest, and where quasi-paramilitaries menace our ports. Last week saw that Passport to Pimlico-esque village of Piddington in Oxfordshire hold a referendum on leaving the UK – with 92% of votes in favour – because of what the Telegraph calls a “migrant camp”. From Reform in particular, one often gets the sense that any degree of contentment is seen as being tantamount to complacent wokeness; as they see it, England is – or should be – a righteously stroppy little country, prone to the raging, nihilistic impulses that Farage et al seem to see as the essence of our national character.
As much as Labour needs a solid, credible approach to immigration, it is going to have to remind people of the truth. We are a country with problems, for sure, but one whose people have not abandoned hope and largely get along with one other – and where, to quote July’s bulletin from the Office for National Statistics, “The cost of living (88%), the NHS (78%) and the economy (70%) were the most commonly reported issues facing the UK today.” Whatever our fears, earlier this month, YouGov reported that 57% of us are “fairly satisfied” with life. Labour should attack Farage, Badenoch et al for their lack of faith in the essential moderation and calm of most Britons; Burnham is the first senior Labour figure in a long time who may have the authenticity, energy and principle to make such talk actually ring true.
And then there are more solid, tangible matters. A fortnight ago, the new prime minister announced £1bn of investment in a new fleet of trains that are going to be built in Derby, “supporting over 350 jobs … and almost 6,000 across [the] UK supply chain”. Self-evidently, we need a lot more of that kind of stuff. Highly visible sites should be quickly set aside for new council housing, so Labour can point at the plots and promise people transformed and secure lives. In our further education colleges, money must soon be spent on teaching the absent skills that will help revive the economy, not least in construction, and provide good, dependable jobs.
The list inevitably goes on, but it may soon mark the difference between the meaningful survival of our democracy and the arrival of a munificently funded barbarism. Labour high-ups ought to remind themselves that that great Labour godhead Aneurin Bevan titled his only book In Place of Fear: in those four words lie this new government’s basic mission, the high stakes involved, and the almost impossibly hard work it will take to even begin to achieve it.
- 
  John Harris is a Guardian columnist

Lithuania seeks full CERN membership as Vilnius hosts particle physics community
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Scientists from the European Organization for Nuclear Research, CERN, are meeting in Lithuania for the first time as the country seeks full membership in the organization at an annual cost of more than 4 million euros.
The weeklong gathering in Vilnius comes as CERN’s Large Hadron Collider in Geneva undergoes an upgrade. The world’s largest particle accelerator was shut down in late June to allow work to begin, with scientists expecting the upgrades to expand their ability to study the fundamental properties of the universe.
The 27-kilometre underground collider accelerates particles to nearly the speed of light and brings them into collisions. Scientists use the resulting data to investigate how the universe developed after the Big Bang.
The CERN community meeting in Vilnius includes scientists working on the LHCb experiment, which studies differences between matter and antimatter.
“At the beginning of the universe we had equal amounts of matter and antimatter. Today the universe is made only of matter, not antimatter. So the fundamental question is: How did that happen? And we still don’t understand it,” said Timothy Gershon, spokesperson for the CERN LHCb experiment.
The LHCb collaboration has published more than 900 scientific papers, said Mindaugas Šarpis, head of the LHCbVilnius group at Vilnius University.
“These are our ideas, our reports on how the universe works,” Šarpis said, noting that the research has also led to discoveries including pentaquarks, particles that scientists had not previously known about.
Vilnius University is one of the institutions participating in the experiment, alongside leading universities including the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Oxford and Cambridge.
“Vilnius University is an equal partner,” Šarpis said. “We can give our students memberships and study the data collected by the LHCb detector. We have billions upon billions of particle collisions that we want to analyse.”
Lithuania became an associate member of CERN about eight years ago, with membership currently costing the government about 1 million euros a year. The country has now begun the process of seeking full membership, which would raise its annual contribution to about 4 million euros.
“The membership procedure has already started,” said Gautier Hamel de Monchenault, CERN’s head of research and computing.
Lithuanian scientists can already work with CERN, but full membership would give Lithuania a vote on the organisation’s council and a role in its governance, Hamel de Monchenault said.
Lithuanian industry would also have opportunities to participate in developing future particle accelerators, he said.
Vilnius University Rector Rimvydas Petrauskas said the financial contribution would be only one part of the process.
“It costs money. The membership fee is quite substantial, but that is not enough,” Petrauskas said. Other member states must also approve Lithuania’s membership and determine whether it meets the required standards, he said.
Lithuanian officials and researchers also point to potential economic benefits from deeper involvement with CERN.
Saulė Mačiukaitė-Žvinienė, a professor at Vilnius University’s Business School, said businesses that have become involved with CERN while Lithuania has been an associate member have seen revenue growth of up to 3% over the past five years.
She said full membership could provide a larger boost, citing research that found businesses in full-member countries can increase revenue and employment by about 14% to 15% annually.
Startups based on CERN technologies have attracted about $4 billion in investment, she said.
CERN’s scientific work has also had broader technological and medical applications. The organisation’s researchers developed the World Wide Web while seeking a way to share large amounts of scientific data, and technologies developed from particle physics research have been applied in medicine, including cancer treatment.

Mass Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow kills two, Russia says
Moscow mayor reports intercepting 1,600 drones during ‘unprecedented’ attack, accusing Ukraine of election interference.
At least two people have been killed and a major refinery has been damaged as hundreds of drones targeted the Russian capital, Moscow, and its surrounding region on the final day of the country’s parliamentary elections.
Moscow’s Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Sunday that more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted and shot down, 450 of which were heading for Moscow.

He also accused Ukraine of attempting to interfere with a tightly controlled three-day election that is set to tighten President Vladimir Putin’s 26-year grip on power.
“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed,” he said on Telegram.
Moscow regional Governor Andrey Vorobyov said on social media that a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man were killed in two separate locations.

Druze general: ‘Nation-State Law turned us into guests in our own home’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:45:28 UTC
15:45:28 KST

Only a few dozen yards separate Amal Asad’s well-kept home in Isfiya from the house of his 94-year-old mother, Dunya. Here, on the slopes of Mount Carmel, the boy who would become an IDF brigadier general was born and raised. From here he left for the recruitment office to enlist in the Paratroopers, five months before the 1973 Yom Kippur War. And this was where he returned on the day his world came crashing down.
It was September 12, 1993. That morning, Asad, then still a colonel, had begun his studies at Israel’s National Security College. Ten minutes into the first lecture, a soldier entered the room, approached Maj. Gen. Yossi Ben-Hanan, then commander of the IDF colleges, and handed him a note.
“Yossi looked at me and asked that the lecture be stopped,” Asad recalls. “He took me into his office, stood in front of me and said, ‘Amal, I’m sorry to tell you that your brother Wafa was killed in an encounter with terrorists in Gaza.’ I said, how can that be? The day before, he had come home from reserve duty to celebrate my birthday and that of his one-year-old daughter, Einav. We were born on the same date.
“I drove home with Col. Nabih Merhi, who was studying with me and was himself killed three years later in the Gaza Strip. The entire way, I kept thinking, ‘How will my mother take this?’ A year earlier, my father, Said, had been killed when his tractor overturned. Now she had lost her son too.”
By the time he reached Isfiya, his mother’s home was already packed with people. “I went inside and saw her sitting there like a noblewoman. My sisters were crying and screaming, and she was trying to calm them down. She was telling them it was God’s will, that this was our fate.”
Sgt. Wafa Asad was killed one day before the signing of the first Oslo Accord. “The patrol jeep he was in drove into an ambush in Shujaia,” his older brother says. “Two Hamas terrorists opened fire. Wafa managed to empty a magazine, but the driver was killed and the jeep crashed into the wall of a mosque. The terrorists approached my wounded brother, shot him to make sure he was dead, photographed him and circulated the pictures.”
Wafa was 27. He left behind a pregnant wife and a daughter. Two other Druze soldiers were killed in the same incident, Sgt. Muwafaq Abu-Shah and Staff Sgt. Ibrahim Shabal, both from Shefaram.
The cell commander, Imad Akel, who was known as “the man with nine lives,” was killed several months later. The second terrorist was arrested and sentenced to life in prison.
“Before the last hostage deal, I said, ‘I am prepared for them to release my brother’s killer in exchange for freeing hostages,’” Asad says in an interview marking the publication of his new book, HaTanach Sheli: Daring, Determination, Compassion, edited and developed with Dorit Lerman. “I saw what their families were going through. In the end, he wasn’t released.”
‘The first slap I got from Jews’
For years, Asad wrestled with how best to commemorate his brother. “I didn’t want another monument. I wanted a living memorial. Wafa loved hiking, he loved running, every day he would run to Elyakim and back, and above all he loved people. I thought about building a trail around the village, but then I said: This isn’t only about my brother. It’s about all the fallen members of the community.
“That is how the ‘For the Druze Sons’ project was born, and it became my life’s work: a 220-kilometer trail beginning in Daliyat al-Karmel, passing through every Druze village and ending at Nabi Shu'ayb. Parts follow existing trails and others were newly prepared. KKL-JNF took responsibility for developing, marking and funding it.”
The idea emerged in 2013. Before there was even a trail, Asad and his friends decided to hold a ceremonial launch for the project with a race near the Muhraqa site on Mount Carmel. “I wrote a Facebook post. I thought a few hundred people would come. Six thousand showed up. I was stunned. Since then, it has become a tradition. Every year we hold a race that draws between 15,000 and 20,000 people.”
The 2026 “For the Druze Sons” race was held Friday near the Golani Junction, with four events: a 10-kilometer run, a three-kilometer run, a 25-kilometer bicycle ride and a three-kilometer public walk. “The trail is now nearing the end of the signage stage, and in March 2027 we will officially inaugurate it,” Asad says.
The Druze community has lost 451 members in Israel’s wars, 13 of them in the war that began after October 7. Among the senior Druze officers killed were Col. Ehsan Daksa of Daliyat al-Karmel, commander of the IDF’s 401st Brigade, who was killed by an explosive device in Jabaliya in October 2024; Lt. Col. Salman Habaka, commander of the 53rd Battalion, who fought at Be'eri on October 7 and was killed in Shujaiya in November 2023; and Lt. Col. Alim Abdallah, deputy commander of the 300th Brigade, who was killed in an encounter on the Lebanon border two days after the Hamas attack.
When Amal Asad enlisted, most young Druze men served in the IDF’s Minorities Unit or in the Border Police. He was among the first Druze soldiers to join the Paratroopers.
In 1974, while taking a squad commanders’ course, his company was sent to evacuate settlers from Sebastia in the West Bank. “During the evacuation, we encountered fierce resistance and a lot of shouting from the settlers,” he writes in his book. “One of them, a young woman named Daniella Weiss, felt the need to yell at us, ‘Jews do not evacuate Jews!’ My friends laughed and told me I could evacuate her without a problem.
“It wasn’t long before she started cursing me and shouting, ‘Arab, what are you doing in the army?’ It was very difficult for me to hear. That was the first slap I got from Jews, and I took it to heart. Fortunately, from the first day I joined the Paratroopers, I felt like a member of the family, with no distinction between me and my fellow soldiers.”
Weiss later became one of the leading figures in Israel’s West Bank settlement movement. In 2019, when former Knesset member Geula Cohen died, Asad went to pay a condolence visit to her son, Tzachi Hanegbi.
“Tzachi said to me, ‘Meet Daniella Weiss,’” he recalls. “I said, ‘I know you.’ She asked, ‘Where do you know me from?’ I told her, ‘Sebastia.’ I told her about our encounter during the evacuation. She didn’t remember it.”
In the late 1980s, shortly after being promoted to colonel, Asad asked to attend a computer course at Mamram, the IDF’s main computing unit. When he arrived, the course commander told him he could not enter the computer room because he lacked the necessary security clearance. Every other participant, all Jewish and including some of his former subordinates, was allowed inside.
Today, that would probably not happen. Druze soldiers and officers serve throughout the IDF and intelligence community, including in positions requiring the highest levels of security clearance.
Among them are Brig. Gen. Hisham Ibrahim, the defense minister’s military secretary, whose position gives him access to some of Israel’s most sensitive security information, and Col. Ayoub Kayouf, commander of the Golani Brigade, who previously served in the elite Shaldag unit. Lt. Col. Mahmoud Kheir el-Din, who was killed during an operation in Khan Younis in 2018, served in one of Military Intelligence’s most secretive special-operations units.
But once they take off their uniforms, after leaving the military or simply while home on leave, many Druze say they feel like second-class citizens. One of the main reasons, Asad says, is the Nation-State Law passed in July 2018. The Basic Law defines Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people and states that national self-determination in Israel is unique to the Jewish people.
“I have left 451 fallen here, including my own brother, and the government says this country belongs more to a Jew living in America than it does to Amal Asad. And I say: Mr. Netanyahu, Mr. Ben Gvir, Mr. Smotrich, who gave you ownership of this country?”
Asad was one of the leaders of the campaign against the law. “The Nation-State Law robbed me of my sense of belonging,” he says. “It is hard to explain what it means to be Druze in Israel after that law was passed.
“A Jew in the United States is first and foremost American. A Druze living in Syria has a clear identity: He is Syrian. A Druze in Lebanon is Lebanese. Most Israeli Arabs see themselves as Palestinian. And what about us, who were born here, who built the country shoulder to shoulder with the Jews, who paid with the blood of our sons and brothers?
“The Nation-State Law turned us into guests in our own home. Welcome guests, perhaps, but guests. In effect, the law says that a Jew living in Brooklyn or Miami has more rights to this land than a Druze citizen whose family has lived here in the same village for 400 years.
“I have left 451 fallen here, including my brother, while that American Jew made $451 million. The government comes along and says: This country belongs more to him than it does to Amal As'ad. And I say: Mr. Netanyahu, Mr. Ben Gvir, Mr. Smotrich, by what right are you trying to turn me into a guest in my own country? Who gave you ownership of this land?”
You have met ministers and right-wing Knesset members. What do they tell you about the law?
“Even if there are Likud lawmakers who oppose the Nation-State Law, they don’t dare speak out. Take Minister Nir Barkat, for example. He was my soldier in the Paratroopers. When he was mayor of Jerusalem, I would visit him and he would hug me in front of everyone and proudly say that I had been his commander. He has become a doormat. Three years ago, he was supposed to come to Isfiya for the Memorial Day ceremony. I wrote a post saying he wasn’t welcome here.” Barkat currently serves as economy and industry minister.
There was a proposal to carve out an exception for the Druze because of their contribution to the country.
“That’s right. Bibi told the Druze: I’ll create a bypass route for you that will distinguish you from the Arabs. I strongly opposed it. I am fighting racism and fighting for equality for every citizen, Jewish, Muslim, Christian or Druze. You want me to be above a Muslim Arab but below a Jew? This law has to disappear not because it harms the Druze, but because it harms democracy.
“I said even then: The fight against the Nation-State Law is first and foremost your fight, the Jews’. Because this is the first crack in the wall of democracy. And I was right. It started with the Druze, continued with the left, with the Kaplan protesters and with Brothers in Arms activists, who are now denounced as traitors. Who knows where it will end.”
And yet, despite all the frustration and pain, a sign at the entrance to Isfiya displays the Israeli flag beside the Druze flag and says, ‘Together we will win.’
“Yes, but if you look at the bottom, you’ll see the logo of a business in the village that put up the sign as advertising. When they hung it, I said: ‘If someone can explain to me what “together” means and what “we will win” means, I’ll buy that sign.’
“Who are we together with? Ben Gvir? The ultra-Orthodox? The Arabs? And who have we defeated in three years of war other than ourselves?”
As a bereaved brother and a senior officer who fought throughout his career and was wounded three times, at the Chinese Farm in the Yom Kippur War, in a raid in southern Lebanon and in an operational accident, perhaps because of those experiences rather than despite them, Asad remains deeply committed to the idea of peace.
In his book, he recounts a meeting several years ago with Jenin Chamber of Commerce head Ammar Abu Bakr. “December 2021. I am CEO of Tirek, a tire-recycling company,” As'ad writes. “At noon, a black Mercedes pulled up at the factory gates. Abu Bakr and another businessman got out and entered my office. The meeting, which was supposed to last a few minutes, went on for more than two hours without us discussing business at all.
“Abu Bakr told me that when I was serving as commander of the IDF brigade responsible for the Jenin area, he had been one of the senior wanted men in the Black Panther organization. He was eventually captured and imprisoned, and was released under the Oslo Accords. But now a different man was sitting opposite me: a father of five, a man with responsibilities, who dreams of a safe future for his children. Years ago, I looked at him through a telescopic sight. Today I look at him through an economic sight. ... When he left the office, I felt as though I were saying goodbye to a friend.
“Peace may be far away, but it is also so close. It sits with you in your office and drives through your gate in a luxury car. It is willing to talk if you are willing to listen.”
Even now, after October 7, do you believe there is someone to talk to on the other side?
“Absolutely. I believe in peace. I believe in dialogue. I believe in human beings. And the problem isn’t only on the other side. Smotrich is doing everything he can to make the situation in the West Bank irreversible. The strengthening of Hamas and weakening of the Palestinian Authority over the years show, in my view, that the government does not want peace.
“Don’t misunderstand me. I think everyone who took part in the October 7 massacre must be eliminated. Every last one. Those people belong underground. But there are millions of other Palestinians who want to live quietly. What have we done to give them hope?
“There isn’t a child in the West Bank today who hasn’t been traumatized by settlers under the army’s protection. Someone who burns down a family’s home, someone who cuts down olive trees, is a terrorist in every sense of the word. Israelis don’t know what is happening there. They aren’t interested either. After October 7, people don’t want to hear about peace or about Palestinians. But it will come back to us.”
‘Sara said: Interesting, but no’
Amal Asad, 71, is married to Suheir. They have two sons, Ram and Amir, two daughters, Reem and Raya, and five grandchildren. He has lived all his life in the Isfiya neighborhood where he was born, apart from three periods when his military service took him to Kibbutz Yad Mordechai, Kibbutz Beit Alfa and the United States, where he attended a military college.
His son Amir, a lawyer, returned to Israel about a year ago after roughly 15 years in New York. “It bothered me very much that he had left the country, not only because I missed him but also on the national level, the Zionist level, the Israeli level. I wanted him to stay here, to build his home here, to raise his children here, to continue the tradition. I’m glad he came back.”
Asad is a people person. Retired senior officers often boast about the famous generals and politicians they crossed paths with during their careers. In his book, Asad repeatedly returns instead to the ordinary soldiers.
“To this day, I have better relationships with my soldiers than with my commanders or colleagues in equivalent positions,” he says.
One of them is Gabi Haberfeld. When Asad was a platoon commander in the Paratroopers’ 890th Battalion, Haberfeld was one of his soldiers. “Today he lives in the United States and is a very successful businessman. I used to meet him every time I visited my son in New York. We eat, drink and spend time together. But even now, as a grandfather himself, he tells me: ‘Amal, I’m still afraid of you.’ Apparently I was a tough commander.”
After being wounded at the Chinese Farm, Asad completed squad commanders’ and officers’ courses and returned to the 890th Battalion as a platoon commander and deputy company commander. “Dudu, the company commander, was about to finish his position and demanded that the battalion commander appoint me to replace him. But I preferred to take the new February 1977 company, so Dudu stayed in the post for the time being.”
A month later, on May 10, 1977, Asad’s company of new recruits was on a march near the brigade training base, then located at Sanur. “A few kilometers before the finish,” As'ad recalls, “a jeep stopped beside me. The training base commander, Yair Rafaeli, got out and said, ‘Amal, leave everything and get back to base. There’s been a disaster.’”
The scale of the disaster soon became clear. A Yas'ur helicopter carrying soldiers from the 890th Battalion had crashed during an exercise in the Jordan Valley. Forty-four soldiers and officers from the company Asad had left only a month earlier, along with 10 aircrew members, were killed in what became known in Israel as the “Disaster of the 54.”
Among the dead was Maj. David “Dudu” Kochavi, the company commander Asad had been due to replace. “My company had to provide the honor guards at the funerals,” he recalls.
Asad later served as deputy battalion commander, and when the First Lebanon War broke out, he commanded the Paratroopers Brigade’s combat engineering company. “When we reached the Chouf Mountains, we discovered that the Syrian commando battalion that had been there had withdrawn. When I tried to understand why, I was told that its battalion commander was a Syrian Druze and that when he heard the Israeli force commander was also Druze, he decided to retreat. I don’t know whether that story is true, but it’s a good excuse.”
It was there that he also encountered members of Lebanon’s Druze community for the first time, a complex and emotional meeting that he describes at length in his book.
His later posts included commander of the Nahal Brigade’s 932nd Battalion, commander of the Menashe Brigade responsible for the Jenin sector, commander of the reserve 5th Brigade and deputy commander of the IDF’s liaison unit in Lebanon during the years of fighting in the security zone.
In 1998, he was promoted to brigadier general and appointed to lead the Israeli side of the Joint Security Committee, the mechanism for security coordination and cooperation with the Palestinians created under the Oslo framework. The committee was part of the Israeli-Palestinian security coordination structure established during the Oslo era.
“We met at Netanyahu’s residence on Balfour Street. He read my proposal and said, ‘Do you mind if I consult my wife?’ I didn’t know her. Then Sara came into the room, sat opposite me, read the paper carefully and said, ‘Interesting. But no.’ Netanyahu accepted her view, and the IDF stayed in Lebanon until Ehud Barak was elected prime minister”
As'ad retired from the IDF after 26 years of service and, ahead of the 1999 election, joined the Center Party led by Yitzhak Mordechai. But after being placed too low on its candidate list to have a realistic chance of entering the Knesset, he left the party and backed Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud. He was even appointed deputy chairman of the Likud election campaign, but that brief political venture did not last either. Since then, he says, he has stayed well away from party politics.
During his short association with Likud, Asad urged Netanyahu, who was then in his first term as prime minister, to withdraw the IDF from Lebanon.
“I told him, ‘Soldiers are being killed for nothing. We have no ability to protect the communities of northern Israel from the Sujud outpost.’ Netanyahu was worried. He said, ‘If we leave Lebanon, there will be chaos.’ I told him, ‘That won’t happen if we do it properly. I’ll prepare an organized proposal for you.’
“I wrote him a four- or five-page paper with a detailed proposal: Announce that on a specified date the IDF will withdraw from southern Lebanon to the last millimeter; leave with a show of force by two divisions, with Israeli flags on the tanks and armored personnel carriers; seal the border; then tell the whole world that the first time Hezbollah fires a missile at Israel, even if it lands in an open area, these are the targets in Lebanon that will be bombed, moving from lighter to heavier targets, including the presidential palace in Beirut.
“We met again at Netanyahu’s residence on Balfour Street. It was Friday at 2:30 p.m. He read my proposal and said, ‘Do you mind if I consult my wife?’ I didn’t know her. Then Sara came into the room, sat opposite me, read the paper carefully and said, ‘Interesting. But no.’ Netanyahu accepted her view, and the IDF remained in Lebanon until Ehud Barak was elected prime minister.”
Despite becoming one of Netanyahu’s sharpest critics in the years since, Asad says he has some sympathy for the prime minister’s criticism of Israel’s prosecution system.
On March 15, 2017, Asad was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit a crime, money laundering, fraud and breach of trust. Prosecutors alleged that he had used his position as a director at Israel Aerospace Industries to obtain work for Druzenet, a company in which his brother was an investor. The investigation ended in a plea agreement under which he admitted to the relatively minor offense of failing to report required information.
“I decided I would rather be smart than right, and I left that chapter behind me,” he says. “I have no doubt that the prosecution needs to be put in order. I don’t support the reform this government is trying to advance, but I can understand Netanyahu’s criticism of the prosecution becoming intoxicated with its own power. It went to their heads.
“Of course, that doesn’t absolve him if he did commit the offenses he is accused of. I have never even accepted a single cigar as a gift. Well, I don’t smoke. But I never even took a piece of baklava.”
‘They throw a party when the state connects a house to electricity’
We drive through the streets of Isfiya in Asad’s jeep. “Look around,” he says. “See what Isfiya looks like and compare it with Yokneam. See what Beit Jann looks like and compare it with Karmiel.
“A shell that falls doesn’t distinguish between a Jewish, Druze, Circassian, Muslim or Christian soldier. But the moment you leave the army, the government, and not only this government, does distinguish between Jews and Druze. And it isn’t only the Nation-State Law.”
His criticism is not directed only at the government. It also extends to the heads of Druze local councils. “You are supposed to be leaders. Any leader would dream of having a community like this to work with. And what have you, the council heads, done so discharged soldiers can build homes? So that the state builds infrastructure in Druze communities?
“You throw a party when the state connects a house to the electricity grid, as if someone has done you a favor. Go to Shoham. Go to Yitzhar. See how people live there and how we live here.”
What can the council heads do?
“For a start, they need to be united. Stop dealing with egos and constantly fighting with one another. A minister comes here and cannot sit with two council heads because they aren’t speaking to each other.
“What have we asked for? To be able to build like normal people on our own land. Every Sunday there is a government meeting where another 2,000 housing units in the West Bank are approved. And what has the Druze community received in 78 years of statehood? Nothing. Not even one new community has been established.”
“I am proud to be Israeli, I am proud to be Druze and I am proud of Arab culture, of which I am a part. But if you ask me what I am, then first and foremost, I am a human being”
Whenever Israel’s Druze are discussed, their contribution to the country’s security is invariably mentioned, and rightly so. But today’s young Druze, Asad says, no longer think only about military careers.
“Some time ago, I met the chairman of an organization working to close gaps within Druze society. I asked what he did for a living and he said, ‘I own a high-tech company. Our offices are in Kfar Saba, but we have a branch in the village of Julis.’ I went there to give a lecture: 90 engineers and software professionals, all Druze.
“A lot of our young people who enlist now go to Unit 8200, cyber or communications units, and dream of careers in high-tech. There is even a woman from Daliyat al-Karmel who works at NASA, the U.S. space agency.”
And when you travel abroad and people ask about your identity, what do you tell them? Are you Israeli first or Druze first?
“I am proud to be Israeli, I am proud to be Druze and I am proud of Arab culture, of which I am a part. But if you ask me what I am, then first and foremost, I am a human being.”
Likud responded to Asad’s account of the meeting at the prime minister’s Balfour Street residence, in which he says Netanyahu rejected his Lebanon withdrawal proposal after consulting his wife: “This is fake news and a gross lie. It is the recycling of bizarre, old lies with no plausibility or basis in reality. Anyone who claims this is how things are conducted is either stupid or malicious, or both.”

Sobyanin claimed that since Saturday, September 19, more than 1,600 drones had allegedly been shot down on the approaches to Moscow, including 450 on their way toward the city.
He said several UAVs reached the territory of the Moscow Oil Refinery. There were no fatalities, Sobyanin added.
According to an OSINT analysis by Astra, the Moscow Oil Refinery (Gazpromneft-Moscow Refinery JSC) caught fire as a result of the attack.
The facility, located in Moscow’s Kapotnya district, is one of Russia’s largest oil refineries. It has a refining capacity of 11 million metric tons of crude oil per year. The refinery supplies about 40% of Moscow’s fuel market and 70% of the Moscow region’s demand for gasoline and jet fuel.
In addition, according to the findings of an OSINT analysis by Astra, the attack also hit a warehouse complex operated by Modern Warehouse Technologies LLC in the village of Sofyino in the Moscow region.
The company’s production and warehouse complex consists of six buildings with a total area of 290,000 square meters. A Pantsir air-defense missile and gun system is located 500 meters from the site.
Earlier, Governor of the Moscow region Andrey Vorobyov confirmed the attack on the region and said the most serious consequences were recorded in the Ramensky district, where Sofyino is located.
It was also reported that Aeroflot had begun adjusting its flight schedule because of the drone attack on Moscow. Due to temporary restrictions on aircraft departures and arrivals at airports in the Moscow aviation hub, the airline was forced to delay some departures on September 20 and cancel several flights.
Some flights arriving at Sheremetyevo Airport were diverted to alternate airports, Aeroflot said.
According to Telegram channels, more than 150 flights at Sheremetyevo were canceled or delayed following the drone attack on Moscow.

Slovak PM accuses West of provoking war with Russia

Slovak PM accuses West of provoking war with Russia
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has accused the West of having "needlessly added fuel to the fire" for more than four years in the context of the Russia-Ukraine war, thereby supposedly provoking a conflict between Russia and NATO.
Source: Fico in a video address posted on social media, as reported by Slovak newspaper Denník N and European Pravda
Details: Fico believes Western politicians are seeking to provoke a conflict between NATO and Russia if Ukraine is defeated on the battlefield.
Quote: "The failure of the strategy of destroying Russia through the war in Ukraine is forcing many Western politicians to conclude that if this cannot be achieved through the Ukrainian army and its full support, then everything must be done to provoke a conflict between NATO and Russia."
Details: Fico noted that "for more than four years, the West has needlessly been adding fuel to the fire in Ukraine".
Meanwhile, he acknowledges that Russia started the war when it invaded Ukraine, but insists: "Russia cannot be defeated in a conventional war, only with nuclear weapons."
"If anyone is interested in provoking a military conflict between NATO and Russia in order to pursue their own national interests, they must take responsibility for such a step themselves and not shift it onto other NATO member states," the prime minister added.
Fico stated that Slovakia would not take part in such a "conflict", despite NATO's Article 5.
"Under my government, no one will send Slovak soldiers outside Slovakia under a fabricated pretext to fight against Russia or any other country," he stressed.
In the video, the prime minister said that 27,000 Ukrainian soldiers are being killed in the war every month. According to Fico, this figure had previously been cited by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
Quote: "I have no reason to question these figures, although deliberately exaggerating the scale of human losses could influence the Western world to increase military and financial aid to Ukraine even further."
Background:
- On 18 September, Fico was due to travel to Ukraine to attend the Carpathian Initiative summit but cancelled the visit due to illness.
- Before that, the Slovak prime minister said he does not want war to come to Slovakia "because of some Article 5" of NATO.

Germany news: Doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs
Published September 19, 2026last updated September 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Polls have opened in key state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
- follow live here
- Germany's famous Oktoberfest is underway in Munich —with flu jabs on offer as well as beer
- Annual anti-abortion marches have taken place in Berlin and Cologne
- A port union has warned that German seaports are at significant risk of cyberattacks and sabotage
Here is a roundup of the top headlines from and about Germany on the weekend of September 19-20, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
German car makers losing ground – study
Germany's automobile giants are continuing to lose ground internationally, according to a new study published on Sunday.
Data compiled by multinational services network EY, previously known as Ernst & Young, found that, while German car manufacturers are still turning over more than their international rivals and still posting a combined profit, the gap is narrowing.
According to the study, German giants BMW, Mercedes and Volkswagen turned over a combined €284 billion in the first half of 2026 – around €1.5 billion more than the second-placed Japanese car industry.
But that figure is down 2.9% on last year and 7% lower than the record-high set in 2023.
Profits are also down, with the €13 billion made by the three German market leaders representing the second-lowest half-year profit since 2017.
US, Japanese, Chinese and South Korean manufacturers, on the other hand, all posted record turnovers for the period.
O'piekst is!: German doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs
Munich's annual Oktoberfest officially got underway on Saturday when the first beer keg was opened with the traditional cry of O'zapft is! ("It has been tapped!").
But another slogan is also being promoted in Bavaria this year: O'piekst is! ("It has been pricked!") — as doctors offer vaccine jabs against flu and Covid-19.
"With so many people coming together in such tight spaces in the beer tents, the risk of infection at Oktoberfest is higher," explained Christoph Spinner, head of infectiology at Munich's Rechts der Isar hospital.
Oktoberfest coincides with the start of the annual flu season, and Spinner warned that less than a third of people who are recommended a flu jab have actually had one.
Beatrix Zurek, a health expert from the city-led initiative München impft! ("Munich vaccinates!") said: "It's our job to go where people are. And that means: Oktoberfest."
Welcome back
Guten Morgen! And welcome back to our coverage of Germany on Sunday, 20 September.
Voters in two more German states head to the polls today as elections take place in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and in the capital, the city-state of Berlin.
We will have all you need to know about those elections in a separate blog which we will be launching when polls open at 8 a.m. local time, so keep an eye out for that.
And for all your non-election Germany news – stay right here!

We are pausing our coverage on Saturday, 19 September and will be back on Sunday, 20 September with more headlines from Germany.
Anti-abortion protests held in Cologne, Berlin
Protests against abortion and assisted suicide took to the streets of the German capital Berlin as well as the western city of Cologne on Saturday, in protest dubbed "March for Life."
Police said some 2,200 took part in Berlin, whereas no figures on the Cologne protests were immediately available. Catholic bishops were among those attending.
Meanwhile in both cities, pro-choice protests were also held.
Abortion in Germany is banned but women are allowed to carry out the measure if the first 12 weeks of the pregnancy have not yet concluded. They are however obligated to hold consultations first, and the abortion can only be held at least three days after such consultations.
Exceptions are naturally if the pregnancy poses a risk to the woman's health.
WATCH: Holocaust survivor on 'very dangerous' AfD Saxony-Anhalt win
Charlotte Knobloch, a Holocaust survivor and one of Germany’s most prominent Jewish community leaders, has voiced her alarm at the Alternative for Germany's (AfD) landslide victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election.
Speaking to DW, she warned that some Jews are once again considering leaving Germany, saying years of efforts to rebuild trust after the Holocaust are being undermined. Knobloch described the rise of the far-right party as a serious threat, urged mainstream politicians to confront extremism more forcefully and called for greater engagement with young people.
Her comments come amid renewed concerns about antisemitism, political polarization, and reported death threats against her.
Far-right AfD holds final rally before Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania election
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party held on Saturday its final rally in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, ahead of the Sunday vote in the eastern state.
Ulrich Siegmund, the party's winner in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, addressed a rally of some 1,000 AfD supporters in Schwerin, according to police estimates.
He said that what happened in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won but without an absolute majority, was also possible in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The latest ZDF Politbarometer poll puts the AfD in the eastern state one percentage point behind the Social Democrats (SPD); at 36% and 37% respectively. Next is the Left Party (Die Linke) at 9%, then the CDU at 6% and the Greens at 5%.
The AfD rally was also attended by the party's candidate in the state, Leif-Erik Holm, who echoed previous remarks that the election "should serve as a signal that this government must finally go." Several other AfD leaders have repeated the same calls since the results of the Saxony-Anhalt state vote.
The far-right party's final rally of the campaign also saw some 350 counter-demonstrators, according to police. No incidents were reported.
Merz schedules CDU meeting with all party leaders to discuss election results
In an unusual measure, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will convene the Christian Democratic Union leadership on Sunday to discuss the results of the state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
Unlike in previous state elections, Merz has invited the entire party executive committee to a formal meeting at 5:00 p.m. (1500 GMT) at the CDU headquarters in Berlin. The committee includes some 25 members, either electees or representatives by virtue of their offices.
Due to attend are the eight influential CDU premiers who backed him ahead of the election.
Compounding pressure has befallen the conservative chancellor since the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month, which saw the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) narrowly missing out on an absolute majority, while Merz's CDU secured half their previous result.
Polls for the upcoming votes are also grim, with the CDU threatened with the prospect of falling below the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament.
In the capital Berlin, where CDU is currently in power, polls suggest the conservative party is in a neck-and-neck race with the socialist Left Party.
Germany's Carsten Breuer to become NATO's Military Committee chairman
Germany's highest ranking military officer, General Carsten Breuer, will be the next chairman of NATO's Military Committee, after being voted into the role on Saturday.
"The support of the chiefs of defense of our NATO allies means a great deal to me. The alliance faces major challenges - for our security and peace in Europe and beyond," Breuer, who is also Germany's chief of defense, told German news agency DPA.
The position is considered among NATO's most influential ones.
Breuer succeeds Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone and will take over as of July 2027.
Breuer was competing for the position against Canada's Chief of Defense General Jennie Carignan. Had she been elected, she would have become the first woman to head the committee.
Cologne opera house reopens after 14-year redo
Cologne's cultural complex, which includes the city's main opera house, theater and children's opera, has finally reopened after renovation works that extended for some 14 years.
"With the reopening of our theaters, we are giving the city back a central place of meeting, inspiration and artistic freedom that belongs to all people of Cologne," Mayor Torsten Burmester said.
The western German state's opera house dates back to 1957, with the theater coming shortly after in 1962.
Since 2012, renovations on the pair commenced with an original budget of €250 million (roughly $287 million) that has somehow multiplied nearly three fold as the years rolled on.
The final price tag on the refurbishments stood at around €800 million.
In the 14 years it took to get the job done, Cologne's opera and theater houses had to relocate to other venues.
Celebrations of the reopening include music, dance, as well as other hands-on activities. On Sunday evening, the opening ceremony will conclude with a concert at the opera house.
Kremlin envoy offers economic cooperation to AfD
A senior Kremlin envoy has offered Russian help with Germany's energy supply in cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which has been widely criticized for its perceived links with Moscow.
The remarks by Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy for international economic cooperation, come as voters are set to go to the polls in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday, with the AfD locked in a close race with the ruling Social Democrats (SPD).
"Mecklenburg-Vorpommern will thrive again when affordable, reliable Nord Stream gas returns through joint work with AfD," Dmitriev wrote on X, using the German name for the state.
"Lower energy bills, more jobs and higher growth," he continued.
"No more German energy and industrial suicide," he added, responding to response to a post by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel calling for political change in the state.
Moscow has in the past offered to resume supplying Germany with cheap gas through the Nord Stream pipelines in the Baltic Sea if sanctions over its invasion of Ukraine are lifted.
The AfD has argued that cheaper Russian energy would benefit the German economy and has called for Russian gas supplies to Germany to resume.
However, critics say that Germany's previous reliance on Russian gas made it prone to energy blackmail from Moscow, while buying it would also serve to fuel Moscow's war machine.
Sunday's state election will have no direct bearing on the issue, with Russian pipeline gas subject to European Union sanctions.
Only one of the original four Nord Stream pipeline strands remains intact following explosions that damaged Nord Stream 1 and 2 in 2022. The remaining strand is not in use.
Oktoberfest opens as Munich mayor taps first beer keg
Crowds rushed onto the Oktoberfest grounds in the southern German city of Munich shortly after the gates opened on Saturday.
Some visitors ran toward the beer tents to claim the best seats after waiting for several hours. Members of the first group in line said they had arrived at 7 p.m. on Friday with camping chairs, sleeping bags and emergency blankets.
Beer could not be served until the official opening ceremony at midday, when new Munich Mayor Dominik Krause of the environmentalist Greens tapped the first keg with the traditional cry of "O'zapft is" — Bavarian dialect for "It is tapped."
"Hop" over to our story for more about the opening of Oktoberfest.
Driver seriously injured in collision with plane at Munich Airport
The driver of a car operated by a cleaning company has suffered serious injuries in a collision with a plane engine at Munich airport overnight and has been flown to hospital by rescue helicopter, police said Saturday.
The car struck both the engine and then a passenger staircase, a police spokeswoman said, saying that the driver might have been affected by a medical problem before the crash.
The accident, which occurred at around 3. a.m. local time (0100 GMT), is being analyzed to determine the exact cause.
There was never any danger to other people, police said, and flight operations were unaffected.
No scheduled flights are permitted at Munich Airport between midnight and 5 a.m.
Germany's Carsten Breuer seeks to chair NATO Military Committee
Germany's highest-ranking soldier, General Carsten Breuer, is standing as candidate for the post of chair of the NATO Military Committee at a vote to take place on Saturday in Copenhagen.
The post is currently held by Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone of Italy.
Breuer, 61, will contend against General Marie Annabelle Jennie Carignan, who is currently Chief of the Defence Staff in Canada.
Breuer himself is the current inspector general of the Bundeswehr, or German armed forces.
The winner of the vote would take over leadership of the NATO Military Committee from July 2027.
The head of the committee is seen as the most influential person in NATO alongside the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (Saceur), a position currently held by General Alexus G. Grynkewich of the US Air Force.
High-profile Jewish representative calls for AfD ban
Charlotte Knobloch, the former president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, has reiterated her call for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) to be banned.
"A lot about the AfD reminds me today about the path the Nazis took to power," the 93-year-old Knobloch told the daily Augsburger Allegemeine.
She said the party "teems with Jew-haters and extremists" — something she said had already existed before, "but once, such parties disappeared from the scene very fast."
This would not be the case with the AfD, she said: "It has broad support in the population, not least with young people."
The party spouts hatred, including "hatred of Jews," she said.
"Unfortunately, no one has managed to clamp down on it so far, so it needs to be banned," she said, even if this is "perhaps difficult legally."
Knobloch called on voters in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday to "read the newspaper, listen to the radio and watch TV; then you can't help seeing that the AfD is a profoundly anti-democratic party."
She also warned that Jews in Germany were "literally under fire once more," with much reminding here of the 1920s and early 1930s.
"There is hatred of Jews from right, from left and from the Muslim milieu," she said.
Knobloch herself was recently the target of a death threat following the AfD's landslide victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,517,990 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:42:50 UTC
15:42:50 KST

Ukrainian mortar soldiers firing on the front line south of Bakhmut, Donetsk Oblast, on Nov. 20, 2023. (Francis Farrell/The Kyiv Independent)
Russia has lost around 1,517,990 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Sept. 20.
The number includes 1,560 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,356 tanks, 25,361 armored combat vehicles, 151,345 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,067 artillery systems, 2,146 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,659 air defense systems, 442 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,695 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the war, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
