Decolonizing perceptions about Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:32:00 UTC
15:32:00 KST

Decolonizing perceptions about Africa
September 20, 2026
The Correct the Map resolution to promote map projections that more realistically reflect the true size of continents endorsed by the United Nations in New York at the beginning of September was a huge success for the African countries that led the campaign. In the General Assembly, 164 member states voted to encourage the use of Equal Earth projection and other equal-area maps instead of the 16th-century Mercator projection.
Robert Dussey, the foreign minister of Togo, which sponsored the Correct the Map campaign at the UN, spoke of a "feeling of pride."
Correct the Map is also supported by the African Union.
"Finally, Africa is fighting to regain its place in the community of nations," he told DW. "The place it has been reserved to this day is unfair. It does not correspond to Africa's reality, not in historical, geographical or economic terms."
Dussey made clear that the debate about global maps was also clearly about symbolically redrawing the maps of facts and knowledge, culture and identity and redressing misperceptions about political and economic realities and power.
Trump's US only state to reject UN resolution
The only UN member state that rejected the resolution was the United States, whose president Donald Trump has engaged in various acts of political symbolism, having issued orders for places to be renamed on maps which he would presumaby also like to redraw Trump has signed executive orders to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, and Lake Ontario as Lake America.
The UN resolution, meanwhile, is part of a broader, global trend, as French historian Romain Tiquet from the African Worlds Institute (IMAF) told DW.
"Since the late 2000s and early 2010s, there has been a great deal of debate about the decolonization of knowledge — in universities, museums and cultural institutions, as well as within social movements and civil society."
He said many questions were being explored: "Who established the categories through which we conceptualize the world? From which locations? And what power dynamics result from this? And cartography fits right into this context."
Mali breaks with former colonial power France
Many African states have also been trying to free the school systems from colonial influence, often for political reasons.
In October 2025, the Malian government decided to remove French history from the school curriculum. The decision was made to stop teaching about the French Revolution but to focus on Malian history and the other ancient West African kingdoms.
In just a few years, the country's military government has made a clean break with the former colonial power. Mali ended its military cooperation with France in 2022, and French soldiers began to withdraw from the country. Burkina Faso and Niger did the same and the three formed the Alliance of Sahel States in 2023.
Philemon Mtoi from Tumaini University Makumira in Tanzania said Mali had made an important step: "As a historian, I believe that a country without a strong understanding of its own history is like a country without clear leadership and direction. This decision is important because it seeks to strengthen patriotism and foster a stronger sense of national identity."
By investing in the research and preservation of African history, Mali — like Africa as a whole — was making a strong contribution to global scholarship, Mtoi explained.
He spoke of "reclaiming and documenting African histories from an African perspective" and said that this was not only "an act of decolonization" but also an "important step toward intellectual independence."
Mtoi said that many other African countries, such as Ghana, Namibia, South Africa and Kenya, had adopted a similar approach. He added that his own country, Tanzania, had also made major changes to the school curriculum recently. He said that "Tanzanian history and ethics" was now a compulsory subject that had replaced global history and that it would be taught in Swahili, the country's national language.
The historian warned, however, that knowledge of other countries and histories should not be erased. He said it was important to acquire a profound knowledge of significant events in global history, such as the French Revolution, but that this could be done at a later stage.
#NotWaiting campaign to abolish stereotypes
School education in a formal setting is only one part of the puzzle. The non-profit Africa No Filter was one of the organizations behind the Correct the Map campaign. It works to challenge and change harmful narratives about Africa.
In a report titled "The cost of media stereotypes to Africa," it says that "Africa could be losing up to $4.2 billion (€3.6 billion) annually in inflated interest payments due to biased media coverage."
Francois Bouda, an officer for arts and culture at Africa No Filter, said that media outlets continued to portray Africa as being poor, corrupt and crisis-ridden. The new campaign #NotWaiting is meant to change this perception.
"We are addressing Africans because we, too, need to change the way we view the African continent. We've accepted the image of a continent incapable of taking care of itself, one that is poor and has no opportunities. We've internalized this and come to believe it, even though many positive things are happening. First of all there has to be an internal change," said Bouda.
'Millions of ordinary people doing extraordinary things every day'
The #NotWaiting campaign is part of a larger movement, which aims to highlight positive developments and initiatives in Africa, to focus on political programs and actors, to counter crisis-reporting.
It comprises figures on the continent and in the diaspora, people who are "not waiting for an external hand to dictate what path to follow," said Bouda.
"This is good for Africans," he said, adding that there were many actors but that the only problem was that they "aren't visible."
The campaign is about Africans themselves painting a positive picture of Africa as a continent on the move, about people sharing stories, which are not curated by international institutions or media outlets.
"We've been building all along," says a video clip to promote the campaign. "From village roads to crowded cities, across the 54 countries that make up the continent, millions of ordinary people doing extraordinary things every day."
This article, to which Sandrine Blanchard and Jean-Claude Abalo contributed, was originally written in German.

Reintroduced dormice face a fox that moved to predator‑free island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Reintroduced dormice face a fox that moved to predator‑free island
The garden dormice released on Suur‑Pakri Island this summer to rewild the species have encountered an unexpected co‑inhabitant who may consider the newcomers gourmet food.
The garden dormouse (Eliomys quercinus), a native Estonian species, went extinct in Estonia due to human activity. The exact cause is unknown. The last wild garden dormouse was seen in 1986. Around the same time, the species disappeared from neighboring countries as well. This summer, the first small colony was released on Suur‑Pakri Island.
"When we last left the island a couple of weeks ago, more than half of the 20 animals released were definitely alive. For a small zoo animal, that's a surprisingly good result. We're optimistic that maybe they'll even survive until spring," said ecologist Marko Mägi.
"Since it's a small animal with a very short lifespan and could end up in a predator's jaws during winter — even though it sleeps through winter — we don't know whether any of them will still see daylight in spring," Mägi noted.
Suur‑Pakri was chosen for reintroduction because it lacked predators.
"Last autumn we carried out control surveys and studied small mammals to determine whether the island was safe for garden dormice. At that time we could say there were no predators that would threaten them. We had a very harsh winter that covered the sea with ice, and a fox easily crossed over to the island," Mägi explained.
"This summer we discovered that a fox is indeed on the island. We saw it on trail cameras, and it was also spotted running through the forest. Now we're curious to see what happens by spring: will the fox win, or the garden dormice?"
"Although the garden dormouse is active at night and gladly climbs trees, where a fox cannot reach, their paths may still cross. But fortunately for the dormice, the island has plenty of other small rodents that interest the fox more. For the fox, the garden dormouse would be a true gourmet meal," Mägi said.

Voters in two German states cast ballots in regional elections on Sept. 20 threatening to weaken Chancellor Friedrich Merz following his party's recent losses to far-right rivals.
Merz scheduled a crisis meeting with his center-right Christian Democratic Union leadership to review results from Berlin and the northeastern coastal state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The 70-year-old chancellor also canceled his trip to the United Nations General Assembly to manage potential political fallout.
The state elections follow a major defeat for the CDU two weeks ago in Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany fell just a few seats short of an absolute majority. Polls indicate the AfD will make additional gains in the latest round of voting.
The AfD polled at 36 percent against the center-left Social Democratic Party's 37 percent in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where popular state premier Manuela Schwesig leads the SPD, according to public broadcaster ZDF. The CDU polled at 6 percent in the state, risking a drop below the 5 percent threshold required for parliamentary representation.
The CDU faces a tight race in the city-state of Berlin against the far-left Die Linke party. Die Linke campaigns on solving a housing crisis and advocates closer ties with Moscow.
Eight CDU state premiers released a joint declaration Wednesday saying the country needs "stability now more than ever" rather than debates over personnel. Pollster Roland Abold said Merz faces a difficult political environment.
"In our last survey in September, 13 percent were still satisfied with his political performance," Abold said. "These are the lowest figures we have ever recorded for an incumbent chancellor."
Merz took office 16 months ago pledging to stimulate the economy, rebuild the military and reduce irregular immigration. His administration currently struggles with surging energy prices driven by conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Berenberg bank chief economist Holger Schmieding said voters tend to blame the ruling coalition for economic difficulties rather than opposition parties. Schmieding predicted Merz will likely survive the current political challenges and serve his term until 2029.

'Messi will take MLS Golden Boot, that does not interest me,' Israeli star soccer striker to 'Post'

Tai Baribo has already scored 14 goals this MLS season, putting the Israel international among the league's leading scorers.

"First of all, I'm not looking at the Golden Boot at all," Baribo told The Jerusalem Post in an exclusive conversation in Washington. "In the end, Messi will take it. It doesn't really interest me."
"I have my goals to achieve, and that's what interests me: my number of goals, getting into the playoffs with the team. That's what I'm aiming for, and that's what I'm going to achieve, God willing."

"When an Israeli player succeeds in a certain league, and people see it, then it really opens the door for the other players," he told the Post.

That growing Israeli presence was on display Saturday night at Audi Field. Baribo started for DC United, while Abada and Toklomati both started for Charlotte, putting three Israelis on the field in the US capital.
Charlotte ultimately won 2-1, but for Baribo and DC United, the most memorable moment may have been a goal that never appeared on the scoreboard.
*'Everybody saw it except the referee'*
Ashley Westwood gave Charlotte the lead in the 22nd minute before DC responded almost immediately after halftime, with Lucas Bartlett leveling the match in the 47th minute.
Allan Saint-Maximin restored Charlotte's advantage in the 71st minute, and the visitors held on for the victory.

Late in the match came the moment that left Baribo particularly frustrated. A DC effort appeared to have crossed the goal line, with replays also shown on the stadium's large video board, but no goal was awarded. Neither the on-field decision nor the review process that followed resulted in the goal being awarded.
Baribo did not hide his frustration afterward.
"In the second half we were much better," he said. "We created a lot of chances, so unfortunately the ball didn't go in, actually, it went in. Everybody saw it except the ref."
"This is unbelievable. You're fighting 90 minutes, you're fighting the whole season, and then they don't see a simple goal. But it is what it is."
"We lost the game. We're still fighting for the playoffs. We hope to make it."
Asked about the fight DC showed in the second half, Baribo returned to the disputed decision.
"It's frustrating," he said. "You have to understand my side. We are running, we are fighting, the owners invest money, and then a simple decision they don't see."
Still, he refused to use the incident as an excuse.

*'The better team doesn't always win'*
Baribo also saw encouraging signs in DC's attacking performance, particularly after a previous match against Atlanta in which chances were harder to come by.
"First of all, it's a good thing that we have chances," he said. "Against Atlanta, I think we maybe didn't have even one. So it's improving, which is good."
"Maybe we conceded the goal and then we started to go forward. We don't need to concede goals to start going forward, but it happened."
"We created chances, we scored, and then at the end they scored the second goal and we were more dominant. I believe everybody saw that we were better today, but not always the better team wins."
Israeli soccer star Tai Baribo praises atmosphere, support from DC United's fans
Baribo also praised the atmosphere at Audi Field as DC pushed forward late.
"We were attacking toward our fans, which really helped us," he said. "The environment was amazing today. They really supported us."
"Unfortunately, again today we lost, but it didn't end. We still believe that we can do it."
For Baribo, the focus remains straightforward: his own scoring targets, DC United's playoff push, and continuing to establish himself in a league where more Israeli players are now following.

AI, Middle East escalation, Ukraine-Russia war on agenda for upcoming UN General Assembly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:28:24 UTC
15:28:24 KST

World leaders gather in New York this week for the UN General Assembly, bracing for US President Donald Trump's return to the rostrum for a second year running, with talks centering on the widening conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine and the risks of artificial intelligence.
Nearly 130 heads of state meet with the post-World War Two order under strain and with the UN itself struggling to remain relevant and weathering attacks from Trump, who has slashed America's contributions and withdrawn from dozens of UN bodies.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping, who last addressed the diplomatic jamboree via video in 2021, will skip New York in favor of one-on-one talks with Trump in Washington on Thursday, fueling debate about the UN's relevance in addressing global crises.
Compounding the crisis of morale and finance are questions about the next leader of the 80-year-old organization: Secretary-General Antonio Guterres completes his term at the end of 2026, with no clear frontrunner in the race to replace him.
The 15-member UN Security Council may hold high-level meetings on Ukraine, AI, and the Middle East, including talks with Arab leaders, diplomats said.
More than a year into Trump's second term, "we would no longer say that the UN is in freefall, but we would say that it's stuck in an open-ended crisis," said Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group.
"The UN may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it seems to be trapped in a trauma center for the foreseeable future," Gowan said.
The US avoided losing its vote at the assembly by paying $725 million in contributions to the regular budget this week, but it still owes the organization more than a billion dollars and makes ongoing demands for cuts and reforms.
AI leaders call for slowdown on development
The assembly meets shortly after several artificial intelligence industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and escape human control.
Guterres has said that AI will be a major topic, adding that countries pushing its frontiers should set up "common guardrails in order to avoid this race to the bottom that could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at the global level."
The secretary-general has long proposed global governance of AI. In 2023, the UN created an advisory body on the technology, with members including tech executives, government officials and academics.
The warning has put Guterres at odds with Trump, who dismissed AI risks as a "hoax," saying there is a "sick conspiracy" against it and that China would benefit from the doubt being cast on its development.
War in Iran, Houthi attacks key issues in Middle Easy talks
The Middle East will again be a focus of discussions, as the US-Israeli war on Iran continues to drive global inflation and destabilize the region. Recent gains by Houthi terrorists threaten shipping in the vital Bab al-Mandab Strait and could further spike energy prices.
"It's very difficult to have a military solution for that problem, and the experience of fighting in Yemen demonstrated how complicated it is to have successful interventions," said Guterres, adding that the UN's envoy on Yemen was making a "huge effort" to advance talks.
Peace talks remain stalled, however, as Iran and the US continue to exchange strikes and Trump threatens a major escalation of the war.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the assembly on Wednesday.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court and will reportedly face protests following his arrival, is due to speak on Thursday.
Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas will for the second year running not be at the gathering in person. The US, a close Israeli ally, again denied him a visa. On Thursday, the General Assembly voted to allow Abbas to appear via video.
There is likely to be a high-level meeting on the conflict in Sudan on the sidelines, diplomats said, although a diplomatic breakthrough is unlikely.
Zelensky seeking to improve Ukraine's position before winter
Also on the agenda is Russia's more than four-year-old war in Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will address the General Assembly. Zelensky will likely seek to shore up Ukraine's position ahead of what is expected to be another tough winter, diplomats said.
The Security Council has been unable to take action to end the conflict because permanent member Russia holds a veto.
Trump has at times appeared frustrated that he has been unable to broker an end to the war, a goal he declared a priority when he began his second term in January last year. The US president spoke with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin earlier this month, but it was unclear whether he plans to meet Zelensky in New York.
Guterres highlighted the impact the war was having on civilians but also on food security and energy prices.
"The effective blockade existing in the Black Sea is creating enormous problems that add to the problems generated by the Middle East crisis, and I think it would be very important to find a way to allow Ukrainian exports and Russian exports of food, fertilizers and energy to take place in a safe way through the Black Sea," he said.

"It is clear that the US has taken a position without considering the details,” he claimed, referring to reforms the PA has begun introducing into its institutions as part of its commitments to the international community.
"It seems that the issue is not the reforms we make or do not make. Rather, it looks like a political issue,” he said, acknowledging that the US administration’s decision to deny Abbas’s entry visa was prompted by the PA’s diplomatic moves at international institutions, efforts to gain recognition for a Palestinian state, and actions with the International Court of Justice- steps the US and Israel consider unilateral.
This is the second year in a row that Abbas has been denied a US visa, forcing him to address the UN General Assembly remotely.
Palestinian officials condemn US move preventing Abbas from attending UN
The Ramallah-based official said there were expectations that, unlike last year, when President Abbas was barred from entering the US to attend the UN General Assembly summit, the United States would take a different approach this year. “We thought that the Americans would enable President Abbas to come to New York and join the gathering with other world leaders. But unfortunately, the Americans did not approve our request,” he said.
However, Abbas will be allowed to address the General Assembly remotely. The official said it has not yet been decided whether the Palestinian president will deliver his speech live by video conference or send a recorded statement.
He confirmed that Palestinian officials have recently pressured the US administration to reverse its decision, but these efforts haven't succeeded. “I believe it’s over. I don’t think we are going to keep pushing. America took its decision," he said.
Asked whether the PA would keep pursuing diplomatic moves at the international level, the official said, “We will do everything necessary according to our interests,” confirming that this includes continuing efforts to achieve recognition of a Palestinian state and to support the Palestinians cause.
The US State Department announced a few days ago that "the PLO and the PA have once again failed to live up to their commitments. This includes taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, including through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ), seeking to bypass negotiations through unilateral recognition, and continuing to pay stipends to terrorists and to glorify acts of terrorism and terrorists in public pronouncements and school textbooks."
"As a consequence of their failure to reform, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials," the US statement said.
In response, President Mahmoud Abbas’s office issued a statement on Thursday rejecting the American stance and stating that “resorting to international institutions and international law is a legitimate right for the State of Palestine and a peaceful and legal means to protect our people and their rights, and that it cannot be equated with the policies of occupation, settlement, annexation, displacement, and settler violence, which constitute the real threat to the two-state solution and to the chances for peace.”
It further stated that “international recognition of the State of Palestine is not a substitute for negotiations, but rather an acknowledgment of the Palestinian people’s inalienable right to self-determination and the realization of their independent state, and support for achieving a just peace based on the two-state solution.”

====================================================================================================

Yom Kippur is about the freedom to choose, former Gaza hostages Keith and Aviva Siegel tell 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:27:47 UTC
15:27:47 KST

Yom Kippur is uncomfortable at its core.
By the holiday’s design, we are meant to suffer for a full 25 hours. We consciously choose to give up food and water, sit with our thoughts, and confront the parts of ourselves that we don’t always like to acknowledge.
But for some, like former Gaza hostages Keith and Aviva Siegel, the whole season is somewhat complex.
This year will mark the first High Holy Days that the hostages who survived their Gaza captivity will be able to observe with their families. Some might fast, others might not, but most importantly, all will have the choice to observe the holiday as they please.
“I think that being deprived of the decisions of how much to eat, when to eat, how to eat, and who to eat with – was a big, huge issue in Gaza,” Aviva told The Jerusalem Post.
“When somebody goes through something like that… and has been starved and doesn’t have any way to control what goes into your tummy and how much you eat and who you eat with and when you eat and what you like to eat… Everything of that was completely and utterly taken away,” she said.
Keith and Aviva Siegel’s Yom Kippur after captivity
The Siegels, 67 and 65, were kidnapped from their Kibbutz Kfar Aza home on October 7.
Aviva spent 51 days in captivity; Keith spent 484. They lost their home, and at least 60 of their close-knit community were killed.
They have previously disclosed that they were starved, denied water, physically and mentally tortured, and watched other hostages be sexually assaulted.
Aviva said that though she will not be fasting this year, she feels as if she has fewer questions than last year, when there were still 20 living hostages in Gaza.
“Then, I had these questions, asking myself: ‘[Since] they are starving, how come you can’t just be hungry for one day, just like them?’ Or ‘Is it okay not to fast anymore while we still have hostages in Gaza, being starved every day?
“I remember looking at the food and saying, ‘No, you decided that you have a different relationship with that in yourself. You’re not going to fast anymore.’”
This year, however, she doesn’t feel like she will have any questions.
“Because of what I went through, and this year because all the hostages are here, I don’t think I’m going to have questions. Maybe it’s not going to be easy for me to eat, but it’s going to be different than last year.”
In her opinion, for released hostages to have the ability to make their own decisions is incredibly important.
“I think that the decision of what we need to do as hostages who came back is to decide. We have that in both hands. And we need to take that because it was taken away in such a brutal way.”
Keith seconded her thoughts, noting that the conscious choice to abstain from eating is very different than being denied food.
“Fasting and starvation are two completely different things for me,” Keith said. “I don’t see any connection between those two.”
For him, Yom Kippur was never about fasting but about taking the time to reflect on the past year.
“The core essence or significance of Yom Kippur is not the fasting. It’s the heshbon nefesh (taking stock of the soul),” Keith said.
“For me, I can observe Yom Kippur and have it [be] very meaningful and significant and not fast.”
Keith told the Post that in captivity his faith also took on a different meaning.
“When I was in captivity, Judaism, or my Jewish identity, became different.” He had prayed frequently while in captivity.
“The terrorists were constantly trying to convince me to convert to Islam. I think the more they did that, I started to think more about my Jewish identity and my faith.
“I don’t know if that would have happened if they had not tried to convince me to convert to Islam, but they did, and it was ongoing, so I thought a lot about it,” Keith said.
“I really felt the strength and the resilience by praying, saying blessings, thinking about my Jewish faith and identity,” he said, adding that he frequently thought about victims of the Holocaust and other disasters throughout Jewish history.
“I kind of felt like: The ones who survived, they survived. And I will survive for those who did not survive, kind of like it is my duty, or my mission, or responsibility, in their honor.”
How captivity changed Keith Siegel’s Jewish faith
The Siegels come from differing backgrounds.
He is from North Carolina; she is from South Africa. He moved here in his twenties, while she made aliyah when she was 9 years old.
He is more soft-spoken, thoughtful, and purposeful with his words. Keith said that growing up in a traditionally Jewish home, he felt a significant amount of pressure to observe holidays, especially Yom Kippur, in the way his parents did.
“As a child, I did it because it was what we did. And to… You know, be a good kid. Please my parents, do what they do,” he said.
Aviva is usually quicker to respond of the two of them, and has a very direct way of speaking. Once or twice during our conversation, they provided the words the other was searching for, which I found really endearing.
In our conversation, Keith and Aviva frequently mentioned anecdotes about their families.
They currently live in Gazit near their daughter and their grandchildren, and mentioned how they frequently meet with them to do Friday dinners or havdallah on Saturday.
When Keith was still in Gaza, the Siegel’s children, grandchildren, and extended family all gathered every Friday to say a special bracha that their daughter, Shir, had written.
“I’ll never forget the first time that Shir read the words (to the Bracha). Every word went into my heart, and cut my heart into pieces. We were all crying like babies next to the Shabbat table,” said Aviva.
“It was important because… it made everybody feel together and cry together. Those are moments that feeling together, [as] part of family, were very very very strong.”
Yom Kippur still carries a special significance for both of them, though. Both told the Post stories of their loved ones and what the holiday meant for them growing up.
Keith fasted when he was growing up to “be a good kid,” though he never really felt like it gave him any spiritual fulfillment. When he moved to Israel when he was in his 20s, he stopped fasting for the most part.
“When I moved to Israel, I kind of felt like it was the… I’m not sure whether to call it the ultimate, but just by living in Israel, the holidays are so much a part of not only the religion but the culture; I can feel Jewish just by living in Israel.”
Aviva spoke about how, when she was young, she and her grandmother spent a lot of time together on Yom Kippur.
“Yom Kippur for me was a very special day. I used to connect with my grandmother, who used to fast with me. We had this special relationship.”
Aviva said that the Yom Kippur she experienced during the 1973 war has remained a prominent memory for her. She remembered that her grandmother continued to fast, despite being told not to.
“I’ll never forget the Yom Kippur War; we were stopped in the middle of the fast. I remember going to her and telling her, ‘You need to stop fasting.’ Because we had been told that nobody fasts from this minute. I remember her saying, ‘No, I’m going to fast until the end.’ There are so many things and emotions about that day.”
Aviva also revealed details of her captivity. She said that she decided in Gaza that she would not fast when she returned to Israel. She was starved and suffered for 51 days, so why should she punish herself more?
“In Gaza, we spoke about it with the other hostages who were with us. I remember myself saying, ‘I’m not going to fast anymore,’” she said.
“What happened to me is the worst thing that happened… that could ever happen to anybody. I’ve been punished, and that’s enough. I don’t deserve to be punished again and to be hungry and starved anymore. “So I’ve got a completely, utterly new relationship with Yom Kippur.”
How the Siegels are rebuilding their lives after captivity
After their release from captivity, the Siegels moved to live near their daughters Shir and Elan and their grandchildren. They can do kiddush on Friday nights with them and focus on spending time with family.
The couple has also spent a significant amount of time volunteering for various humanitarian aid efforts, including their continued advocacy for the remaining hostages – even after both of them were released.
They now volunteer with 255, an organization that provides ongoing support for the former Gaza hostages and their families. It centers the hostages and their families in the rehabilitation process and aims to keep them at the forefront of public conversation in Israel and the Diaspora.
“We have been very involved in a lot of different things in order to both tell people our story and to try to have what happened to us and so many other people not be forgotten,” Keith said.
“I feel like it’s my duty to do good, important, meaningful things.”
Although they were both given a platform that neither of them wanted, they feel that they need to be a “voice for the voiceless.”
“I want the world to understand that we are still trying to pick ourselves up. We’re still carrying a very difficult story,” Aviva said.
“You know, there’s such a big difference between what we look like and sound like and what we feel inside.
“I want the world to understand that we need the support and that we can’t in any way put it [the captivity] aside, and just to know that all of us are, in many times and many moments, struggling.”
For the Siegels, part of Yom Kippur is about tikkun olam and helping to be a part of humanity.
“Yom Kippur is really a day not only of fasting but also of questions. Asking yourself questions and looking for the answers,” Aviva said.
Now, the Siegels no longer have all of the questions they had last year. But with everyone home this year, maybe they will find more room to take stock, focus on the choices they can make of their own free will, and carry them out with their own hands.

Ed Sheeran says situation in Gaza is 'catastrophic and unjustifiable' as he opens Philadelphia show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:27:31 UTC
15:27:31 KST

The English singer-songwriter opened his show sharing his opinions on Gaza, noting that while 7 October attacks were horrific, the Israeli response which killed countless women and children were “catastrophic” and “disproportionate”.
Ed Sheeran opened a concert Saturday with comments about Gaza after controversy swirled around his tour and supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opener Macklemore, who was dropped after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage at an earlier show.
Sheeran began the concert alone on stage with no opener, but was joined by other musicians later in the show.
Sheeran said he wants his music and shows to be about unity and humanity, not politics. But he said that while the attacks in Israel of 7 October, 2023, were horrific, what is happening in Gaza “catastrophic and unjustifiable” and slammed it as “disproportionate”.
“I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet,” said Sheeran during his performance at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia.
The comments before a nearly full stadium came after a tumultuous week that began with rapper Macklemore, Sheeran's original US opener, being dropped in response to saying “Free Palestine” during a 5 September tour stop in New Jersey.
Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday. Within hours of Sheeran’s statement Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew.
Sheeran has performed many songs solo during his Loop Tour concerts, but was joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga before they dropped out in support of Macklemore.
Macklemore was replaced by Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out, and Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out this week.
Before Saturday's show, a small group of pro-Palestinian demonstrators convened outside the stadium.
Hillary Steinberg, 34, said she got concert tickets a year ago but wound up getting a refund and attended the demonstration instead, after she was disappointed that Sheeran refused to take a stand to defend Macklemore or empathise with the plight of the Palestinian people.
“I was, until this week, a big Ed Sheeran fan,” Steinberg said. “I think all art is political, and all music is political, and so this choice — even though he was saying that he wasn’t complicit — is a political choice.”
Diane Savitz, a 53-year-old from Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania, got tickets months ago and attended. She said she is a big Sheeran fan, doesn't think he did anything wrong and a concert is not the place for politics.
“A concert should be for people enjoying the music. Music should bring people together,” Savitz said. “Everyone has their right to freedom of speech, but not every platform is the place for it.”
The Grammy winning artist was adamant earlier this week that he wouldn't be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans don’t come to his shows to hear about these issues. But, as the controversy grew, and ticket prices and sales declined, he decided to address the issue head on.
Sheeran told the crowd in Philadelphia that everyone is welcome at his concerts, and they can have opposing points of view while still singing his songs, which are about “love, hope and unity.”
He also told fans he worries about venues pre-approving performances.
“This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world,” Sheeran said.

Denmark will expedite its 31st military aid package to Ukraine, valued at approximately $275 million, with a primary focus on reinforcing Ukrainian air defense capabilities ahead of the autumn and winter period, the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine announced on Sept. 19

The ministry noted that Denmark has remained one of Ukraine’s primary defense partners since the launch of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, consistently contributing military hardware and pioneering multilateral procurement frameworks.
The Danish government decided to accelerate the delivery of the assistance package, having announced on Sept. 18 its intention to fast-track air defense support for Kyiv. The decision followed a Baltic Sea confrontation on Sept. 14 in which a Russian warship fired signal flares toward a Danish military helicopter.
Baltic Sea naval confrontation
The expedited military aid arrives amid heightened friction between Copenhagen and Moscow following the naval encounter near the Danish island of Gedser.
According to the Danish Armed Forces Command, the Baltic Fleet corvette Soobrazitelny launched two signal flares toward a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter that was conducting routine photographic surveillance over international waters in the southwestern Baltic Sea.

Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen characterized the naval firing as “completely unacceptable” and formally summoned Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin. Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus criticized the Russian crew for “very unprofessional seamanship,” asserting that Moscow’s threshold for operational risk had shifted.

China's space station gets kitchen upgrade for long-term stays
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:24:30 CST
15:24:30 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's orbiting space station has improved its kitchen with advanced appliances and more food choices to keep its residents well-fed during long stays in orbit.
The Astronaut Center of China, working with several private companies, has upgraded the "space kitchen" with a suite of intelligent appliances for drinking water, food reheating and baking, enabling astronauts in orbit to eat hot meals within 20 minutes instead of waiting longer or eating cold food.
At an aerospace medical engineering conference in Tianjin Municipality in north China on Saturday, Liu Weibo, a center expert, gave examples such as a space water dispenser that ensures reclaimed water is safe to drink, and a space microwave heating device that allows rapid reheating at low power with no microwave leakage.
Liu also noted that the hot-air baking oven, the world's first designed for space use, achieves efficient, low-energy removal of cooking fumes and has allowed astronauts in orbit to enjoy baked chicken wings, steak and cake.
The menu on the Chinese space station has also expanded. Astronaut food now includes nearly 200 varieties, while the flight menu cycle has been extended to 10 days. Fresh vegetables, nuts, cakes and meats can be baked and processed in orbit, and yogurt can be fermented in space.
"We are continuing to raise the level of life support for astronauts in orbit," Liu said. "The variety, quality, flavor, appearance and nutrition of space food are getting better."
China's space station, Tiangong, which means Heavenly Palace, has now entered an era of long-term human habitation. One member of the Shenzhou-23 crew will conduct a one-year in-orbit stay, while the country's 2030 crewed moon landing mission is advancing steadily. ■

Interview: China-ASEAN Expo delivers shared development dividends: expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:24:23 CST
15:24:23 KST

MANILA, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- The China-ASEAN Expo (CAEXPO) serves as a bridge for ASEAN and China to boost trade flows and strengthen supply chain cooperation, helping both sides reap shared development dividends, a Filipino expert said.
"ASEAN and China boast complementary economic structures, and the CAEXPO provides a matchmaking venue to connect supply and demand between both sides," said Lucio Pitlo, member of the board of directors and former president of the Philippine Association for Chinese Studies, in an exclusive interview with Xinhua.
Scheduled to run from Sept. 17 to 21 in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, the 23rd CAEXPO draws more than 3,400 exhibitors from over 70 countries and regions.
Pitlo said China supplies high value-added products such as electric vehicles, solar panels and wind turbines, making it an "indispensable trade and development partner" for ASEAN.
He said ASEAN produces high-quality fruits including avocados, coconuts and durians, and is also rich in rubber, oil and gas, and mineral resources, which can meet China's demand for consumer goods and industrial raw materials.
Referring to trade corridors, Pitlo highlighted the Pinglu Canal, which officially opened to traffic Wednesday. He said the waterway will help improve economic activity and deepen connectivity between China and ASEAN.
He elaborated that goods from inland parts of central and southwest China previously had to be shipped via ports in Guangdong for overseas destinations.
"Now with this direct waterway access to the sea, transportation distances will be shortened. ASEAN countries like Vietnam can also deliver fresh fruits faster and more easily to reach Chinese consumers' tables," he added.
Pitlo said mobile payments and e-commerce are playing a growing role in ASEAN countries, areas where China has made much progress, with advanced and mature cashless payment schemes. "Robust and superb technology, supply chains, logistics networks and industry standards" can help ASEAN countries update their online commerce ecosystem.
"ASEAN countries can learn from China's experience in digital transformation. This will help us make more efficient supply chains, find ways to reduce costs, and improve service delivery," he said.
Established in the 1980s, the Philippine Association for Chinese Studies promotes cultural, educational, economic and academic exchanges between the Philippines and China. ■

HONG KONG, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- A public memorial was held in Hong Kong on Sunday for Tung Chee-hwa, former vice chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) and former chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR).
Tung died of illness at the age of 89 in Hong Kong on Sept. 8. He is regarded as an outstanding contributor to "one country, two systems," a renowned patriot, an outstanding social activist and a close friend of the Communist Party of China (CPC).
Tung served as vice chairman of the 10th, 11th, 12th and 13th National Committees of the CPPCC. He was the first- and second-term chief executive of the HKSAR.
While Tung was critically ill, the central authorities expressed deep concern over his condition. President Xi Jinping and other central leaders instructed the Liaison Office of the Central People's Government in the HKSAR to convey best wishes and demanded all-out efforts to treat Tung.
Following Tung's passing, Xi Jinping, Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi, Han Zheng, Hu Jintao and others expressed their deep grief in various forms and extended sincere condolences to his family.
Shi Taifeng, a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and vice chairman of the CPPCC National Committee, Leung Chun-ying, vice chairman of the CPPCC National Committee, Wang Dongfeng, vice chairman and secretary-general of the CPPCC National Committee, Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macao Work Office of the CPC Central Committee and of the Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office of the State Council, and John Lee, chief executive of the HKSAR, attended Sunday's memorial service. ■

China's loan prime rates remain unchanged
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:24:00 CST
15:24:00 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's one-year loan prime rate (LPR), a market-based benchmark lending rate, stood at 3 percent on Sunday, unchanged from the previous month.
The over-five-year LPR, on which many lenders base their mortgage rates, also remained unchanged from the previous reading of 3.5 percent, according to the National Interbank Funding Center.
LPRs, published each month, reflect financing costs for households and businesses and serve as a pricing reference for bank lending. Lower rates can ease borrowers' financing burdens and encourage investment and consumption.
China's one-year and over-five-year LPRs have remained unchanged for 16 consecutive months since June 2025.
Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank, attributed the unchanged LPRs partly to the resilience of the economy. He cited continued strength in exports, a pickup in year-on-year growth in both the consumer price index and producer price index, and a marked acceleration in industrial output growth in August.
Wen also noted that lending rates remained relatively low in August, which provided strong support for the real economy and reduced the need for a policy rate cut.
Data showed that the weighted average interest rate on newly issued corporate loans was below 3 percent in August 2026, about 0.2 percentage point lower than a year earlier, while the rate on newly issued personal housing loans remained unchanged at about 3.1 percent.
China will continue to implement a more proactive fiscal policy and adopt an appropriately accommodative monetary policy in 2026, this year's government work report noted. ■

France's Macron meets Carney to bolster Canada-EU ties amid US trade rift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:23:58 UTC
15:23:58 KST

President Emmanuel Macron is scheduled to visit the French territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon on Sunday, where he is due to meet Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, weeks after US President Donald Trump posted an image on social media showing the archipelago covered by the American flag.
Macron's visit, the first by a French president since Francois Hollande travelled there in 2014, comes as Canada seeks to deepen ties with the European Union amid trade tensions with the United States.
Located off Canada's Atlantic coast, Saint Pierre and Miquelon is France's only remaining territory in North America.
French officials said the trip would underscore France's sovereignty over the archipelago and highlight its close relationship with Canada.
"For a territory of 5,800 inhabitants, it is rare to find so many issues that are important for France as a whole concentrated in a place of this size: France's geostrategic presence in the North Atlantic, at the doorstep of the United States and the Arctic, maritime sovereignty, adaptation to climate change; and cooperation with Canada," a French presidency official told reporters.
Diplomats said the visit, which Macron was undertaking on his way to the annual United Nations General Assembly gathering of world leaders, would also carry symbolic weight after Trump posted a map depicting the United States, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean draped in the US flag and labelled "United States of America".
The image included Saint Pierre and Miquelon and several French Caribbean territories.
France chose not to publicly respond to the post at the time.
Macron and Carney are expected to discuss the energy crisis and Canada's increasingly close relationship with the European Union after the bloc opened the door to Ottawa becoming its first associate member.
More than a decade after the EU and Canada agreed the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), and nine years after its provisional application began, several EU member states have yet to ratify the accord, including France.

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China opened its title defense in women's hockey with a resounding 13-0 victory over Bangladesh at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Sunday.
China quickly took control of the match, with Zhong Jiaqi breaking the deadlock with a smart deflection in front of the goal.
Chen Yang, Li Hong and Zhong each added a goal to give China a 4-0 lead at the end of the first quarter.
Chen, Zhang Ying and Zhong scored in the second quarter as China extended its advantage to 7-0 at halftime.
Just one minute into the third quarter, China's Ma Ning received the ball, adjusted and fired home. Zou Meirong and Chen Yi then scored twice each, while Yang Liu added another goal as China completed the 13-0 victory.
"We made thorough preparations and targeted training before the match, especially for the pace of an early-morning game, the pitch and the time difference, so everyone was able to get into the game relatively quickly today," Ma said.
"As the match progressed, we gradually took control of the game. This opening win has laid a good foundation for our Asian Games campaign. We will remain focused, carefully review the details of this match and give our all in every remaining group-stage game," she added.
China head coach Alyson Annan expressed satisfaction with her team's overall performance, but said that the side could further increase its tempo, particularly in transitions between attack and defense and in the intensity of its pressing.
"The significance of the opening match is to establish a good start, identify problems and build up our form," Annan said. "We will carefully review this match, build on our strengths, address our shortcomings, refine our tactical details and get the team into the best possible competitive condition, so that we can play at a faster tempo, maintain more consistent form and perform better in the matches ahead."
China will face Chinese Taipei on Monday. ■

War update: 234 clashes on front line over past day, Kostiantynivka and Pokrovsk sectors see heaviest fighting
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine in a Facebook post on the battlefield situation as of 8:00 on Sunday, September 20.
The enemy launched 98 airstrikes, dropping 313 guided aerial bombs. In addition, Russian forces used 10,856 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,689 shelling attacks on settlements and Ukrainian military positions, including 58 using multiple-launch rocket systems.
In the Sumy region, the settlements of Bezsalivka, Pustohorod, Bachivsk, Korenok, Ulanove, Rivne, Kruzhok, Potapivka, Obody, Mala Korchakivka, Pysarivka, Sadky, Mohrytsia, Korchakivka, Sumy, Sopych, Hirky, Romashkove, Fotovyzh, and Volfyne came under fire. Ukraine’s aviation and artillery struck four clusters of Russian personnel and equipment, four command UAV posts, four artillery systems and artillery positions, a command post, and an anti-aircraft missile system.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk sectors, four Russian assault actions were recorded. The enemy carried out 122 attacks on Ukrainian positions and settlements.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna sector, Ukrainian units repelled 10 enemy attacks. Russian forces attempted to advance toward Lyman, Artilne, Ternova, Mala Vovcha, Vilkhuvatka, Shevyaikivka, and Dovzhanka.
In the Kupiansk sector, Russian forces made two attempts to improve their positions and conducted assault operations near Kurylivka and Kivsharivka.
In the Lyman sector, Russian forces attacked 15 times near Novoiehorivka, Cherneshchyna, Novoselivka, Zarichne, Stavky, Lyman, and Dibrova. Their attempts to penetrate Ukrainian defenses were repelled.
In the Sloviansk sector, the enemy launched four assault actions near Yampil and Mykolaivka as well as toward Pyskunivka and Orikhuvatka.
In the Kramatorsk sector, Russian forces conducted one offensive action toward Yurkivka.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, 25 attacks were recorded near Kostiantynivka and toward Osykove, Dovha Balka, Illinivka, Rusyn Yar, Mykolaipillia, Stepove, and Vilne.
In the Pokrovsk sector, Russian forces launched 21 attacks. In particular, they attempted to advance toward Dobropillia, Vodianske, Bilytske, Novyi Donbas, Serhiivka and Molodetske.
In the Huliaipole sector, the enemy launched one attack toward Kopani.
No Russian attacks were recorded in the Oleksandrivka, Orikhiv and Dnipro River sectors.
No signs of Russian offensive force buildup were detected in the Volyn and Polissia sectors.
As reported by Ukrinform, total Russian combat losses since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, through September 20, 2026, are estimated at approximately 1,517,990 personnel.

US embassies issue security alerts over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia

2026-09-20

The alerts advised Americans to "be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions" and said the conflict could "escalate rapidly."
US embassies across the Middle East have issued security alerts warning Americans to maintain "heightened vigilance" following attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia.
Embassies in Bahrain, Israel, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE said the "military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly" and that the security environment remained "complex."
The alerts also advised people to "be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."
It comes after the Houthi rebels on Saturday said they had carried out two operations using ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones to target Saudi Arabia in response to Saudi attacks.
"The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu," the group claimed.
A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition forces - which were formed in 2015 to back Yemen's internationally recognised government - later confirmed that the Royal Saudi Air Defense Forces had intercepted a ballistic missile fired towards Riyadh. The spokesperson added that the group had also targeted the cities of Baish, Taif, Farasan, and Yanbu.
On Saturday, residents of Riyadh reported seeing flames and smoke at the capital's King Khalid International Airport.
Video footage circulating on social media appeared to show a towering column of smoke rising from the airport, which flight tracking site Flightradar24 had said was experiencing "major problems."
Yemen's Houthi rebels, who declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, have been launching increasing attacks on Saudi cities and shipping, further heightening tensions in the Middle East.
Saudi Arabia has hit back with its own strikes on the group - which has seized vast stretches of territory in Yemen this month in a lightning offensive - but has failed to stop its advance.
In a press briefing on Friday, Stéphane Dujarric, a spokesperson for the UN Secretary-General, addressed the situation in Yemen.
"Since hostilities escalated in August, the Human Rights office has documented 110 civilian casualties in 31 incidents, including 28 killed and 82 injured, across Taizz, Al Hudaydah and Marib. Insecurity and access constraints continue to hamper our ability to verify the actual number as you can imagine is very likely higher," Dujarric said, according to a transcript shared by the UN.
"We urge all parties, and those with influence over them, to act immediately to de-escalate, protect civilians and facilitate humanitarian access. Every effort must be made to prevent further loss of life," he added.

Hundreds of drones target Moscow on last day of voting in Russia’s parliamentary election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:04:48 UTC
15:04:48 KST

Hundreds of drones targeting Moscow and its surrounding region killed at least two people and damaged a major refinery on the final day of the country’s parliamentary elections, authorities said on Sunday.
The capital’s mayor said that more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted and shot down, 450 of which were aimed at Moscow.
Sergei Sobyanin accused Ukraine of attempting to interfere with a tightly controlled three-day election that is set to tighten president Vladimir Putin’s 26-year grip on power.
“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed,” he said on Telegram.
Moscow’s regional governor said at least two people were killed – a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man – in two separate locations.
A fire triggered by a drone crashing into a 21-storey building also led to 400 people being evacuated, said Moscow regional governor, Andrey Vorobyov, without specifying the drones’ origin.
The attacks come at a time when Kyiv stepped up its long-range drone strike campaign against Russia in recent months, particularly against energy infrastructure to target a vital source of the Kremlin’s revenue to fund its war effort – now in its fifth year.
Ukrainian strikes have knocked out a significant part of Russia’s oil refining capacity, triggering oil product shortages, fuel price increases and long queues at filling stations in many regions across the country’s 11 time zones.
A facility on the territory of the Moscow oil refinery had been damaged, Sobyanin said. No casualties had been reported so far and emergency services were on the scene.
That major refinery has already been hit by Ukrainian strikes in recent months.
Ukraine has not commented on the attacks. Both sides say they do not target civilians.
The latest strike comes after the US president, Donald Trump, said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities.
It also comes after Russians began voting on Friday in the country’s first parliamentary election since Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Only parties that support Putin and the Kremlin’s military campaign have been registered to run. Moscow has also organised voting in occupied Ukraine.
Few Russians doubt Putin’s United Russia party will coast to victory again, but the vote offers a gauge of public support for the war.

Thousands of pregnant women in England are reporting domestic abuse. Midwives are struggling to cope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:09 UTC
15:00:09 KST

About 20,000 disclosures of domestic abuse are estimated to be made to maternity services in England every year, analysis has found.
The figures are likely to be an underestimate of the true scale of disclosures, according to experts, highlighting the role maternity professionals play in identifying abuse.
About 3.3% of maternity bookings made within NHS trusts across England involved a disclosure of current or non-recent domestic abuse.
Applying this proportion to national NHS maternity bookings activity suggests there are approximately 20,000 disclosures of domestic abuse made within maternity services in England every year.
Of the 118 trusts contacted by the charity For Baby’s Sake, 74 provided usable data, and the figures are based on a three-year average of the most recent data available.
Gill Walton, the chief executive of the Royal College of Midwives, said the findings “lay bare” something that midwives already know from their day-to-day practice.
“Midwives are often the only professional a pregnant woman sees regularly and alone, which makes them uniquely placed to spot the signs of domestic abuse and respond with care,” Walton said.
“But recognising a disclosure is only the first step – staff need proper, specialist training to know how to respond and services need the time and resources to follow through with support, so that no disclosure is ever a missed opportunity to protect a parent and their baby.
Experts have also called for midwives to receive adequate support and training on handling such domestic abuse disclosures, while also working long hours on busy maternity wards that can also face staff shortages.
“Midwives and other maternity staff play such a crucial role when it comes to reporting disclosures of domestic violence which are made to them. However, maternity staff also need better support so they know what the next steps are regarding what to do with these disclosures,” Veronica Oakeshott, the interim head of external affairs at Women’s Aid, said.
She added: “They’re already facing immense pressure working on busy maternity wards, so it’s essential that they receive adequate support and training on how to handle these disclosures moving forward.”
Judith Rees, the chief operating officer and designated safeguarding lead at For Baby’s Sake Trust, said: “Having worked as a midwife, health visitor and nurse across 33 years within the NHS, I know how important the relationship between a maternity professional and a parent can be. Creating the right opportunity to ask about domestic abuse, and knowing how to respond when someone says ‘yes’, can be life-changing.”
She added: “Midwives need to understand the impact domestic abuse can have on a parent and their baby, be able to recognise risk and respond safely, and know where to go for specialist support. Pregnancy and the early postnatal period give us a critical window to intervene, and when we get that response right, we have an opportunity to improve outcomes for parents and babies.”
Kate Brintworth, the chief midwifery officer for NHS England, said: “All staff working in NHS maternity and neonatal services are committed to ensuring that any disclosure of domestic abuse will be met with compassion, sensitivity and clear options for support. Midwives receive mandatory safeguarding training, alongside specialist training on how to ask sensitive questions about abuse, and can refer women to specialist domestic abuse services for support with issues such as housing and legal advice where needed.”

====================================================================================================

Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:09 UTC
15:00:09 KST

About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he calls a “penny-drop moment” – that, like countless others in China, his company needed to embrace AI before it was made obsolete by it.
His clients, well-off parents looking to send their children to study overseas, had begun arriving in his office reeling off information and opinions gleaned not from rival firms, but from chatbots.
In response, he started developing his own AI study tool, concluding: “If you can’t beat them, join them.”
The pace and quality of AI development in China is second only to the United States, with the two superpowers locked in an intensifying rivalry as the stakes rise with each new model’s capabilities.
Analysts generally agree that frontier, or cutting-edge, US models are still some way ahead of their Chinese counterparts.
But over the last few weeks the mood music from Silicon Valley has been decidedly sombre, as insider after insider has warned of the potential catastrophes that could result from “loss of control” of the most advanced AIs.
And last Saturday Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei pitched a “worldwide pacing of the frontier” – something he said would “require cooperation with China”.
“China is definitely not receptive” to a slowdown on US firms’ terms, though, said Lian Jye Su from technology research group Omdia.
For the government, AI is a “core sovereignty capability”, and Beijing will not want to jeopardise the progress made in closing the gap with US frontier models.
“It sees these calls [for a slowdown] as a bid to lock in US advantage,” said Su.
Amodei made this explicit, mentioning China specifically when arguing it was key “to keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.
He advocated for measures including continued export controls to China on advanced chips and machinery – the existence of which some argue already amounts to a forced unilateral “pacing”.
China’s foreign ministry responded to Amodei’s piece by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
However, several analysts told the Guardian it would be a mistake to assume this suggested a rejection of the broader concerns raised by the essay.
This week China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework – a document that functions as a “mapping of the AI risk landscape and roughly what one should do about it”, said Gabriel Wagner, a researcher at Concordia, a Beijing-based AI safety consultancy.
Included in the updates are the risks posed by agents, the cybersecurity threats from frontier models and the issue of recursive self-improvement – an as-yet hypothetical scenario where AI becomes advanced enough to improve itself.
“In many ways, I think there is more common ground than people might assume between what Amodei is saying and what the Chinese government is saying,” said Wagner.
That contrasts with US president Donald Trump, who this week called fears AI could wipe out humanity a “hoax”.
Trump is set to meet counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington next week, with AI expected to make the agenda, though analysts are sceptical a major breakthrough will happen.
The ruling Communist party, finely attuned to risks to its political control, has been proactive in ensuring the new technology has developed within boundaries set by the state.
Centralised authority over critical infrastructure and commercial activity means China is generally better placed than the United States “to address any AI disaster”, said Omdia’s Su.
However, Chinese companies do less voluntary monitoring and evaluation work than US ones, said Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (CEIP).
Neither government seems prepared for a loss-of-control incident like those outlined over the last few weeks, she said.
China’s regulation, though, is “iterative … they are quick to adapt and release new measures”, she added.
China has had an algorithm registry since 2022, but warnings on agents released this year suggest a switch in focus “from controlling what AI says to controlling what it does”, per Concordia AI.
Beijing also issued national regulations this year aimed at curbing emotional dependency on companion AIs.
At the same time, AI is being actively encouraged across the economy to promote growth, enshrining this goal in its latest Five Year Plan.
Local governments are offering funding and low rents to companies to help achieve this – entrepreneur But was recently invited to pitch his company, Hampshire Education, to a small city three hours from Shanghai set on establishing a reputation as a tech hub.
Factories across the country’s huge manufacturing base are being encouraged to convert their processes into the AI era.
“Safety and controllability are certainly major concerns, and they are actively discussed,” said a spokesperson for Black Lake Technologies, an industrial agent platform that says it has worked with 40,000 factories globally.
“But in manufacturing, these concerns tend to be much more concrete and operational … what companies care most about is whether the AI is reliable.”
Daily life in China is already highly digitised, with traditionally less discourse around data privacy helping with widespread adoption.
For example, digital health service A-fu, which features AI chatbot versions of prominent doctors trained on real clinical studies, recently hit 150 million users.
“Most people treat AI as an already-useful everyday tool, not an abstract threat, so the practical attitude is to live with it,” said Ni Tao, founding editor of tech website yangtzeer.com.
“There is real anxiety about jobs and misinformation, but it coexists with a strong belief that China must master AI rather than slow down.”

On Trump in general, Farage said at the event that it was “important that our country, and Europe too, get a better, more sensible view of America than it gets of the Trump administration through traditional mainstream media who frankly paint the whole project out to be villainous”.

“Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom,” Farage said. “The people of Northern Ireland neither want a referendum nor unification.”

Chiltern Railways enters public ownership in Labour nationalisation push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:08 UTC
15:00:08 KST

Chiltern Railways has become the latest train operator to enter public ownership as the government closes in on its ambition to renationalise all major passenger rail services.
The operator, which runs commuter rail services on the Chiltern mainline between London Marylebone and Birmingham, on Sunday became the sixth to be nationalised under Labour, with the remaining four to follow by the end of 2027.
The Department for Transport (DfT) said the move would bring more reliable services, with plans to end what it termed the “daily frustration” of overcrowding.
It has promised a package of improvements for Chiltern passengers, including more services and seats, new trains, upgraded stations and better onboard facilities including upgraded wifi.
The government legislated in 2024 to renationalise private train operations as contracts allowed, joining the four operators already in public ownership and Network Rail to eventually establish an integrated body, Great British Railways (GBR).
The rail minister, Peter Hendy, said: “Every transfer into public ownership gives us the chance to tackle the bread-and-butter issues people care about – more frequent, comfortable trains that turn up on time.
“As we set up Great British Railways, we’re putting passengers first. It will not happen overnight, but we will build a railway the country can trust and rely on and that will create growth, jobs and homes.”
Another 25 daily services will be introduced on the Chiltern network from December, with 10,000 extra seats each weekday, as more new trains are rolled out.
Tony Baxter, the interim managing director of Chiltern Railways, said customers would see “improvements made possible thanks to years of planning, dedication and hard work by Chiltern colleagues. Public ownership will further strengthen that progress through closer collaboration across the industry.”
The DfT said the move “also provides a fresh opportunity to deliver East West Rail”, the long-awaited services that should have started under Chiltern last year on a completed stretch of the future Oxford-Cambridge line.
However, it is unclear if a start date for East-West services between Oxford and Milton Keynes has come any closer after the transfer to the state operator, DfTO. Although a variety of reasons have been given for the delay, unions oppose plans to run the trains without a guard.
The RMT union is due to demonstrate outside London Marylebone station on Monday, and members are being balloted for strike action over plans backed by the DfT for driver-only operation.
The row threatens to further cloud the horizon for GBR, as the government seeks to demonstrate the benefits of the publicly owned railway.
The next operator to transfer into public ownership is due to be Great Western Railway in December.
