10 of the best mountain huts in Europe: bunkrooms, bothies and bonhomie
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:08 UTC
15:00:08 KST

Cabaña Verónica, Spain
A good mountain hut, I reckon, should be small and only accessible on foot after considerable effort. Throw in a bit of historical interest and I’m bound to be happy. In which case, Cabaña Verónica in the Picos de Europa is a fine start to this list. It sleeps six, and at 2,325 metres requires a two-hour trek from the nearest cable car station, never mind road. It has incredible views and a friendly custodian who keeps things in good order. Yet the real attraction is that this place was formerly a gun turret of a US navy battleship that was scrapped in Bilbao in 1960. An enterprising engineer, Conrado Senties, had it carried up on horseback and reassembled on a plug of rock in the middle of nowhere. Don’t ask why, just enjoy the eccentricity.
€15, reservarefugios.com
Låktatjåkko, Sweden
An absolute gem just over 100 miles north of the Arctic Circle and 1,228 metres up a mountain, Låktatjåkko is well placed to deliver that other essential experience of a decent hut: cosy conviviality while surrounded by frequently hostile conditions. When I visited, it was hard to find the hut because it was coated in thick ice and half-buried in snow. The snug timber-clad lounge is the perfect spot to sit in front of the fire and read old accounts of Arctic explorers such as Fridtjof Nansen (there is no phone coverage). The kitchen bangs out endless plates of waffles with cloudberry jam and cream as well as more substantial fare. Be warned, however: in winter the chances of being marooned are quite high and the skiing can be a serious challenge due to extreme cold and fast-changing mountain weather.
From 515 Swedish kronor (£40), laktatjakko.se
Gaustatoppen, Norway
Like many other huts belonging to the wonderful Norwegian Trekking Association, this place is small, well-run and traditional. It’s the route up to it that is astounding. You enter a mountainside, take a thundering old-school funicular railway one kilometre inside the granite, then wander through tunnels of military-grade concrete, before exiting through a blast-proof steel door and climbing down a short way to the hut. All that startling infrastructure is the cold war relic of a Nato communications station now doubling up as a museum and underground route to the hut, which dates back to 1893. This unique means of access gives the hut an advantage: you can stay in winter (weekends only) on the summit of the highest peak in Telemark province, Gaustatoppen, a popular ski resort, and then ski down. When I was there, the view was about 10 metres into thick mist. On a clear day, however, they say you can see one-sixth of Norway.
From 1,550 Norwegian kroner (£122), dnt.no
Chata pod Rysmi, Slovakia
The Tatra mountains have some excellent huts, but this is my pick. Close enough to the summit of Rysy (2,501 metres) for an early start to catch dawn on the top, it is traditional, well-run and basic. The weather here can take a brutal turn at any time of year and, like all the best huts, this is in precisely the right position to be a genuine bolthole. If it looks younger than its 1933 start date, that is because it has been destroyed several times by avalanches and rock falls, which is also why it only opens 1 June to 31 October.
€65, chatapodrysmi.kst.sk
Kredarica on Triglav, Slovenia
This is, in many ways, a standard, old-fashioned mountain refuge, but Kredarica has the great advantage of being the last potential stop en route to the summit of Slovenia’s highest peak, Triglav (2,864 metres). Given that every Slovene feels compelled to visit the summit at least once in their lifetime, this can be a busy place in summer, especially as the views are magnificent. The hardcore, however, savour its spartan winter comforts, when the dormitories are unheated bunkholes for those about to tackle the final, rather tricky ascent to the top (ice axe and crampons essential).
€30 half-board, triglavskidom.si
Le Refuge de Ciottulu di Mori, Corsica
One of the attractions of Corsica’s epic GR20 long-distance footpath is its unapologetically old-fashioned mountain huts. No emergency helicopters swooping in when the G&Ts run out: this is gruff, mule-supplied, mountain hospitality. Ciottulu is a good example of the genre: bare bones dining room and a dormitory with communal sleeping benches for 26. Its ambience is more like a bothy set at 2,000 metres in a vast stony panorama with a slightly unpredictable caretaker. 
€15, le-gr20.fr
Breiðuvik, Iceland
The east of Iceland is home to a scattering of superb huts like this one. Breiðvik is actually on the coast and has the usual bunk rooms and well-appointed kitchen. The location is the big attraction: a wild, desolate coastline of volcanic sand beaches and abandoned villages. Together with 39 other locations, Brieðvik is part of a useful network run by the Icelandic Touring Association.
11,500 Icelandic kronur (£70), ferdaf.is
Scotland’s mountain bothies
The UK has always remained aloof from the continental urge to build something cosy on a mountain top. We are much happier sitting inside our leaky waterproofs eating soggy sandwiches. The Mountain Bothy Association is doing a little to encourage us away from such Spartanism, but not too much. Most are former cottages for miners or shepherds; many now have a fireplace or even a wood burner. In some, there are a few supplies left on a shelf by previous guests. I have a soft spot for the hard charms of the least comfortable, where you may find only a stone bench and an open doorway. A few have become over-used and afflicted by visitors who don’t understand the ethos of mucking in, sharing out and cleaning up. For that reason, I’m not sure it’s worthwhile picking out any particular bothy (pictured is the Elphin Bothy in the Assynt region of Sutherland), suffice to say that the roster contains some absolute classics. Go and find them.
mountainbothies.org.uk
Rifugio Nuvolau, Italy
The Dolomites are so blessed with exceptional huts and Nuvolau is one of the best. Only accessible on foot, it was originally built in 1883 as a bequest from the Baron Richard von Meerheimb, the man who coined the term “psychodrama”, something he may have dreamed up while watching a Nuvolau sunset. The impeccable location is famous for its stunning shifts in light and colour. Inside is a dining room that serves excellent food, including a three-course dinner; upstairs is a small dormitory.
€51 B&B, rifugionuvolau.it
Rifugio Lagazuoi, Italy
Many huts in the Dolomites have learned that economic survival is via tourists rather than hikers and climbers. Lagazuoi is one of them. Built as a climbers’ refuge, it has expanded over the years and been connected to the road by cable car, which enables coach parties to stay. And yet, it remains magnificent. The south-facing terrace is lovely and there are fantastic walks all around, not least through the tunnels and terraces of the first world war frontline that lie on the cliff face below. Mount Lagazuoi (2,835 metres) was one location where the Austro-Hungarian empire faced off against Italians. Many years later, in 1965, Ugo Pompanin, a local Alpine guide and rock-climbing pioneer, recognised the potential and built the first hut, which, several additions later, is still run in great style by his son Guido.
From €85 with breakfast, rifugiolagazuoi.com

‘Flip the table and rise up’: Lib Dems’ president in combative mood as party gathers in Brighton
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:07 UTC
15:00:07 KST

Standing outside Toynbee Hall in the East End of London, Josh Babarinde doesn’t exactly look like a rabble-rouser. But despite the well-cut suit and disarmingly large smile, the president of the Liberal Democrats is, apparently, up for a fight.
“There are big modern giants that are getting in the way of people’s ability to thrive, and it is the job of Liberal Democrats to address that,” says the 33-year-old. “How are we going to do that? Well, first of all, we’ve got to flip the table over and rise up.”
Flipping over tables is not behaviour normally associated with Liberal Democrat members, about 5,000 of whom are in Brighton for its annual conference this weekend.
But Babarinde, frequently described as a rising star in the party’s ranks, wants his comrades to channel the spirit of the great Liberal thinker William Beveridge, who finessed his radical ideas on social reform in the 141-year-old Whitechapel building.
Beveridge decried the five evils of want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. However, Babarinde, the Eastbourne MP, is taking aim at targets from big tech to crypto billionaires. “People are looking for a force to help break some of those giants and give power and cash back to people who this country is meant to be working for,” he says.
That people are seeking alternatives to the status quo is undeniable, but whether they are looking at the Liberal Democrats is a matter of debate.
The historic 2024 election result gave the party 71 MPs, yet it has been stuck at about 11% in polls for months.
The Lib Dems gained 153 councillors in England in May and six seats in the Scottish parliament, although the party’s advances were more modest than those of the Greens and Reform UK. The Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, also struggles to command attention. Lib Dem MPs grumble that Nigel Farage only has to sneeze to attract media covverage, while Davey has to resort to bungee jumping.
“You’ve got a very crowded multiparty system. You’ve got Reform saying any old shit in the media and getting coverage for it with no plan for delivering,” says Babarinde. “As Liberal Democrats, we’re not going to fall into that trap. But what we have got to be clear about is the diagnosis of the problem, who it is standing in the way and what needs to be done.”
He dismisses the idea that the party is yet to produce eye-catching retail policies – “There’s oodles and oodles of it!” – but says it needs to reach beyond its middle England strongholds with digital campaigning that is as strong as its much-envied ground game.
Babarinde, who has spoken about his mother being subjected to domestic abuse and how it shaped his politics, has experience engaging with hard-to-reach communities. He set up a social enterprise smartphone repair service staffed by former offenders and at-risk youth more than a decade ago, which earned him an OBE.
After a stroll through the East End, he points to the stand in Spitalfields market where they had pinned up sheets of A4 paper with “Cracked It” written across them in felt-tip, and laughs. “I would never have got my phone repaired there,” he says. “But when people were giving their money over … I was seeing these guys think: ‘Oh my God, wow! Someone wants my skills. They want what I can offer.’”
Do the Lib Dems want what the ambitious Babarinde has to offer? Despite being elected in 2024, he was elevated to the role of president in November, giving him a vital say in strategy and organisation. He bats away the inevitable question about whether he would like the top job – but when asked if he is a natural leader, he smiles.
“I roll up my sleeves and get stuck in,” he says. “When I saw those young people in the East End prolifically involved in crime amid a lack of opportunities. I wasn’t waiting for someone to swoop in to come to address that issue. I decided to come up with a solution.”
So if the problem is that the Liberal Democrats – despite a seemingly advantageous political backdrop – are stuck on 11% in the polls, what does he see as the answer? “The solution is exactly what is in the strategy we’re talking about this week,” Babarinde says.
“I stood to be party president because I thought I had something to offer: to help develop a new strategy for the party so we can reach new heights.”

Reαd carefully: how to spot – and avoid – a homoglyph attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:07 UTC
15:00:07 KST

You’ve read the email carefully and it looks legitimate. The link it asks you to click on has none of the usual red flags: there are no weird numbers or extra parts to the URL. You feel safe to proceed.
But if you had looked slightly closer you may have noticed something slightly wrong with one of the characters. Just as in the headline of this piece where instead of “a” we used the Cyrillic “α”.
Fraudsters can use letters from different alphabets to create URLs and email addresses that look almost identical to the real thing, but in reality send anyone who clicks on them to a spoof website or inbox. From there they can harvest personal details to use in their scams.
There are other letters and symbols that are easily switched. Last year tech experts spotted fraudsters using the Japanese hiragana character ん to look like a / in an address designed to look as though it was on Booking.com’s website.
Jake Moore, global security adviser at cybersecurity company ESET, says the fraudsters “love Microsoft” as a company identity to spoof. “A fake site might use the Cyrillic “с” instead of the Latin “c” (miсrosoft v microsoft),” he says.
Moore says this type of fraud – known as a homoglyph attack – is becoming increasingly popular. A homoglyph is a character that looks very similar, or even identical, to another one.
“Most phishing attacks are designed to point people to links these days instead of downloading attachments. Attachments can easily be scanned and caught by security software if malicious,” he says.
“Therefore, criminals need to design their websites where the links look genuine and casually request people to click on them without thinking.”
Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN, says homoglyph attacks “are really more of a psychological trick than a technical one”, because the fraudsters are typically trying to panic you into responding quickly, rather than taking time to check things out.
“The goal is to create a sense of panic so you don’t look too closely at the URL. They’re betting that when we’re in a rush, our brains see what we expect to see,” Briedis says.
 It just goes to show that the split-second decision you make when clicking a link is often the most vulnerable part of the whole security chain.”
What it looks like
The real thing. Until you look closely.
You will receive an email or text message suggesting you need to click on a URL or email to sort something out.
Some fonts make substitutions almost impossible to detect. In an email address given in comic sans gill, for example, the Cyrillic a does not look at all out of place.
“We’ve spent years telling people to check the website before trusting it but the problem with this technique is that you can do exactly that and still be fooled as it can look as it should,” says Moore.
If it’s a URL, Moore says typically it will lead to a site that encourages you to enter your credentials for the real site, including your username, password and even a one-time passcode.
What to do
If you are sent a link, take a moment to think rather than reacting immediately.
“If any text, WhatsApp or email is asking you to log in anywhere, it is vital that you independently visit the genuine website rather than trusting the link in front of you to save a few seconds,” says Moore.
And apply the same thinking to email addresses. Type in the address you know to be correct, rather than clicking on a link.
Keep your browser updated. It will flag up suspicious websites, and by keeping it updated it will catch the criminals’ latest workarounds.
Put in place two-factor authentication, or multifactor authentication (2FA or MFA), which means you have two steps to log into a site.
If you find that your details have been compromised, change your passwords immediately. Contact your bank and report the phishing attack to Report Fraud.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania election guide: What you need to know
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the fight is between the Social Democrats (SPD) led by the popular Manuela Schwesig and the far-right Altnerative for Germany (AfD).
The 52-year-old Schwesig has made it her mission to beat back the advance of the AfD, which is polling at around 37%, ahead of the SPD at 33%.
"The situation is serious," Schwesig told DW recently. "The AfD would harm our economy; they would harm our social cohesion. Their crude way of speaking, their hate and incitement, is tearing our society apart; there's a renewed propensity for violence, and that will affect us women in particular."
What to watch out for in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
Besides keeping tabs on whether the AfD comes out on top, all eyes are also on how the CDU performs in the state.
CDU is the conservative Christian Democratic Union party that is chaired by the chancellor of the country, Friedrich Merz.
His party is polling at around 7% in the state, which is slightly above the 5% threshold required by a party to enter state parliament.
In the 2021 elections, the CDU had just 13.3% of the vote.
If the CDU fails to achieve the 5% threshold, there's going to be immense pressure on Merz to fight for his job.
Who are the main candidates?
SPD: Manuela Schwesig, also the incumbent state premier.
AfD: Leif-Erik Holm is the AfD's candidate for state premier, whom the party would put forward to head the state government if it can form one, while Enrico Schult is the AfD's candidate leading the party's election campaign in the state. Holm is the better-known candidate out of the two.
CDU: Daniel Peters, who has been the chair of the CDU parliamentary group in the state parliament.
The Left (Die Linke): Simon Oldenburg, who is the current minister for education in the state.
What's the likeliest scenario?
Even if the AfD comes out on top in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, that's not a guarantee that it will govern the state.
In Germany's parliamentary system, a party needs a majority in the state parliament or coalition partners to elect a state premier.
That means that the AfD could be pushed to the sidelines if other parties reject cooperation with it under the so-called "firewall" policy.
Berlin election guide: What you need to know
The campaign so far has been dominated by a battle between the far-left Left Party and Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU)
Both parties are neck and neck, according to polling in recent weeks.
If Merz's party wins the elections, that'll be good news for the chancellor, whose popularity has taken a big hit, especially following state elections in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) trounced the CDU.
Seventeen parties are contesting the election in Berlin, including the Left Party and the CDU. The four other major parties are the AfD — which has consistently polled in third place —, the environmentalist Green Party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the left-wing, populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).
What is the top issue for Berlin voters?
With the German capital struggling with a severe housing shortage in a city where 85% rent their homes, housing and rental costs are voters' top concerns.
Advertised rents have doubled since 2014, and the city needs 211,000 more homes by 2040.
So far, the Left Party has been the only major party that has promised to act on a 2021 referendum when 59% of Berliners voted to have the government take control of apartments from the biggest landlords to protect rents.
For the AfD, Berlin's housing crisis has fed into its argument for restricting immigration that has driven support for the party.
Who are the main candidates?
- CDU: Stefan Evers is the CDU's lead candidate after the outgoing mayor, Kai Wegner, withdrew from the race.
- The Left Party (Die Linke): Elif Eralp will be leading her party into an election as its lead candidate for the first time. She was born in Munich to Turkish parents. She has been compared to Zohran Mamdani, the democratic socialist who won the New York City mayor race following his campaign around an affordability agenda for residents of his city.
- The Greens (Die Grünen): The Greens are fielding a two-person team consisting of Bettina Jarasch and Werner Graf.
- AfD (Alternative for Germany): Kristin Brinker has campaigned on issues of crime and immigration.
- SPD: Steffen Krach, who has experience working in the Berlin city government and was until recently a top politician in Hanover, the capital of Lower Saxony.
Germany's state elections and the fate of Chancellor Merz: What to know
Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a rare campaign appearance for his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at an event in Berlin on Thursday but has largely stayed away from the campaign trail.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU might even fail to make the 5% threshold required to enter parliament.
At the national level, Merz's own approval ratings fell to as low as 14% earlier in the week , while the far-right AfD has surged to first place with 27-29%, according to opinion polls released earlier this week.
Merz's CDU was polling nationally at 18-20%.
The chancellor has been under mounting pressure over whether he's the right person for the job, amid frustration over the slow pace of his promised reforms and the rise of the AfD.
Merz insisted this week that he's still committed to leading the nation and his governing coalition with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).
"I was elected for four years and I want to use this time to solve problems," he said on Tuesday, insisting: "We have to prove that this can be achieved with this coalition."
However, a YouGov survey released on Friday showed that around half of Germans don't expect Merz to still be chancellor by the end of the year.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Morgen and welcome to our coverage of elections in Berlin and the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Polling stations are open for voters to elect members of the state parliaments. There's also a third vote open to EU citizens for electing members of one of Berlin's 12 district or borough assemblies.
While the elections are regional, they are set to have a national impact, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose popularity has severely dipped in recent weeks, struggling to keep his job.
That's due to a host of reasons, including the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) that secured a historic result with nearly 44% of the vote in elections two weeks ago in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
In Berlin, the race is tied between the Christian Democratic Party (CDU) and the Left Party (Die Linke). The AfD has consistently been polling third in Berlin, which is both the capital city and one of the country's 16 states.
In the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the race is tied between the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the AfD.
Stay tuned for the latest developments in these two crucial elections throughout the day.

In the new preface to the 6th edition of his book entitled “The Power of Negotiation”, Iran’s top diplomat wrote that power yields sustainable results only when consolidated through diplomacy.
In the new preface to the book—written in light of current developments and the military aggression by the US and Israel—Araghchi writes, "When the first edition of 'The Power of Negotiation' was published, my aim was to share the fruits of my years in the diplomatic arena, and to speak of a world where dialogue, bargaining, mutual understanding, and persuasion—rather than war and bloodshed—shape the destiny of nations."
At that time, few could have imagined that, in such a short span, the Islamic Republic of Iran would weather two consecutive wars in less than a year, and that Iranian diplomacy would face the most difficult and perilous conditions in its modern history, he added.
Araghchi said that as I write these lines on the occasion of the book's sixth printing, we are still living through historic times.
He further wrote the events of the twelve-day and forty-day wars have now become a significant part of the Iranian nation's historical memory, even as negotiations between Iran and the United States—aimed at reaching an agreement to permanently end the conflict—continue nearly two months after the ceasefire in the forty-day war.
However, a crucial question these days is whether negotiations with the United States are prudent, given that the two previous rounds of talks culminated in war. While this question may appear simple at first glance, it actually presents an inverted version of the truth; those two wars stemmed not from the negotiations themselves, but from the miscalculations of Iran's adversaries.

Germans vote in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, pitting SPD against AfD as Merz faces leadership test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:50:01 UTC
14:50:01 KST

Voters across the eastern German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern cast ballots on Sunday to elect a new state parliament in a tense race.
Premier Manuela Schwesig's centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the far-right Alternative for Germany, known as the AfD, were running neck and neck throughout the campaign.
Polling stations open at 8 a.m. and close at 6 p.m. local time, with about 1.3 million residents eligible to cast a vote.
The electorate included 16- and 17-year-olds voting in a state election there for the very first time this year.
The contest followed the AfD's record 43.8 percent showing in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks earlier, its strongest result yet in any German state.
A final public broadcaster ZDF poll put the Social Democrats (SPD) narrowly ahead at 37 percent, with the AfD trailing just one point behind at 36 percent.
The socialist Left Party polled at 9 percent, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative CDU hovered close to the 5 percent entry threshold, at 6 percent.
The Greens stood at 5 percent, the left-wing Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) trailed at 4 percent, and 21 percent of respondents remained undecided before the vote.
What’s at stake
Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is a thinly populated state on the Baltic Sea, with Schwerin as its capital. The SPD has governed there since 1998 with changing partners.
Schwesig, premier since 2017, won 39.6 percent in the 2021 election and has since governed alongside the Left Party.
A recent ZDF survey found 61 percent would back Schwesig in a direct vote, against just 30 percent for her AfD rival.
Her AfD challenger, federal lawmaker Leif-Erik Holm, campaigned on economic grievances and a pledge to end 28 years of Social Democratic rule.
Possible coalition scenarios
Neither the SPD nor the AfD is expected to win an outright majority in the state parliament, meaning both would need partners to form a government.
Analysts said the likeliest outcome remained a three-way alliance of the Social Democrats, the Left Party and the Greens.
Every mainstream party ruled out governing alongside the AfD, leaving its path to power unclear even in victory.
Beyond Schwerin, the vote doubled as a referendum on Merz, who cancelled a UN trip to New York to stay in Berlin.
Test for Merz
In Berlin, Sunday's election served as a barometer of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's standing, whose support has slid to historic lows.
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU polled around 6 percent, risking a fall below the 5 percent threshold for parliament entry, a result that would leave it without seats in Schwerin for the first time since reunification.
Merz cancelled a UN trip to New York to stay in Berlin, meeting senior CDU leaders late Sunday, with further talks continuing on Monday and a CDU-CSU lawmakers' gathering two days later.
Leadership speculation has built for weeks, though all 8 CDU state premiers backed Merz on Wednesday.
Observers said a strong AfD result paired with another CDU defeat could still spark a leadership fight.

Two people were killed in the surrounding Moscow region and the capital’s oil refinery - which has been hit before - was struck, local authorities said.

Russian electoral officials said on Sept 19 that an online voting system in Moscow had come under cyberattack.
Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a “pseudo election”.
Putin on Sept 18 also accused Ukraine of trying to interfere in the election, citing what he said was a Ukrainian strike on the home of an election official in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region that killed Elena Astanina, the official.
Reuters could not independently verify details of the attack and there was no comment from Kyiv.
Despite what experts see as the election’s predictable outcome, the NEST think-tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, whom Russian authorities have designated “a foreign agent”, said the vote could still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.
“The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on the ballot,” it said in a note.
It said the Communist party and the New People party could attract votes the authorities would prefer to go to United Russia.
Both parties have consistently voted in line with United Russia on major issues.
Putin told the nation in a televised address before the election that the vote would underline support for Russian troops fighting in Ukraine.
“Your choice, and your will, will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory, and love for our homeland, and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us,” said Putin.
Initial results are expected to start emerging at around 1800 GMT on Sept 20 (2am Singapore time on Sept 21), with more complete results available on Sept 21. REUTERS

Germany’s Berlin, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania states head to polls
Far-right AfD defeated German chancellor’s CDU in recent Saxony-Anhalt state election, casting doubt on his future.
Voters in two German states will go to the polls on Sunday, as far-right and far-left gains threaten to affect the political standing of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Merz, according to a report by the AFP news agency, has scheduled a crisis meeting of his Christian Democratic Union party (CDU), skipped this week’s UN General Assembly meeting in New York, and cleared his calendar to deal with potential aftershocks from the votes in Berlin and the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Tens of thousands march across Germany to protest against far-right AfD
- list 2 of 3AfD is rising, but it can still be stopped
- list 3 of 3Germany’s AfD wins in key state: Is far-right on cusp of national rule?
Pressure on Merz has been mounting after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) delivered a major defeat to his CDU party two weeks ago in the key state of Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD fell just short of an absolute majority, which would have allowed it to govern on its own.
And after just 16 months in power, Merz’s approval ratings have plunged to about 14 percent, the latest polls suggest, as he struggles to push through promised economic and social welfare reforms with his centre-left coalition partners, the Social Democratic Party (SPD), raising doubts among fellow party members whether he can continue to lead.
About 2.5 million people are eligible to vote in the capital, Berlin, and nearly 1.3 million in the northeastern coastal state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Polling booths open at 8am local time and will close at 6pm.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Merz’s party is an onlooker to the main battle between the SPD’s popular state premier Manuela Schwesig and the AfD’s lead candidate, former radio presenter Leif-Erik Holm.
While the AfD was polling at 36 percent against the SPD’s 37 percent, Merz’s CDU, at just 6 percent, was dangerously close to the 5 percent hurdle needed to stay in the state parliament, according to public broadcaster ZDF.
In the city-state of Berlin, the ruling CDU is running a tight race against the far-left Die Linke (The Left), which promises drastic measures to solve a dire housing crisis and is popular with young people.
A CDU defeat there would be another blow for Merz, especially at the hands of Die Linke, which wants to curb corporate power and leans towards Moscow.
Regional elections would not usually draw much interest outside Germany, but the AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt, which it sees as the first step towards winning federal elections due in 2029, has sent shockwaves through Europe.

Lightning offensive

“The area is under a hostile aerial threat,” according to a message received just before 3am by Riyadh residents, urging them to stay indoors.

Why has Pauline Hanson joined forces with Muslim and Vietnamese-born MPs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:31:40 UTC
14:31:40 KST

In brief
- Pauline Hanson, Fatima Payman and Dai Le have united to argue parliamentary staffing allocations are unfair.
- The prime minister has significant discretion over personal staff, but the trio wants an independent system instead.
Pauline Hanson and Fatima Payman have clashed over race, religion and politics.
But this week, the One Nation leader and Muslim independent senator stood together, alongside Vietnamese-born independent MP Dai Le.
At the centre of their unlikely alliance is a fight over parliamentary staffing, with the three accusing Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of unfairly determining who gets additional staff and calling for the system to be taken out of the prime minister's hands.
The unlikely trio appeared together at Parliament House on Thursday, arguing the way personal staff are allocated to politicians is unfair and lacks transparency.
Their grievance centres on an unusual feature of Australia's parliamentary system: while MPs and senators employ their own staff, the prime minister has significant discretion over the allocation of additional personal staff.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
That discretion has previously faced scrutiny in parliament.
Why did Hanson, Payman and Le join forces?
Despite their political differences, all three say they are being denied the staffing resources they need to do adequately their jobs.
Payman, who left Labor in 2024 after crossing the Senate floor over Palestinian statehood, currently has no additional personal staff allocated to her.
Le, who defeated Labor to win the western Sydney seat of Fowler as an independent in 2022, has one.
One Nation, meanwhile, increased its representation at the 2025 election but says its staffing allocation did not increase accordingly.
According to AAP, modelling puts One Nation's allocation at 0.83 personal staff per parliamentarian, compared with 4.09 for Labor and 1.47 for the Coalition.
Those figures include different categories of parliamentarians and office-holders, so they are not a direct like-for-like comparison of backbench MPs.
Hanson, Payman and Le argue the differences demonstrate the need for a more transparent and independent system.
According to The Conversation, Le told reporters on Thursday there were "no published criteria, no explanation, no appeal" for staffing decisions.
The three have threatened to pursue legislation changes when parliament returns in October to remove the prime minister's power over non-government personal staff allocations and give the responsibility to an independent authority.
Who actually decides how many staff politicians get?
Parliamentary staffing is divided into different categories, with different rules governing how positions are allocated.
Politicians generally have two broad categories of staff: electorate employees and personal employees.
Electorate staff perform work such as assisting constituents and supporting MPs and senators in their parliamentary duties.
Personal staff can perform different roles, including providing policy advice, research, communications and support for a parliamentarian's work in Canberra.
They are employed under the Members of Parliament (Staff) Act, commonly known as the MOP(S) Act, and cannot legally be employed for party-political purposes.
But additional personal staff are not distributed to every politician according to a single automatic formula.
The Department of Finance says the prime minister determines the number of personal employee positions allocated to ministers and assistant ministers, as well as the allocation given to the opposition.
The prime minister also determines the allocation given to the leader of a minority party, who can then distribute those positions among their party's MPs, and may allocate personal employees to independent parliamentarians.
That means gaining another MP or senator does not necessarily translate into an increase in personal staff members.
Albanese's power over staff members is not unique. The system has given successive prime ministers significant control over personal staffing allocations
Why do extra staff matter?
Additional personal staff provide support across a range of parliamentary duties, and can affect their capacity to carry out parliamentary and electorate work.
They can research legislation, prepare MPs and senators for parliamentary debates and committee hearings, develop policy advice, deal with media and stakeholders and help offices manage correspondence and constituent issues.
Crossbenchers and smaller parties also have fewer parliamentary colleagues and party resources to draw on than the major parties.
The Parliamentary Library has previously noted that staffing levels for crossbenchers have varied significantly over time, and have sometimes changed depending on the political circumstances of the parliament.
When independents held the balance of power following the 2010 election, for example, additional staff were allocated to crossbench MPs. Those arrangements changed after the 2013 election.
Additional personal staff can assist parliamentarians with work including scrutinising legislation, preparing for parliamentary debates and participating in committee work.
Has this fight happened before?
The allocation of personal staff to crossbench parliamentarians has previously been contested, including since the Albanese government took office in 2022.
After Labor took office four years ago, Albanese reduced the number of additional personal staff allocated to crossbench parliamentarians, prompting significant criticism from independents.
A Parliamentary Library research paper subsequently noted that while the overall number of personal staff had increased substantially over the longer term, allocations to crossbenchers and former leaders had not increased in the same way.
The issue returned to parliament in 2025, when senators sought to change how personal staff were allocated to non-government parliamentarians and reduce the prime minister's discretion over the process.
A bill co-sponsored by Coalition and crossbench senators, including Hanson and Payman, proposed guaranteeing minimum personal staffing levels for non-government parliamentarians.
It also sought to limit the prime minister's discretion over those minimum allocations.
The bill passed its second reading in the Senate but was ultimately defeated at the third-reading stage in September 2025.
The Senate nevertheless backed an amendment calling for the government to work with elected groups and independents to develop a "fair and independent staffing model" that accounted for representation, staff wellbeing and workloads.
Reviews of parliamentary workplaces have also previously recommended greater transparency around staffing allocations and an evidence-based examination of workloads.
Why is their alliance so unusual?
Hanson and Payman, in particular, have a long history of clashing politically.
In 2024, Hanson sought to have Payman's eligibility to sit in parliament investigated over questions surrounding her Afghan citizenship.
Payman responded with a fierce attack on Hanson in the Senate, comments she was subsequently required to withdraw.
The political tensions between them remained.
Payman told reporters on Thursday however that politicians should be capable of putting those disagreements aside when they find a common cause, according to a by The Guardian.

California governor signs 13 bills to protect elections from federal interference
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:31:27 CST
14:31:27 KST

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- California Governor Gavin Newsom on Saturday signed a package of 13 bills aimed at protecting the state's November midterm elections from interference, including measures concerning mail voting and demands for voter data, according to his office.
Midterms are congressional elections held midway between presidential elections. In the United States, state law primarily governs election procedures, while federal law sets nationwide standards, according to the Election Assistance Commission.
Among the measures, Assembly Bill 282 makes it a felony to seize ballots, election records or certified voting technology before election results are certified, while Senate Bill 259 makes it a felony for an authority figure to direct someone to interfere with the delivery or return of a mail-in ballot. Assembly Bill 1664 requires local agencies and election officials to promptly notify the state of specified law-enforcement actions involving election records or certified voting technology.
The legislation comes amid a dispute between California and the Trump administration over federal election policies. Trump issued an executive order in March directing federal agencies to provide states with lists of confirmed citizens of voting age and directing the U.S. Postal Service to begin rule-making on standards for mail-in and absentee ballots. California and other states challenged the order in federal court.
The Supreme Court later rejected the request and blocked it from enforcing new restrictions on mail-in ballots ahead of the November midterm elections. California has also resisted federal demands for statewide voter-registration data.
Newsom, Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Attorney General Rob Bonta said the package would protect against federal interference in state election administration.
"This legislative package ensures that California voters will not be silenced or intimidated," Weber said in a statement. Newsom also noted that "These bills today build upon the wall California has built to safeguard our electoral process." ■

He added that Cooper's remarks constituted a "projection and a failed psychological operation to boost the morale of the terrorist U.S. Army's exhausted and worn-out forces in the region and justify the exorbitant financial costs and casualties incurred by the United States in the region."
Shekarchi noted that such claims could not change the reality of the expulsion of the "aggressive" U.S. Army from the region, stressing that the initiative in the Strait of Hormuz remained in the hands of Iran's armed forces.
In a video posted on social media on Saturday, Cooper said, "We've reached this significant milestone while assisting over 2,000 commercial ship transits through the strait by providing coordinated protection. Clearly, the momentum is building."
"Thousands of ships have passed through the strait. Over 1 billion barrels of crude have been shipped from Gulf partners through the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran has exported zero barrels thanks to our ironclad blockade," he added.
Following U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, Tehran restricted passage through the strategic waterway, while U.S. forces imposed a naval blockade targeting vessels traveling to or from Iranian ports. ■

====================================================================================================

Interview: China's Global Development Initiative gives Global South stronger voice, opportunities: former Egyptian PM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:30:42 CST
14:30:42 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's Global Development Initiative (GDI) helps give developing countries, especially those in the Global South, a stronger voice in global governance while creating broader opportunities for development, former Egyptian Prime Minister Essam Sharaf has said.
"After decades of major economic and social transformation, China has accumulated considerable development experience and become more willing to share this experience and its capabilities with other countries, especially those of the Global South," Sharaf, founder and chairman of the Sharaf Foundation for Sustainable Development, told Xinhua in a recent interview.
Sharaf said one of the GDI's most important contributions over the past five years has been to bring development back to "the heart of global attention" at a time of geopolitical conflicts, economic competition and successive crises.
"Development should not become a victim of these conflicts, but should remain a shared priority for the international community," he stressed, noting that peace and development are closely intertwined.
Sharaf said sustainable peace is difficult to build in a world where development gaps are widening, just as real development is difficult to achieve amid conflict and instability.
"One of the most important lessons reinforced by the initiative is that investing in development is, at the same time, an investment in stability, peace and the future," he said.
Sharaf said the GDI also reflects a broader understanding of development that goes beyond economic growth and new projects to improve people's livelihood, reduce poverty, ensure access to food and energy, and strengthen health, education and resilience to crises.
Turning to global governance, Sharaf said the GDI contributes to strengthening multilateralism by promoting greater participation of developing countries in international decision-making.
"From this perspective, I believe the GDI makes an important contribution to shifting from the concept of governance for countries to a broader concept of governance with the participation of countries," Sharaf said.
He said that the GDI's emphasis on participation is particularly important because major global challenges, from climate change and food security to energy and digital transformation, cannot be addressed by any single country alone.
"Ultimately, true multilateralism is not simply about having a large number of countries around one table; it is about ensuring that everyone feels they have a voice, and that their interests and needs are part of the process of shaping a shared future," Sharaf said.
He expected the digital sphere to be one of the most important areas for the GDI's future development, as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly central to one of the fastest technological transformations in human history.
Sharaf warned that if advanced technologies are available only to wealthier countries and societies, the world could move from the traditional development gap to an even more dangerous digital divide.
He said supporting the "Digital South" should go beyond expanding internet access and digital infrastructure to include building human capacity, transferring knowledge, strengthening digital education and scientific research, and ensuring equitable access to technology.
Sharaf said the GDI can play an important role in linking digital development with equitable development, while helping ensure that developing countries benefit from advances in artificial intelligence.
He also pointed to the China-led establishment of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, saying it aims to strengthen international cooperation and global AI governance while promoting the safe, equitable and inclusive development and use of artificial intelligence.
"I believe the GDI has a major opportunity to help shape an important principle for the next phase: the future of technology should not be a future for a limited number of countries, but a shared future for humanity," he said. ■

MOSCOW, September 20. /TASS/. At least two people have been killed in the ongoing massive drone attack on various areas in the Moscow Region, a Russian administrative entity adjacent to the capital Moscow, Governor Andrey Vorobyev wrote on Telegram.
"In Sofyino, a drone hit a three-storey apartment building, damaging six apartments on the upper floor. Unfortunately, a 44-year-old woman was killed," Vorobyev wrote. "One more person was killed in the Orekhovo-Zuevo municipality. An elderly man was in a house that was destroyed and caught fire as a result of a drone attack."
Between 3:00 a.m. and 5:00 a.m. Moscow time (midnight and 2:00 a.m. GMT) on Sunday, at least 249 drones were jammed and destroyed in 17 municipalities of the Moscow Region.
"The attack is ongoing," the governor wrote.
In his words, damage to private houses and apartment blocks have been reported in a number of the region’s municipalities.
In the Ramenskoye district, the roof of a 21-storey apartment block caught fire after being hit by a drone, prompting the evacuation of around 400 people, including 70 children. In addition, 20 cars were damaged there, the governor said.
In Sofyino in the Ramenskoye district, a warehouse was set ablaze. Another serious fire was reported in the city of Kotelniki on Moscow’s southeastern outskirts, where a drone hit an apartment building, setting fire to apartments on three floors.
"Casualty reports are being verified," the governor said. "Firefighters and emergency services are working at the scene."
Later, the governor said three apartment blocks in the Novye Kotelniki residential complex in the city were damaged. It was not immediately clear whether he earlier referred to one of these buildings.

Flights diverted to other airports

About 25 planes bound for Sheremetyevo Airport were diverted to Nizhny Novgorod, Kazan, Cheboksary, St. Petersburg, Samara and Nizhnekamsk.
About 10 flights, namely from Hurghada (Egypt), Tashkent and Fergana (Uzbekistan), Istanbul and Dalaman (Turkey), Dubai (UAE), as well as Russia’s Novosibirsk, Yekaterinburg and Chelyabinsk, were unable to land at Vnukovo Airport.

Forestry agency uses drones to reforest Hualien
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:14:00 UTC
14:14:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency said Saturday that it is using drones to reforest landslide areas upstream of the Mataian River.
Heavy rain from Typhoon Wipha caused landslides near the river and formed a barrier lake in July 2025. Two months later, heavy rain from Typhoon Ragasa caused the lake to overflow and fail, flooding central Guangfu Township, per UDN.
The steep upstream terrain makes reforestation on foot dangerous. The forestry agency’s Hualien branch has therefore used drones to drop seeds and seedlings in materials developed with National Ilan University, per CNA.
The agency conducted its first two rounds of airdrops from December 2025 to January. The third took place from Sept. 5–7, covering about 20 hectares across 67 drop sites and bringing the total area covered to 40.2 hectares.
The latest mission featured three methods:
- Seeds encased in moist gel granules that supply water and protection.
- Germinated seedlings, growing medium, and seeds secured in water-soluble netting.
- Seeds and growing material enclosed in water-soluble capsules.
The agency said drones are also being used to monitor plant growth. Once root systems and ground vegetation become established, they are expected to reduce erosion and the amount of sediment flowing downstream, lowering the risk of river siltation and blockages.

China reiterates opposition to US sanctions on Iran, Russia

China has reiterated its opposition to the unilateral sanctions imposed without the United Nations authorization after US President Donald Trump signed into law legislation expanding coercive measures targeting Russia and extending existing ones against Iran.
A Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson made the remarks on Saturday in response to the US passage of the Russia sanctions bill, saying Beijing opposed unilateral sanctions lacking a basis in international law and would reserve the right to take measures to protect its development interests.
"We have noted the relevant developments. China has always opposed unilateral sanctions that lack authorization from the United Nations and a basis in international law, and opposes so-called secondary sanctions measures taken against other countries on the pretext of involving third parties,” the official said.
“China has always carried out normal economic and trade cooperation with all other countries on the basis of equality and mutual benefit. Such cooperation neither targets any third party nor is subject to disruption or coercion by any third party," the spokesperson said.
The statement came after Trump signed the so-called “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026” into law on Friday, according to a White House release.
The legislation authorizes and expands sanctions, tariffs, and prohibitions targeting Russia, while extending existing illegal sanctions against Iran.
Among its provisions, the law allows the Trump administration to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian oil or natural gas. It also provides for sanctions against Russian officials, banks, and vessels involved in transporting Russian energy.
The legislation further extends sanctions against Iran's energy and defense sectors that were due to expire after the end of 2026.
The bill passed the US House of Representatives on Wednesday by a vote of 262-159, after previously receiving Senate approval in an 86-11 vote, according to Press TV.
The legislation was championed by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who had earned notoriety for his ceaseless warmongering alongside controversial and markedly strong alliance with the Israeli regime. Graham, who had become known by critics as the “merchant of death,” died unexpectedly following a “sudden and brief illness,” earlier this year.

====================================================================================================

Pledges, timed visits and taxes: The strategies diverting tourists from hotspots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:09:20 UTC
14:09:20 KST

Timed visits, taxes and pledges: The strategies diverting tourists from hotspots
For many people, a holiday in a beautiful destination far from home is the perfect way to relax and leave behind the daily grind.
For those who live in tourist destinations, travellers bring business and work opportunities.
But when more and more people flock to the same places, the pressure on locals and their environment can become destructive.
The city of Amsterdam, known worldwide for its picturesque canals, red light district and bike lanes, has stopped investing in traditional marketing altogether.
"Amsterdam is not trying to grow tourism. Amsterdam is trying to manage tourism," Amsterdam & Partners corporate communications specialist Mila de Heer says.
"Our aim is a visitor economy that contributes to the city, respects residents and strengthens Amsterdam's cultural, social and economic fabric.
"Visitors are welcome, but not at any cost."
The Dutch city is not alone.
In destinations around the world, over-tourism has aggravated residents who say they no longer benefit from an industry that is overtaking their infrastructure and contributing to a lack of affordable housing.
Now many of the world's most desirable destinations are saying no to unrestrained mass tourism — but finding the antidote is not simple.
Different strategies are being tested to limit the influx of tourists, including taxes, access restrictions and the closure of hotspots.
Not just 'a lot of tourists'
In 2025, the travel and tourism sector generated $US11 trillion ($15 trillion) and accounted for nearly 10 per cent of the global economy, according to research by the World Travel and Tourism Council.
Western Sydney University sustainable tourism professor Joseph Cheer says it is important to understand that over-tourism means more than just "a lot of tourists".
"At its most basic, over-tourism is when tourism growth starts to create problems at a local level," he says.
Over-tourism manifests as overcrowding, loss of amenities, rapid development that communities cannot keep up with, noise, pollution, waste management issues and increased housing costs, Dr Cheer says.
He says housing in popular destinations often gets used to accommodate tourists because it is more profitable.
"In a situation where we have a housing crisis or housing affordability crisis, this locks out locals from the housing that they would otherwise have had access to," Dr Cheer says.
Accommodation and cruise ship bans
In Barcelona, Spain's most visited city by foreign tourists, authorities announced a moratorium on short-term rentals such as Airbnb to help make the city more affordable for residents.
Mayor Jaume Collboni said the city would scrap the licences of more than 10,000 apartments approved as short-term rentals by November 2028.
Housing is a pain point in Barcelona, where demonstrators have hit the streets the past two summers with water pistols to protest tourism.
Regulation of platforms such as Airbnb has proven successful, according to Dr Cheer.
"It's been able to put limits around the extent to which tourism takes place in local areas. Airbnb had a slogan: 'to live like a local'. The trouble is, no-one asked the locals whether they wanted people to live like them," he says.
The ban is part of Barcelona's wider plan to cut off tourism growth.
"The demand can't grow if there's no accommodation for [tourists]. Already this summer we're seeing that there are people who can't come because they can't find a place to stay. We're not going to respond to growing demand," the city's new sustainable tourism commissioner José Antonio Donaire told The New York Times.
The Italian city of Venice banned large cruise ships from entering its historic centre in 2021, following years of protests by locals.
The community group No Grandi Navi (No Big Ships) attracted media attention for protesting on water, waving flags from small boats.
When a cruise ship full of passengers descends upon a city, facilities and infrastructure can be put under pressure without much economic benefit, Dr Cheer says.
University of Adelaide tourism management senior lecturer Freya Higgins-Desbiolles says the cruise ship ban is a good example of a community being centred in decision-making.
"The local communities should be setting a vision of what they want for tourism in their place," she says.
Tourist taxes and minimum spends
Japan, a favourite destination for Australians, has increased a number of fees aimed at tourists and immigrants amid fears of over-tourism and a surge in anti-immigration sentiment.
This includes the tripling of Japan's international tourist tax, which is attached to airfares departing Japan.
According to the Japan National Tourism Organisation, the fee will "support the maintenance of public works, critical infrastructure at airports and tourist sites, restoration of historic assets, and the creation of online tourist resources".
Closer to home, the Balinese have watched their island completely transform, with its rice paddies and agricultural land turned into villas for tourists.
Foreign visitors have almost tripled in the past 15 years. Almost seven million foreign tourists visited the island last year, more than 1.5 million of them Australian.
But the infrastructure has not kept up with the pace. The island is grappling with a waste crisis, and frustrated locals blamed overdevelopment after the island was hit with deadly floods.
In 2024, Bali implemented a tourist tax. The 150,000 rupiah ($15) payment is collected at the airport, but some visitors have found its implementation confusing.
The charge goes toward conserving ecology and culture while offsetting some of the environmental damage caused by tourism.
Dr Cheer says the effectiveness of tourist taxes is debatable because they do not address the root cause of problems, and it is not always clear whether they will be used to solve the problems created by tourism.
"Tourist taxes are a very blunt instrument that doesn't really change what's happening in the tourism system," he says.
"A 5 euro tax is not going to stop someone from wanting to go to Venice. A $50 Bali entry tax is not going to deter people from going to Bali.
"It's a small drop in the pond when it comes to what they are spending overall."
The Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan has been wary of tourism ever since it opened to visitors in 1974.
The country imposes strict parameters on international travellers, including a ban on mountaineering to preserve its peaks.
Before 2020, a minimum spend of $US200 ($299) per day was required of foreign nationals, as well as a $US65 ($90) daily fee.
Bhutan's reopening to the world after the pandemic saw the minimum spend requirement scrapped in favour of raising the daily "sustainable development fee" (SDF), which the government says is used to offset carbon generated by visitors, to $US200.
In Bhutan, the government can control "who comes in and how much they spend and where they go," Dr Cheer says.
"It might work in Bhutan, but it doesn't necessarily work everywhere else."
In September 2023, in the wake of declining visitor numbers, the country cut the SDF to US$100 per day for the next four years.
Pledges and regeneration closures
In Thailand, the government closes Maya Bay, popularised by the 2000 movie The Beach, for two months every year.
The Phi Phi Islands beach was reopened in 2022 after a nearly four-year closure due to damage to its ecosystem.
The reopening has come with strict rules, including a ban on swimming, and the tourists who have attempted to wade into the turquoise waters have been fined for doing so.
Boats can no longer enter the bay; there is a daily visitor cap and a one-hour time limit for visits.
A similar approach was taken in the Philippines in 2018, when authorities closed the paradisiacal island of Boracay for six months to clean up its shores.
Results from the closure were contentious, but locals say they saw the restoration of the island to its former glory during COVID-19 lockdowns.
From an ecological point of view, closures such as that of Maya Bay and Boracay have been successful, Dr Cheer says, but some outcomes remain to be seen.
"The question remains, if you close and then when you reopen [and] it's business as usual, have you really made any progress? Are you just going one step forward and one step back constantly?" he says.
It can also be difficult for authorities to stick with closures that create ripple effects in the economy.
Even the limited return of tourists to Maya Bay has come with setbacks to the environment, leaving authorities struggling to strike a balance between preserving its ecosystem and sustaining livelihoods.
The Pacific island nation of Palau asks each tourist presenting at immigration to sign a passport pledge to act in an ecologically and culturally responsible way.
"I vow to tread lightly, act kindly and explore mindfully," the pledge reads.
"The only footprints I shall leave are those that will wash away."
Pledges can be helpful in influencing tourists to be more careful about how they visit a place, Dr Higgins-Desbiolles says, but the effect may be limited in an industry as complex as tourism.
"When we shift the focus to the tourist as the consumer, you're not actually getting to the heart of the problem, and you're not making the tourism industry take responsibility," she says.
"I don't think consumer choice is actually going to have the impact that we need, because, of course, it's only the sensitive type of tourists that will be moved by that and engage in that."
The tourism industry's 'growth fetish'
In 2025, international tourist arrivals grew by four per cent, with an estimated 1.52 billion international tourists recorded globally, according to the UN World Tourism Barometer.
That growth has continued but slowed down in 2026 amid the conflict in the Middle East.
Dr Higgins-Desbiolles says the industry must deal with its "growth fetish" if it is to address problems with over-tourism.
"Endless growth is not possible without damaging societies and ecology, so it's got to be managed," she says.
But Dr Higgins-Desbiolles says the industry itself should not be "at the forefront of decision-making".
"They should be a voice in it, but my view is the local people are the ones that have to live with the consequences of tourism, so it's them that should have a strong seat at the table, and often they're not represented," she says.
Amsterdam has put in place a formal "Tourism in Balance" framework, which includes a cap on overnight stays per year.
If overnight stays approach 18 million, the municipal executive must propose measures to prevent the 20 million cap from being exceeded.
The city has made progress in positioning itself as "a place of culture, creativity, neighbourhoods, innovation and local life, rather than as a permissive playground," Ms de Heer says.
"The goal is not more tourists, but better balance. Visitors who behave respectfully, spread across the city and region where appropriate, contribute to culture and local businesses, and do not add disproportionate pressure to already crowded areas."

World leaders return to UN amid wars in Middle East and Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:08:49 UTC
14:08:49 KST

World leaders return to UN amid wars in Middle East and Ukraine
- World leaders gather at the UN General Assembly to address conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, AI risks, and UN challenges amid US funding cuts and leadership uncertainties.
- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urges global AI governance to prevent disaster, contrasting with US President Trump's dismissal of AI risks as a "hoax."
- The Assembly focuses on Middle East tensions, stalled peace talks, and Ukraine's war impact on food security and energy, with key speeches from leaders including Zelensky and Netanyahu.
AI generated
UNITED NATIONS – World leaders gather in New York this week for the UN General Assembly, bracing themselves for US President Donald Trump’s return to the rostrum for a second year running, with talks centring on the widening conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine and the risks of artificial intelligence.
Nearly 130 heads of state meet with the post-World War II order under strain and with the UN itself struggling to remain relevant and weathering attacks from Trump, who has slashed America’s contributions and withdrawn from dozens of UN bodies.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping, who last addressed the diplomatic jamboree via video in 2021, will skip New York in favour of one-on-one talks with Trump in Washington on Sept 24, fuelling debate about the UN’s relevance in addressing global crises.
Compounding the crisis of morale and finance are questions about the next leader of the 80-year-old organisation: Secretary-General Antonio Guterres completes his term at the end of 2026, with no clear frontrunner in the race to replace him.
The 15-member UN Security Council may hold high-level meetings on Ukraine, AI and the Middle East, including talks with Arab leaders, diplomats said.
More than a year into Trump’s second term, “we would no longer say that the UN is in free fall, but we would say that it’s stuck in an open-ended crisis,” said Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group.
“The UN may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it seems to be trapped in a trauma centre for the foreseeable future,” Gowan said.
The US avoided losing its vote at the assembly by paying US$725 million (S$925 million) in contributions to the regular budget this week, but it still owes the organisation more than a billion dollars and makes ongoing demands for cuts and reforms.
Growing AI risks
The assembly meets shortly after several artificial intelligence industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and escape human control.
Guterres has said that AI will be a major topic, adding that countries pushing its frontiers should set up “common guardrails in order to avoid this race to the bottom that could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at the global level.”
The secretary-general has long proposed global governance of AI. In 2023, the UN created an advisory body on the technology, with members including tech executives, government officials and academics.
The warning has put Guterres at odds with Trump, who dismissed AI risks as a “hoax”, saying there is a “sick conspiracy” against it and that China would benefit from the doubt being cast on its development.
Middle East escalation
The Middle East will again be a focus of discussions, as the US-Israeli war on Iran continues to drive global inflation and destabilise the region. Recent gains by Houthi militants threaten shipping in the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait and could further spike energy prices.
“It’s very difficult to have a military solution for that problem, and the experience of fighting in Yemen demonstrated how complicated it is to have successful interventions,” said Guterres, adding that the UN’s envoy on Yemen was making a “huge effort” to advance talks.
Peace talks remain stalled, however, as Iran and the US continue to exchange strikes and Trump threatens a major escalation of the war.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the assembly on Sept 23.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – wanted by the International Criminal Court over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza that Israel denies – is to speak on Sept 24.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will for the second year running not be at the gathering in person. The US, a close Israeli ally, again denied him a visa. On Sept 17, the General Assembly voted to allow Abbas to appear via video.
There is likely to be a high-level meeting on the conflict in Sudan on the sidelines, diplomats said, although a diplomatic breakthrough is unlikely.
Ukraine, food security
Also on the agenda is Russia’s more than four-year-old war in Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will address the General Assembly. Zelensky will likely seek to shore up Ukraine’s position ahead of what is expected to be another tough winter, diplomats said.
The Security Council has been unable to take action to end the conflict because permanent member Russia holds a veto.
Trump has at times appeared frustrated that he has been unable to broker an end to the war, a goal he declared a priority when he began his second term in January 2025. The US president spoke with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin earlier in September, but it was unclear whether he plans to meet Zelensky in New York.
Guterres highlighted the impact the war was having on civilians but also on food security and energy prices.
“The effective blockade existing in the Black Sea is creating enormous problems that add to the problems generated by the Middle East crisis, and I think it would be very important to find a way to allow Ukrainian exports and Russian exports of food, fertilisers and energy to take place in a safe way through the Black Sea,” he said.
