Ed Sheeran returns to stage after calls for boycott over removal of Macklemore
Protesters and police were expected to greet concertgoers in Philadelphia on Saturday for pop superstar Ed Sheeran's first show since he became embroiled in controversy set off after he was asked to remove Macklemore from his performance due to his pro-Palestine remarks.
Rapper Macklemore was booted from Sheeran's US Loop Tour on Monday after the owners of stadiums hosting upcoming shows told Sheeran he would have to choose between using their venues or having Macklemore as a supporting act.
The move comes after Macklemore called for a "Free Palestine" onstage in New Jersey earlier this month.
Sheeran, who has since faced backlash, has denied being behind the decision to remove Macklemore, saying his tour's promoter was responsible.
But four supporting acts soon quit the "Shape of You" singer's tour. They included Sheeran's backing band as well as performer Finneas, who rose to fame collaborating with his pop superstar sister Billie Eilish.
At a time when a growing number of artists are speaking out against the war on Gaza and West Bank Israeli settler violence, the 35-year-old British performer has maintained his apolitical stance.
"I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care," he said on Instagram on Tuesday.
However, he said, "those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum."
The former busker-turned-superstar, accused by critics of failing to stand up to the stadium owners, has been targeted by boycott calls over the controversy.
On Saturday, a pro-Palestinian group urged artists, fans and crew members to stay away from Sheeran's concerts on three continents.
"We now extend our call for boycotting Ed Sheeran's entire world tour, including the upcoming Latin American dates, and the as-yet-unannounced European leg," the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) said in a statement.
"Clearly, there's some real discontent around how this whole situation is being managed, and he's definitely having to do some brand reputation management," said Gretchen Larsen, a professor specializing in the music industry at Durham University Business School in the UK.
Solo show?
No new opening acts or backing bands have been announced, and it was not known how Sheeran planned to carry out his show at Lincoln Financial Field in the eastern US city of Philadelphia on Saturday night.
A pro-Palestinian rally organised by local groups was scheduled to take place near the venue in the afternoon.
City police told AFP there would be an "appropriate police presence" to "help ensure the safety of concertgoers, employees and neighborhood residents."
On the resale market, tickets for the show have been changing hands at a slightly brisker pace since Monday when compared to previous dates on Sheeran's tour, according to tracking site TicketData.
"Some share of the audience isn't tuned in to anything political, or is completely indifferent to it, and has only just now become aware that Ed Sheeran is even playing their city. They're buying tickets with zero connection to the controversy," site founder Keith Pagello said.
The price of the cheapest tickets had fallen from $123 on Monday to $67 by Friday afternoon.
Pagello said the decline was not necessarily linked to the row, as it is common for concert ticket prices to drop as the event date approaches.

Turkey says it could help meet Saudi military needs under defence pact

Breadcrumb
Turkey says it could help meet Saudi military needs under defence pact
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Saturday that Saudi Arabia may have military needs due to the ongoing attacks by Yemen's Houthis and that Turkey was ready to help under a trilateral defence pact that also includes Pakistan.
"We see there are very serious attacks on Saudi Arabia's territorial integrity and sovereignty. We have an alliance agreement in our pact. We are in serious solidarity on this point... They may have some military needs, especially on some technical issues. We would have no issues in meeting these," Fidan told broadcaster NTV.
The joint defence agreement, dubbed the "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement", signed last month stipulates that an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack on all of them.
The Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen, have been launching attacks on Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, a new front in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. The attacks have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, threatening global oil supplies and the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted.
US President Donald Trump has rebuffed pleas from the Saudis for military support to fight the Houthis, who agreed a ceasefire with the United States last year after Washington bombed the group for two months.
Fidan said that it was unacceptable for Saudi Arabia to be made a part of the US-Iran war as it had no desire to join the conflict. He added, without elaborating, that proposals have been conveyed to all sides to end the fighting.
"There are many initiatives, but the sides need to accept these," he said. "There are new proposals, I hope they accept them. Otherwise, the crisis was tolerated until a certain point, but the economic reflections have started to exceed the point of being tolerable."
Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia was open to expansion and did not seek to replace any existing alliances.
Pakistan has said that there were no discussions about a military reaction from Islamabad under the Mecca agreement in response to the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia, but added that Pakistan would act when the "time comes".
Earlier on Saturday, Yemen's Houthis said they attacked "sensitive" sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen near the city's main airport.
Turkey has condemned the Houthi attacks and called for them to stop immediately.

guadagnino, lynch, and the movie directors who design interior spaces

Int. Home – DAY… interior design by Movie Directors
At the end of September, film director Luca Guadagnino and designer Stefano Baisi will release a line with Zara Home that includes nearly 200 sumptuous pieces of interior décor, from squiggly couches that recall Italian Radical Design to tableware that feels snatched from an Italian villa. Through this collection, there is a chance to bring a bit of the energy of Queer, Call Me by Your Name, Challengers, or one of the director’s many other films into a domestic space.
This meeting between interior design and film is not a new one. The visually seductive worlds of David Lynch, Wes Anderson, and Wong Kar Wai have inspired the likes of hotels, home goods collections, and even train cars. For these directors, their cinematic worlds have homes both on and off the silver screen.
Baisi Guadagnino for Zara | campaign by David Sims
Baisi Guadagnino for Zara Home | campaign by Valerie Sadoun
Studio Luca Guadagnino, Zara Home, and the Dior Runway
A few years ago, when Luca Guadagnino was brought up in conversation, those in the know would share, ‘and you know he has an interior design studio!’ The Milan-based director has brought his aesthetic sense to runways, hotels, and villas through Studio Luca Guadagnino, where he began working with Baisi, who would later go on to collaborate with him on Queer, After the Hunt, and Jonathan Anderson’s S/S 2026 Dior runway in Paris. In Rome, monumental spaces within the Palazzo Talìa hotel were redesigned by his studio, complimenting the building’s rich history with contemporary styles.
Palazzo Talìa by Studio Luca Guadagnino | image courtesy of Palazzo Talìa
Baisi Guadagnino for Zara Home | campaign by Valerie Sadoun
David Lynch’s things and places for thinking and listening
‘Every film is going into a new world,’remarked the late American film director David Lynch at the 63rd Venice Film Festival. He talks about following one’s intuition as they navigate the world that is set out in front of them—a world of actors, costumes, dialogue, and sets. Lynch, whose films are characterized by rich colors and liminal spaces, has created a few interior spaces. In 2024, he created A Thinking Room within Milan’s Salone del Mobile. The club Silencio, created in Paris in 2011, features glittering gold walls and takes its name from the Club Silencio in his 2001 thriller, Mulholland Drive. On a smaller scale, the auteur also created a line of speakers with Bang & Olufsen in 2018 that feature his visual art.
interiors of David Lynch. A Thinking Room, curated by Antonio Monda, Salone Internazionale del Mobile, pavilions 5-7 | image courtesy of Salone del Mobile

Bar Luce and the Cygnus Carriage of Wes Anderson
A Wes Anderson movie is so visually particular that it sparked a whole social media trend of creating short videos with symmetrical compositions, a hazy pastel color palette, and yellow, overlaid sans serif text. It makes sense that he would be tapped to create real-life spaces that bring that dreamy cinematic space to real places. At Fondazione Prada’s space in Milan, Bar Luce’s pinball machine and candy-colored seats welcome guests to experience his quaint world over a gelato or espresso macchiato.
Anderson, who staged almost an entire film aboard a train for The Darjeeling Limited, also redesigned the Cygnus carriage for the Belmond train, the British Pullman. In giving the history of the locomotive, Belmond writes that it’s, ‘a carriage built in the 1950s – [which] has its fair share of cinematic history, featuring in the 1972 film ‘Agatha’ starring Dustin Hoffman and Vanessa Redgrave. It is one of eleven on the British Pullman, whose carriages have hosted royalty, carried statesmen and survived World War II bomb raids over the years.’ A very Andersonian space!
Fondazione Prada, which has long championed the cinematic arts, created a sister space to Anderson’s Bar Luce in the form of Wong Kar Wai’s fine dining space, Mi Shang Prada Rong Zhai. The Hong Kong director has long enchanted audiences with his rich, neon images. Think the romantic, intimate space of In the Mood for Love or the luxurious lights of his TV series, Blossoms Shanghai.
Wong Kar Wai’s fine dining space, Mi Shang Prada Rong Zhai | image courtesy of Mi Shang Prada Rong Zhai
Wong Kar Wai’s fine dining space, Mi Shang Prada Rong Zhai | image courtesy of Mi Shang Prada Rong Zhai
Pedro Almodóvar and Roche Bobois
If there’s one thing that unites Pedro Almodóvar’s movies, it’s the primary color palette that runs through his films. There are some films, like The Room Next Door or The Skin I Live In, where he takes a more restrained approach. But in his other films, like Kika, Volver, or Parallel Mothers, this intense use of color in the sets brings the stories forward, making his films seem more like a dream than a retelling of reality. In 2025, the Spanish director created a line with interiors company Roche Bobois, famous for its Bubble Sofa, designed by Sacha Lakic, that brought Almodóvar’s eye-popping palette off the screen and into some of the company’s most iconic silhouettes.

The future of this Australian island is in danger. How its residents are fighting back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
20:34:18 UTC
05:34:18 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Yessie Mosby paces down the beach near his home on Masig, a teardrop-shaped island in the Torres Strait.
As he walks, he points to the crimson fruit of a wongai tree, a marooned yellow rowboat and a tree trunk full of hiding holes — hallmarks of his generations-long connection to this spot.
But not all Mosby's memories are fond.
The Kulkalgal man recalls a day in 2017, when his son recovered the washed-up remains of his great-great-grandmother while playing in the sand.
"They were picking up her bones like shells off the beach. My son grabbed her skull and placed her in a bucket," he says.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Less than three metres above sea level, Masig's sandy shores are slowly being eaten away by rising tides. Areas once safely inland, such as burial sites, playgrounds, roads and family gardens, are receding before its residents' eyes.
The most dire scientific predictions give the Torres Strait's low-lying islands, including Masig, until 2050 before they become uninhabitable. But Mosby, a climate advocate and chair of the Masigalgal Prescribed Body Corporate (a legal entity that holds and manages native title rights on behalf of Traditional Owners), has taken to measuring the encroaching tides in real time.
"When I was young, the island was here," the 43-year-old says, using the sand as a slate to draw a line.
But with the birth of each of his seven children, now aged five to 15 years, that mark has edged further inland.
Finding his ancestor's remains was the final straw.
"That loved one should be resting in peace. She shouldn't be washed out into the sea," he says.
That's when it hit me. I have to try and do something to save this place.
Five years later, in 2022, Mosby was among eight Torres Strait Islanders who won a landmark UN human rights ruling against the Australian government over climate change inaction. The group have been calling for urgent action to protect Masig and its neighbouring islands.
Over the past decade, the federal and Queensland governments have invested millions in the Torres Strait Seawalls Program, installing thousands of sandbags to mitigate coastal erosion. On Masig, they wrap around the island's northwestern side to form a seawall.
But so far, external efforts to hold back the tide have been inadequate.
One way Traditional Owners are seeking to take back control of their future is by establishing a new Indigenous Protected Area (IPA). Unlike other conservation zones, such as national parks or marine reserves, IPAs are voluntarily declared and managed by First Nations Australians.
In 2025, the Masigilgal IPA was created to shelter fragile reef systems, culturally significant species and ancient knowledge from the onslaught of climate change. Officially, it covers the 11 uninhabited coral cays surrounding Masig, but much of the conservation work extends to the island too.
Mosby hopes it will give Masigalgal people, the Traditional Owners of Masig, an advantage in the race to save the island.
"We have the Western knowledge of how climate change works [with] traditional knowledge of how the tide runs, the current flows, what occupies these islands, how the island actually sits," he says.
'It was just bare'
Formerly known as Yorke Island, Masig is a coral cay in the Torres Strait's Central Islands cluster. It is situated closer to Papua New Guinea than Australia and is home to just under 300 people.
Life on Masig is unhurried. It has one narrow landing strip, one supermarket, one primary school and one cafe — MigiYarn Cafe. It's been operating for nearly a decade and is the go-to watering hole for locals to meet and chat.
It's been operating for nearly a decade, but this year, the cafe has cemented itself as the go-to watering hole for locals to meet and chat. Beyond the sound of its swaying hammocks and whirring coffee machine, the lapping ocean is never far away, and a constant reminder of the risks of running a beachfront business on Masig.
Everyone here has a story about climate change. Kimiko Mosby, the cafe's co-owner, recalls a particularly extreme bout of weather in 2018.
"We had the high tides, we had the winds, and we had rain. It was just bang, bang, bang," she says.
"It took a few metres from us."
Mosby had just planted some coconut trees in front of the cafe, which were swept away overnight.
"It was just bare."
So when the opportunity arose to help shape the island's IPA, Mosby jumped at it.
"The consultation process nutted out exactly what we wanted, our input, what our aspirations were, how we saw it and how we wanted to manage it," she says.
After eight years of planning, the Masigilgal IPA was dedicated in July 2025 and now covers 245 hectares of land.
"It's funny, because we always knew Masig and the surrounding islands belong to us, but local people now have a hand in managing our places," she says.
The IPA is run by a small group of environmental rangers from the Torres Strait Regional Authority (TSRA), a Commonwealth agency. Most of these rangers are Masigalgal, or from neighbouring islands, and have become "a vital part of our community," Mosby says.
Revegetation and 'the tree of life'
Life on Masig has traditionally revolved around its trove of ocean goods — from historic pearling and shell trades to modern crayfish and prawn exports. But one resource offers hope for the future.
Known locally as 'the tree of life', and in Miriam Mir (a traditional language of the eastern Torres Strait) as "urab", coconut palms are ubiquitous on Masig — so much so that glaring yellow signs warn passersby of falling coconuts.
At a revegetation site on the island's northwestern side, palms of all heights shoot toward the sky, their fibrous roots holding loose sand and soil in place and helping to buffer against erosion.
Laura Pearson, a Kulkalayg woman and senior ranger supervisor from nearby Warraber Island, is working at the site and explains how they collect ripe, unhusked coconuts and strategically replant them when sprouts form.
"Urab is a really culturally significant plant for us Torres Strait people that provides shelter, slows down the coastal erosion effects, and provides us with water and cooking resources," she says.
The approach is tailored to the island's climate and customs.
"It's important to read our traditional seasons," Pearson says.
Unlike the Western seasonal calendar, the timing and duration of seasons vary according to Masig's traditional calendar. Masigalgal people recognise four seasons — Kuki, Zei, Woerr and Naigai — and look for signs in the wind, weather and wildlife to tell them when one season is expected to change to another.
For example, the season of Kuki — which runs roughly December to April — can be read through signs such as the build-up of big storm clouds and lightning in the far north-west. It's a season when Weiba (rose-crowned fruit doves) become fat and plentiful because of the abundance of ripe fruit on the island.
When SBS News visits, it's leading up to the dry season, which typically runs from September to November.
"We call it Naigai season," Pearson says.
"We don't plant in the dry season; we plant leading up to the monsoon season."
Other native plants are propagated at Mother's Well, the island's plant nursery where rows of green saplings line a polytunnel. Some plants are distributed to community gardens, while others are transported to the IPA's uninhabited islands to boost habitat for local wildlife.
The Masigilgal IPA is a resting spot for more than 30 migratory bird species — including the Eastern Curlew, the world's largest migratory shorebird. According to the Australian Conservation Foundation, global populations have declined by around 80 per cent in the last 30 years. In Australia, the species is now listed as critically endangered due to severe habitat destruction.
Revegetation is a small part of the management puzzle across Masig's uninhabited islands. Rangers must also tackle marine debris, ghost nets (discarded fishing nets), invasive plants and feral species. A day's work might involve dealing with an outbreak of leucaena, a rapidly growing woody weed, or wild pigs that disturb sacred sites, says Pearson.
"Our job is to get in and eradicate it or control it," she says.
"It's never-ending, but it's the best job in the world."
Beyond Masig
Masigilgal is one of five IPAs scattered throughout the more than 274 islands in the Torres Strait. All IPAs are on uninhabited islands covered by Native Title, many of which were historically used for temporary camps and seasonal hunting. As part of the national IPA program, they receive federal government funding to fuel conservation work.
Nationally, more than 95 IPAs span Land and Sea Country from the Tiwi Islands to Tasmania. But Ilana Foster, TSRA's IPA and traditional knowledge specialist, says that navigating a vast body of ocean poses different challenges to mainland Australia.
Sitting where the Coral and Arafura Seas converge, the Strait is the unofficial dugong capital of the world – more than 100,000 of the marine mammals reside in its vast seagrass meadows. It also harbours six of the world's seven turtle species, three of which regularly nest on islands in the region.
However, sea-level rise is beginning to disturb these patterns.
"The high tides are eating away at the sand beaches, so the amount of ground that turtles have to lay in is reduced," Foster says.
Rangers carry out routine marine surveys, checking for changes and deformities in the number of turtle eggs in a nest, called a clutch.
Some IPAs are also facing existential threats, says Vic McGrath, the Torres Strait's first IPA coordinator.
Warul Kawa (or Deliverance Island), an IPA in the far north-western corner of the Torres Strait, is steeped in spiritual significance.
"When you die, all Torres Strait Islanders go there. Your soul heads off to its final place in the west," McGrath explains.
But this sacred island and its IPA are facing a multitude of risks, from shipping lanes and oil spills to the growing threat of illegal fishing.
"Some of those newer IPAs are based on little islands adjacent to shipping channels. I'm concerned about modern impacts", he says.
Amid these dangers, Foster says rangers are documenting vital cultural data.
The reality is that these places are disappearing.
"What else can you do when something is gone but look back on images, recordings, written works," she says.
Since 2009, TSRA's traditional ecological knowledge program has recorded the names of local flora and fauna. Previously, this information had been passed down orally or chronicled in outdated Western anthropological studies, notably from an 1800s historic expedition by AC Haddon.
Now, these community resources developed via the IPA act as a benchmark for monitoring change.
"You can see that the seasons have changed significantly, that they're not happening at the same time," Foster says.
It takes a village
For now, First Nations-led solutions are shouldering a heavy burden.
At Yessie Mosby's camp, rangers have provided makeshift buffers made from densely packed coconut fibres to help fortify the shoreline.
"It's working. I reckon if this wasn't here, this tree would've been washed out," he says.
At times, it can feel like paddling upstream.
Mosby points out that Masig has a tiny carbon footprint, and despite their best efforts on a local level, it will take large-scale action to meaningfully slow climate change.
"We are at the frontline and getting hit by [Mother Nature's] fury. That gets me very upset; it makes my blood boil," he says.
"If the world stops burning fossil fuels and reduces the emissions down to 1.5C, then they will contribute to [saving] an ancient race."
In September 2026, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) released a report warning that global temperature rise is set to cross 1.5C, exceeding global targets.
"You know it's not just an island for us. It's not just our home," Mosby says.
This island is our school. This island is our maternity ward. This island is our science lab. This island is our library.
He warns that climate change drives culture into extinction.
"Masig has a nickname within the Torres Strait. They call this island the teardrop of the Straits. When you leave this island, you shed tears."
Although it is hard to estimate the exact rate of erosion, Masig's distinctive tip is shrinking, slowly being blurred by rising tides.
We know that this island is hurt. She is seeking help
"Already we've got traditional methods of trying to save these islands, but it has to take a village. It has to take everybody to pull as one to try and save these islands."

The baby in this photo isn't the story. What it reveals is
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
20:33:46 UTC
05:33:46 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
The sun is still hours from rising, but Western Australian senator Fatima Payman is already on her first coffee, getting ready for another day of work — and caring for a newborn.
It could be 2am or 3am. She isn't sure anymore. These days, she says time is more of a concept than a clock.
The independent senator isn't just working to an east coast time zone from Perth; she's working around the unpredictable schedule of a new mum.
"Some days it is really tough, and there are some really good days," Payman tells SBS News during an interview in Perth.
I think overall my perspective has shifted in realising how tough women have it out there.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Payman is the first WA senator to have a baby while serving in parliament — a distinction that comes with its own challenges, including the more than 3,600km distance between Perth and Canberra.
Between herself and her husband, Jacob Stokes, a former WA Labor staffer, Payman says they are juggling the demands of parenthood with support from their respective families in Perth.
Their daughter, Aliyah, was born in May this year, the couple's first child, and the family spent the first four months in Perth before Payman returned to Canberra to work earlier this month.
Payman's experience highlights a question that goes beyond one senator: As more women enter politics, has parliament changed enough to accommodate the realities of having a family?
The challenge of motherhood in parliament
Payman's working day now unfolds around the needs of a newborn, with the routines of motherhood squeezed between emails, meetings and the demands of parliamentary work.
There are feeds, nappy changes and playtime, followed by putting Aliyah to sleep and expressing breast milk to ensure there is enough for the day.
In between, Payman reads emails, keeps up to date with political developments and attends virtual meetings.
By the afternoon, she is often driving to community meetings and other events, sometimes with Aliyah in the baby seat, before returning home for the evening routine.
"I am incredibly blessed to have a supportive family around me.
"As they say, it takes a village to raise a baby."
After Aliyah was born, Payman says she did not take an extended break from work.
"I didn't have a maternity leave; it was really right back to work as soon as I could, answering calls," she says.
As an independent senator, Payman's circumstances differ from those of senators in larger political parties, where responsibilities can be shared among multiple members.
She became an independent after crossing the floor in June 2024 to support a motion recognising Palestinian statehood. She resigned from the Labor Party the following month and, in October 2024, launched her own political party, Australia's Voice.
Payman is currently the only senator representing Australia's Voice.
"I had various Labor backbench senators reach out, some have even sent me gifts which are really lovely," she says.
"They told me they would be able to take three to four months of complete maternity leave, and that's a luxury not afforded to independent senators."
A parliament adapting to parenting
Payman's experience comes after years of scrutiny of the parliamentary workplaces and whether they are equipped to accommodate people with caring responsibilities.
In 2021, hundreds of people were interviewed as part of Sex Discrimination Commissioner Kate Jenkins' Set the Standard review into the culture of Commonwealth parliamentary workplaces. Their testimony highlighted power imbalances, gender inequality, a lack of accountability, entitlement and exclusion as contributing to a toxic workplace culture.
The review also identified parliament's long and irregular sitting hours as a factor affecting the well-being of people working there, and made 28 recommendations aimed at creating safer, more diverse and inclusive workplaces.
A 2022 report by UNSW Sydney and the Pathways to Politics Program for Women examined the barriers facing parliamentarians with caring responsibilities, noting that women continue to shoulder a disproportionate share of unpaid care work.
The report warned that if parliament could not reconcile caring responsibilities with its democratic duties, women could be discouraged from entering politics or remaining in parliament long-term.
It proposed five changes to make parliament more "care-friendly", including changes to sitting hours and the parliamentary calendar, formal parental leave for politicians, greater access to childcare and more use of virtual proceedings.
The report also recommended changing rules that classified children as "strangers" and did not permit them in parliamentary chambers.
Some of those changes are now visible inside parliament, from childcare facilities to the rules governing babies in the chambers.
Parliament House has an onsite childcare centre, as well as parents' rooms and facilities for nursing and infant care. The building is also accredited as a Breastfeeding Friendly Workplace.
Senators can breastfeed an infant in the chamber and, at the discretion of the Senate president, briefly care for an infant during proceedings, provided the business of the Senate is not disrupted.
That shift came into focus in 2017, when Greens senator Larissa Waters — now the party's federal leader — brought her baby into the Senate chamber to breastfeed during a sitting.
A turning point for parents in parliament
For Waters, bringing her baby into the chamber exposed a simple mismatch between parliamentary rules and the realities of being a new parent.
"I think all workplaces should be flexible and support new parents. Not just mum[s], but dads should get that flexibility," Waters tells SBS News.
Discussing the watershed moment in 2017, Waters says she was not thinking about making history when she breastfed her daughter during a sitting. Her partner texted her that their daughter was hungry and couldn't wait another five minutes, so she brought her into the chamber to feed her.
"To be honest, I wasn't thinking about the moment it would become; I was just thinking bubba was hungry and I still had to move a motion about preventing black lung disease in Queensland coal mine workers," she says.
Since then, babies have been brought into both the Senate and House of Representatives, including by male politicians. In 2024, Victorian senator Raff Ciccone became the first father to bring a baby into the chamber.
"That modelling of shared care is so important because we know dads only take about 20 per cent of the [primary] parental leave they are entitled to take," Waters says.
"And unless you start that good quality relationship and you share that care from day one, you end up with the mum doing all the work."
Waters says she was able to balance caring for her daughter with her parliamentary responsibilities.
I am a politician and I am a mum, I am both things at all times.
Has female representation changed parliament?
Sue Williamson, an associate professor at UNSW who specialises in areas of gender equality in the workplace, says federal Labor's push to increase the number of women in parliament does not necessarily mean the institution is gender-equal.
"There has been an increase in numbers of women in parliament over the past few years, particularly since the Albanese government got in," she tells SBS News.
"Women now make up almost 50 per cent of parliamentarians, but gender inequalities still exist."
Williamson says gender equality depends not just on who is represented in parliament, but on workplace culture and whether people can balance political careers with caring responsibilities.
Gender equality is more about having equal representation.
"It also goes to the culture of the workplace and we know that historically Parliament House has been a really blokey workplace."
A different challenge for an independent
For Payman, Williamson says being the sole senator representing her party puts her in a unique position, with fewer resources and colleagues to rely on for support.
"Being an independent senator means she doesn't have a lot of resources," she says.
"Already we are hearing from her that she is using her family, her partner, and relatives to provide care for the baby, which is great [that] she has that support network, but not everyone does have that support."
Williamson says Payman's experience, still attracting attention, raises a broader question of whether parliament has changed enough to support politicians with young families.
What really struck me with this story is that, why is this a story? Why are we still talking about this in 2026?
"When male politicians have babies, it's part of life, it's business as usual because they've got someone that can look after their kid."
Waters says babies in parliament can also remind politicians who they are making decisions for.
"There is a sense of delight when there is a baby in the chamber," she says.
"It's one of those moments that really breaks down the political party lines and it is a lovely reality check because it reminds you you are here for people, and that little child's future is being decided by the decisions that you take."
Waters says while parliament has made progress, there is still a broader issue of gender inequality across Australian workplaces.
I think the culture has changed, but we still have a long way to go and more importantly, workplaces around the country have a long way to go.

Conspiracy theories appear to erode public faith in meritocracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
20:00:57 UTC
05:00:57 KST

When people buy into conspiracy theories, their faith in the fairness of society begins to erode. New research published in Political Psychology shows that exposure to conspiratorial narratives directly reduces the belief that resources are distributed based on merit, equality, or need. The findings suggest that suspicions of hidden plots foster a deep distrust of institutions, coloring how individuals view the basic rules of social and economic life.
Meritocracy is the idea that society rewards talent and hard work. Many political leaders and cultural narratives lean heavily on this concept to motivate citizens and justify existing economic structures. Alongside equality and need, meritocracy forms the foundation of what psychologists call distributive justice. This term refers to the perceived fairness of how a community divides its wealth, opportunities, and resources.
Public perception of these justice principles dictates how well a society functions. When people believe the system is fair, they are more likely to cooperate and follow the rules. Alternatively, widespread perceptions of injustice can foster resentment and social instability.
Researchers have extensively studied how income disparities and social mobility affect these views. Little research has examined how conspiratorial thinking influences ideas about fairness. Conspiracy theories typically allege that malevolent, secretive groups are orchestrating events for their own benefit. Because these narratives frame elites as exploitative and corrupt, they naturally conflict with the notion of a fair society.
A team of researchers led by Qi Zhao, a psychologist at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, set out to test this dynamic. They wanted to know if believing in a conspiracy theory makes people less likely to view the world as fair. The team designed a combination of survey analyses and experiments to see if conspiratorial beliefs alter how people perceive the distribution of resources.
In their first study, the researchers analyzed data from the World Value Survey, a large international dataset. The sample included 90,837 participants across 68 different societies. The researchers looked at survey items measuring beliefs in election fraud conspiracies, such as the idea that rich people buy elections or that television news manipulates voters.
They compared these responses to a question asking whether hard work usually brings a better life. The results showed a consistent negative relationship between conspiracy beliefs and faith in meritocracy. People who endorsed election fraud narratives were less likely to believe that effort leads to success.
This pattern held true regardless of whether a country had a highly democratic government or an authoritarian one. The researchers also accounted for national differences in economic inequality, gross domestic product, and expert ratings of corruption. The link between conspiracy beliefs and diminished faith in meritocracy remained intact across these varied environments.
Because the survey could only show a correlation, the researchers conducted an experiment to test for a causal effect. They recruited 403 participants in the United States for an online study. Half of the participants read a news report about a fictional local government misusing public funds, accompanied by evidence supporting the conspiracy theory. The other half read the same report but with evidence refuting the allegations.
Afterward, participants rated their agreement with statements about how resources were handled in the fictional community. Those exposed to the supporting evidence reported lower belief in meritocracy. They also expressed less belief in the principles of equality, which assumes everyone gets an equal share, and need, which dictates that resources go to those who require them most.
The experiment demonstrated that adopting a conspiracy belief directly lowered perceptions of distributive justice. The researchers also tested potential psychological mechanisms behind this shift. They found that distrust in government acted as a primary bridge, explaining how exposure to the conspiracy theory led to lower ratings of fairness.
The researchers then replicated this experiment with 788 participants in China to see if the effect crossed cultural boundaries. Chinese culture traditionally places a stronger emphasis on equality and need compared to the merit-focused culture of the United States. The scenario in this experiment involved a local government colluding with the media to suppress negative news and control the public.
Just as in the American sample, participants who read evidence validating the conspiracy theory reported lower faith in all three justice principles. They were less likely to believe that the fictional society rewarded hard work, distributed resources equally, or helped those in need. Institutional distrust once again served as the psychological mechanism driving these negative perceptions.
To test whether these dynamics exist outside of civic government, the team conducted a final experiment focused on a corporate workplace. They recruited another 403 American participants and asked them to imagine working for an electronics company. The participants read a rumor that the company’s administration was deliberately hiding the presence of dangerous chemicals to avoid bad publicity.
Similar to the previous experiments, participants received information either confirming or debunking the corporate cover-up. Those in the confirmation group displayed a pronounced drop in their belief that the company operated fairly. They doubted that the administration rewarded good work, treated employees equally, or accommodated worker needs.
The researchers concluded that conspiracy theories degrade trust in administrative bodies, which in turn poisons the perception of fairness in an organizational setting. The effect was especially pronounced for the principles of equality and need. Meritocracy perceptions were also reduced, though they remained slightly more resilient, likely because performance-based rewards are deeply ingrained in corporate structures.
A few caveats apply to how these results translate to the real world. The experiments relied on fictional scenarios to manipulate beliefs, which might not perfectly mirror the deeply entrenched narratives people encounter online or in their communities. Real-world conspiracy theories often tie into long-standing political identities, making them harder to accept or reject based on a single piece of evidence.
The studies focused entirely on conspiracy theories involving powerful institutions like governments and corporate boards. It is unknown if conspiracies targeting marginalized groups or ordinary citizens would have the same effect on perceptions of societal fairness. Future research might explore whether narratives about less powerful groups also erode trust in the broader economic system.
Additionally, while the experiments showed that conspiracy beliefs cause a drop in perceived fairness, the reverse might also happen outside the laboratory. Experiencing genuine unfairness might make people more susceptible to conspiratorial thinking. Examining this cycle could help psychologists understand how institutional distrust deepens over time.
The study, “Not a real meritocracy? How conspiracy beliefs reduce perceived distributive justice,” was authored by Qi Zhao, Jan-Willem van Prooijen, and Giuliana Spadaro.

Stop the Bibi bashing and focus on the issues, not the man - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:51:12 UTC
04:51:12 KST

To set the record straight, I have never voted for Benjamin Netanyahu or his party, and doubt that I ever will. But he is the prime minister, and I must respect the office he holds. To do otherwise is a blight on democracy.
People who truly believe in democracy must accept the results of an election. They can voice their protests against the policies of the administration, but they should respect the nation’s leaders.
An attack on the leaders contributes to paving the path to anarchy.
I don’t have a clue how many of the stories about Netanyahu are true or false, but I do know that the more he is attacked by Israelis, the more ammunition is given to Israel’s enemies.
Personally, I think he made a mistake in holding off a state commission of inquiry into what led to the horrific events of October 7. Whether he is considered responsible or not is less important than learning where Israel erred, and how not to repeat the same error, which is commonly referred to in Hebrew as the conceptzia.
They’re blaming Netanyahu, they’re blaming Gadi Eisenkot, they’re blaming Benny Gantz, and a whole bunch of others who were part of the decision making process at security meetings over the years.
October 7 didn’t just happen out of the blue. It was a meticulously planned operation. What’’s important is how it developed below the radar of Israel’s intelligence network, not what time Bibi got out of bed.
How is it that Mossad was able to score points in Iran, but missed the train in Gaza?
It’s not as if there were no warning signs. There were, and they were reported – and they were ignored.
Why?
Were there senior officers who objected to female spotters, and thought they should be concentrating on their domestic skills instead of serving in the army?
Or did they simply think that the young women were panicking because they belonged to the so-called weaker sex, and simply treated their warnings as false alarms?
Every possible scenario must be explored, and any commission of inquiry should include mystery writers and film makers whose creative minds will come up with all kinds of possibilities that may not occur to military personnel.
People change as they get older, and Bibi has probably changed a lot since he was a heroic young soldier under the command of Ehud Barak, and the two rescued hostages from a Sabena plane that was hijacked in flight by Palestinian terrorists, as it traveled from Vienna to Tel Aviv. That was more than half a century ago. Even though I totally disagree with Netanyahu politically, I have every confidence that he is no less a patriot today than he was then – though these days, he’s a lot more cautious.
But Barak, whose voice is frequently heard in anti-Bibi circles, is not cautious. It is perfectly legitimate for Barak, a product and former leader of the Left, to challenge policies set by Bibi, a product and current leader of the Right. But Barak should not be attacking Bibi’s character, especially when giving interviews to foreign media.
To do so encourages further character assassination, such as that displayed in the AI-generated judicial reform campaign video released by Bezalel Smotrich, in which he showed Chief Justice Isaac Amit and Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara being arrested by police and dragged through the streets. This was so outrageously below the belt that even people on the Right who support judicial reform were outraged.
While I understand what it means to bereaved families to have Bibi either admit to being accountable or having a commission of inquiry decide that he’s accountable, it doesn’t really serve any purpose. It doesn’t bring back the dead. It doesn’t heal the wounded. It doesn’t stop the grief and the mourning.
All it does is remove him from office and provide some temporary satisfaction for people who want to see him suffer as they have suffered.
Then again, it’s a different kind of suffering.
Netanyahu has been trying to make amends in recent weeks, but that may be because of the elections, or simply because he’s had more time to think about the situation and to display a more humane side of his personality.
As there is no likelihood of the establishment of a commission of inquiry before the elections, let us at least look at the issues on which the coalition and the opposition agree and make that the foundation of a temporary truce that could lead to greater solidarity in the future. There will still be disputes, but there are disputes within political parties, not just between opposing parties. However, disputes do not need to be violent or disrespectful.
The idea is for each side to understand where the other is coming from and where it hopes to go.
There are people on both sides who do dialogue with each other, just as there are Israelis and Palestinians who are not only neighbors but friends with different opinions.
We need to accept that others do not have to think as we do. The marketplace of different ideas can lead to many great things.
While we continue our internal squabbles, the enemy perceives us as weak. This was among the many theories of what prompted the Hamas attack. Israel’s national unity was crumbling from within – a factor that may have indicated the time was ripe for an external assault.
We dare not make that mistake again. Avoiding it starts with new rules to the game. Be critical of unjust policies, but don’t attack the leader. In other words, stop the Bibi bashing and focus on the issues, not the man.

Man charged in US boy’s disappearance after 33 years
Ishani Desai
- George Burdynski Jr disappeared in 1993 at age 10 near his Maryland home, prompting a large search by police and volunteers that lasted over 33 years.
- Joseph Lynch was recently arrested and charged with second-degree murder and sexual abuse in connection with George's disappearance, after a 47-year-old witness came forward.
- The witness admitted to killing George under Lynch's influence, but has not been charged; George's body remains missing.
AI generated
NEW YORK – When 10-year-old George Burdynski Jr hopped on his bike on May 24, 1993, near his Maryland home, it was the last time his family saw him.
The disappearance of George, who was also known as Junior, shocked Prince George’s County in Maryland and prompted a large search by law enforcement, including the FBI. Volunteers also joined the search.
But the case languished for more than 33 years.
Now, investigators say they have arrested a 61-year-old man, Joseph Lynch, who has been charged with second-degree murder, rape and other sexual abuse charges in connection with George’s disappearance.
Another person, a 47-year-old man, whom Lynch also sexually assaulted, admitted to beating George to death, authorities said.
That unidentified man has not been charged, the Prince George’s County Police Department said. The county state attorney’s office would not comment on Sept 18.
“We held on to hope for 33 years,” said Virginia Burdynski, George’s sister, at a news conference on Sept 17. “This is not what we prayed for.”
Investigators got a break in the case after a witness, the 47-year-old man, stepped forward in June and said he was with George and Lynch at the time of the boy’s disappearance.
The witness, who was 13 in 1993, lived in George’s neighbourhood.
Lynch physically and sexually assaulted the witness on the day that George disappeared, according to a statement of charges.
On that same day, Lynch forced the witness to sexually assault George while Lynch watched, the statement said.
The witness told investigators he could not direct his anger toward Lynch and instead targeted George, who was younger and smaller, the statement said.
“The witness admitted repeatedly punching and kicking the victim until the victim stopped moving,” the statement said. “The witness recalled observing blood coming from the victim’s head and believed that the victim was dead or had been fatally injured.”
Lynch retrieved a knife, tarp and rope and rolled George inside, the statement said.
Lynch and the witness carried George’s body to a location in Prince George’s County and disposed of him, the statement said.
George’s body has never been found.
“Taken together, the suspect’s actions before, during and immediately after the offences establish that he was an active participant in the continuous course of criminal conduct that resulted in the victim’s death,” the statement said. NYTIMES

====================================================================================================

Yom Kippur 2026: Does a text message or social media post count as a real apology?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:34:12 UTC
04:34:12 KST

Aside from fasting for 25 hours, one of the most challenging requirements of the Day of Atonement is asking forgiveness from someone we hurt or offended in the past year.
“Coming to Yom Kippur and banging on your chest doesn’t do anything. God doesn’t forgive on your behalf. It doesn’t work that way,” said Zev M. Shandalov, a former Chicago pulpit rabbi and an educator, lecturer, author, and community rabbi in Ma’aleh Adumim since 2009.
“We have to go to that person and ask for forgiveness with a heartfelt ‘I’m sorry.’ The struggle today versus, let’s say, just 20 years ago is how that apology should appear.”
Avoiding uncomfortable face-to-face confrontations is easier than ever. We can send texts or voice messages, write emails, or post on social media our requests for forgiveness – mehila, in Hebrew.
Do these modern modes of communication count, or are they just cowardly cop-outs?
Be authentic
Hillel Fuld, a tech columnist and Israel advocate with approximately 750,000 social-media followers, spends a lot of time interacting with people online.
Yet when it comes to apologizing, he said, “sending a text message just doesn’t feel authentic. I get a ton of mass messages before Yom Kippur – Please forgive me, blah, blah, blah – but I don’t do that. If you’re going to ask forgiveness, be authentic about it.”
Fuld said that if he feels the need to beg someone’s pardon, “I don’t care if we’re in the digital age or not – I’m gonna get in my car and go meet that person.”
Shandalov, too, said that “the best option is to physically go to the person asking for forgiveness.” He cited the 12th-century sage Maimonides (Rambam), who wrote that proper repentance requires meeting with the wronged party.
“Of course, the Rambam didn’t have WhatsApp, but he could have said it’s okay to write a letter. But he says no, you have to have an interaction with the person and truly ask for forgiveness,” Shandalov said.
“If that’s not possible, do it in a video chat or phone call. However, sometimes saying ‘I’m sorry’ directly is a very tough thing to do. A voice note is the next best option because at least the recipient can hear the inflection in the sender’s voice.”
He considers the least desirable method to be a “general vanilla message on Facebook that says, ‘To all those whom I might have hurt, I’m sorry.’ There’s no meaning behind that.”
Nobody wants to be a checklist item
A different perspective on mass apology messages is offered by lecturer and author Oriya Mevorach, whose Afarkeset Institute provides educational tools, lectures, and workshops for navigating postmodern and Western culture through a Jewish worldview.
“The problem is not the medium,” she said.
“It’s even a blessing today that we have the opportunity to write something general. In the age of social media, we communicate with so many people – sometimes thousands of people – and we can use the same platform to make amends.”
The problem is that blanket social-media apology posts rarely include the elements necessary to trigger a forgiveness response. Instead, they may be perceived as insulting or insincere.
“What people don’t want to see is that you’re saying sorry as a checklist item. Nobody wants to be a checklist item,” she said.
“When I want someone to ask me for forgiveness, first I would like them to acknowledge what they did wrong; and second, to acknowledge that they know I was insulted or offended by what they did. If a general message would include even just the first part, it’s not that bad,” Mevorach explained.
“If a person would write, for example, ‘I know I often come across as offensive and I sometimes attack people online, and I’m aware of this weakness of mine, and I want to apologize to anyone who was insulted by me,’ I think that’s legit,” she said. “The text must be elaborated enough so people understand we are taking responsibility for a specific action.”
The ideal approach, however, is to send a direct personal message containing “the exact words that the recipient would like to hear.”
Because many of us may have difficulty crafting such a message, she suggests using AI tools such as ChatGPT to help phrase a personalized request for mehila.
Accepting a texted apology
The wording of a texted apology will determine how it is received, Shandalov agreed.
“If you feel the text message that someone sends you is adequate, then accept the apology, say ‘thank you very much,’ and put it behind you,” he counseled.
“But if you can’t accept it, you should respond, ‘Listen, I think this requires more of a discussion. I don’t want to make you feel awkward, but we need to talk about some stuff before I could really give you true forgiveness.’ And that’s fine.”
Jewish tradition stipulates that one is permitted to spurn an apology twice, “because sometimes we can’t forgive something or we don’t think the apology is sincere. By the third time you have to say, ‘Yes, I forgive you.’ If you don’t, you are considered a rasha, a bad person – although it depends on the specific situation,” he added.
According to Shandalov, one must ask for mehila even from a deceased person by vocalizing the apology at the person’s grave.
But as Fuld can attest, it’s certainly preferable to seek forgiveness while the wronged party is still among the living.
Years ago, he got into a heated political discussion with an unknown commenter on his Facebook page. “Unfortunately, I lost my cool and called him a self-hating Jew,” he recalled.
A week later, Fuld was asked by the marketing department of a client company to participate in a phone call pitching the company’s story to a journalist.
“At the end of the conversation, the journalist is like, ‘Okay, fantastic, I’ll write the story. Oh, and Hillel, by the way: Remember the guy you called a self-hating Jew last week on Facebook? That was me.’”
Fuld felt devastated.
“When you’re on the Internet, you don’t put a face to it. Speaking to someone whom I called that name was really upsetting for me. So I apologize profusely, and he’s like, ‘It’s totally cool. I know how the Internet works. We get worked up. Totally fine, all good.’ And that was the end of that.”
A few days later, Fuld was shocked to hear that the journalist had died suddenly and unexpectedly. “I was so grateful that I’d had a chance to make it right with him. The fact that I was able to correct my mistake before he died was of astronomic importance to me.”
The Talmud, said Shandalov, encourages us to emulate God’s attributes. “God is described as mohel v’sole’ah, forgiving and pardoning. So it’s important to understand that granting forgiveness is not just repairing a relationship. It’s a godly act.”

The Haredi Public: A politically responsible voice from Israel's ultra-Orthodox public - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:34:05 UTC
04:34:05 KST

Unfortunately, we have gotten used to snarling haredi (ultra-Orthodox) rabbis and politicians who dismiss the concerns of the general Israeli public and disassociate themselves from the burden (actually, the privilege) of running and defending the State of Israel.
By their own admission, all they seek is sinecures for their secluded public, especially the narrowly self-defined Torah/yeshiva “world.”
From this distorted, so-called “Torah perspective,” the task of haredi politicians has been to secure haredi interests against Israeli society and to defend “their people” from “our state” – the “impure” and threatening Zionist state.
Alas, “our” army is not their responsibility. “Our” economy is not their responsibility either. God alone, “their” God, will take care of the bigger picture, along with the beleaguered Israeli taxpayer who pays through his nose and the “suckers” who serve in the Israeli army.
One might have thought that the trauma, suffering, financial deprivation, and household disruption of the past three years in the general Israeli public and in the “Torani” (ardently Torah observant) Religious Zionist community would shock the haredi community out of its crushingly insular shell.
One had hoped that honorable haredi leaders would be stirred toward somewhat increased integration in Israeli society and would nudge forward toward national service in frameworks specially attuned to haredi sensibilities.
One might have imagined great haredi leaders participating in at least one or two of the many funerals for fallen soldiers, or showing up at soldier shiva houses to pay condolences, or quietly taking a minyan (prayer quorum) of their boys late at night to pray at the Mount Herzl military cemetery.
But nada. No movement at the leadership level. Haredi politicians, like the recently deposed MK Moshe Gafni of the Degel HaTorah/UTJ party, spent 40 years insulting and sneering at the secular and Religious Zionist publics and only doubled down on this over the past three years.
Despite October 7, “mainstream” haredi politicians have stuck to the line that “yeshiva boys” (about 100,000 of them) cannot be drafted in any minimal way (whether they are really learning Torah full time or not) or educated any differently.
These leaders are purposefully and devastatingly cut off from the war reality that most Israelis are living. Worse still, they are unflinchingly unfeeling toward the broader public, as their spokesmen unfortunately have made clear.
This is a historic tragedy that has the potential to crash the modern State of Israel, no less, in the Heavens and on earth.
Fortunately, and finally, substantial numbers of haredi Israelis are moving away from this hostile approach. They think for themselves and are seeking alternative political leadership.
They realize that the rejectionist, protectionist posture described above may have been sustainable when the haredi community was a small and embattled minority. It cannot provide a vision for a community rapidly becoming a central pillar in Israeli society. It does not provide a satisfying vision for haredi people themselves.
Enter the Haredi Public party, running for the Knesset for the first time. The new political party begins from a wholly different premise from that of UTJ or Shas: that they, haredi people, are part of the Israeli story.
They do not mean to abandon haredi identity; they believe that haredi Judaism is strong enough to take responsibility for Torah, family, and community, as well as responsibility for sustainable livelihood, defense, civic life, and the future of Israel.
As the visionary chair of the new party’s rabbinic committee, Yehoshua Pfeffer said at the party launch event: “Our initiative means moving from a politics of fear to a politics of hope. It means hope that haredi young people will no longer feel forced to choose between belonging to their community and building a responsible life within the Jewish state.
“It means that the haredi world believes it can grow, mature, and assume a larger and constructive role in strengthening and defending Israel – without losing its soul.
“God did not bring millions of Jews back to the land of our fathers for Israel to fail. Nor did haredi society build its extraordinary world of Torah, family, charity, and community in order to remain forever on the margins of the national story. The next chapter can be different. The question is whether we have the courage to write it.”
The new party, led by its articulate and measured chairman Moti Leitner (a hassidic deputy mayor of Beit Shemesh and a software professional), advocates for protecting those who truly learn Torah full-time while advancing meaningful service for all those who do not, and for giving haredi youth the necessary educational tools to succeed in life and contribute to the Israeli economy and society.
This means working with, not against, the IDF to create haredi service tracks from hesder programs to special brigades and soft military-industrial and civilian-security national service frameworks.
It means rapidly and massively expanding the state-supported haredi school stream that teaches the core curriculum of English, math, science, and civics alongside Torah and Talmud, and which prepares its graduates for potential college study.
Leitner explained that the party was born out of deep conversations with representatives of many haredi communities who felt their voice was not being heard and their needs were not represented within the existing haredi political parties. This includes working haredi people, as well as professionally successful women, haredi immigrants from abroad, and more.
A voice for opportunity and change
These haredim also are horrified by the public and often violent shaming of young haredim who serve in the security force, by campaigns of vilification and terror against even great Torah sages who support cautious change in the haredi world, and by rampant corruption in some haredi municipalities and institutions.
This haredi public also recognizes that too many of its youth are dropping out of schools and feeding the phenomenon of lost street youth without being offered paths that would legitimate a synthesis of haredi identity and professional and national advancement.
Leitner emphasized that the haredi public he represents wants opportunities, not stipends, for haredi young men and women; opportunities to grow and contribute and serve the nation, not to be on the government dole.
The Haredi Public party’s decision to put two women near the top of its Knesset candidate list tells you how bold the new party is. This is unprecedented and long overdue for the haredi public – a breath of fresh air.
The two haredi women in the party – Dr. Nechumi Yaffe (a political psychologist who once worked for the National Security Council) and Ziva Glanz (founder and CEO of the LaShuv olim network) – are impressive leaders.
Rabbi Pfeffer is an intrepid, insightful leader who founded the Iyun Institute at Herut-The Center for Israeli Liberty (formerly the Tikvah Fund), which operates a range of groundbreaking haredi leadership programs and publications.
He is a respected religious court judge, served in the IDF, chairs the public board of Netzah Yehuda, the haredi Nahal brigade, clerked at Israel’s Supreme Court, and is a professor at Hebrew University’s law school.
Pfeffer is truly a model par excellence of a haredi community leader “taking responsibility” for the future of Israel, not shunning and deprecating Israel. I am proud to consider him a close friend!
In fact, I am considering voting for the Haredi Public 40 days from now, even though I do not belong to the ultra-Orthodox community and I dissent from the party platform, which would still give, at least for the next while, a broad exemption from conscription for full-time yeshiva men (not including hesder programs).
This new party – this bold new haredi movement – needs electoral support. Recent polls indicate that it has captured the imagination of the haredi street and the support of about 10% of haredi voters, amounting to about 100,000 voters (or 2.5 Knesset seats), and rising.
This is an astonishing achievement that portends even greater success in the future, but the minimum threshold for election to the Knesset this year will probably be around 150,000 votes (or four seats).
So the new party needs a boost from non-haredi voters who understand the urgency and promise of the Haredi Public and want it to succeed. This will be a worthwhile investment in the long-term health of Judaism and Israeli society!
The writer is managing senior fellow at the Jerusalem-based Misgav Institute for National Security & Zionist Strategy. The views expressed here are his own. His diplomatic, defense, political, and Jewish world columns over the past 30 years are at davidmweinberg.com.

Israel's ultra-Orthodox community can no longer avoid the hard conversations - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:33:51 UTC
04:33:51 KST

Haredim (ultra-Orthodox) made up roughly 2% of Israel’s population 60 years ago. Today, that number is around 13%, and demographers expect it to climb toward 20%, and even 30% within a generation or two. Growth on this scale changes what a community owes the country it lives in.
The haredi community can no longer function as a small group on the margins while others carry the weight of the economy, the army, and civic life. We are becoming a central pillar of this country, and pillars have to hold weight, not just take up space.
Parnassah (livelihood) has turned into something closer to a daily emergency for enormous numbers of haredi families, and I say that from watching it happen to people I know, including myself. Families are large, expenses grow faster than income, and parents find themselves colliding with a reality they were never given the tools to handle.
Our schools do extraordinary work building the spiritual and intellectual life of our children, but somewhere along the way we stopped teaching baseline skills such as arithmetic, English, and skills that any adult needs to earn a living in a modern economy.
Furthermore, about half of haredi students who eventually try to catch up through post-secondary study drop out, because they’re starting from too far behind. That’s a structural failure we built ourselves, and we can unbuild it without touching the yeshiva system meant for those who are meant to sit and study full time.
In my own city, Beit Shemesh, serious plans were underway to build a vocational training complex in the heart of the city, close enough that residents in a community soon approaching half a million people could reach it by bus or on foot and walk away with a trade.
Due to fear of militant elements in the community declaring war on that project, it has stalled. Sadly, this is not an isolated story, but happens across haredi cities whenever anyone tries to build a real path toward employment.
This is an act of harm against thousands of families, dressed up as a defense of Torah values. Torah values include the responsibility to support one’s household. Hazal, our great sages, never envisioned a community where the majority of people live from hand to mouth.
Political leadership bears direct responsibility for where we’ve landed. There is a sitting party leader who has spent the past year traveling the country, threatening institutions that try to switch educational networks to a state haredi system that includes more comprehensive studies in English and math, and this leader told administrators things like, “I’ll come to your house, and I’ll drop a torpedo on it,” and other more graphic language that I won’t share. This is bullying, and it has nothing to do with protecting Torah study.
There are currently 18 haredi Knesset members sitting in the government, and whatever leaves their mouths in public, their operating goal has been singular: make sure no haredi ever serves in the IDF. Everything else is theater.
Haredi hesder yeshivot combine Torah study, IDF service
Since October 7, the army has needed thousands more combat soldiers and thousands more in support roles, and the haredi community is one of the most available sources of manpower in the country. Fourteen haredi hesder yeshivot already exist, some for over a decade, combining serious Torah learning with military service, preserving kashrut, prayer, and ongoing Torah study for soldiers who serve.
These programs work. And yet they get little to no government funding, no institutional recognition, and are treated with open contempt by the same politicians who claim to speak for the haredi public.
When soldiers from our own community went through combat courses, the people who should have stood up publicly to thank them, to embrace them, men like haredi party leaders Yitzhak Goldknopf, Arye Deri, and Moshe Gafni, said nothing.
Worse, our young men who serve report being ignored, mocked, and undermined by the same leadership that benefits politically from claiming to represent all haredim. If those hesder frameworks were properly funded and expanded, we would not be talking about a few hundred participants. We would likely see thousands, and much of the manufactured tension around this issue would fade, because a respected pathway would finally exist for the many young men for whom full-time study was never realistic in the first place.
Ask any of these politicians what they’ve done to solve any of this, and the honest answer, spoken quietly by people close to them, is nothing. When pressed, the answer is always “yes, of course, someone should serve,” delivered in the exact tone people use when they mean the opposite.
Campaigns repeat the line while doing nothing to build it. That gap between what’s said and what’s done is the actual scandal here, more than any individual policy failure.
None of what I’m describing is really about economics or the army as separate issues. It’s about whether haredi leadership is willing to take ownership of the future it keeps promising to protect, instead of hiding behind slogans while institutions collapse and families quietly drown.
The haredi community has the numbers, the talent, and the values to lift this country into a new and bright future; we cannot be the ones to drag it down. What’s missing is leadership honest enough to admit where it has failed, and willing to build something better for the children, the community, and the country we all share.
The writer is chairman of the Haredi Public Party, a new political home for haredim who believe that protecting the world of Torah requires responsible leadership and practical solutions to the challenges facing our community. The party stands for genuine Torah study, increased educational options, dignified employment, appropriate military or national service, economic self-reliance, and a stronger partnership between the haredi community and all of the people of Israel.

A report at the UAE’s Al-Ain media says that “less than 10 days after the Houthis seized control of Yemen’s west coast, Iran rushed to transform this strategic geographical area into a theater of influence for itself.”
Historically, the UAE and therefore its media outlets have good contacts in Aden and the areas of southern Yemen. The UAE played a key role for years in Yemen, backing the Southern Transitional Council against the Houthis.
Now the report indicates that Iran may be playing a role in the area the Houthis captured on September 11 in Yemen. The Houthis launched a rapid offensive up the coast, capturing Mokha and also the areas along the Bab al-Mandab Strait. This is a strategic area.
“Security and media sources revealed that Iran has deployed radar systems in the commanding heights on the western coast, in addition to using the coastal strip as an outlet for smuggling military equipment from Somalia after field visits by its experts,” the report says. It doesn’t say what type of radar may have been placed nearby.
The report argues that this information “reveals Tehran’s efforts to exploit its Houthi arm to transform the Yemeni coast from Hodeidah to Bab al-Mandab into an advanced line of defense for its regional influence network.”
The Houthis have been increasing attacks on Saudi Arabia since the mid-September offensive. The Iranian-backed militias in Iraq also attacked Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline.
In addition to the radar, the Houthis are also involved in smuggling. “Iranian equipment and weapons shipments have recently arrived for the Houthi militias via the western coast.”
Iranian smuggling into Yemen faces challenges
In the past, the Iranians had an easier time smuggling systems into Yemen. Missiles and drone parts arrived by sea. The Iranians recently tried to reopen an air corridor to Yemen in July. The Saudis opposed this. The US has a maritime blockade of Iran. It is unclear how Iran would smuggle items to Yemen.
The sources told Al-Ain that shipments are being unloaded. “After their arrival from the coasts of Somalia, [the shipments] were supervised by Hassan Al-Attas, who is the head of the Fisheries Authority in the Red Sea, based in Hodeidah.”
Al-Ain says that “Attas runs a smuggling network that is a model of an integrated functional hierarchical structure closely linked to the leader Ibrahim Hassan Ismail Al-Madani, while the prominent leader Shaher Al-Qahoum, who trained in Iran, provides it with security cover.”
This type of name-dropping is typical of Al-Ain stories on Yemen. It illustrates the kind of messaging and sourcing behind the report. This is why these reports can matter.
“Al-Attas is also responsible for recruiting fishermen and those with deep maritime experience for the militias, managing smuggling operations from Iran by sea to the shores of Hodeidah, receiving shipments upon arrival, and delivering them to the Houthi militias, as recently reported.”
Houthis intend to create new reality along Red Sea
The goal of the Houthis is to create a new reality along the Red Sea. They are digging trenches in the mountains to prevent the government forces from re-taking the area. They are also increasing activity on the coastline.
“Sources have revealed the installation of radar systems and newly established sites in the highlands overlooking the western coast and the new areas of control.”
The report also says there is activity on Zuqar Island near the Hanish island chain in the Red Sea.
“These steps come as an outcome of visits and field tours conducted by Iranian experts to vital sites, including Bab al-Mandab, the port and airport of Mokha, during which they met with engineers of the Houthi missile force to establish a new phase of threats to international navigation.”
