Detroit Tigers infielder Lee Hao-yu on Friday set Taiwanese MLB records for home runs in a season and hits in a game as he helped his team rally past the Chicago White Sox 11-8.
The 23-year-old went four-for-five with three RBIs and two runs scored, tying the game at 8-8 with a two-run homer in the eighth inning.
The blast was his 10th homer of the season, while his four hits set a single-game MLB record for a Taiwanese.
Photo: AP
“When I actually saw it go out, I just blacked out,” Lee said in a post-game interview, recalling his reaction as the tying home run cleared the wall. “I don’t know what I said or did.”
The Tigers never gave up despite falling behind early, he said, crediting his teammates with responding to their manager’s call for quality at-bats.
Asked what fueled his energy on the field, Lee said: “I mean, I like to win. I don’t like to lose. I helped the team, that’s why I’m so happy.”
Lee’s 10th homer surpassed the previous Taiwanese MLB record of nine set by Yu Chang in 2021 and made him the first Taiwanese to reach double figures in an MLB season.
He also became the first Taiwanese to collect four hits in an MLB game.
Lin Tzu-wei and Chang had previously recorded three-hit games, while Lee had done so twice earlier this season.
Photo: Matt Marton / Imagn Images
Batting ninth and starting at third base, Lee grounded out in the third inning before singling to right field off White Sox starter David Sandlin in the fifth and later scoring.
Detroit, who fell behind 6-1 early and trailed 8-5 after five innings, cut the deficit to 8-6 in the sixth when Lee doubled to deep center field off reliever Chris Murphy. The two-out hit was his 16th double of the season.
In the eighth, Eduardo Valencia was hit by a pitch with one out before Lee sent a pitch from Sean Newcomb over the right-field wall. The homer ignited a five-run inning in which Dillon Dingler delivered the go-ahead RBI single and Riley Greene added a two-run home run.
Photo: AFP
Lee singled again in the ninth to complete his four-hit game, raising his season batting average to .264.

Unknown Publisher

Cuba was plunged into its seventh massive blackout of the year on Friday as fuel shortages wear on the US-blockaded island.
Just five percent of residents in the Cuban capital Havana had power on Friday evening.
“A total disconnection of the electrical system has occurred,” Cuba’s Ministry of Energy and Mines wrote on X.
Photo: Reuters
The nationwide blackout, the 12th since late 2024, occurred after a failure “in the transmission lines” paired with “unstable weather conditions,” state-run utility UNE said.
The island of more than 9 million people endures constant power cuts due to the poor state of its aging thermoelectric plants, but the situation has worsened significantly since January, when Washington imposed a de facto energy blockade on the island in a bid to pressure Havana’s communist government.
A severe lack of fuel makes it difficult to supply Cuba’s power plants and backup generators, which typically run on imported diesel.
“It’s one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity,” schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez said. “Honestly, I don’t know how we haven’t gone crazy.”
Over the past few weeks, blackouts have lasted more than 30 hours in the capital, while in provinces, they have sometimes stretched past 60 hours.
Retiree Francisco Rodriguez said his home had already gone without power for 28 hours on Friday.
“I thought they might at least turn the electricity back on for a few hours soon, but now... I think we won’t have light for several days,” he said.
The cuts have also affected the island’s water supply and mobile phone network, and general living conditions are extremely tough for residents.
“It’s no longer just the electricity. We’re having problems with water and gas as well,” Lazaro Reyes said.
Havana blames the crisis on an array of US-imposed punitive measures, while Washington attributes the hardship to poor internal management.
Another retiree, Zunilda Garcia, took the latest blackout in stride, stepping outside to charge a small lamp with solar energy.
“We have to wait and stay calm,” Garcia said. “We can’t lose hope.”

Former German lawmaker counters pro-China UN resolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:04 UTC
01:43:04 KST

Former German member of the European Parliament Reinhard Butikofer on Thursday urged the international community to counter China’s use of UN Resolution 2758 against Taiwan.
He made the comments at a conference hosted by the Taipei Representative Office in Berlin, saying that the deliberate misinterpretation of the resolution is an aspect of Beijing’s “lawfare.”
Resolution 2758, passed in 1971, states that the People’s Republic of China (PRC) is the only legitimate representative of China at the UN, which enabled Beijing to replace the Republic of China (ROC), Taiwan’s official name, as a permanent member of the UN Security Council.
Photo: CNA
Butikofer, who chaired the event, said that the essence of China’s legal warfare is to export its domestic system of rule by law as part of the global order.
The EU as a whole, including Germany, does not recognize China’s interpretation of UN Resolution 2758 as making Taiwan part of its sovereign territory, he said.
As Beijing is aggressively seeking the support of foreign countries to lend legitimacy to its claims, democracies around the world must take a stronger stance against China’s false narrative, he said.
The resolution was concerned with determining China’s representation in the UN, without making any reference to Taiwan, its legal status or representation in the UN framework, he said.
Beijing’s push to conflate its distorted version of the resolution with the so-called “one China” principle has repercussions not only for Taiwan’s representation in international organizations, but also peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region, Representative to Germany Ku Jiu-Sheng (谷瑞生) said.
Germany and the EU have voiced the view that Taiwan’s participation in global frameworks should be encouraged, and that this policy stance does not conflict with the resolution.
The global strategic landscape has changed since the resolution’s passage in the 1970s, transforming the West’s strategic ambiguity from an advantage into a weakness that China’s “gray zone” warfare could exploit, he said.
Western nations should re-examine the prosperity of their “one China” policy and consider whether it should be replaced by a “one Taiwan” policy, he said.
Berlin’s “one China policy” in no way resembles Beijing’s “one China principle,” he added.
Germany, the UK, France, Canada, Australia and Japan should form a coalition of the willing to support Taiwan’s defense by actions including the passage of warships and other shows of resolve, he said.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Lin Chien-chi (林倩綺) told the conference that, in discussions of Resolution 2758, it is important to distinguish between the resolution’s original intent and the “additional meanings that have emerged through more than five decades of political interpretation, so that political claims are not gradually treated as established facts of international law.”
Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) Legislator-at-Large Liu Shu-pin (劉書彬) said only Taiwanese should decide Taiwan’s future.
The resolution should not hold Taiwan back from contributing to the world in key domains including secure supply chains, she added.

Pottinger urges Taiwan to focus skepticism on CCP promises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:03 UTC
01:43:03 KST

“Skepticism toward the US” and “skepticism toward Taiwan are essentially myths, said former US deputy national security adviser Matt Pottinger in Taipei yesterday, stating people should instead scrutinize the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) promises and shift the focus toward “skepticism toward the CCP.”
Pottinger, now chief executive officer of the risk research and advisory firm Garnut Global, made the comments in a keynote speech at the 2026 Resilient Taiwan for Sustainable Democracy International Forum hosted by the Presidential Office.
He said that during past visits to Taiwan, he has repeatedly called on Taiwan to urgently strengthen its military capabilities and resilience, advice which the current administration is evidently heeding.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
The government’s urgent and targeted approach to self-defense is evidenced by the improved format of the Han Kuang annual military exercises, urban resilience drills and leap in drone production, he said.
Taiwan exported 3,000 drones in 2024, and the figure is expected to increase a hundredfold by the end of this year, Pottinger said, adding Taiwan has laid down the foundation to be a major player in the uncrewed systems industry.
Yet, Beijing and Moscow are colluding in an algorithm-boosted disinformation campaign on social media to spread skepticism of Taiwan and the US in a bid to undermine the two nations, he said.
The “America skepticism” theory, in which the US is described as an unreliable partner, emerges in Taiwan is essentially defamation wrapped in myths, he said.
The matter truly deserving of Taiwanese skepticism is China’s utter inability to keep its promises, as Beijing has demonstrated time and again in its repression of Hong Kong, he said.
The imprisonment of media freedom champion Jimmy Lai (黎智英) and democracy advocate Joshua Wong (黃之鋒), despite Beijing’s agreement to make no changes to Hong Kong’s democratic constitution for 50 years after the handover, he said.
Macao’s former pro-democracy lawmaker Au Kam San (區錦新) was also imprisoned in a secret trial, he added.
Pottinger highlighted former US president Franklin D. Roosevelt as a steadfast ally of the Republic of China in its fight against tyranny, quoting Roosevelt’s famous words: “The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.”
He urged people not to let doubts undermine Taiwan’s confidence in its own achievements and determination, or its resolve to continue strengthening its defenses and resilience.

Lai launches global disaster alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:03 UTC
01:43:03 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday announced the establishment of the World Alliance for Disaster Management (WADM), calling it a major breakthrough in Taiwan’s participation in international organizations over the past half-century.
Lai made the announcement at the opening of the Resilient Taiwan for Sustainable Democracy International Forum, hosted by the Presidential Office in Taipei yesterday. It also marked the second anniversary of the establishment of the Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Committee.
The WADM, an international organization spearheaded by Taiwan, is set to link governments, and disaster prevention agencies and organizations around the world to advance joint training and exercises, as well as mutual assistance and information sharing, with the aim of making Taiwan a cross-border hub for disaster prevention and response coordination, Lai said.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
The organization’s founding members consist of 11 of Taiwan’s official diplomatic allies with UN seats and the Republic of Somaliland, he said.
The WADM is made up of central and local governments, disaster prevention agencies and organizations from 21 countries, including the US, Japan, the UK, Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, Turkey and the Philippines, he said.
“Together they form a cooperation network that spans the globe,” Lai said. “The establishment of the WADM is a major breakthrough for Taiwan in over half a century of efforts to take part in international organizations.”
The committee was established two years ago with the goal of boosting Taiwanese society’s resilience through public-private cooperation, and to help the government continue to operate effectively, and society and essential services to function as normal should the nation face any type of disaster, Lai said.
Taiwan is confident that it has something to offer the international community, he said, citing as an example last month’s Han Kuang military exercises and the Urban Resilience Exercises, which enabled non-military government agencies at the central and local levels to conduct simultaneous drills under the same conditions.
As president, his role is to “ensure Taiwan is better prepared and has greater strength to maintain the status quo, and to prevent peace from being undermined by unilateral provocations,” in the face of dramatically changing international landscape and intensifying threats from China, Lai said.
Taiwan’s defense budget has doubled over the past decade, Lai said, adding that his administration has for the first time proposed a defense budget that exceeded NT$1 trillion (US$31.44 billion) for next year.
The NT$1.1225 trillion budget would put defense spending above 3 percent of GDP, and it is expected to reach 5 percent by 2030, he said.
“We are determined to strengthen Taiwan’s self-defense capabilities and to safeguard peace through strength,” Lai said.
“Taiwan will continue to expand its participation by contributing to the world, to build trust through professionalism and to connect to the world through cooperation,” he said.
He also urged democratic societies to cooperate with each other and spread confidence through resilience when authoritarian forces seek to spread fear and create discord and strife.
“Peace through strength, strength through resilience and resilience through unity,” Lai said, adding that all the preparation aims to protect the welfare of Taiwanese, preserve Taiwan’s free and democratic way of life, and defend peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region and across the world.
With an increasingly extreme and unpredictable climate, resilience preparedness also enables society to absorb shocks, recover quickly and ultimately achieve sustainability, he added.
The forum brought more than 500 local and international defense experts, officials and business representatives to Taipei yesterday. They exchanged views on climate change, “gray zone” aggression and geopolitical risks, and discussed comprehensive resilience models around the world, military-civilian cooperation, psychological defense and resilience partnerships.

Taiwan in Time:  Making the Grand Hotel grand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:02 UTC
01:43:02 KST

Sept. 21 to Sept. 27
When the Shah of Iran became the Grand Hotel’s (圓山大飯店) first head-of-state guest in 1958, it was hardly the landmark it is known as today.
A Chinese-style, two-story structure with just 36 rooms built on the former site of the Taipei Shinto Shrine, the hotel was still referred to as its original name, the Taiwan Hotel (台灣大飯店), in an official newsreel detailing Mohammad Reza Pahlavi’s visit.
Photo courtesy of Stephen Liu
The video lavished praise on the hotel, pointing out its “beautiful architecture and magnificent appearance” and noting that it had just been renovated.
After being greeted personally by then-president Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石) at the airport and receiving a military welcome, foreign dignitaries typically rode with Chiang in a motorcade, with guard cars and motorcycles leading the way. They traveled down Dunhua N Road, east on Nanjing E Road and then north on Zhongshan N Road for the 9.5km journey to the Grand Hotel.
Tens of thousands of spectators lined the route waving flags and cheering, while music and folk performances, including dragon dances and stilt walking, were staged.
Photo courtesy of Taiwan Film and Audiovisual Institute
On the last night of his six-day stay, the Shah held a banquet for Chiang and his wife Soong Mei-ling (宋美齡) at the larger Golden Dragon Hall (金龍廳), which had been added in 1956. The ornate, palace-style Qilin Hall was completed in 1963, featuring a luxurious presidential suite. In 1967 or 1968, Fortune magazine named the Grand Hotel one of the world’s top 10 hotels.
But there was still room to grow. In 1973, the bright-red, 14-story main building replaced the original hotel, adding 640 rooms and state-of-the-art facilities.
FROM SHRINE TO GUESTHOUSE
Photo courtesy of Academia Historica
The site of the Grand Hotel originally hosted the shinto Taiwan Grand Shrine. Built in 1901 by the colonial government to honor Prince Kitashirakawa Yoshihisa, who died during the 1895 Japanese campaign to take control of Taiwan, it was upgraded to Grand Shrine status in 1944. But before its inauguration, it was heavily damaged when an aircraft crashed into it.
A bronze dragon fountain that once stood outside the shrine was preserved and moved to the Golden Dragon Hall. In 1987, it was gilded with 24-karat gold leaf.
After the war, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) dismantled the remains of the shrine. The exact chronology of the postwar years is unclear, but the government began developing the former shrine site as a place to host foreign dignitaries.
Most sources indicate that a small, 36-room Taiwan Hotel was completed around 1951 and initially managed by the state-run Taiwan Travel Agency. In 1952, it was taken over by the The Duen-Mou Foundation of Taiwan (台灣敦睦聯誼會), led by Soong, and renamed the Grand Hotel.
Soong appointed her niece and goddaughter, Kung Ling-wei (孔令偉), as the hotel’s general manager. Kung enjoyed considerable privilege growing up and reportedly was a headache even for Chiang Kai-shek. She wielded considerable authority over hotel affairs, even after a board of prominent political figures was established in 1961.
Kung resided in a house on the complex, accessible through the eastern escape tunnel. Both the house and tunnel were opened to the public in 2021.
LAVISH EXPANSION
With US support and aid growing and more countries opening diplomatic missions in Taipei, the hotel expanded its facilities, writes Lee Jung-chien (李榮建) in the book Memories of Yuanshan (記憶園山). The Golden Dragon Hall was added in 1956, followed by the Cui Feng Hall in 1958. Both were designed by Yang Cho-cheng (楊卓成), who later used a similar fusion of traditional palace-style and modern architecture in his designs for Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall and the National Theater and Concert Hall.
According to the book’s anecdotes, later dignitaries began staying at the Golden Dragon Hall, including then-US president Dwight D. Eisenhower, whose entourage booked 90 rooms for his two-day stay in 1960.
The next expansion was the opulent, three-story Qilin Hall (麒麟閣), which was built by Chinese Civil War veterans on a flattened hill. Opening in May 1963, it had 70 rooms — including a presidential suite designed specifically for heads of state. It was connected to the Golden Dragon Hall via skybridge.
The first heads of state to stay there were then-King of Thailand Bhumibol Adulyadej and Queen Sirikit, who spent three nights there in June 1963.
In 1970, the original main building was torn down to make way for the 14-story current structure. Yang was enlisted for the job once more. Legend has it that Kung, who also oversaw previous expansions, found the original 12-story, 200-room design insufficiently grand and ordered it torn down mid-construction and rebuilt on a larger scale.
Not only was it lavishly adorned with traditional palace-style motifs and decorations, but each room also had an AM radio and a 19-inch color television. In addition to dim sum, Chinese banquet and an American-style barbecue restaurant, there was also a bar and two 24-hour coffee shops. The presidential suite had a private entrance, a dining room for 10 to 12 people and a kitchen.
NOTABLE EVENTS
On Dec. 15, 1978, the US and China announced that they would establish diplomatic relations and break ties with Taiwan. The news sparked outrage in Taiwan. When then-deputy US Secretary of State Warren Christopher landed at Songshan Airport to meet with officials, his passage to the Grand Hotel was anything but smooth.
Once his car left the airport gates, protesters began pelting it with tomatoes, eggs and other objects. A bamboo stick smashed through a window and scratched Christopher. Alarmed, he ordered the car to drive instead to the US military residences in Yangmingshan, avoiding the angry protesters waiting at the foot of the hill leading to the Grand Hotel. Only after the protesters had dispersed was he able to check in.
On Sept. 28, 1986, with Taiwan still under martial law, the Democratic Progressive Party defied the ban on new political parties and held its inauguration ceremony at the Grand Hotel. Although the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) refused to recognize the new party, it did not take drastic action to suppress it.
Filipino opposition politician Benigno Aquino also spent his final nights at the Grand Hotel in July 1983. He was assassinated upon arriving in Manila.
On June 27, 1995, a huge fire broke out on the top floor of the Grand Hotel. A flame ignited during repair work on the tiles of the penthouse’s glass room and, fanned by strong winds, soon spread across the roof, engulfing the top floor. A total of 104 fire trucks, ambulances and aerial ladders rushed to the scene, while about 100 military police also joined the effort. Three hours later, the fire was extinguished, but the top three floors were completely damaged, along with valuable artifacts and furniture in the presidential suite.
A lawmaker reportedly proposed rebuilding the hotel as the new Legislative Yuan, but the idea was quickly shot down. During the three years it took to repair the damage, international dignitaries and important banquets and conferences were moved to other hotels, breaking the Grand Hotel’s monopoly.
However, it reopened in June 1998 with a fireworks ceremony and a newly illuminated roof, making the hotel even more grand.
Taiwan in Time, a column about Taiwan’s history that is published every Sunday, spotlights important or interesting events around the nation that either have anniversaries this week or are tied to current events.
The comical bit of parachute journalism by Simon Shuster in the Atlantic last week under the title “Will Taiwan Just Give Up?”, drew much attention for its numerous minor errors, largely forgivable, its total lack of understanding of Taiwan and its history and its strange, pro-China interpretations, including taking Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) seriously. The laughter and indignation that essay generated among Taiwan aficionados is an indicator of how far Western journalism on Taiwan has come. Twenty years ago, it would have been another piece for the pile. Today, it is an obvious outlier. Shuster’s piece was
For a small nation, Taiwan has an unusually long list of territorial disputes. In part or in whole, it has disputes over the Spratly Islands (Nansha Islands, 南沙群島) with Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei. It also has another territorial dispute with Vietnam over the Paracel Islands, and with Japan over the Senkaku Islands (Diaoyutai Islands, 釣魚台). Of course, the biggest territorial disputes are with the People’s Republic of China (PRC), which not only claims all of the above, but also Pratas Island (Dongsha, 東沙島), Kinmen, Penghu and all of Taiwan itself. This creates considerable headaches politically for the government, especially

It sits entrenched in forest vegetation amid the tall, spindly bodies and spiky heads of the betel nut trees; the air is cool, and its surroundings are mostly silent save the sounds of late-season cicadas. Anduril founder touts defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:42:59 UTC
01:42:59 KST

Anduril Industries founder Palmer Luckey yesterday told a forum in Taipei that “freedom is the most powerful weapon that Taiwan has.”
Luckey, who was sanctioned by China last year due to his defense firm’s weapons and drone sales to Taiwan, made the comments during his keynote speech on Responding to Emerging Threats and Modern Warfare, which was part of a discussion at the Resilient Taiwan for Sustainable Democracy International Forum of the Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Committee hosted by the Presidential Office at the Grand Hyatt Taipei.
Talking about building his first company and seeing Chinese companies take US-developed technologies and them being protected by their government, Luckey said that he realized what China cannot copy is “a country where people are free to improvise, experiment, to ask, act without permission and come up with a lot of this technology in the first place.”
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
“Freedom usually gets described as the thing that Taiwan is defending, but I think freedom is the most powerful weapon that Taiwan has,” he said.
Luckey said Taiwan can use this advantage and turn it into resilience, not only economically, but also militarily, and change how Taiwan fights and how Beijing calculates its victory.
Explaining the three aspects of resilience that Taiwan can work on, he said “operational resilience” is not about making scientific breakthroughs that change the nature of technology, but figuring out how to integrate, assemble, mass produce them cost-effectively and use them effectively on the battlefield.
“The kinds of technologies that Taiwan needs to steel itself against adversaries’ assaults are already abundant,” Luckey said, adding that Taiwan is already a leader of many technologies in the industrial and consumer realm, but it needs to apply them to defense.
Luckey said Taiwan needs to ask itself “what the final stage of Taiwan’s deterrence will look like, one that will persist for years, decades and centuries, and start working towards that steady state today.”
He said Taiwan can already make cost-effective and high-quality machine tools, semiconductors, precision components, advanced composites and others, but these production lines need to become increasingly interchangeable with weapons production at volumes measured in the millions.
Luckey said Taiwan’s domestic demand is not enough to sustain the defense industrial base that it needs for a deterrence level that is unstoppable, and that it should make countries depend on the nation for advanced capabilities the way the world already depends on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co for commercial capabilities.
“The goal should be for everyone in the world, whether they’re buying from you or just afraid of you, to see a label that says, ‘designed in Taiwan, made in Taiwan,’ on a weapons system, and immediately understand what it means,” he said.
He said this “fortress of freedom” can only be built together by the people from the inside — to convince Beijing that the cost of winning is insanely high and there is no victory in invading Taiwan, as what the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) believes would be a short military operation, would actually be the beginning of a fight that could continue for years.
If Taiwan can reach a durable, shared view of its own future, even though it might look slightly different for everyone, and if the CCP understands that this view can survive any political fight, disagreement, campaign or economic coercion, Beijing would know this war could be winnable, but is not worth winning, he said.
Asked by moderator National Security Council Deputy Secretary-General Lin Fei-fan (林飛帆) to assess China’s military buildup and capabilities, Luckey said the seizure of Taiwan is China’s major strategic objective, so it has been preparing well, but “Taiwan has a lot of home advantages.”
“It is going to be much harder for China to fight on your shores than it will be for you. You don’t need to go and invade China. You just need to make it so painful for them and for them to know that it’s so painful that they don’t come for you,” he said. “I think that that is absolutely a doable task.”
As China spends about eight to 10 times more on defense than Taiwan, Taiwan must “cheat” in fighting back, he said. “You can’t fight fair. You need to come up with things that are more asymmetric… You need to have no honor in fighting.”
Nobody in Taiwan should believe it is a hopeless fight, and that those who say it have a reason to believe it, including many who are funded by adversaries, who want people in Taiwan to give up hope and want to take away their right to self-determination, he said.
If it is an easy win for the adversaries, they would not be flooding social media with ideas of helplessness to make people believe nothing can be done, he added.

“We regret the decision to extend the denial of entry visas for members of the Palestinian delegation for a second year in a row,” said Anouar El Anouni, a spokesman for the EU’s diplomatic service. “In light of its existing headquarters agreements with the UN and its obligations as host state, we urge the United States for this decision to be reconsidered.”
Photo: Reuters
The administration of US President Donald Trump denied visas for the Palestinian delegation last year, forcing Abbas, a regular at the UN General Assembly, to address the body of global leadership by video.
The General Assembly voted 152-3 on Thursday for Abbas to be able to appear virtually once again this year.
As it stands, only members of the Palestinian mission to the UN would be able to attend the meeting, which begins on Tuesday.
On Friday, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also expressed regret at Washington’s decision, adding he was concerned about its impact “on the ability of the State of Palestine to participate fully in the work of the United Nations.”
The department said Washington also opposed Palestinian “actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict including through the International Criminal Court and International Court of Justice, seeking to bypass negotiations through seeking unilateral recognition.”
They accused them of “continuing to pay stipends to terrorists and to glorify acts of terrorism and terrorists in public pronouncements and school textbooks.”

Low birthrates a sign of evolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:42:53 UTC
01:42:53 KST

Over the past several decades, Taiwan has undergone a transformation in its societal values surrounding survival, ways of living and the meaning of life itself — all within the span of just two or three generations. Generational conflict is the inevitable consequence of the shift from a mindset of collectivism to one of individualism. In an agrarian society marked by an era of material scarcity, and during the transition to more labor-intensive agriculture, industry and commerce, human beings were the primary source of productivity.
Older generations endured great hardship to raise and sustain their families. Motivated by the belief that “even a blade of grass is nourished with a drop of dew” (一枝草，一點露) and the minimal cost of child-rearing, adding another child to the family meant little more than providing one extra pair of chopsticks. Three generations living under one roof could support one another, and having many children and grandchildren not only was a great help with farm work, but also served as a vital pillar for parents facing the burdens of poverty and illness in the last years of their life. Raising children was thus a way to secure support in old age, enjoy family life and carry on the family name.
However, the spread of Western ideology brought individualism to the East, changing the purpose and meaning of having children. Young people, fearing they cannot afford to raise a family, now choose to opt out of marriage and having children. Instead, they pursue material comforts, travel and personal enjoyment, believing this to be the key to achieving a happy life. We cannot fault them for this. Perhaps it is some form of divine foresight — a precautionary measure taken to reduce birthrates and cut the world’s population — to prepare for the era of artificial intelligence (AI), avert mass unemployment and prevent famine. Only by aligning with the course of nature can we face the widespread adoption of AI in the coming decades without risking mass starvation.
Israeli historian Yuval Noah Harari warned in his book Homo Deus: A Brief History of Tomorrow, that future technologies could give rise to a vast “useless class” — a group who could become economically and politically redundant due to AI and automation — causing many people to be left behind. If society insists on the mindset that people should have more children for “the good of the nation” and maintains high birthrates, the next generation could grow up struggling with structural unemployment and an unequal distribution of resources. The younger generation’s collective subconscious tendency to not marry or have children might well be a biological instinct — a form of herd response to dramatic environmental changes.
This could be a mechanism meant to substantially reduce the population before the widespread adoption of AI takes hold, avoiding the collective tragedies of mass unemployment, world hunger and social upheaval in the decades to come.
Wang Chin-ho is retired.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

China’s electric cars are not Europe’s real problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:42:53 UTC
01:42:53 KST

Europe’s attempts to protect itself from the onslaught of China’s car exports appears to be turning into an expensive game of Whac-A-Mole.
Tariffs in 2024 targeted Chinese electric vehicles with duties as high as 45 percent. The result has been rising imports of hybrids, which are exempt, in turn prompting demands for more restrictions. Carmakers appear to be lost. Europe already makes almost nine times as many plug-in cars as it did in 2019, while conventional vehicle production has fallen about 40 percent — but they are lobbying Brussels to water down emissions targets, while cutting 100,000 jobs. This does not look like the robust domestic industry that protectionism was meant to incubate.
That is because policy gets the problem back-to-front. Europe is restricting imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles, but allowing unrestricted trade in the batteries that power them. The set-up is congenial for the continent’s carmakers, which would rather use cheaper Chinese cells than invest in alternatives. If your aim is to support advanced European manufacturing, however, it is disastrous.
You only need to look at the history of China’s own auto industry to see why. National champions SAIC Motor Corp and BAIC Motor Corp, each founded under Mao Zedong (毛澤東) and still controlled by the municipal governments of Shanghai and Beijing, have lost 70 percent and 93 percent of their market values, respectively, since peaking in 2018. The biggest winners from the shift to EVs are privately owned companies that barely existed two decades ago. At this point, the entire listed single-focus Chinese car sector is worth less than Contemporary Amperex Technology Co, or CATL, the world’s biggest battery maker.
Chinese car brands are causing plenty of political tremors in the EU, but still make up just 6.6 percent of sales. Meanwhile, Chinese batteries, whose local market share has almost doubled in two years to more than 50 percent, are barely discussed. Imagine if Britain had spent the 1930s protecting its aircraft companies, while remaining dependent on Germany for the engines they needed to fly.
The goal here should be building a handful of European-owned battery champions capable of competing at global scale, without trying to exclude the Asian companies whose technology and expertise can help them get there. The moment is ripe for such a shift: Europe’s battery market is roughly as large as China’s was in 2022, giving the region the scale needed to drive down costs and foster essential know-how.
With Chinese EV growth slowing amid saturation and weak consumer demand, Europe might even have the edge. Over the five years through 2031, the continent’s passenger vehicles would likely require an additional 255 gigawatt-hours of batteries, compared to 250GWh in China, according to Bloomberg.
The problem is that Europe’s carmakers are funneling the benefits of this coming production boom offshore, allowing domestic expertise to wither. Automotive Cells Co, or ACC, a battery venture between Stellantis NV, Mercedes-Benz Group AG, and TotalEnergies SE, has been slashed to about a quarter of its planned size as its investors tied up with CATL instead. Volkswagen AG’s PowerCo SE has shelved four of its planned gigafactories in favor of working with CATL and Gotion High-Tech Co, another Chinese player.
Fortunately, many of the elements needed for a better policy are already in place. The EU’s Battery Booster program promises 1.5 billion euros (US$1.72 billion) to support gigafactories in their ramp-up stage. It should be expanded to 10 billion euros and remain available until a company hits 100GWh of capacity, roughly the level needed to compete globally.
Europe’s “resilience criteria” rules, intended to stop public support for clean technology deepening its dependence on dominant foreign suppliers, should help. In cases of clear subsidies, countervailing duties should be imposed on the Chinese-made battery, not the car as a whole, a distinction that has precedent in the US approach to aluminum automotive parts.
In general, Chinese investment should be welcomed. Outside expertise would be vital in resuscitating Europe’s battery industry, as ACC discovered when it had to bring in engineers from Guangdong-based Eve Energy Co to kickstart its troubled production lines. With sufficient protections in place for the power cells that really matter, finished Chinese EVs should be allowed in duty-free, to discipline local automakers.
Batteries lack the political salience of cars, but they are ultimately far more important, sitting at the foundation of an industrial ecosystem stretching far beyond passenger automobiles, into trucks, ships, drones, power grids and data centers.
Europe needs to recognize that the world is changing before it is too late. At the moment, it is applying infant-industry protection to incumbents who have been around since Queen Victoria was on the throne. Meanwhile, its actual infant industry — battery manufacturing — has been left exposed.
David Fickling is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering climate change and energy. Previously, he worked for Bloomberg News, the Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times.

Officials address challenge of election interference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:42:49 UTC
01:42:49 KST

Diplomats from the US, UK and EU yesterday underscored the need to counter electoral interference and cognitive warfare operations ahead of Taiwan’s year-end local elections.
They made the remarks at this year’s Resilient Taiwan for Sustainable Democracy International Forum hosted by the Presidential Office, saying that electoral interference from authoritarian regimes has become a pervasive threat to democratic countries.
British Office Taipei Representative Ruth Bradley-Jones said election interference in Taiwan is the matter that concerns her the most.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
Every democratic country is being targeted by electoral interference, a threat that has become ever more severe with the prevalence of the Internet and advances in artificial intelligence, she said.
Taiwan is “nearest to the fire” of electoral interference, and is bearing the brunt of the damage when it can least afford it, she said, adding that Taiwan must urgently shore up its defenses against meddling.
Head of the European Economic and Trade Office Lutz Gullner said foreign information manipulation and interference, disinformation and cognitive warfare are among the most complex threats confronting the modern state.
For democracies that treasure the freedom of speech, these dilemmas pose a common challenge that defies easy answers, Gullner said.
Dealing with cognitive warfare requires an understanding that disinformation is not about exchanging information or communication, but an instrument in the hybrid warfare toolbox to control, influence or destabilize a targeted society, he said.
A coherent counter-narrative, media literacy and the awareness of the happenings in a country’s informational environment together form the answer to neutralizing foreign information manipulation and influence, he said.
Taiwan’s civil society has demonstrated a remarkable facility in the last of these capabilities, and the government would do well to integrate it within an official strategic framework to counter foreign meddling, Gullner said.
American Institute in Taiwan Director Raymond Greene said that democratic governments must use social media platforms and civil society to fight disinformation effectively.
Cooperation with social media platforms is essential, as they possess the tools capable of targeting fake news within the massive amounts of data social media platforms distribute, he said.
Democracies must counter malicious disinformation without trampling on speech and press freedoms, making it crucial for civil society to be in the spotlight of the fight against hostile cognitive warfare, Greene said.
Neutral groups not aligned with a political faction or ideology can have more credibility among members of the public who do not support the ruling party to reject Internet-based political meddling, he said.

The government is set to impose tougher penalties for drug driving, including vehicle confiscation and fines of up to NT$270,000 for drivers who refuse drug tests, after 23 people were killed in drug driving-related incidents in first half of this year, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said.
President William Lai (賴清德) on Aug. 17 promulgated amendments to the Road Traffic Management and Penalty Act (道路交通管理處罰條例), increasing penalties for drug driving and drug use, Public Transportation and Supervision Division director Hu Ti-chi (胡迪琦) said yesterday.
The amendments include higher fines, license revocation, liability for passengers traveling in the same vehicle, higher fines for driving without a license after revocation, mandatory addiction treatment and vehicle confiscation, he said.
Photo: Taipei Times
The ministry is preparing to implement the revised rules and has announced planned amendments to four related regulations.
Under the previewed amendments, drivers caught driving under the influence of drugs would face penalties based on the type of vehicle they were operating.
For a first offense, motorcycle riders could be fined NT$120,000, while car drivers face a NT$150,000 fine.
For a second offense within 10 years, the fines would increase to NT$210,000 for motorcycles and NT$240,000 for cars.
From the third offense, an additional NT$90,000 would be added to each fine, with no upper limit on the total amount.
Drivers who refuse to take a rapid saliva test would face even steeper penalties, the planned amendments say.
A first refusal would result in a NT$270,000 fine for motorcycle and car drivers. A second refusal within 10 years would raise the fine to NT$450,000, while each subsequent refusal would add another NT$180,000 to the previous penalty, again with no cap.
For drug-driving violations and related offenses resulting in license revocation, authorities could publish the offender’s name and photograph, and suspend the vehicle’s license plates for two years, the planned amendments say.
The new measures would allow vehicles to be confiscated on the spot when a driver is caught driving under the influence of drugs or refuses a drug test, while anyone caught driving while their license is revoked would face an additional NT$80,000 fine, and the vehicle would be impounded.

In hydropowered Bhutan, solar starts to rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:42:46 UTC
01:42:46 KST

Engineer Rinzin Galley stands on a platform overlooking a former military shooting range on the edge of Bhutan’s capital, Thimphu, now home to a field of solar panels.
With abundant waterways, Bhutan has long relied on hydroelectric power to meet its electricity needs and stay carbon negative.
However, demand is growing, and in winter, when rivers run low before the mountain melt arrives, Bhutan already relies on imported Indian electricity.
Photo: AFP
“Solar projects are booming,” said Rinzin, senior engineer at Norion Renewable Energy.
The company’s biggest project to date is the Dechencholing solar farm on former military land, with an installed capacity of 4.45 megawatts (MW).
Dechencholing is one of several solar fields developed in recent years, including the country’s first mega project — Sephu, with capacity of more than 22MW.
That is relatively modest, especially compared with the vast solar fields installed in neighboring China, but it represents a new direction for Bhutan, where hydropower exports account for up to 15 percent of GDP, according to the World Bank.
“Our plans are to develop about 5,000 megawatts,” said Chhewang Rinzin, managing director of Druk Green Power Corp, the country’s generation utility.
Bhutan can generate about 3,700MW from hydro, but that capacity falls by about 80 percent during the winter, he said.
Winter demand has increased to 1,500MW from 400MW, creating a significant shortfall being met by electricity imports from India.
Officials attribute part of the growing demand to a construction boom, but Bhutan has also bet on bitcoin mining to boost revenue. A planned special economic zone known as the Gelephu Mindfulness City is expected to host energy-hungry data centers.
The problem was already clear in 2008, when a goal of generating 10,000MW from hydropower by 2020 was agreed.
However, the plan ran into a series of obstacles, including financing.
“When you’re looking at constructing 10,000 megawatts in hydropower capacity and each megawatt probably costs you about [US]$1.5 million ... for a small economy like ourselves, that’s quite difficult,” Chhewang said.
Solutions have included liberalizing foreign investment rules and increasing solar targets in the energy mix.
The country now aims for 25,000MW by 2040, with solar accounting for one-fifth of that.
Finding sufficient space for projects is challenging given Bhutan’s largely mountainous terrain.
“When we do solar projects on the ground mount, it takes a huge amount of area to get certain capacity,” Rinzin said.
The country’s high altitudes, circuitous routes and roads frequently damaged by landslides pose further problems.
Part of the push has involved training up a corps of solar engineers, including through the De-suung royal skilling initiative.
Norion has trained about 450 De-suung volunteers “to build in-house capacity in the country,” Rinzin said.
Several dozen work at Norion, which has a goal of installing 30MW of solar by next year, much of it on rooftops.
Rooftop solar is now a common sight in Thimphu on government buildings and businesses, but the incentives for individual consumers are still slim.
Electricity is comparatively cheap in Bhutan and installing solar remains expensive.
Om Pradhan, a former minister and ambassador, had long advocated for solar in Bhutan and was keen to install panels at home.
“I thought that firstly it would benefit me personally, in the sense that my electricity bills would go down,” the 79-year-old former minister for trade and industries told reporters. “The second thing is that I’ve always been an advocate for solar power.”
However, the 600,000 ngultrums (US$6,300) it cost him to install the system remains far out of reach for most Bhutanese.
“Many people calculate that if you put that money in the bank, the interest would pay your electricity bills,” he said.

White House turns away CNN, MS NOW, Politico reporters after Trump's ban

All three news outlets separately said their teams' press passes were confiscated on Saturday morning when their journalists went to the White House. A CNN statement on Saturday called the ban "an illegal assault" on its constitutional right to do journalism without interference from the government. In separate statements, MS NOW and Politico said they would "defend our First Amendment rights."

The New York Times in a statement called Trump's latest ban "yet another retaliatory and unconstitutional threat" and said the newspaper "stands in support of the news organizations being unfairly targeted by the president."
The Washington Post in a statement on Saturday said its access to the White House is a "non-negotiable constitutional right," and called the president's actions "a clear form of intimidation meant to silence coverage."
Trump previously has tried to keep certain news outlets or specific journalists out of press gatherings.

Learning about the opposing party’s vaccination rate influences health choices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:00:49 UTC
01:00:49 KST

Public health campaigns often rely on broadcasting facts and statistics to encourage healthy habits. People are more likely to express an intent to receive a COVID-19 vaccine after learning that vaccination rates among members of the opposing political party are higher than they previously thought. The findings, published in PLOS One, suggest that public health campaigns highlighting low vaccination rates to urge action might inadvertently discourage people from getting immunized.
In the United States, political affiliation heavily influences healthcare choices. Currently, whether a person identifies as a Democrat or a Republican is a stronger predictor of their COVID-19 vaccination status than their education level, race, or health insurance coverage. Past research indicates that people often judge the severity of the pandemic and the necessity of government interventions through a partisan lens.
Public health officials frequently attempt to change behavior by providing the public with new data. The success of this strategy heavily depends on what the audience already believes. If a person thinks a virus is exceptionally rare, hearing that it actually infects one in five people might prompt them to take precautions. If that same person already assumed the virus infects half the population, the identical statistic might make them feel safer and less likely to act. Researchers refer to this gap between an individual’s preconceived belief and the actual statistic as an information shock.
Researchers Brandyn F. Churchill of American University, along with Xiaoxue Sherry Gao and Rong Rong of the University of Massachusetts Amherst, wanted to test how these information shocks interact with political identity. They specifically wanted to see how learning new facts about the health behaviors of opposing political groups shapes personal medical decisions.
To establish a baseline of actual COVID-19 experiences, the researchers first conducted an initial survey of 200 adults on an online research platform in May 2024. The group consisted of 100 self-identified Democrats and 100 self-identified Republicans. The participants answered questions about their recent experiences with the virus, including whether they had contracted it or sought medical care. They also reported whether they had received a vaccine, experienced side effects, or vaccinated primarily to protect others.
The initial survey revealed that both political groups experienced similar rates of infection. Both groups also sought medical care for the virus at similar frequencies. There was, however, a vast divide in vaccination behavior. Nearly 46 percent of the Democrats reported receiving a recent COVID-19 vaccine, compared to only 28 percent of the Republicans.
Building on these baseline figures, the researchers designed a main experiment in August 2024 involving 579 different participants. This group included 288 Democrats and 291 Republicans, representing a mix of ages and backgrounds.
The researchers asked these individuals to estimate the responses given by the people in the initial survey. Half of the participants were asked to guess the survey answers of their own political party. The other half were asked to guess the answers of the opposing political party.
To ensure participants answered honestly rather than simply expressing a political bias, they were offered a financial bonus. The participants placed digital bets on how a randomly selected person from the first survey had answered the health questions. If their estimates closely matched the actual data, their chances of winning a monetary reward increased.
The estimates revealed widespread misunderstandings about the realities of the disease. Across the political spectrum, participants overestimated how frequently people caught COVID-19 by about 20 percentage points. They also overestimated how often the virus required medical intervention by 22 percentage points.
Both Democrats and Republicans tended to underestimate the prevalence of vaccine side effects. They also underestimated how many people chose to get vaccinated specifically to protect others.
Participants were no better at accurately estimating the behaviors and experiences of their own political party than they were at estimating those of the opposing party. Both groups consistently overestimated how many Republicans were vaccinated against the virus.
After the participants locked in their estimates, a computer program randomly selected one of the five health topics. The program then revealed the actual statistic from the initial survey to the participant. By comparing the participant’s original guess to the newly revealed statistic, the researchers could measure the size and direction of the information shock. Finally, the researchers asked the participants if they intended to receive an updated COVID-19 vaccine within the next twelve months.
Learning the true statistics regarding infection rates, disease severity, or side effects did not alter the participants’ stated plans to get a vaccine. Seeing the true vaccination rates of their own political party also produced no changes in their intentions.
When participants learned the actual vaccination rate of the opposing political party, their behavior shifted. Participants who realized they had underestimated the opposing party’s vaccination rate became more likely to state an intention to get vaccinated themselves. Those who learned they had overestimated the opposing party’s vaccination rate became less likely to seek a vaccine.
The researchers conducted mathematical tests to ensure this relationship was not a statistical fluke. When they swapped the data to pretend the participants had seen a different health statistic, the effect disappeared. When they looked at whether the information changed past vaccination behavior, there was no connection. This adds weight to the idea that the specific information about the opposing party’s current vaccination rate drove the change in their future intentions.
The researchers attribute this pattern to a social pressure model. In this framework, people are more inclined to adopt a health measure when they see others adopting it. When people learn that a group they view as generally opposed to a behavior is actually participating in it, they may feel increased social pressure to follow suit.
The results present a potential hazard for modern public health messaging. Health agencies often try to motivate the public by emphasizing that vaccination rates are falling below optimal levels. Because people generally overestimate how many of their peers are vaccinated, broadcasting low compliance rates serves as a negative information shock. Hearing that few people are getting the shot could reduce social pressure and inadvertently depress vaccination numbers even further.
While the experiment highlights shifts in stated intentions, an expressed intent to receive a vaccine does not guarantee that a person will actually schedule an appointment and get the shot. The researchers did attempt to follow up with the participants four months later to ask if they had received a vaccine. Many of the participants did not respond to the follow-up survey, meaning the researchers could not reliably track how often intentions translated into real-world behavior.
The study design also limits the ability to explain the underlying psychological mechanisms. The data show that participants reacted to the habits of the opposing political party, but the study does not reveal exactly why this specific information proved more persuasive than data about their own peers. The overall number of participants also constrained the researchers’ ability to analyze differences across more specific demographic categories, such as age, race, or income brackets. Future studies will need to investigate the cognitive pathways that make discordant political information so influential in personal medical decisions.
The study, “Partisan differences in healthcare decision-making: Evidence from a vaccine experiment,” was authored by Brandyn F. Churchill, Xiaoxue Sherry Gao, and Rong Rong.

The price of oil and diesel is rising as a direct result of his own policies, which increases ground shipping costs and transfers those expenses directly to the American consumer. As James Carville famously warned Bill Clinton in 1992, "it's the economy, stupid"—making economic performance the primary concern for American voters.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent explicitly noted that the administration's goal is to collapse the Russian economy by targeting its energy infrastructure. While Trump may enjoy seeing war-porn briefings of burning Russian refineries, he fails to realize the global economic impact. Trump understands these economic consequences because high fuel prices severely threaten his party at the upcoming November midterm elections.
Sputnik Question: What has been the response in the US establishment to Russia's retaliation strikes against Ukrainian ports, logistics warehouses, and rail infrastructure, and to what extent has this changed the calculus in Washington?
Scott Ritter Answer: Statements made by senior US government officials closely conform to narratives produced by Ukrainian intelligence regarding heavy Russian casualties and limited Russian military capacity. US intelligence analysts regularly produce reports that validate official policy postures to secure promotions and bonuses rather than providing accurate assessments. Ukraine is completely bankrupt, unable to pay its soldiers or buy weapons, and seizing frozen Russian assets would end Europe's economy. Ultimately, if economic strain and supply chain disruptions ruin Christmas for American families, voters will severely punish incumbent politicians on election day.
Tehran Times Question: How much of the media campaign regarding the contract between the United States and Venezuela for access to oil is true, and will it solve the economic problems facing the US economy?
Scott Ritter Answer: It is not true at all. Venezuelan oil fields have been maintained haphazardly over many years, with many fields shut down, requiring an extraordinarily expensive and lengthy infrastructure restoration before oil can flow meaningfully. Trump's pressure on American oil companies will not generate significant income or produce substantial oil quantities beyond current levels, making the initiative a policy fantasy. Furthermore, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve of the United States has been exhausted with no capacity to recharge it. Simultaneously, Saudi Arabia is becoming a non-functioning oil producer due to repeated attacks by Houthi forces and Iraqi militias, threatening broader global energy instability. Trump's claim that Venezuelan oil will act as a quick solution represents pure fantasy rather than fact.
Tehran Times Question: How long can the United States economy tolerate this situation and the economic pressures caused by these wars?
Scott Ritter Answer: The United States maintains an illusion of economic stability by printing money excessively and relying on financial smoke and mirrors. The country operates under record-high budget deficits, while government bond yields rising above 5% divert a massive portion of GDP toward paying growing national debt. Leading economic analysts project a major economic crisis emerging around January. While the US may manage to fake it through one more cycle, a structural collapse of the American economic system remains inevitable. Furthermore, efforts by China to establish pro-Yuan trade agreements with Gulf Arab nations threaten to erode the dominance of the petrodollar.
Sputnik Question: Polish Foreign Minister Sikorski claimed that NATO could easily defeat Russia in a conventional war due to overwhelming air power; based on US and Israeli air force operations over Iran, does NATO possess overwhelming air superiority over Russia?
Scott Ritter Answer: NATO has nothing close to air superiority. Establishing air superiority requires generating sustained combat sorties, which demands well-maintained aircraft, fuel, ammunition, active airfields, and functional airborne command and control networks. In any conflict with Russia, NATO's command and control infrastructure would be disabled on day one by advanced Russian electronic warfare. NATO forces have spent two decades operating in undefended airspace dropping guided munitions, but their system failed when applied against Iran, where 39 days of operations failed to inflict a decisive blow.

The F-16 fighter jets transferred to Ukraine were expired aircraft requiring complete refurbishment. Additionally, NATO lacks the required forward airfields, ramp space, fuel storage, and ammunition reserves, all of which would be destroyed on day one, while long-range Russian interceptors would disrupt aerial refueling tankers.
Sputnik Question: Setting aside traditional aviation, how does the rest of NATO compare to Russia in terms of drone and missile capabilities?
Scott Ritter Answer: NATO nations, including Germany, possess zero national air defense capacity. NATO stripped its own air defense inventory to supply Ukraine, whose air defense network was subsequently dismantled by Russian suppression operations. Utilizing drones alone, Russia retains the capability to darken European skies and destroy selected targets without effective opposition. Following the US withdrawal from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty, Russia deployed long-range Iskander-1000 missiles and advanced cruise missiles capable of striking across Europe. Russia maintains sufficient conventional power to destroy NATO's military infrastructure, defense manufacturing, and command centers without utilizing nuclear weapons, granting it total escalatory dominance. While a nuclear exchange would result in the absolute destruction of Europe, Russia maintains survival capabilities, though Moscow seeks peaceful security arrangements rather than conflict with NATO.
Tehran Times Question: How much truth is there to the 60 Minutes interview with the American pilot who was reportedly rescued after his fighter jet was targeted by Iranian air defenses over Iran?

UK jury clears student activist of expressing support for Hamas
A student activist has been cleared of voicing support for Palestinian political movement Hamas, which was proscribed by the UK in 2021.
The jury unanimously found Sarah Cotte not guilty of expressing support for the Palestinian group -- a charge which carries up to 14 years in prison under UK anti-terrorism legisation.
The acquittal — which deals a major blow to campaigns targeting Palestinian rights activists in Britain — came after less than two hours of jury deliberations at the end of a five-day retrial at the Old Bailey Central Criminal Court.
Cotte's supporters hailed the verdict as a “massive victory” for the pro-Palestine movement in Britain.
Cotte, 22, expressed her “unconditional solidarity” with the Palestinian armed resistance against the Israeli occupation during a speech at the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London college on 9 October 2023, the Old Bailey was told.
The prosecution had argued that even though she did not name Hamas, her comments at the gathering were “thinly veiled references” to it.
Cotte had denied that her comments were about Hamas, saying she had been supporting “the right to resist” according to the international law and norms.
In June, during her first trial, Sarah faced two charges. The first was inviting support for a proscribed organisation, referring to Hamas, through a public speech, and the second was expressing an opinion or belief supportive of a proscribed organisation through messages in a closed WhatsApp group. Following that trial, the jury unanimously acquitted Cotte of the second charge. However, they failed to reach a definitive verdict on the first charge, leading the prosecution to demand a retrial, which began on Monday.
In the retrial, the prosecution's case rested on the 2023 speech delivered by Cotte — who is Ethiopian and also holds French citizenship — just two days after the start of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza. Speaking at SOAS, she defended the internationally recognised right of peoples, including the Palestinian people, to resist occupation by all means, including armed struggle. She referred to the Palestinian resistance broadly and never mentioned Hamas by name. Cotte, who was 19 years old at the time, referred to the "Al-Aqsa Flood" operation as a legitimate act of resistance.
Cotte concluded her testimony before the court by reaffirming her stance against Zionism, racism, and colonialism, describing it as a matter of principle.
At the end of January 2024, the Met Police’s counter-terrorism officers arrested Cotte after she was reported by UK Lawyers for Israel. The pro-Israel group had also reported Cotte to the University of London. However, the university refused to expel her, reaffirming its commitment to the principle of freedom of expression and opinion.
In remarks to The New Arab, a spokesperson for the Revolutionary Communist Group, to which Cotte belongs, described the acquittal as "massive victory for the principled anti-Zionist, anti-racist and anti-imperialist stance".
The group accuses the British state of “desperately attempting to criminalize the pro-Palestine movement” following its failure to convict Cotte under the Terrorism Act in June.
It pledged to continue fighting against “all criminalisation of supporters of the risen people of occupied Palestine in their righteous struggle against settler-colonialism and genocide”.
