Trump Is Betting on the Wrong Europe
The far-right parties the White House favors have a foreign-policy agenda that won’t serve American interests.
Donald Trump says he wants a Europe that is more capable of defending itself. But the nationalist-populist movements he is championing there will not advance this agenda and may put Europe at odds with the United States over China.
Earlier this month, the nationalist-populist Alternative for Germany party came just a few seats short of an outright majority in a regional parliament, its best-ever result. This Sunday, Germans will vote in two more regional elections. The ruling Christian Democrats are behind in both races, and the AfD is expected to do well in one. On Wednesday, Chancellor Friedrich Merz canceled his visit to the United Nations General Assembly next week, sparking speculation that he could soon be forced to resign.
U.S. officials are ebullient. Trump greeted the AfD’s recent electoral victory with a triumphant message on Truth Social that finished with “MGGA” (Make Germany Great Again). Richard Grenell, Trump’s former ambassador to Germany and now a presidential envoy, called the result “a huge win and a new day in Germany.”
The Trump administration has consistently embraced Europe’s nationalist-populist parties as ideological partners, and even launched a State Department fund to support MAGA-aligned European groups. It surely sees the AfD’s ascendance as a sign that politics are moving in its direction. But that is true only if Trump’s real goal is a fragmented Europe that accommodates Russian and Chinese power and is unable to punch its weight. Such an outcome would be catastrophic for U.S. interests.
Some people in the administration insist that the idea is not to weaken Europe but to shift the burden for its conventional defense to the Europeans themselves. Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, for example, reject claims that the administration is soft on Russia and say that they are calling instead for greater European self-sufficiency. Colby advocates for what he calls NATO 3.0, in which Europeans would take on the primary responsibility for their conventional defense.
But the nationalist populists do not share this view. The AfD has called for an end to all arms deliveries to Ukraine and a lifting of all sanctions on Russia. Its co-leaders, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, boycotted Volodymyr Zelensky’s speech to the Bundestag in 2024, dismissing the Ukrainian president as a “war and beggar president.”
In France, Marine Le Pen, the parliamentary leader of the nationalist-populist party National Rally and the front-runner for next spring’s presidential election, has promised to take France out of NATO’s integrated military command (France would remain a member of the alliance). Such a withdrawal would hardly help the Trump administration shift the burden of NATO’s defense to Europe.
The Trump administration’s affinity for Europe’s nationalist-populist right seems to be almost entirely cultural and civilizational, and based on the notion that Europe’s populists are fighting the same culture wars—including against immigration—as their counterparts in the United States. J. D. Vance explicitly praised then–Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán as an ally in defense of Western civilization at an election rally in Budapest on the eve of the Hungarian elections. And the Trump team seems to see the European populist right’s enemies—the European Union and national political establishments—as versions of its own domestic foes. This commonality appears to take precedence over foreign-policy concerns.
Trump officials have blasted centrist European governments for being too soft on Beijing but have said nothing about the populist right’s position on China. Some of these parties—particularly the AfD and Fidesz, in Hungary—favor much closer ties to the American adversary. The AfD’s Weidel lived in China for six years, speaks Mandarin, and wrote her doctoral dissertation about China’s pension system. Chrupalla, her co-leader, accused the German government of waging “economic war” against China for proposing a tougher trade policy toward Beijing. They have both called for warmer relations with China. Orbán, who was defeated in the Hungarian elections earlier this year, blocked the EU from criticizing Beijing, initiated an “all-weather comprehensive strategic partnership” with China, and welcomed Chinese investment in Hungarian infrastructure.
These largely transactional attitudes toward China and Russia may reflect a broader worldview among the nationalist populists, who praise Trump but are deeply skeptical of American power. In an analysis for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Jeremy Cliffe argued that the AfD supports a multipolar world order and believes that great powers, such as China and Russia, should possess spheres of influence—a perspective that Trump seems sympathetic toward. The AfD, Cliffe wrote, “may regard Trump as a civilizational ally, but its senior figures have long described the United States as a raumfremd in Europe, a hard to translate German word that means something like ‘territorially alien.’”
If parties with these views take power, they could reduce American influence in Europe while making common European action on Russia and China much more difficult. They will also make Eastern Europeans nervous about German rearmament. In 2011, Radek Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister, said, “I fear German power less than German inaction.” He recently revisited that remark, telling the German newspaper Handelsblatt, “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as the largest economy in Europe, to play a strong role in securing our common security. But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany can lead in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party—and that is exactly what the AfD represents.”
Senior Trump-administration officials say they are building a Europe that will carry its own weight. Maybe they are so beguiled by the nationalist populists’ domestic agenda that they have not yet realized it will come at the expense of NATO 3.0. Or maybe Trump doesn’t care about Europe’s defense, doesn’t see it as a U.S. interest, and doesn’t believe that Europe has any contribution to make to America’s security.
Trump and Vance seem to be laying the foundation for a more divided Europe that is incapable of deterring Russia, ever more dependent on China, and at odds with itself. If the administration continues on this path, it may get the European culture war it wants, but the United States will lose its ally.

What neuroscientists thought was a biological signature for IQ might actually be socioeconomic privilege
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:00:33 UTC
20:00:33 KST

A child’s neighborhood and socioeconomic background appear to shape the function and structure of their developing brain more powerfully than any other behavioral or environmental factor. Brain activity patterns previously thought to represent innate intelligence are actually a reflection of socioeconomic status, likely driven by environmental stressors like sleep deprivation, according to findings published in the journal Science.
For years, neuroscientists have mapped single human traits to brain imaging data. Researchers typically look for the biological basis of a specific cognitive ability, such as intelligence quotient, or a clinical symptom, like anxiety. They compare these traits against physical brain measurements to find overlapping physiological patterns.
However, the environment in which a person grows up exerts an enormous influence on their physical and cognitive development. A team led by Scott Marek, a researcher at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, wanted to evaluate how a vast array of different lifestyle, environmental, and cognitive variables relate to brain biology simultaneously. By looking at hundreds of factors at once, the researchers could determine which aspects of a child’s life are most strongly tied to brain organization.
The researchers utilized data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study. This massive project tracked the development of thousands of nine and ten year old children across the United States. The team analyzed two common brain measurements taken via magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI.
The first measurement was resting-state functional connectivity, which maps how different regions of the brain communicate. It works by tracking spontaneous blood flow while a person is resting, revealing which brain networks naturally fire together. The second measurement was cortical thickness, which measures the physical depth of the brain’s outer layer of gray matter.
The team took these brain scans and compared them against 649 different non-imaging variables, evaluating the strength of the association for each one. These variables spanned a dozen categories, including physical health, parenting, personality, substance use, and social adjustment.
Out of all 649 variables, socioeconomic measures exhibited the strongest and most reliable associations with the children’s brain data. The single most powerful association was linked to the socioeconomic opportunities afforded by the child’s home zip code. This metric captures neighborhood-level factors like school quality, environmental toxins, and access to resources.
Other highly ranked variables included sleep duration and the amount of time children spent on screens. Traditional metrics of cognition and overall mental health symptoms ranked much lower on the list.
The researchers then mapped out exactly where these socioeconomic associations appeared in the physical brain. They found that socioeconomic status was strongly linked to differences in the primary motor and sensory regions. These are areas of the brain that process physical movement and immediate sensory input.
To understand what this specific biological pattern meant, the team compared it to established reference maps of the brain. They looked at positron emission tomography scans tracking neurotransmitters, brainwave recordings monitoring sleep patterns, and imaging that captured the physical effects of task-based reasoning.
The socioeconomic brain pattern closely matched the biological signatures of physiological arousal, sleep deprivation, stress, and the effects of stimulant medications. The pattern did not map onto the frontal and parietal cortices. These are the associative regions of the brain known to handle higher-order cognitive tasks, such as logic, mathematics, and complex thought.
The team noticed an unexpected similarity when they looked at the brain map for intelligence quotient, or IQ. The physical pattern associated with IQ scores was nearly identical to the socioeconomic pattern. It was concentrated in the exact same motor and sensory regions, completely bypassing the brain areas actually responsible for complex reasoning.
Suspecting a mathematical overlap, the researchers adjusted their data to remove the statistical influence of socioeconomic status from the test scores. After this adjustment, the strong associations between the brain and IQ scores largely vanished. The faint pattern that remained shifted away from the sensory and arousal regions and looked slightly more aligned with known cognitive networks.
The researchers tested this overlap further using multivariate analysis, an advanced machine learning technique. They trained computer models to predict a child’s IQ score based entirely on their brain connectivity patterns. The team manipulated the data fed into the models, restricting some training sets to only include children from high socioeconomic backgrounds.
When the models were trained exclusively on affluent children, they completely failed to predict test scores in a new, separate group of participants. The predictive models only worked when the training data included children from neighborhoods with lower socioeconomic status. The researchers concluded that the algorithm was engaging in shortcut learning.
Shortcut learning happens when a computer model relies on a secondary, background variable instead of the intended target. In this case, the algorithm was not detecting a biological signature for intelligence. It was simply detecting the socioeconomic status of the child, which happened to correlate with their test scores.
These population-level associations observe data across large groups at a single moment in time. Group averages cannot predict the future outcomes or cognitive potential of an individual child. Socioeconomic opportunity only explained about 16 percent of the total differences seen across the children’s brain scans, meaning many other biological and environmental factors contribute to human development.
The findings do challenge the notion that IQ scores measure a fixed, essentialized biological trait. The results suggest that past studies linking brain networks to intelligence were likely documenting the physiological toll of environmental stressors.
Future longitudinal research is needed to track these developmental pathways as children age. Researchers might also investigate whether interventions focused on sleep quality and stress reduction can positively influence brain development in under-resourced communities.
The study, “Patterns of brain-wide associations reflect socioeconomics,” was authored by Scott Marek, Meghan Rose Donohue, Nicole R. Karcher, Caroline P. Hoyniak, Roselyne J. Chauvin, Ashley C. Meyer, John Miller, Andrew N. Van, Anxu Wang, Noah J. Baden, Vahdeta Suljic, Kristen M. Scheidter, Julia Monk, Forrest I. Whiting, Nadeshka J. Ramirez-Perez, Samuel R. Krimmel, Athanasia Metoki, Sarah E. Paul, Aaron J. Gorelik, Timothy J. Hendrickson, Stephen M. Malone, Rebecca F. Schwarzlose, Carlos Cardenas-Iniguez, Megan M. Herting, Steven E. Petersen, Joan Luby, Anita C. Randolph, Michael J. Shanahan, Eric Turkheimer, Benjamin P. Kay, Evan M. Gordon, Timothy O. Laumann, Deanna M. Barch, Damien A. Fair, Brenden Tervo-Clemmens, and Nico U. F. Dosenbach.

Can Kevin Warsh Change the Federal Reserve?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

On Sept. 15 and 16, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh presided over his third Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, the body responsible for setting the interest rates that shape the American economy.
With August jobs numbers coming in stronger than analysts expected, the Fed unanimously decided to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point for the first time since 2023. Its new benchmark interest rate sits at a target range of 3.75% to 4%, and markets are expecting at least one additional interest rate hike by the end of the year. That decision unfolded against a striking backdrop: inflation has run above the Fed's 2% target for more than five and a half years.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” stated Warsh. Few economists disagreed with Warsh’s determination and the Fed’s decision—but President Donald Trump did.
Trump quickly critiqued the committee’s undivided vote to raise rates via social media. “LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” he cried.
And upon landing in North Carolina for a campaign rally, the president told reporters he blamed Warsh’s Board of Governors for the decision. “I told Kevin, I said, ‘You might as well vote with the board because it’s just not going to matter.’ The board is very hostile,” he said. “They’re very political. They’re doing the wrong thing. They’re a bunch of politicians.”
Warsh took the helm of the more than century-old institution earlier this year and has moved quickly to put his stamp on it, launching five task forces within his first month, each charged with developing recommendations across a different area of the Fed's mandate. How far he can take that reform agenda will depend on his ability to build coalitions among fellow board and FOMC members and to hold the confidence of financial markets.
At the press conference following his first FOMC meeting in June, Warsh announced several initiatives covering the Fed's communications strategy, balance sheet, data sources, productivity and jobs, and inflation framework. Each is led by three outside experts drawn from academia and industry. The groups are expected to deliver preliminary findings this fall, with most wrapping up by year's end.
The pace and ambition of the efforts signal that Warsh is serious. Whether it proves truly transformative remains an open question.
Watch the data, not the Fed
Of his five reform areas, communication has drawn the most attention, and Warsh moved on it before the task force even convened. He stopped offering long-term projections on Fed policy actions and simplified its press releases, signaling a clear break from recent practice. At the heart of this shift is Warsh's belief that markets have grown too dependent on Fed communication, paying more attention to what officials say than to the underlying economic data. He argues this creates a feedback problem: if markets are reacting to the Fed rather than to the data, the Fed gets a distorted read on where markets actually stand.
Central to this critique is his skepticism of forward guidance, the practice by which Fed officials provide long-term outlooks to signal predictability and transparency. Forward guidance in various forms has been used since the 1990’s but became central as a policy tool when the policy rate reached “the zero lower bound” during the 2008 financial crisis. It was never fully retired. Warsh wants to end it, arguing that it ties the Fed's hands and leaves officials with less room to respond to new information as it arrives.
"The role of forward guidance should be limited and circumscribed. Otherwise, it risks creating ambiguity in the name of clarity. Oversharing policy deliberations and overcommitting to future decisions can lead markets, businesses, and households astray,” argued Warsh. “And I believe when policymakers make quasi-commitments on interest rates through the cycle, we inhibit our own freedom to make the right calls when it's time to decide."
Yet even a more restrained communication style does not insulate a Fed chair from market scrutiny. After his second FOMC meeting in July, Warsh learned that lesson firsthand. Many observers felt he underperformed at the press conference, and markets responded with alarm, raising questions about his credibility at a moment when inflation remains stubbornly high and the chair, while acknowledging the problem, has appeared reluctant to deploy his most powerful tool: raising interest rates.
To be sure, Warsh is not the first Fed chair to rattle markets during a first-year press conference. Both Jerome Powell and Janet Yellen had similar stumbles early in their tenures. What matters is the recovery, and Warsh moved quickly to make one. At the annual Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium in Wyoming at the end of August, he delivered a forceful address on the state of the economy and the urgency of bringing inflation to heel, reassuring markets and resetting the tone ahead of September's meeting.
Warsh's push to streamline Fed communication extends to the meeting calendar itself. He has proposed reducing the number of annual FOMC meetings from eight to six, which would mark the first such structural change since the 1980s. Fewer meetings, he argues, would give the committee more time between sessions to absorb incoming data and deliberate before acting. Critics counter that the tradeoff is agility. With only six scheduled meetings a year, the Fed would have fewer opportunities to respond to fast-moving economic conditions without resorting to emergency sessions and inter-meeting moves. Importantly, Warsh has not convinced critics that the current schedule leads to worse policy outcomes.
Every corner of the Fed under review
Among Warsh’s remaining reform areas, the balance sheet and inflation framework task forces carry the greatest consequence. After the 2008 financial crisis, the Fed began purchasing long-term government bonds and other securities to inject liquidity into the economy, a practice known as quantitative easing. Its balance sheet swelled from roughly $1 trillion before the crisis to nearly $9 trillion in the wake of the Covid pandemic. It currently stands at $6.7 trillion, a level Warsh views as excessive. Bringing this total down is one of his stated goals, but doing so is acutely market sensitive. Any reductions will need to be phased in gradually and communicated with care, as an abrupt shift risks triggering the kind of market disruption the Fed is expressly trying to avoid.
The inflation framework task force operates under similarly intense scrutiny from policymakers and markets alike. The 2% inflation target itself is not on the table. The task force will instead examine the drivers of inflation, how it is measured, and what tools are available for delivering price stability in a changing economy.
The fourth task force examines the economic impact of technology, and artificial intelligence in particular, on the Fed's dual mandate of keeping prices stable and employment high. The fifth focuses on data sources, evaluating new information streams and methodological changes to improve how the Fed collects data and measures inflation. The goal is to give policymakers more current information on the state of the economy.
What Warsh needs
To enact any of these changes, whether on the balance sheet, the inflation framework, or the number of FOMC meetings, Warsh will need to bring his fellow policymakers along. The chair has the authority to convene the task forces and shape their composition, but any resulting changes require approval from the seven-member board of governors, or in the case of FOMC meetings, the full 19-member committee. All proposed reforms will face intense internal debate. The recent frequency of dissents during FOMC meetings suggests that not all members will greet the reform agenda with equal enthusiasm. How transformative Warsh's tenure proves to be will therefore depend not only on the ambition of the proposed reforms but on his ability to bring a majority of colleagues on board. And as his July press conference demonstrated, financial markets will be watching and rendering their own verdict throughout.
Warsh has taken over the Fed at a turbulent moment. Inflation has been running above the 2% target for half a decade. Supply shocks from the conflict in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, combined with repeated tariff threats from the White House, have injected fresh uncertainty into the U.S. economy. Meanwhile, the effects of artificial intelligence, beyond an immediate boost to economic activity, and the potential productivity gains as well as the potential job losses, remain difficult to measure and even harder to predict. And with midterm elections approaching, political pressure is only likely to intensify. Trump has repeatedly called for lower interest rates, and he seems unlikely to quiet his calls.
Faced with these pressures, Warsh has set out on an ambitious reform path. Whether he succeeds will come down to two things: the pace at which he can advance his agenda, and his ability to bring enough of his fellow Fed members with him. Most importantly, Warsh and his colleagues will need to convince the public, the financial markets, and Congress that the changes adopted will lead to better policy making.
This is his ultimate challenge.

Forget the AI Slowdown—the Vulnerability Explosion Is Already Happening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Welcome to the inaugural edition of Kernel Panic! A weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
AI doomers have recently traded one worst-case scenario for another, putting aside a potential software vulnerability apocalypse to focus on the possibility of rogue AI causing mass human death in the next decade. As AI leaders consider a cooperative slowdown on frontier model development, though, one aspect of the cybersecurity sea change has already arrived thanks to existing, broadly available capabilities in mainstream AI products, including open weight models.
A tidal wave of vulnerabilities uncovered using AI has only accelerated in recent months—piling more pressure on under-resourced, and very human, IT and security teams and straining volunteers who maintain crucial open source software. Researchers found and disclosed a vast array of vulnerabilities before the rise of AI-enhanced bug hunting as well, but the recent surge is clear.
Microsoft said last week that it has issued patches for 974 CVEs so far this month, setting a new record. (CVEs, or common vulnerabilities and exposures, is cybersecurity jargon for confirmed software flaws.) In July, Oracle shipped 1,448 patches compared to 309 in July 2025. Google Chrome’s two major version releases in June included 1,072 patches, more than all of the vulnerability fixes shipped in the prior 23 big releases combined. And Mozilla said in April that it found 271 vulnerabilities in Firefox during one bug hunting sprint using Anthropic’s Mythos model.
Across the board, there have been a stunning 66,401 CVEs recorded as of Wednesday this week, according to Jerry Gamblin, the head of research at Empirical Security and founder of RogoLabs, which runs the CVE analysis project cve.icu. By September 16 last year, cve.icu had logged a total of 33,512 CVEs—almost half the current total. For all of 2022, the year OpenAI launched its first version of ChatGPT, cve.icu recorded 25,000 CVEs.
Among both security and AI researchers, experts have been divided about whether this spike and other impacts of AI on cybersecurity will be catastrophic or instead magnify existing dynamics and challenges. Some have pointed out that slow patch adoption and lagging investment in cybersecurity broadly already gave attackers many advantages that led to hacking disasters before the rise of AI. But as vulnerability discovery numbers have continued to rise, and the discussion has become less theoretical, the two sides have seemed to move a bit closer.
“I don’t think it’s overblown,” Gamblin says of the apparent explosion in vulnerability findings across the industry. “What I would push back on is the idea that a bigger number is itself the harm. More CVEs is not more vulnerability. It's more known vulnerability, which is mostly the system working.”
The fear, though, is that vast vulnerability discovery will mean developers getting outpaced on patching, software users who can’t patch fast enough, and an array of escalating cyberattacks fueled by more attackers discovering novel vulnerabilities on their own using AI. As Britain’s National Cyber Security Center puts it, “Just finding vulnerabilities does nothing to improve your security.”
For now, many researchers tell us that there is at least a tenuous balance between AI accelerating bug discovery and AI aiding defenders. “Actors, just like industry, are trying to figure out, ‘where do I use AI?’” says Matthew Olney, director of threat intelligence at Cisco Systems.
As the situation continues to evolve, an AI slowdown of whatever form—be it regulation or an industry accord—could perhaps/hopefully prevent AI from carrying out a mass human extermination event, but it cannot stop the vulnerability tsunami that has already arrived as a result of existing AI tools.
As RogoLabs Gamblin puts it, “Discovery scales with compute. Remediation scales with people—and people are the part you can't buy more of in a quarter.”

After deaths of nine women, South Africans gather to run, mourn and demand change
JOHANNESBURG – South Africans gathered for memorial runs and protests this week after the killings of nine women near Johannesburg reignited anger and fear over violence that many say mirrors the dangers women face every day.
Police have found the bodies of nine women in Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg, over the past two months and are investigating whether the killings are linked.
Most of the victims were in their 20s and 30s. Some were found stripped of their clothes and showed signs of sexual assault.
A memorial run in Johannesburg on the morning of Sept 19 honoured one of the victims, Elizabeth Moselakgomo, who disappeared after going for a run and was found dead days later. Runners lit candles and carried a banner reading: “Enough. Stop Femicide.”
“We are here because we’ve lost a runner. But we are not safe anywhere,” said Lerato Lentsela, one of dozens of people who dressed in black for the memorial run.
“We are not safe running, we are not safe at a post office, we are not safe on a date, we are not safe in our own homes, we are not safe in an Uber.”
The killings have reignited anger over violence against women in South Africa, where gender-based violence was declared a national disaster in 2025. Many women say the heightened attention and official promises have done little to make them feel safer.
“Enough is enough. Our women deserve to live, walk, run and exist without fear,” the Uyinene Mrwetyana Foundation, a charity that campaigns against gender-based violence, said in a statement.
President Cyril Ramaphosa said on Sept 17 that South Africa could not allow itself to grow accustomed to such violence and pledged that no stone would be left unturned in the investigations.
But policing in South Africa is weakened by corruption and lack of resources. Only about one in 10 murders is ever solved.
“We need to relook at our policing. The only reason these nine women were found was because there was more police presence in the area. This problem is countrywide,” said Merlize Jogiat of Women for Change, which held a memorial event in Cape Town on Sept 18.
Some women also criticised police advice urging them to take extra precautions when exercising or walking alone.
“Stop placing the responsibility of our safety back onto us,” Women for Change said in a social media post. “Women should not have to organise their entire lives around surviving violence and not being next.” REUTERS

Israel plans to ask for US additional defence capabilities as a "compensation" after Washington agreed to sell F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, according to Israeli media.
Tel Aviv will seek to purchase weapons systems that US President Donald Trump's administration had previously declined to approve, Israeli news website Walla reported on Friday.
Israel’s military focus extends beyond advanced fighter jets and next-generation stealth aircraft to space-based weapons and the development and production of interceptor aircraft, the outlet said.
Weapons to be demanded by Israeli officials also include "bunker-busting munitions and underground systems capable of operating deep beneath rocky mountains,” it added.
The move is intended to secure a “compensation” from Washington following the F-35 deal with Riyadh, the website said.
On Thursday, the US State Department approved a possible $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia.
The package also includes 49 Pratt & Whitney F135-PW-100 engines, along with cryptographic equipment, electronic warfare support, training and logistics packages, according to a notification sent to the US Congress.
If completed, the deal would make Saudi Arabia the first Arab country to acquire F-35 fighter jets, while Israel is currently the only operator of the aircraft in the Middle East.
Israeli officials have repeatedly criticised Saudi Arabia over its refusal to normalise relations with Tel Aviv before the establishment of a Palestinian state along the 1967 borders, a condition which the international community supports while Israel continues to reject.

Turkey detains nine Israelis in a sweeping probe into an alleged global investment scam that defrauded victims of $266 million

- Nine Israelis detained as Turkey targets global investment-fraud network
Nine Israelis detained as Turkey targets global investment-fraud network
The alleged scheme began with multilingual call-center employees approaching potential investors
Turkish authorities have detained nine Israeli citizens in a sweeping investigation into an alleged international investment fraud operation that prosecutors say stole at least $266 million from victims across several continents.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that it had received reports of the arrests.
“Yesterday, Friday, September 18, reports were received regarding the arrest of several Israeli citizens in Turkey on suspicion of involvement in criminal activity, apparently as part of a broader wave of arrests,” the ministry said. “The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is handling the matter and working to ensure that the Israeli citizens’ rights are upheld.”
The Israeli detainees were reportedly employed at call centers connected to the alleged scheme. Investigators are examining a total of 239 suspects associated with 42 call centers and 28 companies, according to Turkish authorities.
Police searched 236 locations across Istanbul and the southwestern province of Mugla in an operation coordinated with Turkey’s National Intelligence Organization and Interpol.
Investigators allege that the businesses formed part of an international network known as “Scam Empire,” which used fraudulent online trading platforms to target victims in Europe, Asia and Africa. Turkish officials claim that individuals linked to Israel controlled the companies and received the proceeds.
According to investigators, multilingual call-center employees approached potential investors and directed them to trading websites displaying fabricated account balances and apparent profits. Victims were then encouraged to deposit additional funds.
Authorities say the money was subsequently moved through foreign bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets. Reported losses ranged from about $10,000 to several hundred thousand dollars per victim.
One suspected organizer, identified by Turkish officials only by the initials Y.A., is described as an Israeli citizen who also holds a Portuguese passport.
Investigators believe some of the groups transferred their operations from Israel to Turkey to reduce the risk of detection. The call centers allegedly operated through shell companies and recruited employees who spoke languages including Japanese, Hindi, French and Spanish.
New recruits were reportedly trained to use aliases and fabricated personal histories to gain victims’ trust. Some employees were allegedly assigned fictional qualifications, including degrees from prestigious universities, and instructed to present themselves as representatives of investment platforms whose names were frequently changed.
Turkish officials further allege that prospective employees underwent polygraph examinations intended to uncover possible connections to law enforcement or intelligence agencies. Hebrew was reportedly prohibited inside the offices, and Israeli citizens were excluded from the network’s list of potential targets.

Tired of Cluttered Productivity Apps? This One’s Just a Text Document
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

I've spent decades testing, reviewing, and (most importantly) using different to-do list applications. It's a career, yes, but it's also a bit of an obsession.
And I think we can all admit that most of these apps are way too complicated. A to-do list is just a list. Humans have been making lists for thousands of years, long before computers existed. Paper works well, but so does a stone slate if that's what you've got handy.
It's possible that you, a modern human, absolutely need a to-do list application with bells and whistles—due dates, recurring tasks, sharing features, and maybe even an AI integration. But there's a good chance all you need is the digital equivalent of a piece of paper: A simple list of things that need to get done.
And that's what Tasks.txt, a totally free Mac app, offers. From Ukrainian programmer Yevhen Kharkivskyi, this tool is based on the todo.txt system developed by Gina Trapani. It's a complete alternative to a to-do list app that is based on a single text file.
The important thing here, though, is that it offers more than just a text file. This is a well-executed app. Open Tasks.txt and you'll see a simple list broken down into three categories: Done, Next, and Backlog.
The general idea is to use "Next" for the tasks you want to accomplish today and "Backlog" for the things you want to do later. The "Done" section is populated as you check things off, then cleared out at the beginning of every day.
It's possible to use this application using only the keyboard, which I love. Open the window and you can just start typing tasks—your cursor is already active in the text box at the bottom. Hit Enter and your task will be added either to Backlog or Next, depending on what you choose in the drop-down menu to the right of your text box. Press the Tab key to switch from the text box to your task list. You can use the arrows to change which task is currently selected. Pressing the Enter key adds a note below the name of a task, and Cmd+Enter marks a task complete. You can also move tasks up and down the list using Cmd+Up/Down.
There are no unnecessary controls or interface elements in your way. You can open this application, decide what you need to do, then get to it. And you aren’t stuck using keyboard shortcuts—using the mouse is just as intuitive, if that's what you prefer.
The to-do list is the heart of the app, but there's also an Archive and Scratchpad tab. The Archive includes every task you’ve completed in the past—everything from the Done section is moved here at the end of each day. The Scratchpad is just a blank text document you can use for keeping notes.
All of this, notably, is stored in a couple of text documents. You can find these documents in the app’s settings and open them with any text editor. It's pretty easy to look at the document and figure out what's going on.
Your task list isn't in some database in the cloud—it's on your computer, in an open, human-readable format. This simplicity means you can easily grab your tasks to use in some other application later, if that's what you want.
And Tasks.txt makes it clear that your tasks are completely private. "There is no account, no cloud sync, no telemetry, no analytics, no crash reporting," the website states. "There are no servers. Nothing leaves your machine." This is a rarity in the modern age, where every piece of software is trying to hold your data hostage to sell a subscription. This alone makes this an app worth considering.
Mostly, though, I just think it's a well-implemented app that gets the basics extremely right. It won't work for everyone, sure, but it might work perfectly for you.

Russia is trying to sell the world an image of a great power without which, supposedly, it is impossible to resolve international problems. However, the results of a survey conducted in July–August 2026 in 34 countries commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation show a different picture. Only 26% of respondents are prepared to view Russia’s leading role in world affairs positively. Half of respondents view such leadership negatively. In developed countries, support for Russia’s role is just 13%
It is noted that what is even worse for Moscow is that a significant part of the world perceives Russia not as a leader, but as a threat. On average, 42% of respondents called it a serious danger to their own country. In Poland, the figure is 78%; in Norway and Sweden, 73% each; in the United Kingdom, 67%; and in France and Germany, 64% each.
Particularly telling is the gap between Europe’s perception of Russia and Russia’s own view of itself. For years, the Kremlin has tried to impose the notion of the Russian Federation as a state that sets the rules of international politics. Instead, in a significant part of Europe, it is viewed primarily as a source of military threat
Russian propaganda traditionally tries to compensate for its isolation in the West with claims of support from the countries of the Global South. But here, too, the picture is far from the Kremlin’s version. In developing countries, only 40% of respondents are prepared to view Russia’s leading role positively. In other words, even there Moscow does not secure majority support for its claims to global leadership.
The Kremlin can call Russia a “center of power” and claim to be shaping a new world order as much as it likes. Outside Russia’s propaganda bubble, these ambitions have little public support. For a significant part of the world, Russia is neither a model of development nor a desirable global leader, but a state from which threats and conflicts are expected

With the start of the main stage of voting in the pseudo-elections to the Russian State Duma, Russian propaganda launched a large-scale information campaign, attempting to create the illusion of a mass “patriotic upsurge” in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.

From Human Reasoning to Belief: An Empirical Account
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:23:00 UTC
19:23:00 KST

Joshua Mugg’s book, From Human Reasoning to Belief: An Empirical Account draws on a vast empirical literature to develop and defend a single-process theory (SPT) of human reasoning against popular dual-process theories (DPT). In the second half of the book, it leverages its SPT to help explain various empirical results from belief and belief formation.
DPTs have cropped up in virtually every part of psychological and neural science (Evans & Stanovich, 2013; De Neys, 2021). They distinguish between Type-1 processing, which is often described as “fast”, “intuitive”, “automatic”, etc., and Type-2 processing, which is often described as “slow”, “reflective”, “controlled”, etc. The labels ‘Type-1’ and ‘Type-2’ are fashionable today because they maintain neutrality on different characterisations of the distinction. The common commitment, as Mugg points out, is that the distinction, whatever it is, “is supposed to cut cognition itself in two” (19).
However, Mugg notes that DPT has been engaged in a steady retreat for decades. At first, DPT was associated with massively conjunctive claims, like that cognition itself was cut into two, where one side consisted of processes that are fast and intuitive and automatic, etc. and the other side consisted of processes that are slow and reflective and controlled, etc. Mugg notes that these are most charitably interpreted as statistical, clustering claims (a laSamuels, 2009). This is often known as “Standard Menu” DPT.
Decades of functional dissociation studies have called this view into question: it’s proven easy to find processes that are fast but reflective, slow but intuitive, etc. So, dual-process theorists have retreated to what I’ll call “Essentialised” formulations of DPT: cognition itself is cut into two, where one part has one property, and the other part lacks that property. For example, Evans suggests that Type-1 processing doesn’t involve working memory, while Type-2 does (Evans & Stanovich, 2013). Since Essentialised DPT makes no clustering claims, it is quite resistant to functional dissociation studies.
The retreat from Standard Menu DPT to Essentialised DPT is cause for concern, though. It is reminiscent of what Lakatos (1970) calls a “degenerative” research program. It started off making many specific predictions, which were then falsified. In response, DPT has protected its core theoretical commitment (that cognition itself is split in two) by reducing the empirical content of its auxiliary hypotheses (rejecting conjunctive claims about Type-1 and Type-2 processing), resulting in fewer, less specific predictions (as in Essentialised DPT). (To be clear, I’m not saying that DPT is degenerative—just that it’s reasonable to worry it is.)
The apparent degeneracy of Mugg’s target, DPT, puts him at a significant advantage since he aims to defend a particular instance of single process theory (SPT), which he calls the “Soundboard Account of Reasoning”. Unfortunately, I worry that his account squanders some of its advantage: the first half of the book presses objections against DPT that seem to be mutually inconsistent, and then halfway through the book, Mugg shifts his focus from human reasoning to belief. The beleaguered DPT will live to see another day, I suspect.
Chapter 1 lays out some of Mugg’s starting commitments. He endorses Craver- and Khalidi-style weakenings of Boyd’s account of (natural) kinds (Boyd, 1991; Craver, 2009; Khalidi, 2023). He endorses the view that belief is a kind in this sense—i.e., it is individuated (at least partly) by a cluster of functional properties. It’s a bit difficult to tell from this stage why all this matters, but I think this chapter was meant to provide connective tissue between Chapters 2 and 3 (which focus on cognitive architecture) and Chapters 4–6 (which focus on belief).
Chapter 2 is more focused. Most of this chapter is dedicated to reviewing experimental literature on DPT. His review does well to highlight DPT’s (apparent) degeneracy—although the Lakatosian framing is mine, not his. Consistent with my Lakatosian framing of DPT’s problem, though, Mugg opts to present its problem in the form of a dilemma.
The first horn is Standard Menu DPT. It is rich in empirical content, so it makes bold, testable claims. The problem is just that these claims are widely disproven. Standard Menu DPT is interesting but empirically inadequate, then. The second horn is Essentialised DPT. It rejects the inadequate empirical content of Standard Menu DPT, but at the cost of explanatory power. Essentialised DPT is empirically adequate, but uninteresting (non-explanatory).
Even if we think Essentialised DPT is a retreat from Standard Menu DPT, it isn’t obvious that this is untoward in any way. Rejecting clustering claims is probably a good idea. Why not think, as Evans & Stanovich (2013) clearly seem to, that Essentialised DPT is a disciplining of Standard Menu DPT’s excesses? It’s not enough to say, as Mugg does, that this retreat “reduces the explanatory power of DPT” (31). Giving up some explanatory power for a lot more plausibility and empirical adequacy might be a perfectly acceptable bargain for DPT.
However, it seems like Mugg wants to say that Essentialised DPT has no explanatory power at all. At one point, for example, he complains how “it becomes unclear how to test these nuanced versions of DPT” (33). At another point, he even says that “the Logical Intuition Model renders itself compatible with the results at the cost of making the theory explanatorily and predictively inert” (35–36). If true, this is a serious problem. No amount of plausibility and empirical adequacy would be worth that much sacrifice in explanatory power.
Suppose Mugg is right. Essentialised DPT has no empirical content. All that’s left to it would be two bare claims about type-individuation: (a) some processes have a property-like access to working memory, while others don’t and (b) that property difference is sufficient for them to be different types of processes. Mugg appears to disagree with the latter claim, since he goes in for clustering accounts of types, such that we can change the type a cognitive process belongs to only by making sufficiently large changes to sufficiently many of its properties.
If that’s right, then Mugg’s disagreement with Essentialised DPT is metaphysical, not empirical. But then it’s strange that Mugg attempts to give an empirical argument against DPT at all (via inference to the best explanation). We can expect an empirical argument to work against Standard Menu DPT (since it has empirical content), but it shouldn’t work against Essentialised DPT. If Mugg does want to disagree with DPT on empirical grounds (as seems to), then he’d need to clearly attribute empirical content to DPT.
Chapter 3 introduces Mugg’s Soundboard Account of Reasoning. His account is centred on a metaphor: that reasoning has a soundboard architecture that is modulated with knobs and switches. Put literally, reasoning is such that it can be adequately characterised by dynamical functions over independent parameters, continuous (“knobs”) and/or discrete (“switches”). It’s the independence of the parameters that distinguishes this view from Standard Menu DPT (which maintains clustering and hence, dependence between the parameters).
As Mugg notes in Chapter 2, though, most dual-process theorists today endorse Essentialised DPT. By itself, though, the Soundboard Account is fully consistent with Essentialised DPT, which agrees that the parameters are independent. Essentialised DPT just insists on an additional commitment—that one parameter is privileged, such that changing the value of that parameter (but not any other parameter) makes a type-difference to the whole reasoning process (this works best if the parameter is discrete).
Mugg anticipates this worry:
One might think that I am…retaining diachronic Type 1 and Type 2 processing, which really makes the Soundboard Account a specific version of default-interventionist DPT. This is not so. Initial responses (as a category) and subsequent responses (as a category) will be too heterogeneous on the Soundboard Account to constitute kinds or serve as helpful constructs because the properties on the Standard Menu crosscut one another on my account, even for initial settings. (43)
However, this response begs the question against Essentialised DPT, which rejects that initial responses must have a different cluster of properties than subsequent responses in order to belong to different types of processes.
I think it would have been better if Mugg had just granted the metaphysical claim that default vs. intervening processing would be different types if the former were diachronically separated from the latter (perhaps by a discrete event like metacognitive control), and then he could insist that the empirical evidence suggests there is no discrete distinguishing event like this, and hence, there is no type-difference between default vs. intervening processing. For example, Grayot et al. (forthcoming) press an empirical objection like this against my proposed formulation of Essentialised DPT (Rumana, 2023).
Chapters 4–6 take a significant turn. Mugg stops critiquing DPT and starts critiquing various accounts of belief formation: Chapter 4 criticises Spinozan accounts of belief formation, Chapter 5 criticises conventional explanations of implicit bias results, and Chapter 6 criticises doxastic involuntarism.
In personal correspondence, Mugg has clarified that he meant to show that we “can indirectly test competing accounts of belief by tying them to cognitive architectures”.[1] As such, his Soundboard Account is meant to provide a standard by which to arbitrate different accounts of belief. Since many accounts of belief draw support from outdated formulations of DPT (like Tamar Gendler’s account of aliefs), I think he’s quite right that support for these accounts can be undercut by reiterating criticisms against these forms of DPT. Therefore, I would encourage readers (especially readers interested in belief and belief formation) to read Chapters 4–6 in light of this.
Nevertheless, the book itself provides a different (and less plausible) justification for these chapters: “my aim in [Chapter 3] was not to argue for the Soundboard Account, but merely to build the theory. My argument for the theory will come as an inference to the best explanation [in Chapters 4–6]” (61). My review will take the book at its word that the Soundboard Account draws its justification from the content of Chapters 4–6 (especially since no other justification is provided for it, at least relative to Essentialised DPT).
I doubt the content of Chapters 4–6 can justify the Soundboard Account, though. First, Mugg himself admits that (at least some of) the accounts he criticises could also be couched in terms of his Soundboard Account (65). That seems true for all the accounts. Prima facie, that might seem like a problem for Mugg: if the Soundboard Account is equally compatible with all accounts of belief formation, how could confirming any account of belief formation confirm the Soundboard Account? One would start to worry that this is a real-life case of Clark Glymour’s (1980) tacking problem.
Mugg endorses Elliott Sober’s (1999) contrastive account of confirmation (fn. 4, p. 15), so perhaps he could forestall this objection by taking his explanations of belief formation to confirm his Soundboard Account against DPT, but not to confirm the Soundboard Account tout court. If that’s right, then confirming his account of belief formation can confirm the Soundboard Account against DPT only if his account of belief formation is better accommodated by the Soundboard Account than by DPT. Mugg suggests that it is, but he only considers the Standard Menu DPT (whose empirical inadequacy is already well-known).
Again, though, Essentialised DPT seems equally capable of accommodating accounts of belief formation, since empirical explanations of belief are neutral to type individuation. Thus, it’s hard to see how various explanations of belief formation can help arbitrate the disagreement between SPT and DPT. As a result, Chapters 4–6 may read like a long digression if you, like most dual-process theorists today, are more interested in the viability of Essentialised DPT (and if you take the content of these chapters to be justification for the Soundboard Account against DPT).
Chapter 7 tries to wrap everything up. It’s clear from this conclusion that the focus of the book has shifted from human reasoning to (various observations about) belief (and its formation). I’m left thinking that the title “From human reasoning to belief” should be taken as a literal description of the book’s focus. Perhaps, it’s unfair that my review hasn’t been more willing to follow this shift. I do expect this book can inspire a reader with interests in both belief and human reasoning to see the explanatory relationships between them. Either way, this book does not provide the sustained critique of DPT and empirical argument for the Soundboard Account that it promises.

Russia reports online attacks on electoral system on second day of parliamentary vote

Russia reports online attacks on electoral system on second day of parliamentary vote
MOSCOW – The Russian authorities reported attacks on voting systems and communication lines across the country on Sept 19, the second day of a three-day parliamentary election that Moscow is treating as a test of public support for the war in Ukraine.
The State Duma election, the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in February 2022, is widely expected to see the ruling pro-Putin United Russia party retain its dominance in Russia’s tightly controlled political system.
Most anti-war candidates were excluded from the ballot before voting across Russia’s 11 time zones got under way, after the Supreme Court ruled in August that the liberal Yabloko party, which wants a ceasefire in Ukraine, breached electoral rules, something it denied.
Some Yabloko candidates, however, are still contesting single-member constituencies, which account for half of the 450 seats in the Lower House of Parliament. The party has traditionally polled in the single digits.
On Sept 19, the authorities said the online voting system in Moscow was subjected to a strong attack overnight, but that the situation was under control.
The attacks were continuing, Central Election Commission (CEC) chairwoman Ella Pamfilova was cited as saying by state media, but all were being successfully repelled.
Russia’s digital ministry said it registered a sabotage attempt on communication lines in the country’s Far East, but that the attack was thwarted, and all communication had been restored, state media reported.
President Vladimir Putin earlier accused Ukraine of trying to interfere with the vote, without providing evidence.
Nationwide turnout as of mid-day on Sept 19 stood at 32.58 per cent, according to CEC data cited by state media.
In Moldova’s separatist pro-Russian Transdniestria region, the election triggered a diplomatic dispute with Chisinau over its objections to the Kremlin’s plan to open 15 polling stations for Russian nationals there.
Moscow says the 220,000 residents of Transdniestria, a sliver of land that broke away from Moldova in 1990 at the end of Soviet rule, hold Russian passports and are entitled to vote. REUTERS

Deflating Mental Representations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:18:00 UTC
19:18:00 KST

I found this book illuminating. A font of fresh ideas, it challenges the currently dominant Representational Theory of Mind and develops an alternative account of mental states and processes that is worthy of close attention. I was not in the end persuaded by its main claims, but I came away feeling that I had learned a lot in thinking about those claims and evaluating them. The book also offers some ancillary benefits, such as an outstandingly clear account of the nature and scope of computational cognitive science.
The principal claim of the Representational Theory of Mind can be expressed as follows:
RTM: A wide range of mental items (including every propositional attitude, every concept, and every perceptual state) constitutively involve mental representations that are directed on, or represent, objects, properties, events, or states of affairs.
Adherents hold that RTM captures a key architectural assumption of folk psychology and contemporary cognitive science, and they advocate a robustly realistic reading of it, according to which the mind really is populated by mental representations, and representations really are the objects over which the cognitive processes postulated by folk psychology and cognitive science are defined. Contemporary versions of RTM allow that mental representations can take many forms—sentences, images, simulations, maps, place cells, and so on—but they agree that representations of all these kinds bear forms of the generic relation X represents Y to portions of extra-mental reality. Most advocates seek to naturalize this relation by explaining it reductively—that is, without using any semantic, intentional, or normative concepts. It is acknowledged on all sides that a fully satisfactory reduction has yet to be found, but many advocates think that a successful reduction is gradually emerging in the current literature (e. g., Neander, 2017; Shea, 2018).
Egan’s main objection to this picture is that attempts to explain the relation X represents Y are never naturalistic in the advertised sense. They aim to honor the intuition that each representational vehicle has a unique content, but there are always multiple candidates for the role of content, and selection among them is determined pragmatically—that is, by the explanatory interests of the relevant theorist—rather than naturalistically. Consider, for example, Neander’s attempt to show that a certain representational vehicle V in the toad’s optic tectum represents the complex of low-level properties moving worm-shaped object rather than a higher-level ecological property such as nutrient (Neander, 2017). In making her case, Neander points out that attributing the lower-level content to V better serves the purpose of describing the causal process that supports the toad’s feeding behavior. After all, experiments show that a toad will gobble up any moving worm-shaped object it perceives, regardless of whether the object is nutritious.
It follows that the properties moving and worm-shaped are triggers of the process that eventuates in V, and that nutrient makes no proprietary contribution to the process, but is merely co-instantiated with the properties that actually do the causal work. As Egan points out, however, a biologist whose dominant theoretical interest is in explaining the toad’s survival and flourishing in its ecological niche would have an equally strong reason to say that the vehicle V represents nutrient or a niche-equivalent property such as toad food. On what basis could a representationalist philosopher or scientist decide between these two competing hypotheses about the content of V? Egan’s answer appears to be that there are no naturalistic facts that provide such a basis. Rather, preference for one hypothesis over the other can only be justified by context-dependent pragmatic considerations, and in particular, by the explanatory goals of the person making the choice. Someone interested in explaining how the toad’s perceptual system works would prefer the moving worm-shaped object hypothesis, while someone interested in explaining how the toad manages to survive would prefer the nutrient hypothesis. This being so, she concludes, neither claim “will naturalize content in the advertised sense, inasmuch as the content attributed has a pragmatic rationale” (28).
According to Egan, then, representata are not determined naturalistically. Prima facie, this thesis calls the naturalistic credentials of the whole representationalist enterprise into question. Intuitively, however, representationalist explanations of behavior can be extremely illuminating and may even be conceptually necessary, given that naturalistic explanations in terms of neural states and processes are likely to be forbiddingly complex. Can Egan’s anti-naturalist conclusion be reconciled somehow with this observation about the value of representationalist explanations? She thinks it can. Her account of how this is possible begins with a distinction between a scientific theory proper and a gloss that scientists add to the theory.
To illustrate, in the case of the prey-catching behavior of the toad, a theory proper would consist of a naturalistic specification of a physical process involving a mechanism M in the toad’s brain that takes visually acquired information about a distal stimulus S as input and yields a protrusion of the toad’s tongue as output, where S is the target of the protruded tongue. A representationalist gloss on M would designate a state R of M as a mental representation and would add that R represents the external stimulus S. The gloss would therefore make contact with key components of the causal process running from S to the protruded tongue, and could therefore be said to track or model an illuminating physical explanation of the toad’s prey-capturing behavior.
But the gloss would not be unique. One possible gloss would claim that R represents S as a moving worm-shaped object, and another would claim that R represents S as a nutrient. Since, according to Egan, the physical facts of the case would be neutral between these two interpretations of them, we have an example of how representationalist glosses can have explanatory value without being naturalistically determined. A choice between them could only be motivated by the explanatory goals of scientists providing the glosses.
After providing an eagle’s eye view of her proposal in the first half of the book, Egan turns in the second half to examining representationalist accounts of three prominent cognitive domains, arguing in each case that it would be a mistake to view the account as literally true, but maintaining that each account is illuminating when understood to be a representationalist gloss on a set of physical facts. The domains are propositional attitudes, bodily sensations, and visual experiences. Unfortunately, space limitations preclude discussion of Egan’s views about more than one of these domains. I will focus here on what she has to say about propositional attitudes, but her ideas about bodily sensations and visual experiences are different and no less worthy of consideration.
Egan’s proposal about attitudes is complex, but for purposes of this review it can be simplified as follows. Consider an agent who possesses a functional architecture that conforms to the requirements of folk psychology. Thus, the agent has internal states that are linked to each other, and to external stimuli and types of behavior, by a system of causal relations that meets those requirements. Suppose also, however, that the agent only weakly realizes folk psychology because the states in question are individuated purely in terms of causal relations, with intentional contents playing no role. Given this restriction, it can’t be literally true that the states count as beliefs and other intentional states; but even so, we can use terms like “belief*” and “desire*” in describing the agent, provided that we thereby mean only that the so-designated states have the causal roles attributed to beliefs and desires by folk psychology. Egan would, I think, regard a theory of the agent that is guided by these assumptions as a theory proper of the agent’s mind. (Egan does not use starred terms like “belief*,” but they are useful tools for streamlining the exposition. Their use is warranted because we are considering a functionally defined structure with states that meet the causal conditions specified by folk psychology, which assigns differentiating causal roles to the class of beliefs, the class of desires, and so on.)
As I interpret Egan, a gloss on this theory would take the form of a function F mapping sentences of a spoken and written language to the agent’s belief*s, desire*s, and so on. The mapping would associate sentences with attitude*-states in such a way that inferential relations defined over the sentences would correspond uniquely to causal relations among the belief*-states and desire*-states. Thus, for example, if the F-images of sentences of the following forms were belief*-states:
If P, then Q.
P
those belief*-states would have a strong tendency to cause the belief*-state corresponding to Q under F. Here the sentences would have truth conditions and syntactic properties in the literal sense, but their images under F would not.
To appreciate that the theory proper we have been considering admits of multiple representationalist glosses, we need only recall that representational contents are not uniquely determined by causal relations. This is shown, for example, by the causal chain problem, which points out that if a mental state has one external cause, then it has many. In more positive terms, it is shown by the fact that friends of representationalism like Neander and Shea find it necessary to supplement appeals to causal relations with appeals to more complex properties in analyzing the relation X represents Y. (Readers of Neander and Shea will remember that Neander appeals to information functions in analyzing this relation, and that Shea appeals to stabilized task functions. (Neander, 2017; Shea, 2018)) Now as we saw, the internal states specified by our theory proper are individuated purely by causal relations to each other, to external stimuli, and behavior. It follows that if we want to map sentences with determinate truth conditions onto our agent’s attitude*s, we will have to make a choice among possible mappings that is not determined by the causal facts. Egan would say that pragmatic considerations provide the only possible basis for such a choice.
I have several reservations about the foregoing components of Egan’s position.
First, I worry about her initial argument that it is pragmatic considerations rather than naturalistic factors that determine the acceptability of hypotheses about representational contents. As becomes apparent on inspection, the argument presupposes that representationalism is committed to the following two theses:
(1) There is just one representation relation binding mental states to representata.
(2) Pairs of hypotheses about content like these:
(i) Mental state S represents the property-complex moving and worm-shaped object.
(ii) Mental state S represents the property nutrient.
are in competition to specify the unique representatum of a given mental state.
Given these presuppositions about the commitments of representationalism, a naturalistic version of representationalism would have to provide a naturalistic basis for choosing between the two hypotheses. As Egan sees the situation, however, there is no such naturalistic basis for choice. On her view, the principal difference between the hypotheses has to do with what they can be used to explain: the first hypothesis contributes to explaining how a visuo-behavioral mechanism works, and the second hypothesis contributes to explaining how the toad survives in its niche. Accordingly, giving preference to one of the hypotheses depends on the explanatory goals of a philosopher or toad scientist, which means that it depends on contextual pragmatic factors.
I have concerns about this argument because I see no reason to think that representationalism is committed to (1) and (2). It seems entirely compatible with the spirit of representationalism to allow that there are two or more representation relations linking internal states with properties of external objects, where each of these relations can be explained in naturalistic terms. To accommodate the case at hand, for example, we might distinguish between causal mechanism representation and ecological significance representation, perhaps explaining the first in terms of the teleo-causal apparatus that Neander presents (2017), and the second in terms of the ecological apparatus that Millikan constructs (1989). (Both of these proposals are fully in keeping with the requirements of naturalism.) It follows from this that hypotheses like (i) and (ii) are not in competition. Indeed, they can both be true, provided that they are understood to be concerned with different representation relations. To be sure, if a theorist chooses between them, the ground of her choice will no doubt be pragmatic, having to do with her explanatory interests, but she could choose both if her interests were sufficiently broad. After all, they can both be true. Moreover, there is nothing special about a situation in which a scientist bases a choice between true hypotheses on explanatory interests. That is in fact how scientists generally proceed when confronted with pairs of true hypotheses, and they do so without in any sense deflating their theories. (Representational pluralism is advocated at length in Hill, 2022.)
Second, I have apprehensions about Egan’s treatment of propositional attitudes. One reason for worry is that she assumes without explanation that the natural language sentences that model functionally defined belief*-states and desire*-states have a full share of meaning, including truth conditions. It seems that if the idea of mental states with representational contents is problematic, the idea of syntactically individuated sentences with truth conditions should be equally problematic. Also, functions like the function F cited five paragraphs ago are not well defined. As we saw, given an inference involving premises P1,…,Pn and conclusion C, F is supposed to map these sentences onto belief*-states B1,…,Bn+1 just in case B1,…,Bn cause Bn+1. But there will be many sets of n + 1 belief*-states that meet this weak causal condition.
Egan’s deflationary account of the representational contents of beliefs is quite different than her accounts of bodily sensations and perceptual experiences. The present concerns about the former account do not apply to either of the latter. However, the earlier point about multiple representation relations would seem to raise general questions about the motivation for Egan’s deflationary project as a whole.
REFERENCES
Hill, C. S. (2022). Perceptual Experience. (Oxford: Oxford University Press).
Millikan, R. G. (1989a). “Biosemantics,” Journal of Philosophy 86: 281–97.
Neander, K. (2017). A Mark of the Mental: In Defense of Informational Teleosemantics. (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press).
Shea, N. (2018). Representation in Cognitive Science. (Oxford: Oxford University Press).

The US spent a month approving Germany’s transfer of 10 Patriot missiles to Ukraine

The US spent a month approving Germany’s transfer of 10 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Germany received US approval to transfer 10 PAC-2 GEM-T missiles worth $29.6 million to Ukraine only after a month. The munitions may be enough for one massive attack.
It took the United States a month to approve the transfer to Ukraine of 10 PAC-2 GEM-T surface-to-air missiles for Patriot systems from Germany. Berlin submitted the request back on August 14, but received authorization to re-export the American missiles only a month later, Defense Express reports, writes UNN.
Details
The total cost of the 10 missiles is $29.6 million. PAC-2 GEM-T missiles have a range of up to 160 km and are primarily intended to counter aircraft and cruise missiles.
The delay is related to the U.S. procedure for the re-export of weapons: the U.S. Congress has 30 days to review the proposed transfer and the ability to block it.
The transfer could have been approved faster
Defense Express points out that U.S. legislation provides for an Emergency Waiver mechanism, which allows the transfer of weapons to be expedited in the event of an emergency. However, it was not applied to these missiles.
PAC-2 GEM-T missiles have limited capabilities against ballistic missiles compared with the newer PAC-3 MSE. They do not use the principle of direct kinetic interception but destroy the target with a warhead explosion near it.
According to Defense Express, in the best-case scenario, 10 such missiles may be enough for Ukraine to repel one massive attack. The publication also points to a severe global shortage of ammunition for Patriot systems.
