Yom Kippur through the centuries: The prayer books that preserve centuries of Jewish history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:26:33 UTC
17:26:33 KST

From a World War II soldier’s mahzor (prayer book), to manuscripts from the Cairo Genizah, to a recently reunited prayer book from Portugal, the National Library of Israel’s impressive collection of prayer books and other holiday-related items immeasurably enhances our appreciation of the High Holy Days.
Dr. Chaim Neria, the NLI’s curator of the Haim and Hanna Solomon Judaica Collection, was excited to share a bevy of Yom Kippur-related artifacts, including rare prayer books, from its vast archive. It holds millions of items, both physical and digital, including books in Hebrew and those on Jewish topics; Jewish journals and magazines; Hebrew manuscripts; personal archives; and Jewish music.
In an interview with The Jerusalem Post, Neria explained how the NLI came to house thousands of prayer books, noting that “it fits into the overall mission of the library.”
He shared the extent of the library’s commitment to assembling a “very deep and broad” collection; ideally, it will include “every book printed about the Jewish people – and eventually have the best documentation of the Jewish people since the invention of printing.”
One reason the NLI has such a large collection of prayer books is that they were widely produced. “People needed them, and used them,” he noted. He even playfully pointed out that given their popularity, a printer would be making a “safe bet” if he produced prayer books.
The mystery of the Jewish soldier who fell on Yom Kippur, 1944
Neria began our tour by sharing a relatively “new” prayer book, where careful research and detective work by the NLI solved a mystery of a Jewish soldier in the US Army who fell on Yom Kippur, 1944.
A particularly peculiar two-volume Yiddish and Hebrew prayer book, printed in New York in 1942 by Ziegelheim Press, a publisher who had immigrated from Vienna to Manhattan before World War II and continued his work from the Big Apple, showed up at the NLI with many unanswered questions.
It contained the following inscription in Dutch with some Hebrew: “In memory of our son, David Meyer Wald, of the American Army. September 27, 1944 – Yom Kippur 5705, who fell in the liberation of Holland. May he rest in peace in the cemetery of Margraten, Plot Nn, row 9, grave number 222.
“Zelg and Hania Wald. Please commemorate his soul.”
The prayer books were apparently donated in memory of an American Jewish soldier initially buried in a cemetery in Holland. Researchers learned that David Meyer Wald was one of 8,288 soldiers buried in the American military cemetery near the village of Margraten, in southern Holland.
They later pieced together key aspects of his life: he was born in 1923 in Timkovichi, now in today’s Belarus. His family immigrated to the United States in 1938 and settled in Pittsburgh, PA. He served in the 325th Infantry Regiment, a unit belonging to the US Army’s 82nd Airborne Division, and was killed in Holland in 1944.
Wald was initially buried in Holland and re-interred in 1949 in Montreal.
Researchers at the NLI were puzzled about the prayer book until they discovered in 2007 that a Torah scroll was dedicated in memory of the same deceased American soldier by his parents. It was donated to the synagogue closest to his burial place in Holland. The Walds also donated two prayer books and perhaps other books to the NLI at the same time.
It is still unclear exactly how the books reached the NLI, or why it mistakenly contained another label – the Jewish Cultural Reconstruction, Inc., often abbreviated as JCR, which worked after the Holocaust to save books stolen by the Nazis during the war from Jewish libraries and from private collections across Europe.
Yet one thing was clear: the books were donated in memory of a Jewish soldier who gave his life fighting the Nazis and who died – on Yom Kippur – “for the sanctification of God’s name,” as stated on his gravestone in Hebrew.
This is a case, Neria noted, “in which one mahzor opened an entire story of an American soldier who died while liberating the world from evil. It gives new meaning to Yom Kippur, Jewish history, and the Israel experience. The story is very touching and unique.”
A remnant of one of the oldest Yom Kippur prayer books in existence
Neria took our tour further back in time – to the Cairo Genizah, which contains hundreds of thousands of complete Jewish documents and fragments of documents, including holy books, letters, and business and legal documents. They were all discovered in the attic of a synagogue in Fustat (the ancient city of Cairo) in the mid-1800s.
Neria explained the centrality and importance of the city. “Cairo was the center of Jewish activity, partially because it was a city where many merchants and rabbis arrived; it was a religious center and also a center for commerce.” The synagogue in Cairo was similarly important in the history of nusach (traditional wording and music).
Among the treasures in the genizah is a fragment of a page from an ancient Yom Kippur prayer book. It was written in the late 11th or early 12th century by a scribe named Hillel Ben-Eli, a cantor from Baghdad who immigrated to Egypt and worked as the official scribe of the Cairo rabbinical court.
Certificates in his handwriting appeared between 1066 and 1108. He is one of the most important scribes whose writings were found in the genizah. The prayer book from which this fragment comes is the oldest in the NLI’s collections, and one of the oldest in the entire world.
Those familiar with the Yom Kippur liturgy may recognize the name of Rabbi Eliezer Kalir, one of the greatest poets in Jewish history. On one side of a page from the genizah is a paragraph from a piyut (liturgical poem) by Rabbi Kalir called “Please Answer My Whisper.”
According to Neria and his team, in the third line, one can make out the Hebrew words “[Honi] hamulat kodesh, umehallelim behadarat [kodesh]” (“[My riches] are holy noise, and they praise in [holy] splendor”). On the other side are prayers related to the Yom Kippur service in the ancient Temple.
Neria explained the importance of the poets who wrote the poems that have made their way to prayers we recite on various holidays. They include slihot (penitential poems and prayers read before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur), kinot (elegies on Tisha B’av), and yotzrot (liturgical poetry read before the “Shema” on four designated torah portions).
“They even wrote new piyutim for each Shabbat.”
The discovery of the piyut from the genizah shows that, nearly 1,000 years ago, Jews gathered in synagogues and recited prayers similar to the ones that we recite today. And we are still familiar with these piyutim.
The Lisbon Mahzor that wandered the world
Neria completed our tour of the library’s prayer book gems by sharing one from Lisbon, produced in the period just after Jews were expelled from Spain.
“This was a very unique moment in history,” noted Neria, since the Jews had just been expelled from Spain and were briefly permitted to live in Portugal before also being expelled from there as well.
King John II of Portugal recognized a personal opportunity that would also benefit his country if he allowed tens of thousands of Spanish Jews to settle in Portugal, as the Jews possessed commercial skills and an important trade network.
Soon after, things began to worsen for Jews living in Portugal. There were new restrictions, Jewish children were seized and shipped to Portugal’s colonies, and families had to pay large sums to renew their right to remain in Lisbon. Often, Jews faced forced baptism.
Many of the Jewish community’s manuscripts – precious works of art – disappeared; others were smuggled out of the country.
The Lisbon Mahzor eventually reached the Jewish community of Aleppo and was guarded alongside the famed Aleppo Codex. The three-volume prayer book contained all of the liturgy for the Jewish year: one volume for daily prayers, and two others with the festival services for Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
In 1957, one volume of the Lisbon Mahzor was given to then-president of Israel, Yitzhak Ben-Zvi by the Jewish community of Aleppo, where it remained in the archives of Yad Ben-Zvi.
The whereabouts of the other two volumes remained a mystery until recently, when the missing volumes appeared in the catalogue of the Kedem Auction House. When the NLI learned of their availability – and knowing their incredible importance – it appealed to acquire them directly without public auction.
They claimed that they were treasures belonging to the Jewish people. The purchase was made possible with support from the Haim and Hanna Solomon Judaica Foundation, and the Zukier family.
All three volumes have now been reunited at the NLI and are accessible online.
Neria couldn’t contain his excitement as he showed off these treasures.
“This is why the National Library is here, to tell us about our roots and traditions – from 2,000 years after the piyutim from the Cairo Genizah were written (and read until today on Yom Kippur), to a soldier who died on Yom Kippur, with his parents’ words continuing to move us! This is a living tradition!”

====================================================================================================

Wine talk: The grape and the word
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:26:30 UTC
17:26:30 KST

Wine guys love wine to the depth of their being. To them, it is more than a drink.
It’s not just fermented grape juice or liquid grapes. Wine can be a window into all kinds of worlds. These include agriculture, archaeology, economics, gastronomy, geology, history, politics, religion, technology, and peoplehood.
It gives insight into the “people of Israel” and the “places of Israel,” from the first sprouting of the Jewish people in biblical times to the start-up Israel of today. Above all, we like to talk about wine and share experiences to enthuse others… and be enthused.
Wine also has a wide-ranging literature. You only have to see the number of wine books in a wine lover’s private library to understand what is obvious to me: wine is aspirational. We love to read about wine, learn about it, and immerse ourselves in the wine stories of others. Some of us like to read about wine and talk about it as much as drink it.
In the next few months, some books will be published that should be on every wine professional’s and wine lover’s bookshelf.
Hugh Johnson’s Pocket Wine Book
Hugh Johnson’s Pocket Wine Book, edited by famous wine writer Margaret Rand, is the largest-selling wine book in the world. It is not new. The first one was published in 1977.
Englishman Hugh Johnson is the world’s most famous and prolific wine writer. He remembers James Mitchell saying to him: “You know, Hugh, everything anybody really needs to know about wine could go into a little book like this…” and pulling out his diary. (Once there really was something called a pocket diary!) This was the invention of the Pocket Wine Book, published by Mitchell Beazley, and it has continued every year since then.
The Pocket Wine Book is a mini-reference book for anyone who buys wine – in wine stores, restaurants, or on the internet. It is a comprehensive up-to-date annual guide that has retained its popularity despite the accessibility of online information.
Hugh Johnson never believed in giving wines scores, but he does rate wineries from one to four stars.
Explanations are in brief note form and in British understatement, though the experts contributing cover the world. The book is close to being a kind of Michelin Guide for wine, with information about wineries and wines, grape varieties, matching food to wine, and the best values and vintages.
Even Israel gets a mention. Where else will you find a ranking of 45 Israeli wineries ranked by an international book? The entry includes large commercial wineries, small wineries, and boutique wineries; some kosher, others non-kosher. It also gives a heads-up about new-ish, tiny wineries of interest, which are below the radar.
Included are wineries owned across the spectrum: from haredi (ultra-Orthodox) to liberal Jews, right-wing settler wineries from the Central Mountains Region to left-wing kibbutz wineries, Israeli Arabs, and Christian Monks. This is part of why I say “Wine is the beautiful Israel.” Wine represents the rich mosaic of Israelis and the Land of Israel.
In Israel, we act very loudly in wine. We are active on social media like a wine giant. So it is a wake-up call to see our relative importance. In the Pocket Wine Book, Israel is part of the Eastern Mediterranean Region, and we are allocated a total of one and a half pages.
At the beginning, Israel did not feature at all, but slowly and steadily we found a voice. We were first mentioned in the 1980 edition, but it was only a few lines. The Golan Heights Winery was the first Israeli winery to be awarded stars in the late 1990s and the first to be awarded three stars. Domaine du Castel was the first to be awarded four stars in 2008.
In the new book, there are three Israeli wineries with four stars outright, and another three which earn two or three to four stars. Hugh Johnson’s Pocket Wine Book 2027, published by Mitchell Beazley, was released last week.
The World Atlas of Wine
IT WAS IN 1971 that Hugh Johnson wrote the first The World Atlas of Wine. He believed that wine was liquid geography. The publisher, James Mitchell, was interested in the idea of matching precise cartography to viticulture. Hugh Johnson liked the idea of mapping the main vineyards and vineyard areas.
It took him two years of travel, research, and writing, and it became a classic. Other editions followed. It was reprinted four more times between that first edition and 2001. Each time, the content advanced considerably as the wine world expanded in terms of quality and awareness.
In the early 2000s, Jancis Robinson MW, today’s most famous wine critic, joined him as co-author. This certainly made the ultimate dream team. Three more editions were published, and they are not reprints. The texts are rewritten, and the maps are updated, and they somehow manage to squeeze in all the new wine information that has come to light since the last edition.
Israel used to feature in the World Atlas alongside our neighbors in a page headed “Eastern Mediterranean.” From the eighth edition published in 2019, we were honored with our own full page and map! This is repeated in the ninth edition as well, except the maps and texts have been totally updated to take into account changes in the last seven years.
The ninth edition of The World Atlas of Wine by Hugh Johnson, Jancis Robinson MW, and Julia Harding MW will be published on September 24, 2026.
The most serious tome in the wine lover’s library is The Oxford Companion to Wine edited by Jancis Robinson MW. This is the one wine professionals studying for the WSET Diploma or Master of Wine use as a textbook. It is the ultimate in wine expertise and scholarship, and it covers every aspect of wine, written by the relevant world experts in every field.
The contract for the first edition was signed in 1988, and after years of graft, it was published in 1994 to acclaim throughout the wine trade. It won every book prize possible.
Since then, there have been four new editions. The latest is the fifth edition, which was published in 2023. It has more than 4,000 entries from over 250 global experts and is over one million words in total. The subjects of particular interest to us are “Israel” and “Kosher,” each of which has its own entry.
Any wine professional, expert, or connoisseur will have this book and is likely to purchase each new edition as soon as they come out. The fifth edition of The Oxford Companion to Wine is edited by Jancis Robinson MW, Julia Harding MW, and Tara Q. Thomas, and published by Oxford University Press.
If The Oxford Wine Companion is too academic for your needs, there is a new wine encyclopedia being published which is geared more to the wine lover. This is The Encyclopedia of Wine: A Definitive Guide to the World of Wine, edited by David Williams and published by Dorling Kindersley, which will be released in October.
An alternative is The New Sotheby’s Wine Encyclopedia by Tom Stevenson and Orsi Szentkiralyi, published by National Geographic. Both are excellent, comprehensive, and bulging with information. The only difference is that the Dorling Kindersley book is brand new and up-to-date. The Sotheby’s book was published in 2020.
So if you are buying a present, it is a better bet to choose the newer book. However, both are thoroughly recommended. All the books recommended are available from the publisher, bookstores, or Amazon.
The Bible of Israeli Wines
THOSE INTERESTED in wine books on Israel have a smaller choice in English, but there have been a few I picked up over the years that I still have and occasionally refer to.
The first one was The Bible of Israeli Wines by Michael Ben Joseph, published by Modan Publishing in 2002. I know the author as Mimi. He is in his 90s and still occasionally attends tastings. He wrote the first serious wine books in Hebrew that brought many into the wine world in the 1990s.
The book is way out of date, but it is like a time capsule of Israeli wine at that time. Furthermore, some of it still reads well. I still dip into it occasionally. If you find a copy in a book sale, it is a worthy purchase.
The next book worth having is The Ultimate Rogov’s Guide To Israeli Wines published by Toby Press. The late Daniel Rogov, a food and wine writer initially for The Jerusalem Post and later Haaretz, was Israel’s most important wine critic. He published his annual wine guide, and I still return to it.
It is useful for checking out winery stories and when certain wines were launched. However, if you only have one, it would be the last edition before he passed away, published in 2012. The best bet is a secondhand bookshop.
Then there is a series of publications of The Wine Route of Israel, with its striking green vine leaf cover. It was edited by Eliezer Sacks and published by Cordinata. The last English edition was in 2015. The essays, including a comprehensive history of Israeli wine, are still relevant. The sister book Wine of Israel, also by Sacks, was published in 2020 by Cordinata.
Both of these may be found at winery visitors’ centers, and Cordinata still has a few.
Wine Journey: Israeli Adventure
THE NEWEST and most up-to-date book is Wine Journey: Israeli Adventure by Itamar Gur, Guy Haran, David Silverman, and Roni Saslove. It is a paperback that was first self-published in 2021.
It proved popular, and an updated edition was printed in 2025. This format is practical and primarily for tourists, but there is a lot of information about Israeli wine, too. The book may be found in winery visitors’ centers or can be purchased online: www.israeladventure.wine
For a fun read, I recommend two books that cover two Israeli success stories. The Golan Heights Winery celebrated its 40th anniversary in 2023, and Domaine du Castel had its 30th year in 2022. These are Israel’s two most famous wineries, and the stories will warm the cockles of your heart.
Golan Heights Winery: Forty Years of Quality, Innovation and Authenticity and Domaine du Castel: The Biography are still available (if you are quick) at the relevant winery visitors’ center. Both books are self-published, and they have something else in common: they both won major awards at The Gourmand Awards, the Oscars of cookery and wine books.
These are the wineries that Israel put on the international wine map. Wine lovers, Zionists, or anyone interested in Israel will enjoy a good read and an insight into the Israeli wine industry.
In case anyone is in the know, I can confirm some involvement of sorts in many of the publications mentioned, but that is not relevant, and I make the recommendations on merit alone.
What I will claim ownership of is the ultimate Israeli wine book that was written but not published. I had a formal agreement to write a book with a major international specialist wine publisher. The book was to include Cyprus, Lebanon, and Israel, which was a unique approach and an exciting joint venture.
Unfortunately, Israeli and Jewish academics, artists, scientists, and authors are experiencing tough times due to Israel’s image abroad. Boycotts, cancellations, and unpleasantness are the order of the day.
After the work had been completed, the agreement was canceled – retroactively, to my surprise, regret, and disappointment. I was told verbally that it was because of Israel’s image. This is where we are. The book on Israeli wine has been written. Let’s hope we can find a way amid the opposition to get it published. Until then, invest in a wine book.
Dive in! Happy reading! ■
The writer is a wine trade veteran and winery insider turned wine writer, who has advanced Israeli wines over four decades. He is referred to as the English voice of Israeli wine. www.adammontefiore.com

The surprising history of Kol Nidre: How Yom Kippur’s legal formula became a sacred anthem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:26:16 UTC
17:26:16 KST

The iconic Kol Nidre theme – with its distinct modal inflections, expressive leaps, and solemn cantorial contours – has accomplished something rare in Jewish liturgy: it crossed the threshold of the synagogue into secular culture. For centuries, this ancient melody has fascinated everyone from classical composers and avant-garde musicians to film directors and pop artists.
Yet, the tension at the heart of Kol Nidre is striking. Fundamentally, the text is not a poetic prayer or a plea for mercy; it is a dry, legislative formula written in Aramaic for the annulment of personal vows. How did a dry legal disclaimer become bound to the most emotionally charged melody in the Jewish calendar?
“The text for Kol Nidrei dates from the eighth or ninth century, and already then it was controversial,” explained Cantor Eliyahu Schleifer, professor emeritus of Sacred Music and former director of the School of Sacred Music at Hebrew Union College in Jerusalem, who is one of the world’s foremost authorities on Jewish liturgical music. “The primary dispute was whether or not one can annul future vows.”
He noted that during the Middle Ages, the text initially referred to the year to come: “From this Yom Kippur until the next Yom Kippur which comes to us for good.” However, because scholars debated whether future vows could legally be absolved, many communities shifted to referring only to past vows: “From the past Yom Kippur until this Yom Kippur.”
“But nowadays,” Schleifer observed, “we refer to both past and future vows: ‘From the past Yom Kippur until this Yom Kippur, and from this Yom Kippur until the next Yom Kippur which comes to us for good.’”
That legal flexibility came at a heavy cost. In the Middle Ages, antisemites weaponized the formula, claiming that in the Kol Nidre prayer – one of Judaism’s holiest – Jews absolved themselves of any and all agreements and promises. This false pretext led to the systemic imposition of the humiliating “Oath More Judaico.”
The struggle over Kol Nidre’s legal text
In response, during the 19th century, leaders of the nascent Jewish Reform movement attempted to alter or drop the text entirely.
As Schleifer noted, “In early 20th-century American Reform prayer books, the text for Kol Nidre was omitted altogether.”
Instead, the rubric simply read “The Kol Nidre Chant,” and the organist or choir would perform the traditional melody without the Aramaic words. In other non-Orthodox traditions, alternative German psalms were substituted for the original legal formula, or cellists were brought in to perform Max Bruch’s famous instrumental fantasy on the theme as part of the service.
The text was only widely reinstated among non-Orthodox communities during the rise of Nazism in Europe, as Jews reclaimed their ancient liturgy under the ethos of “this is how our forefathers prayed.”
While Sephardi traditions feature a wide variety of regional recitatives and chanting styles – differing from community to community and cantor to cantor – the Ashkenazi melody developed into a single, widely standardized theme across Europe.
It is categorized as one of the “Mi-Sinai” tunes – traditional Ashkenazi melodies so deeply revered that oral legend attributed their origin to divine revelation at Mount Sinai. In reality, its roots are a complex tapestry woven in 15th- and 16th-century Germany.
ACCORDING TO Schleifer, the theme represents a synthesis of Ashkenazi biblical cantillations (derived from the haftarah), virtuoso cantorial improvisations, and secular medieval German folk songs sung by Minnesängers, German poet-musicians.
Historical records show how early rabbinic authorities shaped its performance.
“Our teacher, Rabbi Ya’acov Ben-Moshe Levi Moelin (the Maharil), one of the greatest rabbinic figures of the late 14th and early 15th centuries, described a traditional theme that is recited three times, with the cantor increasing his voice each time,” Schleifer noted. “Theologians still debate whether he meant increasing dynamic volume or raising the pitch by melodic steps. Today, cantors do both.”
However, whether the Maharil was referring to the exact melody sung today remains doubtful. Without musical notation from the 14th century, musicologists believe the early medieval theme likely differed from the modern version.
The melody was first transcribed in print in Berlin in 1765 by Cantor Aharon Beer, but it was Louis Lewandowski in 1871 who formalized the standard choral and cantorial arrangement known worldwide today.
How Kol Nidre’s melody conquered the secular world
The emotional gravity of the Ashkenazi theme inevitably attracted non-Jewish and secular classical composers.
The most famous adaptation remains the 1880 fantasy for cello and orchestra, Kol Nidrei, by the Protestant German composer Max Bruch. Bruch transcribed the theme directly from Jacob Abraham Lichtenstein, cantor of the Old Synagogue in Berlin.
Though scholars like Leon Botstein note that Bruch was drawn to the piece primarily as a folk music enthusiast rather than a philosemite, his composition permanently etched the melody into the classical music repertoire.
Decades later, Arnold Schoenberg created his own modern and deeply spiritual Kol Nidre (Op. 38). For Schoenberg, who had converted to Christianity before formally returning to Judaism as the Nazis rose to power, the piece was a deeply personal act of repentance.
Schoenberg embedded texts from Lurianic Kabbalah alongside the traditional prayer. He also subscribed to a popular myth: that the theme originated among Sephardi Conversos singing secretly in cellars during the Spanish Inquisition.
“That legend has no historical basis,” Schleifer clarified. “If it were true, you would hear the theme in Sephardi synagogues today. Schoenberg’s work is derived entirely from Ashkenazi cantillations.”
Myths surrounding classical masters and the melody extend even further back. Rumors have long persisted that Ludwig van Beethoven quoted the Kol Nidre motif in the Adagio of his String Quartet Op. 131.
“In comparison with the actual theme of Kol Nidre,” Schleifer reflected, “I don’t believe that to be true.”
Beyond the classical canon, Kol Nidre migrated into 20th-century popular culture. It was recorded by pop crooners like Perry Como, adapted into psychedelic rock (such as The Electric Prunes’ 1968 track “Kol Nidre”), and featured prominently in cinema – from Al Jolson in the groundbreaking 1927 film The Jazz Singer to Neil Diamond’s 1980 remake.
Why has this specific melody crossed so many cultural boundaries?
Beyond its connection to Yom Kippur’s theme of repentance, Schleifer believes the answer lies in its core musical architecture.
“The theme came to symbolize the fate of the Jewish people,” he reflected. “It begins in a solemn minor key, but ultimately transitions into the major scale – symbolizing a profound sense of hope and salvation at the end of days.”

Archaeologists discovered a mysterious Roman burial with the body placed face down
Kyiv • UNN
A burial with the body face down and four glass vessels was discovered in the necropolis of ancient Salona. The reason for the ritual has not yet been established.
Archaeologists in Croatia have discovered an unusual Roman-period burial in which the deceased was placed face down in the grave. Several glass vessels were found alongside the remains, including an unusually shaped perfume bottle, Croatia Week reports, according to UNN.
Details
The burial was one of 16 recently examined in the western necropolis of ancient Salona—the capital of the Roman province of Dalmatia. The excavations are being conducted by specialists from the Croatian Institute for Nature Protection and the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts.
In the grave containing a body placed face down, archaeologists found three glass bottles and a small glass vessel. One of the perfume bottles was made in the shape of a date.
Unusual burial among cremated remains
The find is particularly notable because most of the other nearby burials examined contained cremated remains. In 12 graves, the remains were placed directly in the ground; in several others, ceramic urns were used, while in one case archaeologists discovered a stone urn.
In another burial, a glass bottle, a bone needle, and a ceramic oil lamp were found together with the cremated remains.
Researchers have not yet determined why one of the deceased was buried face down. Such burials differ from standard burial practices and may be of particular interest for further research.
Overall, archaeologists have already examined more than 150 graves on the territory of the necropolis of ancient Salona.

Leonardo DRS to power South Korea’s newest destroyer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:22:30 UTC
17:22:30 KST

- Leonardo DRS will supply the electric propulsion system for South Korea's KDDX destroyer, the Republic of Korea Navy's first full-electric-drive surface combatant.
- The six-ship KDDX program, led by Hanwha Ocean, is valued at roughly $5.7 billion, with the lead ship due by 2032.
Leonardo DRS will build the electric propulsion system for South Korea’s next-generation KDDX destroyer, the company announced, supplying technology for what will be the Republic of Korea Navy’s first full-electric-drive surface warship.
DRS signed the contract with Doosan Enerbility, which will work alongside the American company to build the ship’s complete power and propulsion system, covering everything from the prime movers that generate power to the propellers that turn it into thrust. DRS is providing its 100-Series permanent magnet propulsion motors paired with matching variable-frequency drives, hardware the company says is built to be more compact and power-dense than older electric drive systems. Hanwha Ocean is building the lead ship under a separate contract with South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration.
Electric propulsion lets a ship dedicate more of its power to sensors and weapons rather than the mechanical drivetrain connecting engines directly to propellers, an arrangement that matters more as warships add power-hungry equipment. “Our advanced electric-propulsion technologies are designed to deliver the power capacity, efficiency, reliability and adaptability required for advanced radars, advanced EW systems, directed energy systems, the charging of unmanned vehicles, the launch of drone swarms and other increasingly power-intensive mission capabilities,” said John Baylouny, president and chief executive officer of Leonardo DRS.
The KDDX program is South Korea’s first indigenously designed and built destroyer class, intended to fill the gap between the Navy’s 4,200-ton KDX-II destroyers and its larger KDX-III Sejong the Great-class Aegis ships, while replacing the aging three-ship KDX-I Gwanggaeto the Great class. The full program covers six destroyers of roughly 6,000 to 7,000 tons and about 155 meters (509 feet) in length, at a total program cost estimated near 7.8 trillion won, or roughly $5.7 billion. South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration awarded Hanwha Ocean the detailed design and lead-ship construction contract in July 2026, worth about $580 million, after the company narrowly beat rival HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in a competitive scoring process that followed more than two years of delay over how the contract should be awarded. The lead ship is due for delivery by 2032, with the remaining five ships following by around 2036.
The destroyers are planned to carry mostly Korean-made systems, including a domestic combat management system, Hanwha Systems’ integrated mast, a dual-band active electronically scanned array radar, and Korean vertical launch systems. Propulsion for the class appears to combine gas turbines with the new electric drive system: GE Aerospace said on Sept. 1 that it would supply 12 LM2500+G4 marine gas turbines across the six ships, with Hanwha Aerospace manufacturing engine components, assembling the turbines, and providing local support.
DRS’s role builds on a longer relationship with the Republic of Korea Navy. The company has supplied hybrid electric drive systems for 20 anti-submarine warfare frigates across the Navy’s FFX Batch II, III and IV programs over more than a decade, and has scaled similar propulsion technology for the U.S. Navy’s Columbia-class submarine program. “For more than a decade our systems have supported Republic of Korea Navy FFX II/III/IV frigates, and we have demonstrated the ability to scale our electric-propulsion technology for the most demanding naval applications, including the COLUMBIA-class submarine program,” said Jon Miller, senior vice president and general manager of Naval Power Systems at Leonardo DRS.

BRUSSELS – The European Union said on Sept 18 it regretted Washington’s decision to deny visas for the second year running to Palestinian officials seeking to attend the UN General Assembly, urging a rethink.
The US State Department said this week it was refusing to grant visas to Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas and other members of his delegation ahead of next week’s meeting in New York.
“We regret the decision to extend the denial of entry visas for members of the Palestinian delegation for a second year in a row,” said Anouar El Anouni, a spokesman for the EU’s diplomatic service.

The PA recently reformed this system, allocating welfare payments to families on a needs basis rather than political affiliation or prisoner status.

The half-empty glass: Israel’s wine industry battles falling demand, cheap imports and growing stockpiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:07:17 UTC
17:07:17 KST

For years, wine was an almost automatic part of a meal, a night out with friends or an office gathering. Now the world around it is changing. Young people are drinking less alcohol, consumers are tightening their belts, restaurants and the events industry are still dealing with the effects of the war, and Israel’s high-tech sector, once a major engine of happy-hour culture, is not operating as it once did.
The impact is being felt clearly at wineries: fewer bottles are being sold, more consumers are looking for lower prices and some warehouses are filling with inventory that is increasingly difficult to move. Even ahead of Rosh Hashanah, traditionally a seasonal peak for wine sales, wineries are seeing weaker demand for holiday gift packages.
“This is no longer just a market fluctuation. It is a symptom of a cultural, economic and health shift, and of something deeper, a change in the human experience of spending time together,” says Haim Gan, an expert on the Israeli and global wine markets and owner of Ish Ha’anavim, the Grape Man wine culture center.
Gan says consumers are increasingly focused on health and well-being, while younger drinkers in particular are choosing less alcohol. This does not necessarily mean complete abstinence, but rather new alternatives emerging as part of a generational and cultural shift. Major wine exhibitions are featuring more alcohol-free and low-alcohol brands.
At the same time, global production is increasingly affected by extreme weather, creating greater volatility between vintages and making supply less stable. Combined with warming temperatures, that helps explain why red wine, particularly heavier, full-bodied reds, increasingly has to justify its place, and not only among younger consumers. In France, where wine is almost a native language, the industry is already speaking in terms of an existential shift. It is becoming clear that this is not merely a passing fashion, but a new vocabulary and a change of direction.
“We live in a lifestyle-driven world where people constantly monitor their workouts, body temperature and sleep on their wrists,” Gan says. “In several major markets, the discussion is no longer only about declining consumption, but about wine’s difficulty in winning over younger palates compared with other categories. When young people do not enter the wine market, even if quality improves, the market contracts.”
‘Young people prefer protein’
Ilan Hasson, owner of the Five Stones boutique winery and the Masada Group, which imports wine and alcoholic beverages to Israel, is equally candid about the decline in wine and alcohol consumption in Israel and abroad.
“Our winery CEO, Or Ohayon, has just returned from a customer tour in the United States, and people are drinking less wine there as well,” Hasson says. “I can’t point to one exact reason, but what we mainly see is that people are looking for cheaper brands and want to spend less on a bottle.”
Or have they simply switched to protein drinks instead of Cabernet and Sauvignon? 
“Yes. People say it’s because young people prefer protein, and maybe there is something to that, though I don’t know how thoroughly it has been tested statistically. But if wine or alcohol was once a way to get a buzz, young people today have found other ways. Price also affects consumption. 
"It’s no secret that life in Israel is relatively expensive, and that applies to both Israeli and imported wine, so people are looking for alternatives. Fortunately, our winery has a loyal customer base, and by reaching it directly and thinking outside the box, we have managed to maintain our sales and production levels.”
Do you see local wineries that are unable to maintain sales?
“Definitely. You see it at boutique wineries and medium-sized wineries, and you see wine producers offering bottles at prices you know cannot be profitable. That clearly reflects inventory planning that created quantities they can no longer sell at the higher prices.”
What can be done?
“In a properly functioning country, the Economy and Agriculture ministries would join us in encouraging consumption and helping save the industry, as happens in many countries where governments support wineries with marketing budgets and export assistance. That doesn’t happen here. Foreign exchange is also hurting us dramatically. If two years ago a winery exported a bottle at a certain price in shekels, today we are getting 20% less because of the exchange rate. When the U.S. market is your main market and Trump has added a 15% tariff, you are already down 35% compared with two years ago. That has a dramatic effect. The state should have stepped in, but it hasn’t.”
So what are you doing? 
“We’re going out into the field more, holding wine events, meeting more customers and encouraging promotions and sales to put the focus on our winery and on the Israeli wine industry compared with other countries. We are also trying to expose as many people as possible, especially young people, to the winery itself. There is no doubt that the visitor-center phenomenon that developed here during COVID is helping compensate for the decline in wine consumption at home or in wine bars.”
Wine bars keep opening. How do you explain the paradox? 
“Wine bars are opening in what would once have been defined as wine shops, because they need to create another economic growth engine for the point of sale. If a wine shop used to sell 100 bottles and now sells 70, it looks for a way to make up the missing 30 by serving wine on site at retail prices with a very low corkage fee.”
Restaurant consumption is another issue because of the war. 
“Restaurants also stopped operating during COVID, but back then we were sitting at home in a mood that encouraged more cooking, and wine became the perfect accompanying product and began arriving at people’s doors by delivery. But during a war, when people are running to shelters, wine is not the obvious product. If we get some quiet and tourists return before the end of the year, it will be significant, because tourists consume more than Israeli customers,” Hasson says.
Vineyards left unharvested
There are other factors behind the downturn: younger generations socialize differently, instability in the high-tech sector over the past year has meant fewer company happy hours and fewer gift deliveries to employees, and young people are less inclined to sit over expensive bottles of wine and spirits, preferring cheaper forms of entertainment. Then there are the stocks piling up in winery warehouses because the war has sharply reduced the number of events in recent years.
“After COVID, Israel immediately went into a state of war. Activity at event halls dropped sharply, and as a result, wine that had already been sold to those venues was not consumed. That meant the halls did not buy additional bottles from wineries,” says Gil Doron, owner of HaYogev 8 Winery.
“The market for inexpensive wines effectively disappeared in recent years. Beyond that, the market for more expensive wines sold to restaurants also shrank because there are no tourists here. When a tourist comes to Israel for a week, he goes to a restaurant every evening and orders at least one bottle of wine for the table. In a week, he consumes at least five bottles. That has not existed in Israel for three years.”
The situation is pushing buyers toward lower prices. Event halls, restaurants and bars increasingly look for bottles that, including delivery, cost around 30 shekels. Israeli wineries cannot compete at those prices, so importers are bringing in reasonably good wines at lower prices from Italy, Spain and France.
The pressure is so severe that some large Israeli wineries have decided not to produce wine this year. They are leaving grapes on the vines and not harvesting them, choosing not to deepen losses after becoming stuck with lower-priced wines originally intended for weddings and other events that never took place.
“Wine imports to Israel, particularly from Europe, have indeed become very intensive,” Gan says. “Israeli wine looks very expensive on the shelf because an Israeli boutique bottle might cost 120 to 130 shekels, around 40 euros, while imported wines are priced much lower. The decline in consumption is not only local, it is global, and Europe is also stuck with wine stocks it needs to sell.”
“But the industry there is subsidized and supported by governments that assist exports. So is it any wonder we are seeing an inflation of European wines in Israeli restaurants at the expense of Israeli wines and wineries, which have been living through war for three years?”
Gan adds: “You also cannot ignore the fact that the war has led many people around the world to stop drinking Israeli wine and to look at Israeli bottles differently. Right now, we are a pariah state in the world. Wine exhibitions and fairs are showing less interest in Israeli wines, not because of the price, but because of the political situation.”
Yael Guy: “No one talks or writes openly about the growth of the Muslim population, but it is whispered about in industry conversations. And it is not only in Europe but also in the United States. Fewer people are drinking wine”
And what about event halls stuck with stock? 
“That definitely hurts wineries,” Gan says. “If an event hall that already buys wine very cheaply is sitting on, say, six pallets, it will first work through them at the events it does have and will not buy more wine from wineries. The wineries then experience fewer sales. The entire food chain is affected.”
Gan says the crisis also presents an opportunity for Israel’s wine industry to rethink pricing, production costs, regulation, branding and, above all, wine education, which he says remains badly underdeveloped.
“It is time we finally started educating people in Israel about Israeli wine. Has the Grape and Wine Council ever carried out one major campaign encompassing all Israeli wineries? Millions are poured into press conferences. What about a campaign showing the growers, the 30,000 families who make a respectable living from this industry? Why doesn’t the state wake up and understand that this is a product that brings tourism to Israel and uses relatively little water? Where are you, Agriculture Ministry, Economy Ministry, Tourism Ministry?”
Looking for cheap wine
“The Israeli market is getting smaller because young people consume less wine and there are no tourists, and all of that is pushing the market toward promotions,” Doron says.
“What used to be three bottles for 100 shekels has become five for 100, meaning 20 shekels a bottle for the consumer. That means the supermarket paid no more than 12 shekels, and that barely covers the cost of the grapes. In other words, somebody is selling wine at a loss.”
Why? “Because some wineries are sitting on four years’ worth of inventory. Sales have fallen since COVID and the war, and they have to sell that stock. The first thing they do is reduce production, which means we are seeing wineries no longer buying all the grapes produced by the vineyards.”
“This year, many growers who once sold directly to wineries are looking to sell grapes on the open market to anyone willing to buy. You see advertisements on growers’ sites saying, ‘I have 10 dunams of these grapes and 15 dunams of those grapes that will be ready for harvest in a week.’”
And when they cannot sell them? 
“Then they leave them to dry on the vines. There are also growers in Israel already talking about uprooting vineyards, and that is a major crisis.”
Doron says understanding the economics of a winery helps explain why the situation is so difficult. Planting one dunam of vineyard, about a quarter acre, costs around 20,000 shekels. Under Jewish agricultural law, grapes cannot be harvested for wine during the first three years. Throughout that period, growers must irrigate, fertilize and tend the vines, while any fruit is cut off and discarded.
“Only in the fourth year do you harvest the grapes and make wine. Red wine then spends 12 or 18 months in barrels and later more time in bottles. So the first bottle I sell from a vineyard I planted may come six years after I invested in it. And where is all the investment in the vineyard and the work?”
He says seedlings have also become more expensive. “In France, they sell me a grapevine seedling for one euro. Here it costs between 16 and 18 shekels, 450% more, and then people ask why I can’t sell wine for five euros. Why? Because the costs for boutique wineries reach 40 to 45 shekels per bottle before kosher certification and before VAT. That is my base cost before I have made a single shekel.”
Haim Gan, Ish Ha’anavim: “You cannot ignore the fact that the war has led many people around the world to stop drinking Israeli wine and look at Israeli bottles differently. Right now, we are a pariah state in the world. Exhibitions and fairs are less interested in Israeli wines because of the political situation”
So you would not recommend that romantics dreaming of opening a winery go into the business?
“Every week someone sits at my bar and tells me, ‘My dream is to make wine.’ That’s wonderful, as long as you make one barrel, a few bottles and hand them out to family and friends.”
“The problem starts when people fall in love with the idea and begin producing thousands of bottles. Then they make investments without understanding the economics, how much it costs, how to market it, who will buy it, what the Health Ministry license involves and what about land administration, permitted land use and taxes?”
“It is different in Europe, where the state gives you grants. When I built my winery, I received no support from any government body. I only received a bill for land fees. Anyone thinking of opening a winery today is crazy and has no economic justification for doing so.”
“There is no doubt the industry will go through a shake-up in the coming years. We are already seeing wineries closing and growers stopping production. I know at least four wineries in Israel, and I won’t name them, that decided not to make wine this year and instead only sell the bottles they already have in stock,” Doron says.
‘The government only talks’
“This year, we actually had a shortage of red grapes, and the surpluses held by large and medium-sized wineries made large quantities of grapes available for us to buy,” says Moti Teperberg of Teperberg Winery. “That tells us something about the years ahead and the possibility of another surplus of wine inventory in the local market because of excessive vineyard planting by wineries that did not correctly calculate consumption.”
Why only in the years ahead?  We already know there is a grape surplus this year. You needed grapes and clearly found people willing to sell. 
“True, but at least in Israel there are currently buyers for those grapes. What concerns me more is wine imports. I see more and more large and medium-sized wineries getting into imported wine, which points to what we already know: grapes abroad are much cheaper than in Israel, and that encourages wineries and importers to flood the market.”
“What also concerns me is the quality of some of the wine reaching Israeli consumers, without real oversight or standards. It is wine with no mother or father. People will buy those cheap wines once and then not buy them again.”
But when imported wine costs 30 or 40 shekels, price matters. 
“There are also Israeli wines that cost 30 to 40 shekels. The price depends on the source of the grapes, growing methods and winemaking. But there are cases where an imported wine priced at seven euros is not even worth two euros. And then what? You flood the market and hurt Israeli growers. For what?”
“Wine is a baby. It needs a mother and a father. The house that wine comes from matters,” says Teperberg, who is marking 50 years in the wine industry at the winery, Israel’s third largest, whose roots date back to 1870.
Still, Israeli wines are very expensive compared with the range of imported wines. “Because everything in Israel is expensive. Isn’t milk expensive? Aren’t cheese and rent expensive? The government says it will fight the cost of living, but that’s bullshit. They only know how to talk and load more and more payments on us, while taxes keep going up.”
“You can’t have everything rising, water, electricity, municipal taxes, fuel. The growers tell us fertilizer prices have risen and land costs have risen. Who finances that? Where do you expect us to cut prices? And the government? It just talks instead of asking where it can actually begin reducing the cost of living. I can make slogans too. My soul is rooted in this industry. I’m completing 50 years in it, and it hurts me to see how things are being handled.”
Ilan Hasson, Five Stones Winery: “In a properly functioning country, the Economy and Agriculture ministries would be joining us to encourage consumption and save the industry. Foreign exchange and Trump’s tariff are also having a dramatic impact”
Fewer holiday gift packages
On the eve of Rosh Hashanah, the broader trend is also affecting holiday wine sales. Gan says 40% of wine sales in Israel take place around Rosh Hashanah and Passover, and this year sales are declining.
Part of that, he says, reflects high-tech companies giving fewer expensive gifts and holding fewer events. Another factor is the oversupply of cheaper wines still sitting in distribution channels, which are being bought as holiday gifts instead of boutique bottles or premium ranges from local wineries.
Shaked, however, insists business remains broadly normal. Tal Shaked, marketing director at Shaked, which imports a range of wine brands and owns the Derech Hayayin wine-store chain, recognizes the broader decline in wine consumption but says holiday gift package sales have not fallen significantly.
“Because of greater health awareness, people eat and drink less, and when they do consume, they choose higher-quality products,” Shaked says. He also points to the growing trend toward zero-alcohol wines.
“Alcohol-free wine has about a third of the calories, and the category is growing by around 10% a year and has reached a market of two billion euros in Europe.”
Are you seeing a decline in holiday wine package sales this year? 
“We are seeing a small decline in the volume of wine sold for the holiday, but not a decline in revenue.”
How does that make sense? 
The whole industry is talking about declining wine consumption. “When it comes to holiday packages for employees of high-tech companies, banks and so on, those deals are arranged in advance. Right now, we are seeing an average holiday season, even though the holiday came early and is close to the back-to-school period, when people are less focused on gifts. But when it comes to holiday packages, we are meeting our forecasts.”
Still, a 30 shekel bottle from Europe leaves an 80 shekel Israeli bottle sitting in the warehouse, and that is what producers are talking about. 
“If you shop at Shufersal or Rami Levy, or stay at an Isrotel or Dan hotel, kosher certification is important. A large share of the imports coming into Israel is not kosher, although it gives Israeli consumers more options. And by the way, there are also Israeli wines at low prices. It isn’t only imported wine,” Shaked says.
Boycott of Israel
Israeli wine exporters, particularly those selling into Europe, are being hit both by the global decline in wine consumption and by boycotts or restrictions targeting Israeli products.
According to Yael Guy, export manager for Golan Heights Winery and Galil Mountain Winery in Europe, Asia and Latin America, the consumption crisis is being felt strongly alongside a changing attitude toward Israeli products, including wine.
“We are facing a difficult situation in European markets,” she says. “In 2024, Finland announced that it was removing all Israeli wines from its selection. They hid it behind claims of low demand and weaker sales, but that is bullshit.”
“In addition, official sanctions are supposed to come into force in the Netherlands banning the import and sale of wines from the territories and the Golan Heights. They have gone even further by restricting Israeli wines from advertising on importers’ websites and appearing at exhibitions. There is a similar trend in Ireland, Britain and Spain. We have already seen stickers saying ‘child killers in Gaza’ placed on Israeli wine bottles.”
“We discussed this with the Economy Ministry because what is happening in the Netherlands, for example, does not only affect wine. It also affects date growers and other food products exported to Europe.”
Gil Doron, HaYogev 8 Winery: “When a tourist comes to Israel for a week, he goes to a restaurant every evening and orders at least one bottle of wine for the table. In a week, he consumes at least five bottles. That has not existed in Israel for three years”
That is the painful Israeli part. What about the broader decline in wine consumption worldwide?
“The whole world is seeing declining alcohol consumption among younger generations, and on top of that there is a glut of wine in global markets,” Guy says.
“Immediately after COVID, there was a major boom in wine and gastronomy around the world. We produced and exported to Europe and Latin America, and markets became flooded. Beginning in 2023 and continuing through 2024 and 2025, markets began feeling a shift in the alcohol and wine category, and importers were left with inventories they needed to sell.”
“In Europe, the war between Russia and Ukraine also created economic problems, and middle-class consumers are reconsidering their spending habits.”
Guy raises another factor she says is discussed privately within the industry: the growth of Muslim populations in some markets.
“No one talks or writes about it openly, but it is whispered about in industry conversations. And it is not only in Europe but also in the United States. Fewer people are drinking wine.”
There is another important factor, the age of loneliness and touchscreens. People simply meet less often. “When fewer people eat together, fewer bottles are opened. Wine is not only a drink. It is a ritual,” Gan says.
He argues that despite the global trends, Israel still has a strong culture of shared meals, family, friends and community, something that could provide the local industry with a comparative advantage. “In Israel, we also have to understand that our strength is our local cuisine: spicy food, salads, the sea, the grill. Israeli wine has to stop imitating some imaginary European dining table and start making wine for the real Israeli table.”
“The world is drinking less wine, but it has not stopped looking for meaning. If we know how to read this period not through fear but through attentiveness, perhaps we can turn the global crisis into an opportunity,” he concludes.
What is happening around the world?
France is offering grants to uproot vineyards, Italy is cutting support for producers and in South America wine sells wholesale for less than one euro a bottle as the global industry wrestles with falling consumption and oversupply
Global wine consumption in 2024 was estimated at around 214 million hectoliters, down 3.3% from 2023 and marking its lowest level since 1961. The downward trend continued in 2025 and into 2026.
In the United States, wine consumption has fallen by more than 15%, while production declined by 6% last year. The drop has been particularly pronounced among consumers aged 20 to 35, who are increasingly turning to alcohol-free drinks.
The decline follows decades in which wealthy companies and investors bought wineries for romantic reasons and planted large vineyard areas, creating an oversupply of grapes for which there are now fewer buyers.
The result has been vineyards being uprooted and bulk wine sold in huge quantities to marketing companies producing private-label brands. Costco, for example, can sell its own-label wine for $3 to $5 a bottle after acquiring bulk wine at extremely low prices, in some cases for less than $1 per liter.
The wineries squeezed hardest are often mid-sized producers that previously sold bottles for around $12 and are now scaling back, selling assets and uprooting vineyards and equipment.
France is facing an equally severe crisis. Excess vineyard acreage has pushed wine prices sharply lower, with bottles selling in European supermarkets for as little as five euros. Profit margins for wineries have been squeezed, and the French government has allocated hundreds of millions of euros to programs that pay growers to uproot vineyards.
Italy, meanwhile, has moved to reduce support for wine producers as it seeks to shrink the industry.
China has planted thousands of additional dunams of vineyards in recent years to serve its domestic market, against the backdrop of trade disputes affecting major wine imports from Australia and New Zealand.
South America is also facing a deep crisis, with the average bottle of wine selling wholesale for less than one euro.

Pizza dough and TV prison dramas: how Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe survived jail in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:44:09 UTC
16:44:09 KST

It is a TV show about women confined to prison in the US, but Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe found watching Orange is the New Black with her fellow inmates a strange comfort after smuggling episodes into her Iranian jail cell, downloaded on to an illegal USB stick.
The British-Iranian former charity worker was detained in 2016 for more than five years and kept in the notorious Evin prison in Tehran.
She told an audience at the Big Brue festival in Bruton, Somerset, that she thought she would never be released, so did not mind risking her freedom by sneaking in contraband.
This included USB sticks preloaded with Netflix shows. She said: “We watched Breaking Bad, Prison Break and Orange is the New Black. It was very unusual, but it kind of connected us to the life we had before. Orange is the New Black is a whole different kind of genre of somebody who’s in prison.”
Zaghari-Ratcliffe also danced with her fellow prisoners to contraband Zumba videos and cooked pizza for them in an oven she managed to cobble together money for and have sent to the prison. “I was the queen of the pizza dough in prison,” she said.
She also discussed how she got permission to use the prison sewing machine, which helped her pass the time as she sewed clothes for her young daughter and her friends, the other prisoners.
This newfound artistic hobby spawned a collaboration with London’s Imperial War Museum and the fabric department of Liberty, creating three new prints that explored her experience as a prisoner.
The riskiest item of contraband she snuck into prison was a Swiss Army knife. She said: “I realised, they don’t care what I do. I’m just a political hostage. So I can basically do anything in prison. I can be naughty. I can smuggle things, and once I smuggled this massive whopping Swiss knife.”
She placed it in her shoe, but said: “It was so chunky, I just couldn’t walk. Having a knife in prison is a real crime. But I felt if they had found it, they would have given me what sentence? I was already in prison, and they couldn’t have done anything else to me.”
Zaghari-Ratcliffe was released in March 2022 after the then Conservative government paid back a multimillion debt the UK owed to Iran. The Iranian regime had accused her of spying – a charge she denied and for which no evidence was ever produced.
It became increasingly clear she was being held as a state hostage to try to force the UK to pay back its debt arising from a military deal struck with the deposed Shah of Iran.
Though she is still traumatised by her time in prison and is visiting a therapist, Zaghari-Ratcliffe said she had continued to find solace in sewing.
“When the military attack on Iran happened at the end of February, for five days, I didn’t do anything. I just couldn’t do anything. The only thing that I could do was sit at my sewing machine and sew,” she said.
“I thought, I don’t even know where my parents are. There was an internet blackout for a good two months, and I just couldn’t control the world around me, but I could control my own world. Sewing was the only thing that could calm me down. So yes, still, that’s still my refuge.”

Economic Watch: China's five-year plan to elevate electronic information manufacturing sector
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:07:54 CST
17:07:54 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- As artificial intelligence (AI) plays an increasingly significant role in reshaping the global industrial landscape, China has recently unveiled a plan to advance its electronic information manufacturing sector, a critical foundation for AI development, over the next five years.
The development plan for the electronic information manufacturing industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), jointly issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and the National Development and Reform Commission, aims to further consolidate the pillar role of the industry by 2030.
Industrial firms in the sector with an annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan (about 2.96 million U.S. dollars) are expected to see their combined revenue surpass 30 trillion yuan, and R&D investment intensity of the sector will rise to 3.5 percent, according to the plan.
TO ENHANCE INDUSTRIAL BASE
The electronic information manufacturing industry is a major force in the new industrialization drive. By the end of 2025, China's electronic information manufacturing industry had led the country's 41 major industrial sectors in terms of revenue for 13 consecutive years.
Building on that foundation, the plan presents a systemic framework to strengthen the industrial base, spanning integrated circuits, electronic components and materials, intelligent sensors, specialized electronic equipment and measuring instruments, and the photonics industry.
The framework aims to tackle bottlenecks in key areas and build an independent and controllable industrial base, said Liu Bin, an official with the MIIT.
Liu pointed to photonics as an example, noting that advancing breakthroughs in core technologies and establishing pilot testing platforms for key areas and shared needs will strengthen the sector from the ground up. These efforts, he said, will lay a solid foundation for development and accelerate both technological innovation and industrialization process.
As a representative sector of the electronic information manufacturing industry, China's integrated circuit industry is entering a new phase of rapid growth, driven by the explosive global demand for high-end computing and memory chips brought about by the AI revolution.
Customs data shows that in the first seven months, the country's integrated circuit exports reached 216 billion U.S. dollars, up 99.5 percent year on year, already surpassing the full-year total of 2025.
A semiconductor technology company in southwest China's Sichuan Province has already completed its first half-year production targets, and aims to double its output value from last year, according to its general manager.
TO STRENGTHEN COMPETITIVENESS
While strengthening the industrial base, the plan also sets out strategies to boost the competitiveness of whole devices and systems. This includes enhancing industrial chain resilience in key areas, developing a robust computing ecosystem, and promoting innovation in consumer electronics, among other initiatives.
Terminals form the basic foundation of industrial scale and serve as the gateway through which smart technologies reach hundreds of millions of users, said Liang Linjun, a researcher at China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT).
The plan outlines a dedicated push for innovation in key consumer electronics products, ranging from high-end mobile phones and personal computers to virtual reality devices. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), China's output of core consumer electronics, including mobile phones and computers, maintained a top global ranking.
The accelerating evolution of a new generation of AI is bringing new demand, new product forms, and new ways of development to the electronic information manufacturing industry, while raising higher requirements for basic hardware supply and system coordination, said Liang.
Liang called for efforts to open up typical application scenarios, develop standards for agent collaboration, high-speed computing interconnect, and hardware-software compatibility, increase long-term capital supply that matches innovation cycles, and train more talent with expertise in both AI and electronics manufacturing.
The plan also addresses rising concerns over cutthroat competition in the industry. It calls for timely revisions to industry norms, coordinated planning and early-warning systems for capacity across subsectors, and a comprehensive effort to curb cutthroat competition.
As the "hardware foundation" of the digital world, the electronic information manufacturing industry is undergoing profound changes in its strategic position, competitive logic, and growth model, said Ao Li, vice president of the CAICT.
Turning scale into systemic strength, as well as moving from leading in volume to winning on quality, will be a major task for China's electronic information manufacturing industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period, Ao said.
Industry insiders say government, industry, academia, research institutions, and users need to work together to translate the plan into results by strengthening the industrial foundation and making the supply chain more resilient.
Such a collective push is expected to put China's electronic information manufacturing sector on firmer footing, with a more complete chain and more active innovation, and to lay a solid base for the country's goals of building itself into a manufacturing powerhouse and a cyber powerhouse, they said. ■

World Organization for Science Literacy debuts in Beijing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:07:42 CST
17:07:42 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- The World Organization for Science Literacy made its debut in Beijing on Sunday.
At the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Conference on Science Literacy, the organization pledged to promote exchanges and cooperation, deepen collaborative innovation and foster positive interaction between science and technology and society, so as to jointly enhance public science literacy and support the beneficial development of an intelligent society.
As an international sci-tech organization, it currently has 32 founding members from 21 countries across Asia, Europe, South America, Africa and Oceania.
The organization was initiated with the support of the China Association for Science and Technology and registered in Beijing in June this year.
With sci-tech issues getting increasingly globalized, cross-border dialogue and collaborative action on science popularization have become ever more urgent.
In recent years, China has stepped up efforts to advance science popularization. In 2025, the proportion of Chinese citizens with scientific literacy reached 16.74 percent, a leap from a relatively low level to a medium level.
Meanwhile, the country has actively engaged in global science popularization cooperation, helping improve scientific literacy in economically underdeveloped regions and among key demographic groups.
Elies Molins, Co-President of the World Federation of Scientific Workers, said scientific literacy is more critical than ever. Only by enabling the public to fully understand both the potential and the risks of technological progress can the risks brought by new knowledge be reduced, he said. ■

ISLAMABAD, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Pakistani security forces killed five militants and rescued 23 abducted civilians during an operation along a key highway in the country's southwest Balochistan province, the military said on Sunday.
The Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military's media wing, said in a statement that the operation was launched after militants attempted to set up an illegal checkpoint on the Pakistan Highway (N-25) near Kalat on Friday night to abduct travelers for ransom, extort money and hijack vehicles.
Security forces responded swiftly, triggering an intense exchange of fire in which five militants were killed, said the military.
Troops also raided a militant hideout and rescued 23 abductees, while recovering six trucks, three buses and two cars that had allegedly been seized by the militants, according to the ISPR.
A large cache of weapons, ammunition and explosives was also recovered during the operation, the military said.
The military added that clearance operations were continuing in the surrounding areas to eliminate any remaining militants and ensure the safety of local residents and traffic along the strategic national highway. ■

China's August power use tops 1 trillion kWh again, load hits record high
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:07:16 CST
17:07:16 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's electricity consumption, a key barometer of economic activity, topped 1 trillion kilowatt-hours (kWh) again in August, while the electricity load hit a record high last month, official data showed on Sunday.
Power use totaled 1.03 trillion kWh in August, rising 1.7 percent year on year, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA). Electricity load hit a record high of 1.56 billion kilowatts, 49.69 million kilowatts higher than the previous year's peak.
A breakdown of the August data revealed that power consumed by the primary industry rose 2.7 percent year on year to 16.9 billion kWh, while power consumed by the secondary industry increased 2.4 percent to 612.4 billion kWh. Power use by the tertiary industry reached 215.5 billion kWh, up 5.1 percent year on year.
Notably, electricity consumption by the high-tech and equipment manufacturing sector reached 122.2 billion kWh in August, an increase of 7.2 percent. Computer and communications equipment, automobile manufacturing, general equipment manufacturing, special equipment manufacturing and electrical machinery manufacturing saw power use rise 7.5 percent, 7.6 percent, 7.6 percent, 8.2 percent and 12.3 percent, respectively.
The charging and battery swapping service sector and internet data services reported rapid growth in electricity consumption in August, rising 51.2 percent and 37.9 percent, to 17.2 billion and 10.2 billion kWh, respectively.
In the first eight months of the year, China's total power use reached 7.17 trillion kWh, up 4.3 percent year on year, the NEA said. Power use by the primary, secondary and tertiary industries rose 3.3 percent, 4.4 percent and 7.1 percent, to 104.6 billion kWh, 4.53 trillion kWh and 1.43 trillion kWh, respectively.
During this period, high-tech and equipment manufacturing electricity consumption climbed 9.3 percent to 845.1 billion kWh. Electricity use by charging and battery swapping services and internet data services grew 55.1 percent to 114.7 billion kWh and 42.5 percent to 69.5 billion kWh, respectively. Residential power use rose 0.3 percent to 1.11 trillion kWh.
In recent years, China has made major strides in terms of its power infrastructure, helping ensure a stable electricity supply during peak periods and effectively supporting economic and social development as well as meeting people's basic needs, the National Development and Reform Commission said in July. ■

Bear boards fishing boat before falling into sea in Japan's Miyagi
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:07:10 CST
17:07:10 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Several bear encounters have been reported in Miyagi Prefecture, northeastern Japan, over the weekend.
In the city of Shiogama, a bear climbed aboard a moored fishing boat through its gangplank at around 8:30 p.m. local time on Saturday. The roughly one-meter-tall animal dozed off on the bow before falling overboard and disappearing into the sea, Kyodo News reported.
Three crew members aboard the vessel took refuge in a locked room and were unharmed.
Police said bear sightings had been reported in the area since Friday.
In a separate incident in Iwanuma, also in Miyagi Prefecture, a train struck a bear late Saturday, disrupting rail services for about two hours. None of the crew or passengers were injured. ■

RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Vasco da Gama moved out of the Brazilian Serie A relegation zone on Saturday by cruising to a 5-0 home win over Coritiba.

China launches new group of satellites
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:06:57 CST
17:06:57 KST

JIUQUAN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China successfully launched nine satellites into space from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwest China at 12:03 p.m. Sunday (Beijing Time).
The satellites were carried by a Lijian-1 Y18 carrier rocket and have entered their planned orbits.
They will mainly be used for space environment monitoring, disaster prevention and mitigation and scientific experiments.
The launch mission was a complete success.
This was the 17th flight mission conducted by the Lijian carrier rocket series, which were developed by commercial spaceflight company CAS Space. The Lijian series have so far successfully sent one spacecraft and 121 satellites into space, with a total payload mass in orbit exceeding 21 tonnes, according to the company.
The launch schedule for Lijian-1 carrier rocket has been set through the second half of 2027.
CAS Space is China's commercial space company that has launched the largest number of satellites and the heaviest payloads in the country's private space sector, the Science and Technology Daily reported Sunday. ■
